speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The past two years had us tackling the immediate challenge of protecting lives and livelihoods during the pandemic while building on the foundations of an economically vibrant, socially cohesive and sustainable Singapore for us to call home.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In many countries, the pandemic had exposed cracks and divisions within society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are those against being masked, as well as anti-vaxxers, voicing out against measures amidst the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The difference was our coming together as a united society, helping each other in these exceptional times.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We understood we had a responsibility and the part to play for the greater good of public health.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Volunteers reached out, especially to seniors staying-alone, encouraging vaccination and ensuring the seniors do not feel isolated amidst the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Grassroot organisations distributed care packs, masks, assisted in COVID-19 Support Grants and organised career fairs for those that lost their jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Private organisations such as Ghifari Network, helped to obtain and distribute care packs including for the migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Industries supported each other such as aerospace workers supporting vaccination centres.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Companies took in mid-career workers switching from challenged industries through the SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways Programme.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are many more instances where things could have been much worse, but by coming together and helping one another we have emerged from this pandemic stronger.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The situation in East Europe reminds us peace is fragile.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we emerge from this pandemic, we must position Singapore for the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are at an inflexion point in our history.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is for us to define how we want to grow as a society in this next phase.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must reaffirm our commitment for progress in an inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must continue to impart the right values to the next generation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our ageing population would increase the demand for healthcare and social care.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we, as a society care for our seniors?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we, support our less-privileged families and our low-wage workers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we continue to improve the lives of all Singaporean by growing our economy and staying relevant in an increasingly competitive global economy?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we manage work-life harmony in a future work environment that blurs the line between work and home?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we contribute to global efforts in tackling climate change?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are all pertinent questions we must answer but our means to provide resources for these will come under great strain as the ratio of our working population supporting aged dependents decreases.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We can only get through this stronger if we remain united, helping and working together to ensure that the outcome is greater than the sum of all our efforts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We continue to provide support for workers, businesses and households in tackling the immediate challenges due to the pandemic while positioning ourselves to be future-ready by continuing our journey in transforming our businesses, developing new capabilities and investing in our people.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Budget also reaffirms our societal commitment towards inclusive growth: caring for our seniors, assisting our low-wage workers and preparing for increased healthcare and social care needs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And thirdly, how do we ensure inclusive growth for all?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A Pasir Ris resident, Mr Wong, shared that he worries businesses will increase prices disproportionately at each GST hike in 2023 and 2024.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The outcome will result in a disproportionate increase in cost that is borne only by the end consumer.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we prevent businesses from passing costs straight to consumers instead of everyone shouldering a bit of the pain?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can the Committee against Profiteering identify the singular cause of price increase and hence, identify businesses profiteering from GST in light of increasing cost of supplies, rental, labour, energy in addition to the step increases in GST?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we ensure the committee is effective in protecting our residents?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moving beyond GST, in light of our future challenges, how do we remain relevant in the global economy and drive sector-specific industry transformation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was previously mentioned that the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) will be refreshed by this year to meet the accelerated changes brought about by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is the progress of the ITM refresh?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And given that in this year's Budget, a lot of additional resource is provided to bring about business transformation, how do we ensure companies develop capabilities in line with the refreshed ITMs to take full advantage of the opportunities available in the industry?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will the economic transformation efforts be integrated more closely with the National Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2025 plans?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will the ITM Refresh consider workplace transformation and specifically address the upskilling, retraining and hiring of mature workers, workers with disabilities and other vulnerable workers for an inclusive transformation of the industries?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we leverage on the 811 company training committees (CTSs) set up by NTUC and its affiliated unions to identify the training and skills workers need to keep up with the transformation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will there be a clear direction on how to enhance sustainability efforts in our ITM Refresh?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, in the aerospace ITM Refresh, what will be our direction on sustainability activities such as sustainable aviation fuels, electric hydrogen or hybrid propulsion.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will electric vehicles feature in our land transport industry transformation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we position ourselves for the challenges and opportunities ahead and transform our industry, I am heartened that in this Budget, we have provisioned significant resources to renew and strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our efforts to uplift low-wage workers have been ongoing for the past decade and I believe we can continue to do more to support our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is important to ensure that productivity continues to improve so that wage growth is sustainable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If real productivity is not achieved, there is a risk wage growth would drive up costs and make us less competitive in the global market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The key to sustainable wage growth is upgrading workers' skills to ensure our workers maintain a good job, earn a good wage and have the opportunity to earn more.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we encourage and support SMEs to transform their businesses so that lower-wage workers can be deployed more productively, with more scope for progression?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we get business associations to support more SMEs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am heartened that Progressive Wage Model (PWM) will be extended and wage increase for low-wage workers will be co-funded under the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will be further boosted by the Enhance Workfare Income Supplement Scheme.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While Companies transform to drive real productivity growth, how do we encourage low-wage workers to continuously upskill and upgrade?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we consider a yearly workfare income supplement "bonus" or tiered supplement scheme if the worker utilise his SkillsFuture credit or attend training and courses yearly to upgrade himself or herself?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Disadvantaged platform workers also need assistance to meet their housing and retirement needs as well as with getting an adequate amount of baseline coverage for work injuries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will MOM be able to provide an update on discussions at the Advisory Committee on Platform Workers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Inclusive growth should create opportunities for seniors, workers with special needs and those with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the increasing prevalence of Flexible Work Arrangements including work hours, how will MOM encourage employers to sustain these arrangements?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we create second careers for our seniors who are still able and willing to work but do not want to work full-time?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Ministry consider promoting flexible work arrangement, flexible work hours and work-sharing to create opportunities for these individuals?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even as we make adjustments to foreign worker policies, to increase its effectiveness, we must progress on fair employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How are we progressing at legislating TAFEP guidelines to ensure fair employment practices and treatment at the workplace?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond supporting our workers, we must also ensure that students from all background are given equal opportunities to excel in the skills-based economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How is our education system preparing our students for employment in a skills-based economy?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For students in our ITEs and Polytechnics, can MOE consider apprenticeship schemes where students can work with experienced staff from industry partners, learning job-specific skills and gaining applied competency?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   In the future, Singapore will face an ageing population, with one in four Singaporeans above the age of 65 by 2030.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We also believe that we need to continue to help senior citizens and less fortunate families in our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This means that our healthcare and social needs will increase, while the resources required to support the increase will be limited.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am heartened that this Budget shows that we remain committed to inclusive economic growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The KidSTART and UPLIFT programmes will be expanded further to help more underprivileged students.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Workfare Income Supplement scheme will also be enhanced.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The qualifying monthly income cap for the scheme has been raised, the age eligibility has been extended and the payout increased especially for persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, this is a balanced Budget. it provides support to workers, businesses and households in tackling the immediate challenges brought about by the pandemic while positioning ourselves to be future ready, by continuing our journey towards transforming our businesses, developing new capabilities and investing in our people.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am heartened that we continue to invest in our people and strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have always committed ourselves towards inclusive growth and we will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I rise in support of the Budget.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the concluding paragraphs of the Budget Statement, the Finance Minister highlighted how various sectors of Singapore society rose to the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He applauded the Singapore spirit, as seen from frontline workers to those who set up community care facilities to the footballers and fans at the AFF Suzuki Cup semi-final.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He was emphatic that Singapore would always prevail so long as we stood side by side in solidarity with one another.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, two years on into the pandemic, it is appropriate to start evaluating how governments and people across the world responded to the pandemic, not just in terms of the health and economic impacts, but also what lessons or hints can be drawn about a nation’s culture and innovative potential.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One analysis early on into the pandemic studied how 57 countries around the world responded to the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This study was published early last year in The Lancet by Prof Michele Gelfand, a cultural psychologist at the University of Maryland, USA and several colleagues.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Prof Gelfand divided the countries based on whether they had “tight” or “loose” cultures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, for instance, countries like China and Singapore were classified as having tight cultures, in that our societies tended to be highly respectful of rules and norms; contrast this with a country like the United States, where people tended to defy them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She observed, unsurprisingly, that loose countries had more difficulties enforcing social distancing measures due to the attitude of the people to rules; this in turn was associated with more COVID-19 deaths and serious illness in loose countries compared to tight countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To be clear, these findings were more about the culture of the people rather than what the state did.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For us here, classified as a tight culture, Singaporeans have fared well to comply with rules and guidance; this has contributed to keeping the overall health impacts of COVID in Singapore at a relatively manageable level.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In talking about Prof Gelfand’s study some months later, CNN anchor Fareed Zakaria went further.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He noted that as the COVID-19 pandemic raged on, the development of vaccines shed another dimension on tight and loose cultures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He observed that some of the loosest countries, which fared poorly in managing the pandemic through social distancing measures, were the most innovative and dynamic at developing, procuring and distributing the vaccine.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These loose countries included the United States, Britain, Israel and Chile.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Mr Zakaria posited that the very traits that made it hard to follow social distancing rules, were the ones that helped generate the solution to the problem.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He concluded that these loose countries benefitted from the creativity, risk-taking and rule-breaking that was endemic in their people.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, it is clear how these solutions have benefited humankind across the globe.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While Singapore has done relatively well in the pandemic for health outcomes, it would be opportune to do a stock-take of how we did to invent or create solutions for COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the one hand, there are some indications of significant breakthroughs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, it was reported that a Singapore team from Duke-NUS had developed a COVID-19 neutralising antibody test kit, which was the first of its kind to get approval from the American Food and Drug Administration.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another example is the COVID-19 PCR test kit developed by DSO National Laboratories, that did not require reagents to process samples.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, a lack of locally manufactured solutions is not just a matter of national pride.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We have experienced first-hand how, in a global pandemic, needing to procure supplies from abroad subjects us to market forces and has resulted in supply shortages.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I also note the recent announcement that work has started on a new vaccine manufacturing facility at Depot Road by Hilleman Laboratories.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This facility is part of efforts by the Economic Development Board to strengthen capabilities across the biopharmaceutical manufacturing value chain.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, we should strive to move up the value chain, to be the owners of such intellectual property.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This raises the more general question: what is the state of Singapore’s capacity to innovate?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When one drills down further to why Singapore is ranked highly, we see that this is mainly due to its institutions and market and business sophistication.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We did not fare so well in the area of Creative Outputs and Knowledge and Technology Outputs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For a high income country, we were ranked especially weak in the areas of Knowledge Creation and the Registration of Trademarks and Industrial Designs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The report highlighted that countries like South Korea were particularly active in commercialising and patenting inventions in health-related technologies during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: South Korea was especially strong in registering patents, trademarks and industrial designs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As a high-income country, we can contribute more to improve the quality of life for humankind.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Do we need to do more to nurture creativity and risk-taking?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are there other inhibitors in Singapore’s ecosystem that need to be addressed?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Budget 2022 is entitled “Charting Our New Way Forward Together”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If one looks at its coverage, it does indeed provide measures that support a broad church – from business to households and workers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It also imposes increased obligations on the more able to contribute more to the public purse, while accelerating salary increases for many low-wage workers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For my part, I will just make an observation on the household illustrations used in the Budget Statement on the expected impact of the GST increase.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is a further assumption that all household members are Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To be fair, the Ministry may have used them because the scenarios are typical.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, these illustrations may inadvertently alienate Singaporeans whose households do not fit into the traditional structure.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They also reinforce the stereotype of the man being the major breadwinner.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, these households may experience less severe impacts from the GST increase than other types of households, due to more offsets.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, from a gender perspective, I feel that there is no need for the illustrations to stipulate the amounts earned by husbands and wives separately.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Instead, the indication of the combined household income would suffice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By including some other types of households, we can have a fuller picture of the impact of tax changes on different segments of society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, I believe including them would have an important signalling effect that every household, whatever its composition, is part and parcel of the Singapore compact.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore would do well if it finds a balance between tightness and looseness.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have also made an observation about the household illustrations used in the Budget, which in my view could be more inclusive.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: First, let me just say thank our Finance Minister Lawrence Wong, as well as the team from MOF for putting up this particular Budget that is forward-looking as we move towards the post-pandemic phase to build a greener, as well as more inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: During the last financial crisis in 2008, the Government dipped into our national reserves to support the economy and the amount utilised was probably returned when the economy rebounded strongly, post-crisis.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This time, the Government has again deep into our national reserves for the pandemic, and the amount utilised is actually much larger compared to the last crisis.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Using the same lyrics that was from last year's National Day song – that "we did it before and we'll do it again" – or just wondering whether will the Government be doing it again, and how and when the Government will be able to recoup and return the drawdowns that have been made during the pandemic so that we can return the reserves to our future generations.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I will focus my speech now on three areas that affects the poor, the rich and all.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: On inflation, we are already feeling the pinch of inflation even before the Budget statement was made.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The rise in petrol prices, the higher electrical tariffs, supply chain disruption, higher labour costs arising from the pandemic have triggered across-the-board rise in the cost of living.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: HDB resale price went up, private property prices went up.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Childcare services fees were also increased and taxi fares are all going up.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Cooking oil and eggs prices are also moving up.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Even throwing rubbish cost for now, as refuse removal fees was increased; and soon, even the plastic bags will cost some money, if you collect plastic bags from the supermarket.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And having a sugary drink itself may cost more if the Government decides to implement a sugar tax.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Inflation is making in-roads into the pockets of the man-on-the-street, especially the lower socio-economic groups.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have heard rumblings of higher cost of living as the people struggle to adjust with the cost to the loss of purchasing power.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The cost of running businesses is rising rapidly, although there are various packages from the Government to cushion the impact on the operational overheads.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Yes, under the 2012 Progressive Wage Model (PWM), the salaries of local lower-wage workers were increased.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, these numbers show how inflation is eating into the worker's income.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: GST was first introduced in 1994, with a 3% rate.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Headline inflation then was 3.1% in 1994, and it dipped to 1.7% in 1995.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: MAS allowed the currency to appreciate steadily during this phase.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This helped to contain overall domestic inflationary pressures.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I take reference from the MAS "50 Years of Inflation Experience in Singapore" that was published by Macroeconomic Review October last year.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In 2003, GST was raised to 4% and again to 5% in 2004, and it was up again from 5% to 7% in 2007.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the latter half of the 2000s, exchange rate policy was generally tightened as Singapore's headline inflation rose rapidly, from 0.5% to 6.6% in 2008.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This increase was attributed to the backdrop of strong global commodity prices and also partly due to the China's rapid economic growth and other emerging economies.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: According to MAS, this was estimated to add around 0.4% to 0.5% to headline inflation each year in 2007 and 2008.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: During this period, the price of crude oil increased significantly due to heightened uncertainty, leading to a short bout of high inflation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In 2008, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose above 5% for two months due to skyrocketing gas prices – sounds déjà vu again.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: By the third quarter of 2008, the effect of the US banking crisis impacted our economy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This resulted in Singapore being hit by recession.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: By allowing our Singapore currency to appreciate, it will help to cushion the inflation of imported goods and services but it will also harm our businesses by making our exports more expensive and reduce our competitiveness.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The inflationary effect on the cost of living is permanent.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And they worry for their children and grandchildren having to live with this high costs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And, for businesses, their biggest overheads – wages, rental and property prices, only go one way – they will go up.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Once business costs go up, this will also affect all consumers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As we push for more wage increase for Singaporeans especially the lower-income group, business cost will also have to go up and inflation will increase and erode the purchasing power of these workers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If inflation goes up, it hits people's savings especially the poor, the elderly and retirees.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They would feel the drop in their buying power, and everything is more expensive for them.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Those with savings would find themselves digging deeper, further into their savings than before.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What may previously be an adequate amount of retirement funds could now become insufficient.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How are we to manage wage increases to go up in tandem with this inflation?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, the Government's efforts in helping the workers and employers with the Wage Credit Scheme would be a futile effort.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We need to examine this carefully and how are we to manage inflation when the GST rise kicks in.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The big question is that is it progressive enough or is this just the beginning?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But there is one area where I feel we should take a closer look; that is the property tax.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I feel that there is more room for adjustment.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: From the current Budget, I do not see how the Government can recover the expenses that the Government requires in the coming years in order to reduce the deficit.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Recently, we kept hearing news of record transacted prices of Good Class Bungalows.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Should we have done more to make property tax more progressive, especially for the top-end properties like in this category?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our tax system is based on the annual value of the property which is as I understand is computed based on the imputed rental value of the property.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Because of the land area of GCB compared with a high-rise and more densely populated condominium, the property tax levied on GCB is comparatively lower.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The expanse of land for a condominium would include the many facilities and car parks, but the density is much higher, even for HDB blocks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They could be paying much more property tax per square foot than a GCB.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, my question is – Singapore has only 728 square kilometres of land, of which 14% is allocated for residential housing.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Besides this, I would like to ask whether there is a differentiation between a freehold and lease hold property in the computation of property tax?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Do these companies pay any tax on the value that they are holding since the ownership of the land will go back to them after the expiry of the 99-year lease?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, it would seem that these companies or developers are allowed to hold value without paying any taxes for 99 years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Increasing sin taxes will encourage Singaporeans to adopt a healthier lifestyle and help our Government to support the revenue.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: My last topic will be on sustainability and clean energy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I agree with Dr Tan Wu Meng on what he said yesterday.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is a small city state of just over 700 square kilometres.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The limited size that we have also limits the amount of renewable energy that we can harvest.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Between land for housing, transport, security, healthcare, education and a whole suite of economic infrastructure, we also push out land for infrastructure for Electric Vehicles (EVs) in public and private housing estates, office buildings, public roads and carparks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I know we have embarked on tapping solar energy and explored many other avenues to reduce our carbon footprint, but is it enough?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I know that the Government has been working to import clean energy from ASEAN and various countries.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: All these are fine, as long as the relationship between countries are good and stable and the supply countries do not face any disruption or any sudden domestic needs increase.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With climate change causing a heightened frequency and intensity of climate disasters in our supply countries, this is a real threat.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The concerns over our energy security, as well as resilience, arises if we are significantly rely and depend on external supplies.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The events in Europe are a good eye-opener of how energy prices shot up amidst the disruption and the supply of gas and because of conflicts between countries.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, only France seems to be in a better place than the rest of Europe because its electricity supply is supplied by its own nuclear power plants and this accounts for more than two-thirds of its total electricity generation in 2021.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the Far East, Hong Kong, which is slightly bigger than us, about 1,106 square kilometres, gets its electricity generated from coal, natural gas and also nuclear energy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Hong Kong gets its electricity from a nuclear power plant that is in Guangdong, the Daya Bay Nuclear Power Station.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I have raised this question previously before, that was before the nuclear incident in Japan occurred, whether will Singapore consider nuclear energy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I also raised this question in a written Parliamentary Question (PQ) as well to MTI earlier this year and Minister Gan Kim Yong has replied as a written reply to say that Singapore supports the international effort to strengthen the global nuclear safety as well as the security architecture.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I do support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even as the Workers' Party disagrees with the key proposal of the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my speech, I would like to talk about a carbon tax, our transitions in the petrochemicals and industry and transport, before touching on the GST impact on healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is still broadly similar to the range as proposed by my colleague, the hon member for Sengkang, Assoc Prof James Lim, in his previous speeches.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also hope that the Government will present more details on how they intend to mitigate the impact of the increase of the carbon tax on our households beyond the U-Save vouchers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is an important subject, given the carbon taxes increase over the next eight years and to aim to achieve net-zero emissions, by or around mid-century.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Although some details, such as the exact day of the net-zero achievement and of the transition framework for emissions, intensive and trade expo sectors, as well as the exact quantum of the additional U-Save rebates to help mitigate the cost increases to businesses and households, have not been released, this is a step in the right direction for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Workers' Party agrees with the need to transit our economy to a green one as soon as it is practical.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, the Workers' Party also recognises that while decarbonisation is necessary, it will also impose a cost.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is especially so if we are to provide climate leadership for our citizens and in this region.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Singapore has taken some early measures on sustainable development, such as switching to natural gas for electricity generation instead of more pollutive fuel oil, imposed a vehicle quota system to cap vehicle growth and has introduced a suite of mitigation measures to decarbonize our industry, buildings and households sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We now have a bolder carbon tax trajectory and improve our net-zero climate ambition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Therefore, we need to think carefully about how to bring about this change and not leave anyone behind.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my speech during the "Towards a Low-carbon Society" Motion last month, I have argued that we are in need of a just transition, one that is inclusive and equips those who work here and plan to work here with the necessary know-how, to access good job opportunities in the sustainability sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Today, I wish to talk about the need for a just transition within the petrochemicals industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There have been movements towards a greener transition within our petrochemical industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In November last year, Shell has announced that it is halving its crude processing capacity at its Singapore hub and reduce fuel exports.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The oil major, a major part of our oil and gas industry, is intending to transit from fossil fuels to cut emissions and meet lobal low-carbon energy needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is part of a wider global trend in a transition towards lower carbon fuels and it undoubtedly will affect Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Earlier this year, students from the group Students for A Fossil-free Future (S4F), produced a 68-page report calling for universities to divest from fossil fuels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I empathised with the concerns of these students.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They have proposed that Singapore Universities seek sustainable alternatives to linkages with the fossil fuel industry and implement climate crisis education over the short, medium and long-term.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, while it is true that we do need to transition, what does that mean for the petrochemical industry in Singapore in its current form?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We know that our petrochemical industry has been a strategic pillar of our industrial sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The number went down to 27,000 in 2020, according to MTI's answer to my PQ in April 2021.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We are also a regional trading centre for coal, natural gas and oil products and support dozens of finance houses that specialise in the said commodities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More than a hundred global chemical companies have operations in the city.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As noted above, Singapore's linkages into the current brown economy are deep.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And while we build for the economy of the future, the reality is that if we take away the manpower and capital in the petrochemical industry abruptly, we will cut the oxygen prematurely at a time when our green ambitions have only just begun.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And there is still a need for some petrochemicals in the modern green economy as some petrochemicals can be found in modern solar panels, modern wind turbines and batteries, to name but a few.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Therefore, I ask that the Government provide more details on how it intends to manage the green transition in our petrochemicals industry and if Singapore will continue to attract and keep parts of the petrochemicals industry in Singapore that are relevant for the green economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the Committee of Supply debates, I will focus on the manpower transition in the industry with the hope that Singapore will be adequately prepared for the transition so that our Singaporean workers, young and old, will be able to be optimally employed in the sector as it undergoes the green transition and that we will not need to rely on or import significant foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I filed a question to the Minister for Transport asking for the total number of electric vehicle chargers installed in 2021 and the expected number of EV chargers that will be installed progressively over 2022 and 2025.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The year 2200 appears a long way off the target of 60,000 in eight years' time and I would like to ask the Minister again what are the Government's progressive targets over the next few years and how does the Government plan to step up on the installation of public EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Last year, in my Budget debate speech, I also mentioned that having a critical number of charging points required in all residential commercial car parks and public car parks as well as the design of the car parks and the siting of the EV charging points are important.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Singapore is unlike other countries like the US or Australia, where most people have the luxury of charging their cars in their own garage overnight.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The minimum charging time, even with an incomplete charge with a fast charger, may still lead to queues in HDB or condo car parks, if there are insufficient chargers or if the chargers are inappropriately sited.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A year on, I would like to ask the Minister what the Government's experience with the installation of our initial chargers over the past year has been.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Has the Government done any study to establish a suitable ratio of EV chargers versus the number of cars per car park?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the public car parks be adopting all fast chargers or will there be a combination of fast and slow chargers?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Does the Government have any specific planning requirements for the design of car parks in public, private residential or commercial buildings in respect of the installation and siting of EV chargers in car parks to minimise waiting time and avoid any traffic blockage caused by vehicles waiting for charging?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For existing car parks, does the Government foresee that some or all car parks may require modifications?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If modifications are required, would the assistance offered by way of the current EV common charger grant to MCSTs be sufficient?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Not unlike ICE cars, most vehicles, except for commercial vehicles, will not require daily charging.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, drivers will still have to develop new habits of charging their cars with some forward planning.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: ICE cars may need just 10 minutes in petrol kiosks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But, for EVs, queuing time aside, typically, a fast charger may take between 30 and 40 minutes for up to an 80% charge, and a slow charger may take up to eight hours for a full charge.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Technology is, of course, improving constantly, but depending on the number of cars waiting for charging at any one time, an HDB car park with, say, just three to four chargers, may still possibly create queuing time not currently seen with ICE cars in petrol stations, even with charging operators charging a penalty charge for drivers who leave their cars beyond the charging time required.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will MOT consider using public education messaging on wise and considerate use of public chargers so that we can start engendering good and considerate habits with our drivers while the EV numbers are still small and growing, just as we also want to encourage our ICE drivers not to use slots reserved for EV charging?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is good to get these issues right as early as possible so that we can minimise the waiting time and enhance charging access for EV owners.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Importantly, this will, in turn, have an impact on our efforts to persuade more vehicle owners to convert earlier to the use of EVs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As I have mentioned earlier, the Workers' Party recognises the costs that the decarbonisation move will impose on Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Therefore, the GST hike comes at an inopportune time for Singaporeans, many of whom are dealing with record consumer price inflation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I echo my other Workers' Party colleagues who are asking for the GST hike to be implemented only as a last resort.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Apart from the adequacy of such packages, I note that the assistance package is only available for a few years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I note that GST has only gone up and has never gone down, even if assistance packages will adequately cushion the impact for low-income earners and even the lower-middle middle class in the short term.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The eventuality is that the GST increase will be a burden on the middle class, increasing their costs of living.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And as the sandwich class, this may be something they can less afford, as compared to higher income groups above them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In particular, we need to pay attention to Singaporeans in their 30s to 50s, but the vast majority are not just paying for necessities for themselves but also for their parents and their children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The compounded pain that households will have to deal with is not something we should ignore out of hand.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is particularly so as we expect an ageing population to come in the near future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Singaporeans will be facing more questions on out-of-pocket healthcare prices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government has argued that the Government's healthcare expenditure will increase significantly, but the out-of-pocket costs of healthcare paid for by the people will also increase as a result of the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: GST also applies to premiums of Shield and group medical insurance plans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While Budget 2022 can be said to be matching our climate ambitions to the international standards, the devil is, of course, in the details as we will need to transition away from our current economic structure at some cost.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I look forward to more details from the Government on how it intends to manage the transition, particularly within the petrochemical industry, and the move towards electric vehicles.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am heartened that the Finance Minister is committed to making more investments in our people and social infrastructure to strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   In our rapidly ageing country, each of our youths becomes even more precious.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government and the community should invest in and develop our youths, especially those coming from disadvantaged families, and help them grow and learn in a healthy way.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Youths nurtured with care will grow up to be successful and contribute to our country.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government should allocate more resources to help disadvantaged families to help minimise the adverse impact of family problems on teenagers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When families are struggling, the Government needs to step in quickly to prevent their situation from deteriorating further.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many youth problems, such as school absenteeism, delinquency and addictions, can be prevented if we intervene early to nip the problems in the bud.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope there will be a teenage version of Comlink.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can we hire, retain and train more family support counsellors to help vulnerable families navigate the assistance schemes available to them?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All youths benefit from caring role models, guidance and advice for their studies and future careers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For disadvantaged youths, these are even more vital in order for them to get out of the poverty cycle.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can we increase accessibility to mentorship opportunities and provide better internship and career placement support to them?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I urge the Government to provide more funding to organisations, such as Young NTUC, that run mentorship programmes to support the recruitment and training of mentors and ensure their quality.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Better internship and career placement support is also important.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Funding is needed for allowance subsidies and to support various components of an internship programme, such as the training of company supervisors.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also hope that the Government will consider giving incentives to spur sectoral tripartite cooperation to build a more systemic approach in curating internship and placement opportunities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Creating an internship of quality requires input and cooperation among the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), employers and Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Companies need more help to design good internship programmes that enable the students to gain work experience, make meaningful contributions and gain insights of the industry.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These should help the students gain clarity on their career options and make informed postgraduate choices.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should encourage youths to go beyond their compulsory school internships today and embark on additional ones if possible.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Internships should also benefit companies as opportunities to spot potential talents and employees.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to change our employers’ attitude towards interns and internships as temporary exercises.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Internships should be taken seriously as part of a firm’s long-term human resource management.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If our youths have positive experiences, we may be able to address the problem of local manpower shortage for certain vocations and industries.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A promising approach is to get the employers, unemployed youths and the IHLs to come together to develop a work-study experience.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It can be an apprenticeship plus internship programme or a conversion programme where they learn before commencing work.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This method had proven quite effective for Work-Study Diplomas, a mid-career switch conversion programme.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the process to develop and approve new courses can take some time.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To expedite, the Government, through MOM or NTUC, can take the lead and drive each sector's development in this area.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Government also consider providing funds to help unemployed graduates as union members?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As members, they are entitled to the equivalent of student passes so that they can get further job placements or skills training.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is also important to support ITE students and youths-in-transition from school to the workplace and provide programmes to build up their experiences through internship opportunities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For certain sectors, due to limited internship opportunities, they get some exposure through school projects but this is not the same as work experience.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Special needs youths need help to secure internship opportunities too.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Both the youths and employers would need customised training and support to make sure that the work arrangements can be sustained.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Government please provide more funds and support to incentivise companies to be more inclusive?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would also like to ask for more funding to support IHLs to develop Continuing Education and Training modules with input from sector leaders and companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such an ecosystem will facilitate the development of updated training programmes, which are relevant and in demand by industries.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The programme involves online vocational and on-the-job learning with local and global host companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Indeed, a tripartite approach is the most promising one to ensure timely and relevant curriculum development and good matches to place the trained participants.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In recent years, there has been a sharp increase in the number of platform workers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to rethink our approach to supporting their welfare.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A key factor contributing to the gig economy's expansion was the improvement of digital technology.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This facilitated the matching of workers to tasks.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the relationship between these technology companies and assigned workers is unequal and heavily weighed in favour of the firms, which have access to the data, customers and a wide pool of non-union, unorganised workers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The tech companies have no obligation to the independent workers, which mostly include private hire drivers and food delivery couriers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, although they have flexibility and autonomy, the fact is that they have limited bargaining power and will find it hard to earn a sustaining wage if they do not work full-time.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While many platform workers are young and work part-time, now, the number of full-timers are also significant.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Presently, they are prone to exploitation and have very little say on how much they get paid – they are price takers – and in order to make a decent living, which include the incentive pay, which comes with completing certain assigned jobs, they have to work long hours to reach their target wages.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Due to low barriers of entry, the jobs are attractive to those who have difficulty finding other jobs due to low levels of education, lack of skillsets or credentials, or other reasons, such as a prior criminal record.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While they provide a much needed and in-demand service, they are in dead-end jobs with no prospect of progression.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   To residents of Chua Chu Kang, and platform workers, my fellow Members of Parliament and I will help you get fair wages and rights.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): The least we can do for them is to ensure that they have representation via unions and are treated fairly, in another words, with the full rights and entitlements of employees.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the changes in carbon taxes, companies will face increasing pressure to transform.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the cost of transformation will ultimately be passed on to the consumers and lead to higher costs of living.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With inflation and logistics challenges due to the pandemic, ordinary families will face financial pressures.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: SMEs will also face challenges dealing with the higher carbon taxes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While I support our efforts to go green, both figuratively and literally, I am very worried about the impact on our middle- and lower-income families and the competitiveness of our local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope the Government will assist them more over the transition period.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With this, I would like to conclude with my support for the Budget.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: First, I will cover the topic of a caring and inclusive society, which I will deliver in English.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For the second part, I will speak on a couple of issues related to the Malay/Muslim community in Malay.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: With this in mind, I would like to use my speech to invite the Government and every Member of this House to reflect on the issues that are faced by certain segments of our fellow Singaporeans who may still feel marginalised.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For those who belong to these segments, the phrase "caring and inclusive society" may provoke anger and disappointment rather than any joy or pride.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They are the ones who face challenges in their respective lives due to certain existing Government policies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I want to highlight the difficulties they face and make some suggestions that could alleviate the hardship these citizens face.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The issues I am about to cover are not new.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Rather, they have been discussed before and been raised repeatedly by many Members from both sides of this House, including myself.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I proposed some suggestions which I felt could reduce the burden on motorcyclists and motorcycle owners.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry said it would monitor the situation and will assess what were the best measures that could be taken to address the matter.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The second group of citizens are those whose spouse is not a Singaporean Citizen.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The difficulty they face is in obtaining a Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP) or Singaporean permanent residence or Singapore Permanent Resident status.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe I do not need to elaborate at length as this matter has been raised repeatedly in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, I want to emphasise the negative implications stemming from the situation whereby applications for the Long-Term Visit Pass and permanent residence are rejected many times.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I personally know some of my residents who face such situations, the implication of which is separation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is very sad, because it is far from demonstrating our caring and inclusive society that every Budget claims to want to achieve.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Another stressful situation faced by individuals married to foreign spouses is the cost of schooling for the children of their spouses.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They have to pay high school fees because their stepchildren are student pass holders.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For low-income earners, this is a very heavy burden.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many such individuals are destitute and find themselves out of options and solutions for their financial problems arising from the high school fees.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many of these individuals have already sought to obtain Permanent Resident status in the hope that their children would not be subject to high fees.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, many of those who have applied have been unsuccessful.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a concern for Singaporeans experiencing such a situation, I would like to ask the Government to re-evaluate our immigration policy in order to provide relief in this situation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Alternatively, I recommend that MOE considers establishing a subsidy scheme for such students, especially for those from low-income families and where their stepfathers have legal guardianship status over them.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The next group who feels marginalised are divorcees: single mothers or fathers and also unwed single parents.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many still suffer from failing to find a place to live.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is worrying as there are still many restrictions in our public housing policies for unwed single parents as they and their children do not meet the criteria of a family nucleus under the existing rules.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I and many other Members of Parliament have expressed our concerns on the matter and have been calling to abolish this unfavourable ruling and at the same time, to extend public housing benefits to all single parents regardless of their marital status.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I hope this issue can be given due attention and will result in more positive changes to HDB's existing housing policies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There are two other concerns I have voiced in recent years, which I feel can have a positive impact in our effort in continuing to reinforce caring and inclusive values if they are addressed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One is with respect to the Kindergarten Financial Assistance Scheme, KiFAS.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have asked on several occasions in this Chamber to have this scheme extended to students from low-income families who attend kindergartens run by non-profit organisations such as charities, voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) and religious entities such as mosques and churches.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because parents who wish to send their children to a kindergarten of their choice for certain reasons should not be sidelined or deprived of the opportunity to obtain financial assistance schemes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I do not think this is in line with inclusive values.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Full-time madrasah students may also feel excluded from society in some ways.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: While the move to provide all full-time students at madrasah with Edusave accounts is a welcome one, I note that the Edusave awards, which are presented to students who have performed well or shown good improvement in a mainstream school, remains unavailable to madrasah students.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such awards should be extended to every Singaporean student to further strengthen efforts to inculcate inclusive values in our society, especially students.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have raised this matter in this House, previously citing two individuals who have sought my assistance on their dilemma of being stateless.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Both of them were born and bred in Singapore and have never left this country as a result of their nationality status.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One of them has to bear a heavier financial burden due to ineligibility for medical fee subsidies and the other is unable to access ComCare assistance.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Having stayed in this country for the whole of their life and after giving their youth and energy to the building of this nation, they were repeatedly told of their unsuccessful applications and appeals for citizenship.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Other Members of this House have also separately filed questions relating to the plight of the stateless.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I also note that the Minister for Manpower had said in January 2021 that there were no regulations preventing the employment of stateless persons.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, I note that there are several steps that prospective employers of stateless persons need to take before employing them.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I hope that the authorities will consider formulating streamlined policies to resolve the status of the stateless in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   I would like to bring up a number of issues relating to the Malay-Muslim community, during this Budget debate as well as the Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In today's debate, I would like to touch on two matters, that should be given due emphasis and attention to ensure the well-being of the Malay/Muslim community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: First, on home ownership and second, on education.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: After almost 57 years of independence, Singapore has attained many commendable achievements.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The excellence that we achieved is the result of having awareness, hard work accompanied by sweat and tears, in addition to the spirit, perseverance, commitment, determination and solidarity of our people with a touch of vision and aspiration.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As the people of a multi-racial Singapore, we are cognizant that united we stand, divide we fall.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a result, we can see now that on the world stage, Singapore is increasingly known as an exceptional and reputable brand name.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We are a nation that is far ahead in many areas like economic growth, public administration, quality education, health services, anti-corruption and so on.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, there are still many who are unable to say that they are self-sufficient.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because we are facing critical challenges and problems, brought about by the wave of progress in the name of development, success and prosperity In short, we all face the pressure of a very high cost of living.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This was declared by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) in a joint statement on 23 February.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In this august Chamber, I would like to say clearly and plainly that the increase in prices of goods has adversely affected our people's cost of living.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In this challenging and increasingly stressful situation, the Malay community is the most affected.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This, Mr Speaker, this is not progress but regression.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If every rental flat is occupied by a family of four, it means 74,400 Malays are now living in a cramped, stressful and hampered manner.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This comprises almost 15% of the entire Malay community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like to ask the Government; first, what is being done by the Government to improve the ability of Malays to purchase flats and therefore leave the rental flats?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Second, how many Malays are living in HDB rental flats in 2021?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Third, what are the Government’s short-term and medium-term plans to reduce the number of Malays living in 1-room and 2-room rental flats?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Four, what is the Government's target to reduce the number of Malays living in rental flats by 2030?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am very concerned, looking at the growing number of our children who are more comfortable speaking in English.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This will cause their command of the Malay language as their Mother Tongue to be eroded.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In future, perhaps within another decade, Singaporean Malays will generally feel awkward speaking in their own language.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Children at this age are at a critical stage in their growth development.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: With married couples focused on supporting families, most of these children are placed in childcare centres before being sent to kindergarten.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge that it is important for our people to have a good command of English, and the bilingual policy adopted by the Government should ensure a balance for all mother tongues, including the Malay Language, and on this point, my concern is that if there is no concerted effort, the majority of our 38,668 Malay children will have difficulty mastering the Malay Language, much less being fluent in their Mother Tongue.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The lowest percentage was 97.5% in 2020, and this downward trend began since the beginning of the new millennium in 2001.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Malay community cannot allow this decline to continue on.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is an early indication that a critical step must be taken to prevent this problem from worsening.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some may think that this decline is very small or negligible.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, on this issue, I would like to pose some questions to the Government on the education of Malay children.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This will allow the community to know more clearly the Government's position and stand in ensuring that Malay children are not hindered from the opportunity to learn Malay Language from a young age.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As the saying goes, bend the bamboo while it is still a bamboo shoot.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: First, what will the Government do to address the shortage of preschools offering the teaching of Mother Tongue?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Will the Government provide a bigger allocation to attract more professionals to join the preschool teaching sector to teach the Malay language?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Third, what are the immediate steps that will be taken by the Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs as well as the Mendaki Foundation to improve Malay language proficiency among primary school students who will sit for the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Generally we know that Mendaki Tuition Classes do not offer tuition in the Malay language.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Four, what is the near-term objective of the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) to address the lack of Malay Language teaching in preschools by 2030?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Malay community is always told about our achievement and progress, and when we look that the available statistics, we can see a significant weakness over the last 10 years.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The issues highlighted must be addressed decisively and judiciously.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, we also seek the Government’s understanding to look into the living situation of Malays, with many increasingly living in rental flats.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This has to be addressed quickly to extract them of the cycle and grip of poverty, and all the social problems that come with it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We heard an account of this from the hon Minister for Foreign Affairs in this House yesterday.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Worryingly, I see no end in sight in the immediate future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Financial and economic sanctions on an unprecedented scale have been imposed on Russia by the US and EU countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister was quick to point out that our decision will come at a cost.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The consequence for the rest of the world is substantial and serious.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are already hit with the inflationary pressures arising from the pandemic and supply chain issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I trust that both sides of the House are solidly behind the hon Minister for Foreign Affairs’ condemnation of Russia’s unprovoked invasion of Ukraine and call for the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of Ukraine to be respected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As he eloquently highlighted, our own short history as a tiny island city-state informs us that we too will always be vulnerable to machinations of big powers and must continually be prepared to guard against any existential threat to Singapore and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have little influence in what happens globally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have no choice but to take the world as it is.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is why our defence policy is based on the twin pillars of diplomacy which advocates a rule-based approach to settling international disputes in accordance with the UN Charter and international law; and deterrence, which involves a strong defence capability and ensuring that any enemy will know that there will be a big price to pay if they take us on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is these developments that have guided me to draw hon Members’ attention to one aspect of the Budget Statement which is not specifically spelt out but is the raison d’etre for a number of initiatives stated in the Budget, that is strengthening our nation’s resilience and robustness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am guided by how Princeton professor Markus Brunnermeier has defined these terms in his book published last year titled “The Resilient Society”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He described “resilience” as the ability to rebound from a shock, whereas “robustness” is the ability to resist.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Closer to home, at NUS, environmental scholars at the Lee Kuan Yew School have defined “resilience” as R1 and R2.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first being an ability to mitigate and resist; the second, to adapt and flourish in new circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whatever their names, the two are ways to respond to external shocks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
