text: More importantly, the Lee Kuan Yew School researchers point out that resilience is not a cost-free virtue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, the price of resilience is inefficiency – a point I shall elaborate on below.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Investing in both these capabilities are important to ensure Singapore’s survival in this unpredictable and volatile world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is clear is that we cannot afford to adopt a “feast and famine” approach to building these capabilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Thinking long term to secure Singapore’s future has always been the hallmark of the PAP Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat spoke last year about efforts to strengthen Singapore’s capabilities in biomedical sciences and health infrastructures to be ready for Disease X.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim recounted some of these efforts in her speech just now and aptly described them as a "reassuring development".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also last year, the hon Education Minister Chan Chun Sing announced plans for MOE to roll out mental health education lessons to our children at Primary, Secondary and pre-university levels by next year to help them build up their resilience.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are not short-term plans, with an eye on the next electoral cycle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are for the protection and flourishing of our children, grandchildren, and generations beyond – but already hardwired into our spending today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I applaud these moves and other Government initiatives aimed at making Singapore and Singaporeans more resilient and robust.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: No doubt though, there is a cost – and one we bear today – in developing these capacities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Let us take grocery supply as an example.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It costs less for a supermarket to stock groceries employing a just-in-time inventory, something that hon Member Mr Seah Kian Peng knows very well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Purchase decisions can be made based on current conditions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It makes the business operations leaner but susceptible to disruptions when the suppliers cannot supply.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The other option is to employ a just-in-case model which will allow the businesses to be more agile and respond to sudden demand increases quickly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It does, however, mean that business costs will be higher.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may not be the most efficient way to use resources.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But it may be the better way when dealing with strategic goods.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is where we, on both sides of the House, must come together and affirm that these costs must be incurred progressively over the long term because what is ultimately at stake is Singapore’s survival and viability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My question to the hon Minister for Finance is two-fold; first, could he please let us know what are the strategic areas that the Government intends to build resilience and robustness capabilities for the immediate as well as the long term; and two, have we committed sufficient funds and resources for the building of these capabilities?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My hope is that the Government will continue to eschew the natural tendency, when our country’s fiscal position is relatively weak and there is a pressure to increase social expenditure, to cut back on investments to progressively build such capabilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect to GST, I am glad to note the progressive way in which the GST will be implemented.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is provided for under the Assurance Package and the permanent GST Voucher Scheme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This also means that, on a net basis, it will be the wealthier Singaporeans, who will be bearing the brunt of the impact of the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have carefully considered the reasons provided by the Minister for the tax increases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the Minister’s decision requiring those with more to contribute more tax to fund our social programmes and, in particular, help those whom the hon Member Mr Faisal Manap referred to in his speech just now as "marginalised people" and keep our social compact strong.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, such contributions by the wealthier amongst us will so serve as “investment” not just for the future of the less fortunate but also for their own continued economic well-being and growth.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: After all, the strength of our social compact provides the foundations of our economic growth.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this way, their businesses and wealth will continue to grow, in a society that is stable and fair, where each man feels he has a place.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only that, we should also acknowledge that our tax bases are still relatively low, even with the proposed increases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One point which I wish to emphasise though is the continued need to keep our public expenditure lean.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If we do not and we just continue to fund social expenditure for the less fortunate through knee-jerk increases in tax for the wealthy, then I am afraid the social compact will, ironically, weaken.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There will be a danger that our society will fracture as a result of an “us against them” mentality taking root.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is a point that hon Members who spoke before me also raised.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Already I see warning signs that this may happen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note calls amongst persons who own private landed properties but have no steady income streams asking for Government support.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This, with other measures such as CDC Vouchers and MediSave top-ups for seniors, will allow them to get more than five times the GST that they would have paid in a year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The reality, however, is that with the landed property prices as they are, these persons can well afford to fund their own expenses through readily available reverse mortgages from banks which will allow them to live comfortably in their homes until the end of their lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Thereafter, their homes may be sold and the proceeds applied against loans extended by the bank.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not easy to make these arguments to people who feel very strongly about their properties, but we must, on behalf of a society where more than 90% live in flats, push back against such claims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A similar example involves elderly retired couples in an HDB flat which is eligible for the Lease Buyback Scheme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They would again be entitled to Government support because they are living in an HDB flat without income.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In reality though, they would be able to fund their expenses through the Lease Buyback Scheme which would again enable them to sell the tail end of their lease to HDB and live comfortably in their homes until the end of their life with the proceeds obtained.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some time back, I met an elderly couple who sought ComCare assistance because they are retired and their children are not willing to give them any allowance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I suggested the Lease Buyback Scheme to them as a way to resolve their financial woes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: After some thought, they came back to me and the answer was that they are not keen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The reason is because they want to pass on their homes as inheritance to their children even though their children are not paying for their upkeep.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As parents, they are amazing but as claimants on taxpayers’ monies used in substitution for their upkeep, they become what economists refer to as “free riders”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Private inheritance comes at a cost of public funds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This also means that there is less money for helping a person who may have a more pressing need for assistance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Again, this may be a hard argument to make to the elderly couple, but if we do not, we will be a nation of ComCarers, with a large budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And there is no large budget without large taxes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At some point in time, as our social spending increases, we will have to make hard decisions on whom we should support through social assistance so that we can keep public spending lean and only to be given to the truly need it, while we focus on making our safety “trampoline” – a phrase made popular by Senior Minister Tharman – springier.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With established track records, these Singapore businesses would be able to establish good branding and reputation as leaders in this field, venture into the region or beyond, and undertake larger scale projects to reduce carbon emissions that can be financed through carbon credits.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through this we would have developed a value proposition for Singaporean businesses and allow them an opportunity to participate in the international carbon credit value-chain.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not the natural position of price takers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But while we cannot determine our own price, we can continue to write our own destiny as long as we are a sovereign state, with the will and wherewithal to defend it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To continue to write each page, requires resources and careful husbandry of what we have.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is what our Budget does, and this is why I support it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We are now moving towards life with COVID-19 as an endemic disease, a path which is bound to be fraught with unexpected challenges.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Russian invasion of Ukraine has been a stark demonstration of the fragility of territorial sovereignty in the face of aggression by a larger neighbour.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Building national resilience is a key effort we need to undertake to prepare for current and future challenges.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It has to be a joint effort, borne out of the partnership between the people, society, companies and the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is vital that Government policies must be supportive of this endeavour to build and strengthen resilience.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As I respond to the Finance Minister's Budget Statement, I will talk about seven pillars of resilience I believe that we need to continuously build up our nation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are resilient families, resilient environment, resilient infrastructure, resilient companies, resilient workforce, resilient society and resilient government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This means that 20% of them will not be able to withdraw more than a token sum from their CPF.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many of them struggle with their living expenses and are not able to use their CPF of housing payments.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope that MOF will give careful consideration to the needs of CPF members with lower balances before raising the BRS.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For our children, building resilience starts at home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All parents, myself included, view our kids as precious gems, but we must be careful not to mollycoddle them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let us encourage our children to take part in competitions, whether in sports, games or the arts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Every competition will have only one winner and many losers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let them learn to win with grace and remain resilient in defeat by picking themselves up to fight another day.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let our children take public transport to school instead of ferrying them everywhere by car.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This brings an additional benefit of reducing traffic jams around schools.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I commend schools that disallow parents from turning up at schools with water bottles or homework that their children left at home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In order to realise this goal, Singapore must be prepared to make big investments in emerging green technologies and take decisive steps towards wielding the mantle of climate leadership, regionally and globally.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will set Singapore on a path towards being a global player in the hydrogen industry and benefit Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: NEA is now mulling the introduction of a mandatory plastic bag charge at supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, policies designed to achieve this must take into account the local context.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most shoppers do not throw away their plastic bags but use them to bag their thrash before throwing it down the rubbish chute.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If they do not have enough plastic bags from supermarkets, they might end up buying plastic bags or, worse, throwing their rubbish directly down the chutes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, any policy interventions should strive to encourage intrinsic attitudes towards conservation, not lead to people trying to work around punitive measures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Instead of a per-bag charge, has NEA considered requiring large supermarkets to offer a discount as an incentive for not using plastic bags?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's rapid urban development and ascent on the global economic stage was made possible in large part due to good infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our public transport network has seen improvements in recent years although the convenience and frequency of bus services in some areas like Bedok Reservoir has been a bugbear for many commuters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This has shown up in commuters' surveys which rate bus services the lowest among transport modes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will speak more about this during MOT Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Moving on to digital infrastructure, the prevalence of online scams points to the need for more resilient cyber infrastructure, not only at the backend but also at the frontend, with efforts to detect attempts at social engineering and prevent people from falling prey to scammers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While our public education is important, the financial institutions must redouble their efforts to use technological solutions to detect suspicious patterns of use and stop using SMS as a channel for sending passwords.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The world has entered a stage where cyber warfare is a real threat, as demonstrated by Russia's alleged cyberattacks Ukrainian's infrastructure, long before the air, land and sea invasion began.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Adversaries can potentially maliciously shut down or control critical infrastructure with the click of a mouse.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are our Government agencies putting enough resources into countering this threat and are critical infrastructure providers, like water treatment plants, power grid operators, telcos and public transport operators, ready to counter these threats?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our companies have seen challenging times in this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The pandemic has shown our over-reliance on our foreign workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to transform our economy to boost the attractiveness of local talent to companies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MOM should watch out for companies that circumvent market testing requirements, for example, doing a token posting on MyCareersFuture when they already have a foreigner in mind to hire.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Where there are instances of companies claiming that they are unable to find Singaporeans to take up positions, we need to make a deeper qualitative assessment on why this is so.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, are there gaps in our education system that are preventing our schools from producing market-ready graduates?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On a separate note, I believe that one of the brightest sparks from the pandemic is the mainstreaming of work-from-home arrangements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A large proportion of both employees and employers want to continue remote work, at least part of the time, even after the pandemic ends.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should build on these gains and encourage more companies, especially the traditional SMEs, to provide work-from-home options for their employees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Good economic prospects and technological advances disproportionately benefit the high-skilled.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To make our growth more inclusive, we should engage more Singaporeans economically, including people with disabilities and the elderly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Companies should extend work-from-home opportunities to engage and empower Singaporeans with mobility issues.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Not only do they form a large untapped labour market with valuable experience to contribute, enabling them to work from home will help them to connect better with society, improve their overall well-being and strengthen Singapore's social security.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope MOM can consider ways to incentivise companies to extend work-from-home opportunities to this group of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will disadvantage workers who have extremely low incomes and are forced to work reduced hours through no fault of their own or have unpaid caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister said that this is to encourage part-timers and casual workers to take up regular full-time work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I fear that it will result in the exact opposite.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Workers may decide to drop out of the workforce because their income cannot even cover their travel expenses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I appeal to the Minister to rescind the minimum income requirement, so that all lower-wage workers will benefit from Workfare.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This was a call made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition as well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Building on this approach, would the Minister consider also co-funding for five years the pay increases of all Singaporean workers who are taking home less than $1,300, including those who are not in sectors or occupations covered by the PWM?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will help companies adjust to paying their workers a minimum wage and bring Singapore closer towards implementing a national minimum wage, something that the Workers' Party has been consistently advocating for.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In addition to strengthening our workers' rights, we also need to build more resilience in our local workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some employers have lamented to me about local employees quitting when they are made to work long hours, in contrast to foreigners whom they claimed have no qualms about working overtime.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should not be dismissive about those who may have genuine domestic responsibilities like taking care of children or elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, for those that do not, including many young professionals, I feel it does not hurt to "pia" a bit more during your first job, so you can establish your career and compete more effectively with the global workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Of course, do this without sacrificing your mental and physical health.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A vibrant local sports scene contributes towards building a resilient society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Suzuki Cup football tournament was a great demonstration of how sports can promote national unity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I experienced it myself when I took my son to see one of the matches.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, cheering the Lions once every two years is not enough.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our sporting talents are playing in the international tournaments throughout the year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, Loh Kean Yew's historic victory at the 2021 Badminton World Championships could only be watched live on Cable Television.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Non-subscribers had to wait almost a week to watch it on free-to-air TV.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Featuring more of our local sporting talents on free-to-air TV or local online channels, like meWATCH, will not only imbue a greater national spirit, but will also inspire generation of young sports enthusiasts, who may go on to become future champions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A sizable presence of opposition Members in Parliament will keep the government on its toes and responsive to the needs of the people and increase the resilience of our government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On the other side of the coin, as an efficient and effective civil service, I commend our public servants for demonstrating great resilience in helping our nation through the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I was once a civil servant and, to this day, I hold close to my heart a piece of advice that my Permanent Secretary gave to me when I first joined the service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He told me he expected me to be a subject matter expert on the issues covered by my desk.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He said it was my responsibility to provide objective recommendations in my policy submissions I put up to the senior management and Ministers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They must also not be afraid to respectfully point out policy errors made by political officeholders, as it is in Singapore's interests that the best possible policies are advanced.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The civil service must also remain politically neutral.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The final point I wish to raise is to register my concerns over the planned hike in the GST rates in 2023 and 2024.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I understand the budgetary pressures that come with an ageing society, and I support moves to socialise more provision of more public welfare services, especially for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, only a portion of the GST paid is returned in the form of GST Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MOF should consider other more progressive sources of revenue besides the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has, thankfully, been largely spared the kind of widespread rifts in society caused by measures to deal with the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, we must anticipate that future challenges will only get harder.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let us take the necessary steps now to build a more resilient Singapore, so that our next generation will be better prepared to weather any storm that comes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We had also planted the seeds of growth on the SG Green Plan through sustainability efforts and green financing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our consistent and careful handling of the COVID-19 crisis has led to greater confidence not only in Singapore but the region as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we are not out of the woods yet.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: New challenges have emerged in the course of the past year.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: COVID-19 and its variants have tested our system and the resilience of our people.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But we have prevailed, thanks to the cooperation and understanding of everyone.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is also assisted by the various schemes like the JSS, COVID-19 Relief Grant and the Jobs Growth Incentive (JGI), just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are also facing a period of global economic uncertainty and higher energy prices, given the recent developments in the Ukraine region.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With these challenges we now face, I agree with Minister Lawrence Wong that we have to further strengthen our social compact as one people, more so now than ever before.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, in my Committee of Supply cuts, I will focus on three main areas.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This includes strengthening our total defence and relevance of National Service (NS) to our people and new citizens, maintaining and improving our relationship with other countries in the region and all over the world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, prepare our people to be secure and confident to face a post-COVID-19 world, that means maximising the potential of everyone, especially the most vulnerable, like ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Instead of offenders, they can become overcomers through our help in their rehabilitation and reintegration into the workforce and society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must also look at the retirement security of not only our seniors but entire communities, by considering reforms to make it easier and affordable for Singaporeans to plan for their retirement and their future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Third, invest in our next generations through technology, education and skills required for the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This involves not just targeting young people or students but also working with their parents, educators and industry players.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How we support the young determines how they will grow to support our country in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, all of these goals and aspirations will only remain as a wish list if we do not have the fiscal discipline and proper planning to finance our plans in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Budget 2022 gives us the springboard to do so.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   This Budget is bigger than last year.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although revenue is projected to be higher than last year, this is not sufficient to cover our recurring expenses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, there is a need to increase revenue not just for current and future expenditure but to save for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, anecdotally some Chua Chu Kang residents have informed me that they are already seeing some shops and stalls increasing retail prices.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Taskforce is not something new as it was also set up during the GST hike in 2007.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our GST system is progressive and the features of the permanent GST Vouchers and other transfers have the effect of helping those who need it the most.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, it also results in savings in administrative costs and implementation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The increase in GST alone will not be able to cover our expenditure, especially healthcare expenditure which will continue to increase.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, while the Government had been able to tap on the country's reserves to respond to the COVID-19 crisis, this is untenable for the long term.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to take steps to reduce the budget deficit in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, as stated, this year’s Budget will have an even bigger deficit.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What this means is that we need to do three things: first, work hard; second, spend smart; and third, save more.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, given the continued impact and uncertainty of the pandemic and global situation we have to continue to work hard in our economic recovery and strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am glad that we have come up with many efforts for close coordination between Ministries and agencies in specific areas which would also give us the ability to work harder together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, the Singapore Green Plan 2030 involves various Government agencies working in concert, along with a whole-of-society effort, to meet a global challenge.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just like the saying, "if you want to run fast, run alone.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If you want to run further, run together".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In recent years, MOF had also developed a number of joint Budgets to ensure better alignment and greater efficiency and value.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have seen these efforts in the Smart Nation initiative for example.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What other whole-of-government efforts can be better coordinated across Ministries and agencies so that we can also attain greater efficiency and savings in implementation?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, I would suggest that the recommendations of the taskforce on family violence be considered for potential implementation not just by MSF alone but on a whole-of-Government effort.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With regard to the pandemic, does MOF track the coordination of efforts and resources by MTF and the various agencies and Ministries related to the COVID-19 pandemic?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would be useful for future studies on the impact of the pandemic and how much it cost our country to provide the necessary support and response.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would suggest a multi-Ministerial consolidated Budget or allocation to address any future crisis.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will also provide a more accurate picture of non-crisis related expense by a particular Ministry or agency.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In my work with the Parliament Estimates Committee, we looked at the Government's budget to see how improvements may be effected to increase efficiency.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the course of the past year, we have also introduced various legislation which has helped in this.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With such explanations or regular reports, Singaporeans can understand that the borrowing will not only help “free up” our spending capacity but at the same time not be a burden to future generations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One example is the Land Betterment Charge Act (LBC) which streamlines the previous framework for tax collection.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a good example of making things more efficient.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have a clarification: would MOF be looking into streamlining the imposition and collection of other charges to ensure greater efficiency?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is there a specific department that looks into this?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our tax system is admittedly already simpler and less complicated to navigate than other jurisdictions', but we can still see how to make it more efficient.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps just like how we set targets on right-sizing Government spending with 5-year Block Budget Framework, MOF can similarly set targets to trim down the number and types of taxes too.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Besides cutting on costs and spending smart, we must save more into our reserves.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our country does not have any other viable natural resources.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: NIRC, is already the single largest source of revenue.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We cannot be over reliant on this alone.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Now is the time for us to start planning to put more into our reserves for the future generations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would MOF set some targets within the next five years, to reinvest more of our investment returns to build up our reserves and explore more revenue streams to complement our investment income?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hopefully with such targets we will be able to save more for our children and their children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Economists and market watchers look to be convinced of whether the Budget will make Singapore more competitive and foster GDP growth.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But just as organisations are finding that employees are increasingly looking beyond dollars and cents for companies with a clear and inspiring purpose, I believe that Singaporeans are also looking for more in a Budget: do the values reflected by the policies and initiatives proposed align with our own core values?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because when the values espoused are aligned with your own core values, it is a very special and awesome feeling – just ask any Liverpool fan who has bought into the ethos of "You Never Walk Alone".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is about not just getting results but doing it in a way that makes you deeply proud to be a Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: On this measure, the evolution of the social compact towards a fairer, greener and more inclusive Singapore, as described by the Finance Minister, delivers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These are values and a vision for the future that are shared by the broad middle ground of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The yin and yang of the Singapore way, mutually reinforcing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While reinforcing personal responsibility through tying incentives and support to work, the Budget continues the tilt towards collective support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This has been happening for the past more than 10 years.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government has recognised the need for greater social support, in response to growing inequality, technological change and changing societal expectations, and adjusted the system, very deliberately, over time, including the introduction of the new anchors of our social security system like Workfare, Silver Support and now PWM, and the tightening of foreign manpower policy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Collective support means we all pay, which also ensures that we all understand that nothing we get comes for free.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: By raising revenue in a broad-based way, but spending it in a targeted and fair way, we set ourselves up for a more sustainable fiscal position, while giving time and support for the transition.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: However, one area I urge the Minister to review, in light of recent developments, is the Household Support Package.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many Members of Parliament on both sides of the House have spoken about their concerns over the cost of living.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I must echo this concern, for low- and middle-income households.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I sat and talked to one of my residents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He and his wife have five children, they live in a five-room flat.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His water bill has gone up from $30 to $60, multiply by 12, $360.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His petrol bill, which he uses to work and ferry his kids to and from school has gone from $500 to $800 or $300 increase a month, $3,600 a year.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His food expenditure – they do not cook a lot, so they mostly eat out – has gone up by about 15% to 20%, he says.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fortunately, his spend on healthcare and education have not gone up by much.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But as you can see, these add up pretty quickly.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But long term, the way to make sure that the increased cost of living does not bite too hard, is to ensure that incomes grow faster than expenses at every level of the workforce.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With the expanded PWM, I think we are quite covered with the lower-income workers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For the middle-income, it is vital that we continue to enhance the competitiveness of our economy so that we can continue to create and retain good jobs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is vital that we continue to invest in capability building and take a balanced, tempered approach in implementing the tax and manpower policy changes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In the Committee of Supply, I will speak more on measures to enhance the competitiveness of the economy, build capabilities in our people and businesses, accelerate the green transition and manage the healthcare costs and workforce for an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is a set of leading global companies that are moving past all definitions of “great”, companies that used to focus on scale and strong shareholder returns.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These Beyond Great companies have realised that sustainable competitive advantage in an era of technological, geopolitical and social change, can only be attained by being responsive to the needs of all stakeholders, shareholders, but also customers, employees, local communities, governments and the natural environment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The have agile business models that offer customised solutions to borderless communities of digitally connected customers and are experts at forming flexible ecosystems of partners.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Conscious of their responsibility to the countries they operate in, they nurture local expertise, enable SMEs to participate in global and regional value chains and help the countries they are in to develop customised solutions to their toughest problems.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They are willing to provide jobs and opportunities for a combination of skills, from the highly skilled global professionals who compete with the best in the world, to the middle and lower-skilled workers who may compete more often with lower-cost resources in the region, because they understand that for Singapore to be true to our values, we must have jobs for every Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To attract these companies, we must continue to offer financial stability, predictability, transparency and low taxes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Beyond Great companies will also demand world class digital infrastructure and customs procedures that minimise transaction costs, cross border data sharing frameworks and safeguards, regional trade agreements that harmonise regulations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: All of these are necessary for them to transact international business through digital platforms and fast-evolving ecosystems.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Beyond Great companies also require flexible labour policies and the ability to tap on global employees and freelancers sitting outside the host country and within a country, a workforce that is not only highly skilled with specialised technical capabilities but also people with digital mindsets, who are agile and always hungry to learn, who have motivation and grit.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In my maiden speech at the start of this Parliament, I spoke about the need for the Government and companies to invest in our people.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must also collaborate in public-private ecosystems with these Beyond Great companies to align plans, policies and incentives to achieve mutually shared goals beyond profit and growth.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The second strategy deals with social policy – implement a permanent growth dividend.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I must confess though that when schemes like the Solidarity Payment and Community Development Council (CDC) Vouchers were announced, I was quite bemused.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Did rich Singaporeans really need the $100 to feel solidarity with other Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But after getting feedback on the vouchers from the ground, I must say my position has shifted.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My residents in 5-room, executive apartment (EA), executive maisonette (EM) and Jumbo flats – we happen to have a lot in my division – told me that it felt good to finally get something when, usually, there is nothing for them, even though quite a few of them donated theirs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In the discussion on GST in this and previous Budgets, we have talked about the advantages of GST as a broad-based tax on revenue.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Perhaps, there is something to be said about boosting solidarity through a broad-based distribution, which also provides an additional way to enhance financial security and mitigate inequality for those whose fortunes do not reflect the nation's success.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have done this before with one-off payments like the SG Bonus in 2018, the Growth Dividend in 2011, the New Singapore Shares in 2001 and, of course, the discounted Singtel shares in the 1990s.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It may feel moot to even be discussing this in the context of consecutive years of Budget deficits, but I hope the Minister might consider this as we move forward.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The third strategy deals with shaping our values themselves – build a positive national culture.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our founding Prime Minister, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, famously said in 1977, "You know the Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Or we would not have made the grade.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But let us also recognise that he is a champion grumbler." Forty-five years later, we may laugh and wryly say some things never change.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But who do we really want to be?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Have we thought about how much better and stronger we would be if we were a more positive people?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are three components of a positive national culture that I think are particularly important.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In dealing with people, we must make the effort to get to know them as whole human beings.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It increases the likelihood that they will go the extra mile when we need them to.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The relationship and the trust between the people and the Government and the Public Service are a massive ingredient to sustainable success for our nation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we respect others, we must accept that people have different strengths and weaknesses and support them to use their strengths to flourish and not be stuck with narrow ideas of what good looks like and of what should be valued.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must accept different backgrounds, cultures and viewpoints while not letting society become more and more fragmented.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must speak to one another, on the streets and in this House, with respect and with integrity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Third, aspiration or ambition – always believing that we can do better, be better.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We fight complacency and cynicism by surrounding ourselves with people who push us to aim higher and do better.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We believe that no matter how small we are, our actions matter.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, with respect to climate change, we could take the view that Singapore going to net-zero may not move the needle if bigger countries in the region and the world do not do their part or we could take the view that I mooted in last year's Budget debate that by investing in research and development (R&D) and developing solutions for the greatest existential crisis of our times, we can lead and change the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must cultivate that eternal optimism, that sense of idealism and adventure.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And there are rich findings at the end of that rainbow.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To the young and the not so old, I say, look at that horizon, follow that rainbow, go ride it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Quite a few will find a vein of gold.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But all those who pursue that rainbow will have a joyous and exhilarating ride and some profit." Mr Speaker, building this positive national culture requires a lot of work that has to start early in life – in our schools, communities, workplaces, in our interactions with Government agencies, in social media, in the metaverse.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have to enable and stimulate the building of networks, support groups, mentorship programmes, volunteer groups.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In my youth, we had a lot of public education campaigns on radio and television.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Who can forget Singa the Courtesy Lion, Teamy the Bee and all those jingles?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Now, the same types of campaigns may not be quite so effective with Singaporeans today but we have even more new mediums, tools and talents today to put out relatable and inspiring content to propagate positivity among Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Let us infect one another with positivity, regardless of backgrounds, cultures or political leanings.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: (In Malay):   Not long ago, I received a message over Facebook from a Chinese resident.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Taking pains to say that it was nothing racist but an encouragement to me, our Malay MP in our Sembawang GRC, she shared what she overheard from a group of Chinese women:  "Aiyo, you see, generally Malays are less hardworking … But you see that our Sembawang GRC Malay MP looks so cheerful, so hardworking and active?" Is this racist?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some will say yes, some will say no.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As minorities, the truth is we have always had to work harder than others just to be seen as working as hard as others.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But is there a genuine desire to put in the hard work to change things?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I believe this to be the case with this Government.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is fashionable these days to cry out injustices, to see calls to cancel someone or something.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Sadly, that can sometimes do a great injustice to the hard work being done to change things.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Budget represents a vision of a fairer, greener and more inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A fairer and more inclusive Singapore where the fruits of progress are shared more equally by all augurs well for our community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I hope our community will take full advantage of the commitment to invest in our people, invest in our children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: During this time, we must continue to work on increasing incomes across all levels of our community through our individual efforts to upskill, and through further Government effort.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I also hope that the 4G leaders will continue to build genuine relationships with our community, understand our values, our constraints, but also our talents, our efforts and our hustle.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And then please be our ally and help us develop and use our strengths to benefit ourselves and society.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because we don’t just want to get better than we were, we want to be at par with everyone else.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: (In English) Mr Speaker, Budget 2022 makes a significant move down the path of a fairer, greener, more inclusive Singapore, from which may emerge a vision of a Singapore that is beyond great.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It moves further to build capabilities to keep our economy and our people competitive, scaling up early intensive interventions to boost social mobility.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is a Budget we can be proud of.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I join Members of this House to thank our workers for their hard work and sacrifices during the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes our frontline workers and also those who are providing critical support behind the scenes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In my capacity as advisor to the Healthcare Services Employees' Union (HSEU) and as Senior Minister of State for Transport, I have witnessed how our healthcare and transport workers have stood strong and resilient in the face of challenging circumstances, to care for patients and commuters, and to keep Singapore connected with the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our Labour Members of Parliament will speak about how NTUC and our tripartite partners have worked together to protect, enable and care for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Brother Abdul Samad will share his views on the protection of workers during the pandemic and beyond.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Brother Heng Chee How will touch on enhancing employment for older workers, a topic close to his heart.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Brother Patrick Tay will focus on strengthening workplace fairness and support for professionals, managers and executives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Brother Desmond Choo will talk about providing support and opportunities for younger workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Brother Melvin Yong will speak on improving mental health support for our workers and enhancing consumer protection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Brother Fahmi Aliman will touch on NTUC's efforts to uplift lower-wage workers, reflecting our shared values with the People's Action Party to build a fair and just society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Sister Yeo Wan Ling will highlight how NTUC has provided support for women, family, self-employed persons and workers in small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Brother Seah Kian Peng will share on cost pressures faced by SMEs and how NTUC and our social enterprises have helped Singaporeans to manage costs of living and provided assistance to our members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Together, the Labour Members of Parliament will present how NTUC has championed the interests of our workers and helped them to achieve better wages, better welfare and better work prospects – because every worker matters, and every worker can make a difference.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In his speech at the 1976 NTUC's Second Triennial Delegates Conference, Dr Goh Keng Swee warned about the dangers of having small or no economic growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Without sufficient growth, we have a zero-sum game.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will intensify social conflict because one group can only benefit at the expense of another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And when cohesion is affected, win-lose will soon become "lose-lose".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is why the Labour Movement fully supports the Government’s efforts to grow Singapore’s economy and to ensure that when companies do well, our workers receive a fair share of the gains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The PAP Government has consistently placed emphasis on achieving this win-win outcome through tripartism, to keep improving the lives of our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Mr Lee Kuan Yew said: "It is in the interest of the workers and their unions that we must strive for growth and development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In other words, growth is meaningless unless it is shared by the workers." When Singapore’s economy transforms and the profile of our workforce changes, this important purpose shall remain at the heart of NTUC’s mission.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Even as we evolve "what" we do and "how" we achieve our outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Never forgetting our core purpose and DNA, while moving in tandem with changing times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We could see how this principle was translated into action when NTUC implemented new ideas over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Or when NTUC set up e2i to work with Government agencies and employers to improve productivity and help workers find jobs, which is especially important during a crisis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A more recent innovation is the formation of Company Training Committees (CTCs) between our unions and employers to strengthen our engagements with companies and workers through NTUC’s Training and Placement Ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our ecosystem brings together a comprehensive package of training and placement services provided by e2i, NTUC LearningHub, Ong Teng Cheong Labour Leadership Institute and NTUC’s Industry Training and Transformation team.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Compared to an entity which does only training or only job matching, we provide companies and workers with a wider range of integrated services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our union leaders will mobilise workers to actively upskill themselves and support the company’s transformation plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Depending on their requirements, NTUC can help CTC companies to redesign jobs and implement productivity improvements, improve workplace safety and health, to promote physical and mental well-being of our workers, provide training to existing workers and new entrants and match jobseekers to companies that are growing and expanding their workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also have strong support from Government agencies and employers, which makes a powerful combination for driving enterprise and workforce transformation through CTC as a collaboration platform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They are experienced business leaders who understand tripartism well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Certact Engineering is a local SME that provides precision and plastic engineering services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Managing Director, Ms Ellis Eng, is a strong believer in training and self-improvement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: She started her career as a nurse before she joined Certact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through on-the-job training, she picked up new skills and learnt more about its business functions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Certact Engineering formed a CTC with the Advanced Manufacturing Employees’ Union (AMEU).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Management and union agreed to redesign the role of "Machinists" to "Robotics Operators".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Some of the workers were initially reluctant because they were unsure how they could adapt to the new requirements because they had been working as "Machinists" for many years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But with support from the union and from management, the workers embarked on the transformation journey and, over time, they became more confident and more familiar with the digital tools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: After its transformation, Certact Engineering has more than doubled its revenue and is expanding its operations to take on more contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The growth benefited the workers, too, as they received significant wage increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is a win-win outcome that we want to scale up and achieve together with other CTC companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will now talk about protection for our workers and I will focus on two areas: first, how NTUC can uplift vulnerable workers, including ex-offenders as well as persons with special needs and disabilities, through skills upgrading and job placement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, why the Labour Movement firmly supports the Government’s policy for Singapore to remain open to international trade, investments and foreign workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Because we know that our workers can have better wages and better work prospects when our economy is open and connected with the world and when we allow employers to have a complementary mix of local and foreign workers to grow their business in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I visited Agape Connecting People, a social enterprise that helps individuals turn their lives around through skills upgrading and job placement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The beneficiaries include people who are physically or visually challenged, single mothers and ex-offenders, with the last group forming the majority of their clients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One of its co-founders, Mr Anil David, is an ex-offender himself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He founded Agape Connecting People to help other vulnerable workers by equipping them with job-ready skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He and his team have helped more than 800 vulnerable workers to find jobs and, just as important, to discover their sense of purpose, dignity and self-worth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One beneficiary is Ms Nur Madiah Lim, who was born without hands and legs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When Nur approached Agape Connecting People for help, the company trained and appointed her as one of its contact centre agents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: She has been in this job now for the past three years and continually hones her skills to manage calls, emails and live chats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Nur went on to handle a National CARE Hotline (NCH) and earned her diploma, which was one of the goals she set to achieve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Her other goal was to own an HDB flat, which she has also achieved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Your resilience, determination and positive attitude are a source of inspiration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Together with our partners, NTUC will expand our services to help even more vulnerable workers through training and job placement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The number of vulnerable workers may be a small proportion of our overall workforce, but this is a meaningful area for the Tripartite Partners to focus on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last evening, Mr Shawn Huang spoke passionately about how he and his colleagues have worked with Ms Denise Phua to help a group of vulnerable workers find meaningful employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And what he shared really touched my heart – to build a more caring and inclusive society, we must do our best to leave no one behind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Mr Edward Chia that Singaporean workers are capable, but there are not enough of us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung made the same point during an earlier debate in this House.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We believe a balanced and complementary approach is better for our local workers, instead of rejecting free trade agreements (FTAs) and turning away foreigners and foreign investments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We understand the concerns of local workers regarding competition from foreigners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: NTUC will do our best to protect the rice bowls of our workers and champion fair employment practices for locals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, we know this alone is not sufficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Having an empty rice bowl does not help our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To enable our workers to have better jobs and better lives, we must also protect our rice fields and ensure that the fields are productive and can yield bountiful harvests year after year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Then our workers and their families, their rice bowls will be filled with rice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is why NTUC works closely with employers and the Government to grow Singapore's economy, attract more investments and create more good jobs for our people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Minister Lawrence Wong said in the Budget Statement: "by combining local and foreign professionals, we form the teams in Singapore to create value together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This gives us that extra advantage to excel amidst intense global competition and to create many good jobs and career choices for Singaporeans." Sir, to be clear, there are some employers who do not practise fair hiring and do not invest enough in developing their Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They are the minority among employers, but their behaviours have created a negative impact on the lived experiences of our workers and their families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, we must not react to the small number of black sheep employers by implementing overly tight foreign manpower measures that will hurt our businesses, or worse, by stirring anti-foreigner sentiments amongst our population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Such moves are detrimental to Singapore and Singaporeans as they damage our international standing, erode cohesion in our society and lead to job losses for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Instead, a key part of our response must focus on working with employers and HR managers through tripartism to improve workplace practices for local workers, strengthen the emphasis on developing local talent and invest in building a strong Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last year, I suggested at an event with business and HR leaders that the Government should sharpen the differentiation in how we treat employers with good HR practices and strong relationships with the unions, versus those with poor HR records and do not put in effort to develop their local workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One example is dnata Singapore, which has been badly affected by the pandemic as their main business is ground handling, cargo and catering services to the aviation industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: After they formed a CTC with NTUC and completed their Operation and Technology Roadmap in 2020, the company started offering food services to local business and retail customers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They also invested in upskilling their workforce to support their transformation and to prepare for the recovery in the aviation sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I met three of their staff during my visit – Ms Garmit Kuar, Mr Abdul Faizal and Ms Ferry Carisma.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Garmit and Faizal are locals, while Ferry came from the Philippines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They shared with me their challenges during the pandemic and their upskilling journeys to become trainers in dnata.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They enjoy their new roles as it gives them great satisfaction to help their colleagues acquire new skills and knowledge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I was also happy to learn from Garmit and Faizal that they appreciate having Ferry and other foreign colleagues as co-workers because they contribute to making the team more productive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And when the company does better, everyone gets to enjoy larger bonuses and higher salary increments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dnata's example show that if we can work with companies through our tripartite partnership and CTC platform to create good jobs for locals and develop a strong Singaporean Core, it will help to provide sufficient protection and assurance to our people which will in turn allow Singapore to remain open and connected with the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This brings me to the third and final area, skills upgrading for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Labour Movement believes that a good job is the best welfare for workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And the best protection for their employability is to invest in their continuous training and skills upgrading.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I fully support MOE's plans to give lifelong learning a further boost and Minister Chan Chun Sing's call for all Singaporeans to "learn for life, and to learn throughout life".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Skills upgrading and continuous learning are key priorities for the Labour Movement too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One practical challenge we want to tackle is the jobs-skills mismatch, where employers who are short-handed could not find enough workers with the right skills to fill their job vacancies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The tripartite coordination can help achieve better alignment, improve job placement rates and reduce wasted time and effort for both employers and job-seekers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have some experience with such tripartite collaborations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They have been doing good work to identify new skills required in the industry and preparing existing workers and new entrants with the relevant training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another example is the Singapore Institute of Power and Gas (SIPG) that was set up in 2014 to be a Centralised Training Institute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I was then Chief Executive of the Energy Market Authority (EMA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This has grown into a tripartite collaboration between the Union of Power and Gas Employees (UPAGE), industry and Government agencies like EMA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Under the leadership of Brother Samad, UPAGE worked with SIPG to train our workers in emerging areas, for example, Electric Vehicle charging facilities and wider adoption of renewable energy in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: More recently, NTUC set up the Tourism Careers Hub with Singapore Tourism Board.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also brought in Workforce Singapore, e2i and the industry associations to help employers and workers from the tourism sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The tourism industry has gone through a difficult period during the pandemic, but it is slowly recovering and I am confident it will bounce back.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dedicated career coaches will advise new entrants and existing workers on the training they need to take on higher level jobs in the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Tourism Careers Hub will also facilitate placement of workers within the industry to help employers who are facing manpower shortages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We plan to start with these and grow the list of sectors over time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Tripartite Academies will serve as collaboration platforms at the sectoral level to complement our network of CTCs which are collaboration platforms at the enterprise level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Both platforms are important because they support the larger national objective of transforming Singapore's economy by building stronger enterprise and workforce capabilities which will in turn provide better jobs and better wages for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, we must continue to drive the transformation of businesses to achieve sufficient economic growth, to give our workers better wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must protect their jobs and interests, treat them fairly, and ensure that their skills are constantly upgraded through lifelong learning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They started from a coffee shop in Toa Payoh.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Kok Kuan Hwa, founder of the Chang Cheng Group, became an apprentice chef at the age of 15.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the years, he and his team have worked hard, listened to customers' feedback, and improved constantly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They have improved efficiency, developed new products and brands, and become the food and beverage group it is today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Chang Cheng Group is also working with e2i to improve work efficiency, training employees to perform multiple roles, and help 56 low-wage workers and 15 older workers to upgrade their skills and earn higher wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
