text: Through our tripartite partnership, NTUC will give full support to companies like the Chang Cheng Group and other local enterprises, enhance their competitiveness through transformation, and create more good jobs, better wages and a secure future for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, I have spoken about the importance of Growth, Protection and Skills Upgrading or "GPS".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As a navigation tool, GPS can show us how to get to our destination, but GPS cannot get us there unless we embark on the journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is the journey of transforming and growing our economy to build stronger enterprise and workforce capabilities through tripartism and helping our workers to upgrade their skills to remain employable and to take on the new jobs that are being created.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There will be obstacles and unexpected developments during this journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Sometimes, the GPS may wrongly indicate a turning or we could discover new paths along the way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, we will need to adjust and calibrate our measures as we progress but never lose sight of the direction we are taking and the destination we want to arrive at.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And always remain cohesive so that we can stay together while we move ahead as one united people.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   Budget 2022 provides various forms of support to help Singaporeans cope with the increasing cost of living.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As always, the low-income group should receive such support to help them with their living expenses.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It is also important that employers hire Singaporean workers and make them the first choice.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This approach reflects our openness to foreign workers because we are all aware that there is a shortage of manpower that is needed to continue developing Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The main objective of forming these committees is to allow trade unions and the management to work together to improve the quality and capability of their workers through comprehensive and new skills.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As a result of this effort, I hope that the workers can have better income, career and welfare.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We often hear news reports where Government says that a lot of job opportunities will be made available through new companies that will commence operations in Singapore for the near and long term.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This announcement is very much welcomed and therefore, I encourage all workers to constantly improve your skills and capabilities so that we can take on the jobs that will be offered.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, I would also like to convey my appreciation to the Fatwa Council and our religious leaders in providing guidance to fulfil our religious obligations at the mosques in terms of Friday prayers as well as daily prayers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This includes the mosque committee members and volunteers who have been working hard to facilitate and ensure safe distancing measures, among others, so that the congregants can come to the mosques in a safe and orderly manner.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Sir, I will now begin my speech in English.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened that this Budget reflects the Government's continuous support for workers and businesses that are still impacted as we move to an endemic situation.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget also acknowledges and empathise my fellow workers' plight given the rising cost of living and their stagnating income.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We partnered with Government agencies to help redeploy workers from hard-hit sectors to sectors that had an urgent need for manpower.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For workers who unfortunately lost their jobs, we negotiated for reasonable retrenchment benefits and at the same time, provided immediate employment assistance through our Job Security Council.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For the companies that were still doing well, we pursued the skills upgrading and career development of workers through the company training committees.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: These all are only possible due to our unique model of tripartism.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As our economy shows signs of recovery, and our resident unemployment rate has rebounding to pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is an opportune time to grow jobs and improve the wages, welfare and work prospects of our workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to the first topic of my speech, very close to my heart and indeed all in this Chamber, I believe – Strengthening our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This pandemic has accelerated technology adoption across all industries.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen many positive examples of unionised companies automating lower-level manual jobs and upskilling workers to work with technological solutions to increase their job value and productivity.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As the COVID-19 situation improves and borders are slowly opening, companies should avoid taking the easy way out by bringing back foreign labour as a quick fix solution.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Companies should invest in technology and automation for work processes to be easier, safer and smarter.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that there are some jobs that need to be supplemented by foreign labour but we should build on the momentum to train and transform our workforce to strengthen our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Even with the reduction of the Dependency Ratio, I would also like to see that MOM continues to be stringent in assessing the needs of companies for foreign labour and ensure that such talents that come, complement our Singaporean workforce and augment their skills and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Strengthening our Singaporean Core applies to workers of all levels, including our Professionals, Managers, Executives (PMEs).

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The demands for good and high-skilled jobs that would attract PMEs are also growing, and this provides opportunities for localisation of jobs and career development.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The NTUC-SNEF PME task force reported that younger PMEs, aged below 40, opined that their employers are not investing enough to equip them with relevant skills to prepare them for the future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Companies should not take advantage of the recovering economy to bring in foreign talents but instead put in place career development for their Singaporean workers to take on these jobs and grow their careers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While we could continue to embark on the transformation journey, together with enhancing foreign manpower and companies' policies, we acknowledge that it is important for us to keep up with the demands of the evolving job market, hence it is imperative that companies continue to invest in training, to build deep capabilities in our local workforce for us to strengthen our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC is very committed and ready to partner with companies to form CTCs to identify relevant training to upskill and transform workers in tandem with industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Such efforts must lead to better wages, better work prospects and better welfare for our workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: These three outcomes will be the catalyst to encourage workers to attend training.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, amid the COVID-19 outbreak, NTUC Learning Hub swiftly augmented its training capabilities to respond to training needs and the national agenda to upskill.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC Learning Hub also launched their Learning eXperience Platform (LXP) late last year to encourage online learning at one's own pace, anytime and anywhere.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is to also encourage our workforce to embrace lifelong learning and upskilling – complementing CTCs' efforts in partnering companies to transform their business and workforce towards Industry 4.0 and Worker 4.0.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As a strategic partner for industrial transformation, companies can tap on NTUC's Training and Placement network for a smoother business transformation journey, mobilise workers for upskilling and into new jobs to meet the aspirations of their workers, for better staff retention.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For Singapore to remain its Airhub status, there needs to be a continuous and healthy pipeline of talents to perform these good skilled jobs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: With this support, companies need to ramp up their technological solutions and also train their workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Companies should also find ways to retain experienced workers through better salaries and benefits while at the same time, improve internship opportunities for Polytechnic and ITE students.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Besides aviation, tourism is another severely impacted sector and have been facing severe manpower shortage.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Workloads have increased and sadly, salaries have not increased much since pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Now and post pandemic, companies are and will continue to change to be leaner and more efficient in their operations, where skilled manpower is sought after.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: There are efforts to upskill the workforce so that it enables companies to cope with international demand when it returns.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: These are good jobs where a worker who has picked up the relevant industry knowledge and has the passion to contribute can rise very quickly to take up management level positions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We hope companies could increase the local Polytechnic and ITE graduate entry level salaries to attract Singaporeans and retain them in the long run.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, the salaries offered by the gig economy will draw them away from these industries.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, while Singapore gradually expands vaccinated travel lanes, there remains economic challenges and COVID-19 fear.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: These put additional pressure on effective recovery of international tourism.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I hope and I call on the Government to review and extend similar support to the hotel sector too.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Next point that I would like to raise is on the rising cost of living, with my focus towards extending more support to the middle-income earners.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We are all aware that inflation has been on the rise.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For the whole of 2021, overall inflation rose to 2.3%, and in fact, this is the highest since year 2013.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Based on the feedback and sentiments from my peers and fellow workers, inflation is quickly emerging as a key challenge this year, as households face rising prices on multiple fronts, ranging from food, education to housing.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We are really heartened by Government's initiatives such as the GST support package to help lower- and middle-income households as well as retirees to cope with the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: On this note, we hope that it could be further increased so that it can be extended to middle-income Singaporeans to help them cope with the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: To my fellow workers, rest assured that the unions and NTUC hear your concerns and anxieties on the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We are also paying close attention and finding avenues to better support you.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Our NTUC's social enterprises are committed to continue helping members and workers to moderate the cost of living and stretching their hard-earned dollars.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Each of them is created to primarily address specific concerns that weigh on the minds of fellow Singaporeans, from rising food costs, catering to the broader needs of Singaporean working parents and their families to staying relevant throughout their working lives.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: They will continue to roll out initiatives to help Singaporeans cope with the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I would close my speech by making two key points.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: One, as our economy recovers, we should build on the momentum to train and transform the Singaporean workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Together with the strong support of the Government, we will continue to walk this journey with you, raise local workforce capabilities through upskilling and reskilling.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Unions and NTUC will continue to protect our workers, and the social enterprises will continue to cushion the impact of the cost of living through our various initiatives.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Together, unions, NTUC and our social enterprises are committed to serve our members and workers better.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We are and will always be by your side, because every worker matters!

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is indeed a Budget that is well-considered and targeted in giving our nation, economy and society a strong boost for the future while supporting our fellow Singaporeans to ride through this pandemic and easing their concerns over the cost of living today.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is one that invests more in our people and social infrastructure so that together, we can bring Singapore out of the COVID-19 shadows and re-inject the nation with resilience and strong growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is important that we continue to build a vibrant economy with thriving companies, supported by a future-ready workforce that can access good jobs and wages, and ensure that no one is left behind.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Being part of NTUC and as Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Chair for Education, I believe in investing in our workforce and our companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As shared by fellow Labour Members of Parliament, Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat as well Labour Nominated Member of Parliament, Brother Abdul Samad earlier, as well as many other hon Members of this House, we are glad to see further investments in our people – not just the young but also supporting Continuing Education and Training, and Lifelong Learning for all, especially our mid-career workers amidst an ageing workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By training our workers and equipping them with good and in-demand skills, and giving them good jobs and opportunities, we want them to have better income stability to manage their daily cost of living and tools for success to achieve their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In my last Budget debate speech, I made a special highlight on a segment of our workforce which the COVID-19 pandemic has impacted immensely.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are the Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs) in Singapore, especially those in the ages of 40s to 60s.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In response to our local PMEs’ call for assistance, NTUC and SNEF want to strengthen their employment and employability and ensure that they can compete fairly and effectively to meet employers’ manpower and skill demands in a dynamic labour landscape.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am heartened that the Government has taken the NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce recommendations into serious consideration, as reflected in the Budget Statement made by Minister Lawrence Wong.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, strengthening the Singaporean Core through enhancing the Employment Pass framework.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While many of us, including the local PMEs whom the NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce surveyed, recognised the contribution and complementarity of foreign PMEs to Singapore’s economy and the need for us to stay open and competitive, there remained ground concerns and perceptions that an overreliance on foreign PMEs has led to an unnecessary increase in competition in the local job market and employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To safeguard our Singaporean Core and curb discriminatory hiring, we must ensure that Singaporean PMEs have access to a level playing field for jobs while at the same time, balance companies’ manpower needs in the immediate and longer term.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Today, the eligibility criteria for Employment Pass (EP) applications generally focus on the individual applicant’s educational qualifications and salary.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With the qualifying salaries of both the EP and S Pass holders raised in the past, and with further increases announced in Budget 2022, this will go some way to level the playing field for local PMEs as it ties in with the rise in their median wages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, I opine that such a system, by itself, is inadequate to level the playing field for our local PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is therefore pertinent that the EP framework be further enhanced to meet the objective of ensuring that foreign professionals complement our local PME workforce and that employers practice fair hiring as well as improve the diversity of their workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am elated that Minister Lawrence Wong announced earlier that the Government will refine the EP application framework so that there is complementarity, transparency and diversity of the foreign workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We believe that such a system will provide the flexibility to let employers who have justified genuinely and adequately, secure foreign talents to complement their local PME workforce and restrict access to foreign talents for the errant companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And for our local PMEs, we believe both a refinement of the EP system, coupled with the workplace fairness legislation, will go a long way to give better protection and stronger assurance to our local PME populace, especially those 40 to 60 years of age.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, imposing a penalty framework for egregious cases of workplace fairness.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am glad MOM has formed the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness and I hope to see a set of recommendations which will include establishing a robust framework to help achieve workplace fairness for our local PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This should include measures to strengthen enforcement against errant companies and management personnel who adopt unfair practices and require their remedial action.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The measures should also be supported by grievance handling processes that will be entrenched to facilitate the therapeutic resolution of grievances at company level for our local PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, protecting the confidentiality of whistle-blowers of discriminatory practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This brings me to my third point on mandating whistle-blowing policies and procedures to ensure that employees can speak up safely, especially with the forthcoming workplace fairness legislation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In my engagements, I have heard from various HR professionals and PMEs who have witnessed or experienced discriminatory practices at work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, in most cases, they do not report such practices for fear of potential reprisals or consequences in their workplace or in their industry.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is beneficial for those who experienced workplace discrimination or harassment to come forward so that problems can be resolved and positive norms can be established.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We will therefore need to incorporate legal protections to promote transparency and fairness by safeguarding employees’ confidentiality and preventing retaliation by the employer.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this aspect, I hope that policies can be put in place to mandate that employers set up formal grievance handling processes that are communicated clearly to employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Equally important in the process, is to ensure confidentiality of the whistle-blowers and prohibit retaliation against employees, ex-employees and potential employees, who report discrimination or harassment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Fourth, helping mature PMEs transit into new roles through short-term salary support.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In an online survey with 1,000 PMEs last year in April, we found that as compared to younger PMEs who are 20 to 40 years old, a higher percentage of the mature PMEs who are 40 to 60 years old, attributed their age to be a disadvantage to them at workplaces.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In another online survey conducted last year in July with another 1,000 mature PMEs, majority of these mature PMEs expressed challenges in their search for employment and attributed their age to be the key reason.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will better encourage and support companies in hiring our mature PMEs and ensure that mature PMEs get the opportunities they need and deserve.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the long-term, and with an ageing population, I hope that the JGI can be translated or even entrenched to a permanent short-term salary support initiative to assist our mature PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is done by helping companies, who hire unemployed mature PMEs, in mitigating their costs and risks associated with hiring this group of PMEs, who may possess the relevant skills and experience needed by the companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will also allow companies to assess the mature PMEs’ suitability for the job roles and continue to keep them in the company's workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We recognise the growing need to ensure PMEs are adequately protected, have access to good jobs and are equipped with relevant skills.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As we prepare for the new normal, it is important that we continue to entrench progressive and fair practices at workplaces and extend schemes to support our local PMEs, especially the more vulnerable ones.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is crucial to create a level playing field for Singaporean PMEs, strengthen the Singaporean Core, eradicate all forms of discrimination through tougher measures and targeted legislation, and support PMEs and workers in general, to transit effectively and less painfully between jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One of the best ways to protect PMEs and help them progress is through having better wages and better jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: NTUC will help support PMEs with the four Ups – Up their Skills, Up their Employability, Up their Protection and Up their Employment Opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At NTUC, we will champion these for all workers because every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As we pivot and transform to the next normal of work, employers and workers alike will have to find new ways and new avenues to navigate the kinks and curves that the uneven and uncertain future presents.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is thus imperative that we renew our commitment and resolve to uplift society as Singapore continues to recover from the corollaries of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am encouraged by the central theme of this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we continue to find ways to deal with the ever-evolving nature of the pandemic, we must also set our eyes on how we can prepare Singaporeans for a post-pandemic future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Only by doing so can we “Chart Our New Way Forward Together.” My esteemed colleagues and I in the Labour Movement strongly support and welcome the slew of measures introduced to alleviate the hardship that Singaporeans have experienced as a result of the pandemic as well as improve all facets of society as we transit to a post-pandemic future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am heartened to note that the Government will be allocating more resources to help vulnerable groups in society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we chart our way forward, we should remain sensitive to the challenges and concerns of our vulnerable workers, especially our lower-wage workers and migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The best way to help workers cope with cost of living is through better wages and better jobs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Many of our lower-wage workers are frontliners in our nation’s fight against the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Spanning from security to cleaning sectors, our workers have toiled to keep Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As the number of COVID-19 cases soared, our workers continued to work tirelessly to keep Singapore going.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In doing so, they stepped up despite the risks to their health and took on additional precautions to limit the transmission of COVID-19 in our community.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In my Budget speech last year, I spoke about the ongoing efforts to support lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In particular, I reiterated that the formation of the Tripartite Workgroup on Lower-Wage Workers is a testament to our commitment to ensure that the interests of our lower-wage workers are protected.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Over the past year, the collective support from various stakeholder groups to uplift the incomes of our lower-wage workers have been encouraging.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC, alongside our tripartite partners and various other stakeholder groups, will remain committed to help workers improve their income security and quality of life, and give them confidence in navigating their careers, equipping them to participate in new growth opportunities.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: But how can we work towards this goal?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: What are some areas we can continue to look into?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It will also allow employers to voluntarily raise wages for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Having said that, at NTUC, we are cognisant that efforts to help lower-wage workers is a long-term strategy.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In particular, I would like to know if the Government will make special provisions for these industries.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: On the subject of PWM expansion and as mentioned in my Budget speech last year, NTUC has identified two sectors for the implementation of PWM, namely, strata and facilities management and pest management.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC has conducted several engagements with stakeholders in the respective sectors and the response has been very encouraging thus far.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In sectors where services are outsourced, we ought to incentivise service buyers from the private sector to adopt outcome-based contracting to ensure that PWM wage increases are sustainable in the long run.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Consumers and service buyers should also become more socially responsible and reject service providers that provide services at a low cost but at the expense of the welfare of such essential service workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Instead, service buyers should adopt an outcome-based contracting model where contracts are awarded to companies with progressive employment practices that give due recognition to workers, rather than basing these decisions on price alone.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In 2018, NTUC launched the Smart Sourcing Initiative that gives funding to service buyers in security, cleaning and landscape sectors that implement outcome-based contracts and train procurement staff to be familiar with the best sourcing principles.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The introduction of this initiative is encouraging but it also reminds us that there are sufficient opportunities and latitude to incentivise service buyers from the private sector to adopt outcome-based contracting.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In order to do this, I call on the Government to provide funding for trade associations to engage consultants to develop an outcome-based contract guide.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Depending on the industry, the consultants would develop bespoke guides for employers in varying industries.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By incentivising private sector employers to implement outcome-based contracts, due recognition can be accorded to our workers, ensuring that they can progress and perform higher-value roles and our PWM wage increases will be more sustainable in the long run.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Another vulnerable group adversely impacted by the pandemic would be our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I will not be the first to thank our migrant workers for their hard work and contribution to the development of our nation, all while working in challenging conditions, distant from their homes and loved ones.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC has perennially been advocating for enhanced medical coverage for the welfare and safety of our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We are pleased that the Government has heeded our calls for greater protection.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: At NTUC, we strongly believe that our migrant workers deserve to be insured against risks within and beyond the workplace.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In December last year, NTUC Migrant Workers' Centre (MWC) introduced its Associate Membership to offer holistic protection and benefits that are specially tailored to serve migrant workers' lifestyle needs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Collectively, I am confident that the Government's provision of enhanced protection and NTUC MWC's Associate Membership programme would ensure that our migrant workers are well protected against uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: MOM also claimed that the electronic payment of salaries has proven to be beneficial, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, because it ensures that foreign workers continue to receive salaries even when there are movement restrictions in place.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Once again, I urge the Government to consider mandating electronic payment of salary for migrant workers to protect them from exploitation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   At this year’s Budget Speech, the Government announced the Household Support Package to provide support for daily essentials.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Assurance Package for GST to cushion the impact of the planned GST increase, and enhancements to the permanent GST Voucher scheme to provide continuing help to defray the GST expenses of lower-income to middle-income Singaporean households, beyond the transitional support covered by the Assurance Package.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Support is also provided to lower-income households to cope with the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: For example, the 2021 Public Transport Voucher (PTV) Exercise will be extended to support lower-income families to cope with any fare adjustments.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These schemes announced by the Government would undoubtedly assist in defraying the costs of living for Singaporean households, including the Malay-Muslim community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By strengthening our social compact, the assistance rendered is beyond defraying cost but also provide opportunities for all to enhance our social support pillars.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We will be able to focus on our children’s education through the expansion of Uplift and Kidstart to support more young children from lower income families.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The budget will immensely benefit our Malay-Muslim households in Singapore in coping with the cost of living as Singapore transitions to a post-pandemic future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The majority of Singaporean households will receive at least five years’ worth of additional GST expenses.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is important for the family to take this opportunity to, firstly, continue to find a stable job that provide protection for us now and in the future; second, encourage the spouse to get back to workforce and support the family income; and third, upgrade and upskill to prepare for job in the growth sectors.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We can all take a leaf from 47-year-old Brother Ahmad Sadiq's lifelong learning journey.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: To ensure a brighter future, Brother Ahmad Sadiq pursued part-time courses to climb the academic ladder, beginning with a NITEC in Mechanical Technology, then a diploma in Mechanical Engineering, and finally, a Bachelor's in Mechanical Technology with Honours (Distinction).

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: All this education was fully self-funded, alongside a study grant from the Union of Power and Gas Employees (UPAGE), as well as SkillsFuture Credits.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As a Mechanical Engineer and now as a union leader, he continues to champion lifelong learning and leading by example.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, he is currently pursuing an energy manager course supported by his company, and plans to pursue shorter courses that are aligned to his personal interests.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Moving forward, NTUC will also join hands with the Malay/Muslim community to address the community’s various needs and concerns.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: At NTUC, we firmly believe that the best approach is to empower our workers to access better jobs and earn better wages with better skills.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This MOU is part of M3 Focus Area 4’s key strategy to uplift the Malay community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This partnership is a prime example of how NTUC enlarges our efforts in empowering our workers, forging collaborations with community-based and self-help organisation partners to enhance our reach to workers and communities that would benefit from our national-level resources in training and job placement.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We will do this by leveraging our training ecosystem with NTUC LearningHub and NTUC’s e2i.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: And through this ecosystem, the Malay/Muslim community’s efforts to train and upskill, can be augmented and scaled up, so that they remain employable and competitive in the job market.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Malay Muslim union leaders are also deployed in the M3@Towns to rally the Malay Muslim workforce and provide the last mile support for job placements.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: With continued support from the community, NTUC's efforts will go a long way in our cause to uplift the Malay/Muslim community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): Sir, in conclusion, the COVID-19 pandemic has tested our resilience as a nation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Singaporeans have remained steadfast despite the challenges they faced during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Whilst we have come a long way, there will inevitably be many more challenges along the way.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, as a country, we have weathered similar storms and emerged stronger together.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Rest assured, NTUC will continue to champion all workers because every worker matters.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Every country is faced with an apparent trilemma when it comes to labour policies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What seems to be fair often does not cultivate a competitive workforce and what appears to do both ends up with high costs of living or taxes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore's answer to this comes from the PWM the Singapore Labour Movement pioneered.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Done prudently with meticulous negotiations amongst the tripartite partners, it rewards improved productivity and quality with a wage increase ladder suitable for individual industry sectors.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Two upcoming PWMs will be in the retail and food services sector.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The workers in these sectors touch our lives and hearts everyday and yet, we have taken our workers in these sectors for granted.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many Singaporeans start our day with a kopi that is served by their usual good neighbourhood kopi soh.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When we celebrate with our families birthdays, anniversaries, New Year and Christmas, our workers in the restaurants are right there with us, even if their own families are spending time away from them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our retail frontliners have also been there for us when we buy our first set of furniture, when we pick the freshest produce from our grocers, when we scoot down to our convenience stores at 2.00 am to pick up emergency supplies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our workers in these sectors have been keeping Singapore and our lives running with their hard work, sacrifices and good cheer.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: F&B and retail are price sensitive, where a rise of prices in a kopi or a plate of economy rice at the food court will draw much attention.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, our retailers have told me how price spotting even amongst essential items have become ever more keen with the advent of online shopping, cutting their margins razor thin.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The pandemic has shown that this sector’s veterans and newcomers alike do thrive with the help of technology.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Radha Exports Private Limited is the company behind the ValuDollar chain of stores.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During COVID-19, the team was caught in an onslaught of challenges to their supply chain and manpower.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was the necessity for change that pushed the company to digitalise and upskill their workers in this process.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This increased productivity generated new and better paying jobs by helping the company justify a better pay for their employees.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I visited with the company and was delighted to have met with Uncle Rafi, as he is affectionately known.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He has been working with the company since 2004, and has moved from being a deliveryman to now their warehouse supervisor.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, Uncle Rafi is 65 years young, and he proudly tells me of his lifelong learning journey in Radha, from taking inventory using paper and pen, to creating rooms filled with filing shelves, to now being able to use their warehouse software to call up the smallest bar of chocolate from the aircon comfort of his newly computerised monitoring room.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The moral of the story is clear: upskilling works and tech is here to help.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The PWM ensures competitive pay comes from justifiable reasons.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the PWM continues to reach out to more lower-wage workers, as a Labour Movement, as a Tripartite Partnership, as a country, we need to stand together.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is the heart of the matter: the PWM stands for Singapore’s commitment to uplift workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is about companies investing in our hardest working workers, unions protecting them with promise and hope, consumers making sure that those who labour can find ways to make ends meet with dignity, and Government ensuring that companies, workers and consumers are supported while we all are playing our own part in uplifting the lives of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As many countries battled the economic downturn in the face of the COVID-19, the gig economy has provided crucial lifelines for many, allowing workers from affected industries to seek freelance jobs in food delivery and ride-hailing services.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The growing importance of this economy has seen a greater emphasis to protect the interests and welfare of these workers, workers who are not considered employees and thus are not afforded the protections and benefits salaried employees enjoy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The study cited that the "lack of savings and voluntary CPF contributions, being stuck in platform work poses additional challenges to future aspirations, such as home ownership".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a progressive Labour Movement, we are sensitive to changes in the evolving Singaporean workforce and have witnessed, like many in the House, including Mr Saktiandi Supaat, the growing popularity of gig work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As such, the Labour Movement has been at the forefront of Singapore’s push to accord greater protection and welfare benefits for workers in the gig economy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We thank Mr Supaat for his feedback and suggestions for protecting freelancers in the education sector and hope that Mr Supaat can continue his good work with us in our associations and our unions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over the years, we have set up and advocated for safety nets for our gig workers such as offering protection and representation in the event of illness or injuries and care support for income loss or training assistance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, there are miles to go before we sleep.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even as these efforts are encouraging, such measures do not sufficiently protect workers, particularly those who rely on the gig economy as their primary source of income.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Without basic labour protections, one can ill-afford to fall sick or face sudden emergencies without facing a loss of income.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If this is their hard-earned rice bowl, should we not then provide them with the required protection they deserve?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If our workers are contributing to the enterprise value of their partner platforms, should we not then also insist on platforms also contributing to the retirement safety nets of their partners?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the Adviser to the NTUC’s National Taxi Association, National Private Hire Vehicles Association and the National Delivery Champions Association, I have heard loud and clear from the ground the need for better protection and representation of our gig platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of our brothers, Raymond, met with an accident last year.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While covered by his platform partner’s insurance package, he felt that the claim process was onerous to a point where he decided not to pursue the insurance, as he would be able to earn back in one day what he would have received in the claims.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Brother Joseph also spoke to us about gaps in their platform partner’s support when their app went down and drivers were not able to earn their full day’s livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our associations assisted to compile the list of bugs as the app went back up so that our drivers would have a coordinated voice on what impacts their livelihoods most.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are just some of the many small inconveniences and I would say large tribulations our gig economy workers face as the gig economy and its ecosystem of platforms evolve and grow.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we look to provide greater protection and welfare benefits for workers in the gig economy, the Tripartite Partnership must strive to support a healthy diversity of career options and sustainable, dignified livelihoods brought about by the gig economy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In this respect, I look forward to the recommendations of the Advisory Committee for Platform Workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is a good significant beginning for a more coordinated approach to supporting our growing gig worker population.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On the topic of evolving workforce, one of the greatest lessons learnt has been on the importance of accommodating diverse profiles as a design feature of our labour force, rather than a design fault.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In particular, the interests of two groups of employees – women returning to work, as well as single mothers – must be paid attention to.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement has long recognised the distinct challenges women face at work that primarily stems from women having to saddle a greater proportion of domestic responsibilities and have accordingly championed and provisioned to advance this cause.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, our NTUC Learning Hub has started to co-create with our Women and Family Unit, confidence training courses as well as skills-based programmes to give women returnees the much needed boost when it comes to re-entering the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We has also introduced a Women Mentoring Women programme that consists of Women Union Leaders joining forces with female grassroots leaders in mentoring women who need support with careers and livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The primary thrust of these supports have been to alleviate the pressures that our women face both at home and the workplace, so that they can engage more productively and meaningfully in both spheres of their lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To this end, the Labour Movement has sought to continuously enhance Flexible Work Arrangement standards to stay responsive to changing family and workplace needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we celebrate these strides forward, we should also be mindful of ongoing gaps.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is my firm belief that changes in organisational culture is just as important as formal frameworks and enhancements to FWA policies must be accompanied by parallel changes in attitudes and values.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As companies consider FWA a long-term feature, ground issues such as fair performance evaluation of employees on FWAs, and the availability of FWA options to employees in all job roles become all the more real on the ground.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On this, I call for more support from our Government to help employers upskill their HR and line managers to manage a workforce with employees on FWAs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mothercare, is a name many mothers are familiar with, and it is not surprising that they have championed my heart for women.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I was at their store, I delighted in meeting with Mdm Fadilah who has four children and has worked her way in from Sales Assistant to Store Manager in just eight short years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She was not alone and I met another three teammates of hers, who were moms with three to four children each.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are committed to job redesign and providing flexible working arrangements especially for their moms at work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that we ladies can have our cake and eat it too with the support of our workplaces.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I look forward to the measures our Government will introduce to encourage and support our employers to take on the challenge of job redesign.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These people are those who interact with us in our everyday life – our colleagues, neighbours, relatives and friends.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are the coffee aunty whom we meet every morning, and the smiling lad at the convenience store, the restaurant waiter whom we celebrate birthdays together, and the aunty cashier who gives us discount at the supermarket counter.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workers must constantly upgrade their skills and companies must invest in technology.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Helping low-wage Singaporeans is the mission of NTUC, the investment of the companies and the duty of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Helping businesses pivot to capture new capabilities in digitalisation and upskilling and allowing for employees to share in the fruits of advancement; creating deeper safety nets for the freelance ecosystem, ensuring parity for single mothers and sparking deep attitudinal changes at workplaces for women.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are the opportunities we must latch onto as they present themselves in a Singapore economy that awaits thoughtful reconstruction as #EveryWorkerMatters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Budget theme “Charting Our New Way Forward Together” is especially apt for a group of Singaporeans with the most vested interests – our younger Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is a loose moniker covering people from late childhood to early adulthood who are coming of age during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has changed the workforce, workplace and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: New opportunities abound but also new threats lurk.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Technology has accelerated the creation of higher-end jobs but also commoditised lower-end ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Young workers preparing for a changing economic order before COVID-19, now find themselves facing a vastly altered one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, they also have opportunities beyond the reach of earlier generations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some worries I have heard from younger Singaporeans include how fundamental economic shifts will impact their job prospects and, of course, inflationary pressures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They want to pursue the future with energy and passion but are faced with a nebulous environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Generation COVID are the future leaders of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to address their anxieties and worries and, importantly, work with them to fulfil their potential to the fullest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I do appreciate that I am perhaps unable to adequately understand the predicament faced by Generation COVID.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, for a start, I would like to explore some of their concerns from three aspects: jobs, education and changing aspirations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some members of this Generation find their skills eroded substantially even before they graduate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Others are graduating into depressed sectors, such as tourism-related industries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet others, majoring in oil and gas, are entering the decarbonisation era.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Reskilling and rapid adaptation are the new game.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, we can consider expanding the reach of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The use of SkillsFuture credits has shown a strong uptake in the past year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Courses related to skills in the IT, healthcare and professional services sectors are seeing the highest demand, alongside good employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is especially for those who have graduated but find themselves unable to tap on growth opportunities due to a mismatch in skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Young NTUC’s survey also showed that a majority of young people find such skills workshops useful.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, we can also increase subsidies for targeted SkillsFuture courses, especially those that support young Singaporeans to explore industries in growth economies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because of the shifting skills landscape, many younger Singaporeans will possibly need a more significant skills upgrade via a second subsidised diploma or degree.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is merit to such bigger moves because some skills acquisition just cannot be done through micro-courses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, every Singaporean enjoys one bite of the cherry – one subsidised diploma and/or degree per person.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With a shrinking cohort of Singaporeans every year, there is already capacity within the IHLs for people seeking a career boost.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, hard technical skills are already baseline expectations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These can be taught within educational institutions or academies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, there is a greater industry emphasis on soft skills, such as career management and interpersonal skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some of these soft skills are not transferable through courses and are perhaps better picked up through the sharing of experiences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, there is great demand for structured mentorship in today’s workplace to assist our younger people in navigating the professional workspace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mentorship will be especially valuable for Generation COVID younger people from the lower- and middle-income families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some of them might not have easy access to mentors, unlike their better-off counterparts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have some nascent endeavours, such as Young NTUC’s LIT Mentorship.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is also WeConnect 2.0, an initiative by the Mentoring Alliance For Action (Singapore).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But for the Singaporean workforce to differentiate itself from competitors, we must see mentorship as a national capability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is also part of the ethos espoused by this Budget – Singaporeans looking out for one another.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must still preserve the ground-up mutual help movement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, creating national centres of excellence for mentorship can accelerate and boost the impact of mentorship.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Tripartite partners, such as NTUC and SNEF, can develop such centres because of their deep industry connections.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Ironically, the new opportunities from the post-pandemic world, or the endemic-pandemic world, would also have made career navigation a lot more difficult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The current model of navigation starts from the school in the form of career guidance offices to national placement centres, such as e2i or Career Connect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The transition is not seamless and might not also meet the needs of younger workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Young workers have often asked about the possibility of a one-stop centre that houses career counselling, mentorship, internships and employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I can imagine that even the approach to career navigation might be quite different if it primarily serves younger workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Government consider working with tripartite partners to develop such a capability?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, on how we can better tailor our policies to Generation COVID, shaping Singapore into a country that they are proud to call home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Indeed, Generation COVID youths are different from the youths we were.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They hold different aspirations for Singapore and have a stronger sense of social justice and activism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of them are interested in political and social causes, actively seeking avenues to be heard, to contribute meaningfully to such discourse.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: During the pandemic and even now, many youths have founded and expanded mutual aid networks to help the less fortunate around us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They also hope that their professional work aids in the advancement of social causes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Increasingly, we see our younger people seeking the expression and advancement of such issues not only through their personal lives, but also their professional work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This intersection of work and social activism is both exciting and less understood.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must first seek to understand Generation COVID’s views on a deeper level, by creating safer spaces for them to candidly share their thoughts, views and aspirations for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What is their desired workplace and work culture?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What is the new compact with our younger workers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC is working towards a deeper understanding of the aspirations and needs of our younger workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We welcome partners to join us on this journey.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is that critical first step in building a new and sustainable compact with our young workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To many of our Generation COVID, greater strides must be taken to tackle mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As part of a generation who ascribe greater significance to having a purposeful balance between work and mental wellness over traditional aggregators of success, this issue is one Generation COVID feels strongly for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The pandemic has normalised hybrid workplaces and work-from-home culture.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the changing face of the workplace has afforded more flexibility, it has also blurred the boundaries between work and personal lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: New entrants to the workforce have a much harder time adapting to the hybrid work model without the benefit of an established support network.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, they are more exposed to stresses that were never present before the proliferation of hybrid workplaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe we can spark more conversations on mental health on the national level, thereby normalising mental health issues across the nation and within workspaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Key stakeholders, such as employers, must remain sensitive and understanding towards persons struggling with mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement will work closely with our tripartite partners to champion mental health within the workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can consider establishing a code of practices for working from home and increasing peer-to-peer support as an avenue to advance mental wellness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Peer support is a crucial part of primary care at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is not meant to replace professionals but, instead, is a vital link to get people to seek help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must ensure that Generation COVID is well-prepared to face the uncertainties of the global economy and even the next pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will chart this journey together with Generation COVID, working with them to emerge even stronger from the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The bills come, not just from the price of security and safety today, but for the education and investments of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The rising inflationary pressures come from different sources and are complex in nature.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The impact, however, is simple and direct – a dollar today can buy more than a dollar tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I want to speak on two groups that are particularly hard-hit – small businesses and the cost of living for the ordinary men and women.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Many SME suppliers are all struggling now to manage the cost increases that are coming from all fronts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Whether it is raw materials, freight, manpower, packaging or cost of energy, everything is more expensive now.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Added to that, the headwinds from tough weather, floods and logistical disruptions due to COVID-19 restrictions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For SMEs, in particular, where profits can be razor-thin, it is about cost pressures and stresses of managing rising costs in many areas, and these, sometimes, can appear to be faceless corporate troubles.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But when businesses fail, jobs are lost, too.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And behind each SME is a group of men and women with dreams and families.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One SME owner shared with me that the cost of his raw materials for soya sauce includes soya beans.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The current conflict that is taking place in Russia and Ukraine will add further cost pressures to businesses.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Amongst other things, Ukraine is a major supplier of sunflower seed, sunflower oil, whilst Russia is a major supplier of wheat, which will impact raw materials supply and cost of wheat-based products.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Ukraine is also a major producer of corn.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Corn supply shortage may also impact price of livestock feeds where corn is a major ingredient.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, many egg suppliers have told me that their cost has gone up very significantly where energy cost and corn, which is the feed for the chicken, are major cost items for them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In its annual survey last year, the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry sought feedback from more than 1,000 businesses, 92% of whom are SMEs.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Many say their costs have gone up quite significantly and, as a result, they have suffered losses.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: SMEs form an important part of the Singapore economy, including as a source of jobs and meaningful livelihood.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And, often, the voices of small business owners go unheard.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, what can we do to ensure that SMEs have a place at the table?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, trade associations play an important role in gathering feedback, as well as explaining new policies and schemes to its members.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Such associations may run on a tight budget, which constrain their effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister consider providing some one-off grants to such associations?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On the impact of cost increases, I think some price increase in products and services may be expected.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Of course, there are those few errant businesses which may take advantage of the situation to profiteer.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Like everyone else in this House, I have no sympathy for them and they should be taken to task.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am sure the Committee against Profiteering headed by Minister of State Low Yen Ling, when the committee is formulating the guidelines against profiteering, will, with the help of the community, step up their vigilance in light of the current situation and ensure that those who use, whether it is “inflation” or “GST” or whatever, to cover a multitude of price increases, will be taken to task.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But at the same time, we should not begrudge businesses and SMEs for legitimate and reasonable price increases for the reasons that I shared earlier.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Given the important role that migrant workers play in Singapore’s economy, I would like the Government to give some flexibility to businesses and, in particular, SMEs in hiring such workers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am not sure about the rest of you but my grandparents, parents, peers and now my own children, they are also talking about it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think no one will ever say things were cheap during their time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our forefathers carried those worries too, but through determination, hard work and with support from various people and the Government sectors, they not only survived but prospered and built the foundation of a thriving Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, NTUC FairPrice, "Welcome" then, was born at a time of rising prices in the oil shocks of the 1970s.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We ran similar "Stretch Your Dollar" programmes in 2007 to 2008 during the Global Financial Crisis and again from 2010 to 2011 during the economic downturn.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Overall, NTUC’s focus is on ensuring workers in Singapore remain competitive and employable for life, as well as enhancing their welfare.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To do this, NTUC strives to help workers of all collars and ages get better jobs and earn better wages.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, NTUC supports workers and their families by moderating the cost of living through various programmes, including sustainable wage increases in the form of PWM, subsidised training, financial assistance schemes and affordable daily essentials and services through the NTUC group of social enterprises.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Within the NTUC group, we have various charities and foundations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They include U Care Fund, FairPrice Foundation, Orange Aid, Eldercare Trust and Bright Horizons Fund to ensure those who have less, they are not disadvantaged.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Over the years, the NTUC Enterprise group have evolved to be significant industry players today, whilst continuing to take care of the needs of not just workers, but also their multi-generational families, across their different life stages.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We strive to play our part to moderate cost of essential goods and services, serving as price benchmarks and addressing underserved needs.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Of course, we are not the only ones doing this, and there are many, many helping hands all over Singapore to help those in need.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This can either be in the form of giving guidance on specific items or tax incentives for doing so.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yes, we need to extend more help to those less tech-savvy workers to apply for Government schemes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They are often the ones who need it most.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Even as we help address their welfare needs, we can also help them see where they need help in terms of upgrading their skills and securing jobs.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As Singapore develops, aspirations today are understandably different from the past.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We are better educated, technologies have empowered convenience and lifestyles have evolved.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But one thing remains: we continue to want the best for our children and for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the past, a dollar’s value is measured in its ability to buy a home, to go to school and put a meal on the table.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, a dollar can already do this for most of us, and we want it to buy more.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What we need to buy with our dollar is security for all Singaporeans, to be able to continue our common dream of peace and prosperity amidst rising and uncertain seas.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.50 pm until 4.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This Budget comes on the back of significant global inflationary pressures, at a time when rising cost of living is a major concern for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The proposed increase in GST will no doubt add to consumers' concerns.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While we understand the need to raise revenue, I am heartened that the Government has decided to delay the GST increase to 2023 and to stagger the increase over two years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Doing so will provide time for the various measures introduced to tackle rising inflation to come into effect.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: At CASE, we believe more can be done to help consumers make informed purchasing decisions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: That is why we launched the Price Kaki mobile application in 2019 to allow consumers to compare prices of household essentials, groceries and hawker food, make informed purchase decisions and stretch their dollar.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To tackle rising prices, consumers can also consider purchasing house brands for their daily essentials.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to Price Kaki's data, house brand products can cost 10% to 25% cheaper than brand goods.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: House brands can be just as good and have similar nutrition value as regular brands.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would encourage consumers to look beyond the advertising and give house brands a try.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The same taste for a much lower cost may come as a pleasant surprise.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But comparing prices alone is insufficient if a retailer chooses to maintain the price but reduce the quantity of the product.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mandatory unit pricing is already practised in countries such as Australia, Argentina and Chile.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This might have been a logistical and administrative challenge in the past when price tags were printed on paper placed manually on the shelves.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With the wide use of digital price tags today, supermarkets should have no difficulty displaying unit pricing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As part of our commitment to price transparency, CASE will display unit price alongside the retail price for items listed on Price Kaki.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While the CDC vouchers have been a major help, more can be done to help our neighbourhood merchants transform their businesses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Heartland shops are facing immense pressure as higher prices of goods and utilities are weighing down heavily on their profitability.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They are also facing stiff competition from online retailers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As consumers' purchasing behaviour shifts to e-commerce accelerated by the pandemic, I thought it would be helpful to onboard our heartland merchants and hawkers onto a major e-marketplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will help them tap on the huge e-commerce potential.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am therefore glad that Lazada Singapore has partnered Radin Mas to launch the Radin Mas Marketplace @ Lazada.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will be Singapore's first e-marketplace for heartland shops.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
