text: Lazada will onboard all interested merchants and hawkers in Radin Mas, which number close to 600 and allow them to list their first 100 items on the e-marketplace at no cost.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lazada will also teach our merchants how to better engage with younger customers such as through livestreaming.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Merchants and consumers can also benefit from the occasional promotional campaigns organised by Lazada.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we transform our economy and chart our way in the post-pandemic future, we must ensure that our heartland shops will continue to remain part of our Singapore Story.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, we need to watch out for these three "invisibles" that could stand in the way of raising salaries – the invisible competition for jobs, invisible skills mismatch and invisible threat of burnout.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has completely transformed the way we work and has accelerated the "work from anywhere" trend.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Competition for jobs can now come from digital nomads working from any corner of the globe as long as the candidate has the right skills, a computer and a good Internet connection.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There is even a new word recently invented called "workcation" where people travel and work remotely at the same time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Countries are now seeking to attract these digital nomads as they reopen their economies and try to revive their tourism and hospitality sectors at the same time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Financial Times recently reported that Thailand is offering 10-year visas to attract skilled professionals working remotely.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to Investopedia, Thailand is not alone, with Germany, Mexico and Norway – just to name a few examples – trying very hard to attract these digital nomads.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: He highlighted how it is important for Singapore to continually transform ourselves and help our local workforce perform higher value jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But the reality is that digital nomads are competing for higher value jobs – jobs such as creative professionals, coding specialists and data science analysts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Simply put, companies today need not hire people based physically in Singapore to fill jobs here and our PMETs are particularly at risk of being displaced by an invisible competition, sitting by the poolside of a resort in Phuket.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While the increase in minimum qualifying salaries for Employment Pass and S Pass holders may be a short-term measure, I urge the Government to study this trend and review if our existing labour policies would continue to remain relevant in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Do we need to adjust our policies and economic strategies to account for this invisible global competition for local jobs?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to data from MOM, Singapore had a record high of 98,700 job openings in September 2021, with the number of job vacancies more than double the number of unemployed people.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: On the ground, however, the Labour Movement has received feedback from PMETs, particularly those in their mid-career, that they find it difficult to land these jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What could be the reason for the disconnect?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One answer is likely a mismatch in skills.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The CTCs help address the two most common questions that workers have when it comes to training – train what and train for what – by aligning the training needs with the company's future business and operations roadmap.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Therefore, I encourage all companies in Singapore to work with NTUC and partner with us to create and implement training programmes that are suitable to upskill and reskill your workers effectively.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, I would like to touch on workplace burnout, a real but often invisible threat to the well-being of our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For the first time, the Workplace Safety and Health Council will introduce a new workplace mental health category at this year's Workplace Safety and Health (WSH) Awards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, there remains much more to be done.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Clearly, our tired working professionals deserve a right to disconnect so that they can have protected time to rest and recharge after work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge the Ministries and our Government agencies to lead by promulgating clear directives on after-hours work communications for their staff.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Good workplace mental health is good for productivity and business.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Government can provide grants to encourage more employers to implement Employee Assistance Programmes at various workplaces to support its workers with mental health needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Rising energy prices, inflation and a rapidly ageing population are just some of the difficult hurdles that Singapore and Singaporeans will need to overcome.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: At NTUC, we believe that every worker matters and the best way to protect them through these challenges is through better jobs and better wages.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We will continue to walk alongside our brothers and sisters and help them take advantage of all the help that are available.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Earlier, the hon Member Mr Melvin Yong spoke of the threat of shrinkflation, which is that the price is the same, but the items get smaller.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That is the pressure that inflation can put on consumers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But, Sir, not everything, however, is going in that direction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There are certain things which are going in the opposite direction and one of them is the longevity of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Singaporeans are living longer and there are implications, and it is to this direction that I will now turn.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, I thank the Government for beginning to implement the recommendations of the Tripartite Workgroup on Older Workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is important for these steps to be undertaken while conditions permit, because 10 years might sound very long, but it passes much faster than one thinks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For workers to be able to maximise their CPF retirement savings gained from work, they need to be in work for as many years as they are willing and able to, and for them to be able to qualify for both employer and employee CPF contributions as pay levels change with time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Hence, there should be periodic reviews of the qualifying criteria for employer CPF contributions to ensure that, as pay levels improve over time, the proportion of pay that qualifies for CPF keeps pace and does not become materially eroded, of course, taking into account prevailing economic conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This will enable us to strike and sustain a fair, judicious and necessary equilibrium between employers’ legitimate cost concerns and workers’ legitimate need for retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Clearly, this would greatly help with an older worker’s financial position and retirement savings, much more than any other measure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This was why the Tripartite Workgroup on Older Workers had recommended increases in the statutory retirement and reemployment ages to be accomplished within this decade, moving from 62 to 65 and from 67 to 70 by the end of the decade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Government had previously announced that the first step in this journey is to add one year to both the statutory retirement and reemployment ages in July this year, that is, in July 2022.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I fully support this step as our economy is projected to grow this year at a still healthy clip.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Just like the improvements in CPF contribution rates, we must take incremental steps while we can, so that we will reach the goal within the timeframe that the Tripartite partners had agreed upon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The enactment of the Retirement Age Act and its subsequent expansion to encompass Reemployment represent overt Government and legislative intent and support for older Singaporean workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I, therefore, look forward to the outcomes of the Tripartite Workgroup on Workplace Fairness and, in particular, its recommendations to safeguard and strengthen the interests of older workers for fair consideration and treatment at work, including for training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Government has also put money where its mouth is to spur the continued hiring of older workers through a range of policy incentives: training subsidies, hiring incentives, CPF offset measures and so on, all stacked in favour of the hiring of older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is all the more remarkable, because these improvements happened even in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic that we are experiencing here in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: When we compare this achievement with the large-scale shedding of older workforces in many other countries over the past two years, then we know that we must not take this support and investment in our older workers for granted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This did not come naturally and it is not by chance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That said, I want to point to two areas that I urge close attention and coordinated action on in the coming years, to make sure that these hard-won gains are sustained and not eroded.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We have also heard that the proportion of Singaporeans aged 65 and above has grown from 9% of the population in 2009 to 16% in 2019 and will reach 25% in 2030.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These figures all, basically, show that Singapore is ageing very rapidly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The implication of that on healthcare costs is clear and has been extensively discussed, including in the Budget speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, I will not dwell on that one.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But there is another significant implication, which is the implication on mature workers’ employment rate, that we must not miss.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As I had said in previous Budget debate speeches, there is a significant trend of departure from work among female workers from around middle age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: By some estimates, there could be some 30,000 such work-able persons in our population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is likely to be due to care responsibilities, that is, the fact that they had left work is likely to be due to care responsibilities at work, and such care responsibilities, given that if they are leaving at middle age, are likely to be related to caring for senior members in the family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This trend, we must expect, will intensify as our population bulge of baby boomers age into their 70s and beyond, and that would trigger a corresponding increase in pressure on middle-aged family members, especially women, to have to leave work in order to care for their senior family members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If this happens, the impact on household income and the retirement adequacy of caregivers on the one hand, and the implication on the availability and mix of our workforce to companies on the other, will be big.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Traditional measures to help retain more middle-aged workers with care responsibilities either at work or to allow a return to work include the promotion of flexible work arrangements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is correct and must, of course, continue.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Conceptually, this would be similar to the thinking behind providing affordable childcare services so that the parents, especially the mothers, can have a practical option of choosing to work, rather than, out of no choice, to have to stay at home to look after the babies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, if you flip it to the other end of the population, conceptually, it is the same.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But that, in itself, brings about its own complexities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Doing so will also allow us to create viable jobs in this sector, turning the unavoidable population ageing into an opportunity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I turn now to my final point, which is that we need to focus attention on jobs and occupations that employ significant numbers of older workers that we know will be impacted significantly by fast changes in technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In this regard, we must pay special attention to the subset of such jobs and occupations that our switch to a low-carbon economy will likely put additional pressure on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The vulnerability of older workers in such settings is quite self-evident and I think, earlier on, my colleague Mr Melvin Yong and, before that, Mr Patrick Tay had also given examples of how the middle-aged PMEs are also facing these difficulties and pressure, including the three invisibles that Mr Melvin Yong spoke about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For older workers, if they are displaced, then their risk of structural unemployment will be higher than the rest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Even if they are rehired, their earnings will likely be lower and, therefore, negatively impacting their retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Such efforts can certainly tap into NTUC’s growing network of Company Training Committees (CTCs) in order to systematically, deliberately and proactively do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And where there is ultimately an excess of manpower, parallel efforts to help the older workers reskill and convert to other job possibilities elsewhere will be equally crucial.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This means that we must look at what is coming ahead and rally the whole of Singapore society to face it together and thrive, leaving no one behind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As for NTUC, we will continue to champion better wages, jobs and work prospects for all workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Every worker matters and we believe that this is the best way to care for their present and to uplift their future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our older workers are a valuable and growing part of our local workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Let us work together with them to shape that better future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The past two years had been like a roller-coaster ride in the dark.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We do not know where the twists and turns are but we have, together, shoulder-to-shoulder, ridden over one peak after another, and it seems like we are now in the midst of another one.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This has never been a fun ride, especially for our frontliners.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To Team MOH and the healthcare workers who are once again called up to the fore, thank you, and I salute you for valiantly keeping our country going, not forgetting my fellow educators, who face students every day to provide normalcy amid a dynamic landscape.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Alongside our Public Service officers, our healthcare workers and educators have taken up multiple, varied and new roles, which underlie their unwavering commitment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am grateful as they give us the much-needed confidence to see the light at the end of this dark roller-coaster ride.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I urge that we continue to provide our Public Service officers, especially our healthcare workers and educators, with the best support and work-life balance possible.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How many hats can one person wear to remain effective?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps, it is also time that we set clear guidelines on work hours, introduce timeouts and enforce the time for disconnect.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Replying to non-urgent emails can wait but our families cannot.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must also continue to create and upgrade channels for communication between staff and this does not include the bi-annual staff appraisal.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am also aware of the abuse they face and the pressures of work from the stakeholders, and we should do more to create practical ways to allow them to come forth and be provided with the necessary support and protection.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I support the Finance Minister's call to renew and strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It resonates strongly with me and I will touch on two areas: education and mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To sustain something lifelong requires us to acknowledge that one may be susceptible to physical and mental burnouts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my previous speeches, I mentioned that one way to mitigate this is to provide opportunities or rather, phases for individuals to: discover, re-discover and re-invent themselves.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I will cover two of them today, although all three are aptly represented in this year's Budget announcement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The first phase, "discover", begins from early childhood.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Within this phase, we must provide our children with the opportunities to discover their strengths and interests.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I hope that we can also curate programmes for those in the middle class in the future, especially those who may be struggling or facing sudden change in their situation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As shown through the pandemic, being on a balance means that one can be tipped over fairly easily.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I understand the need to hold these major exams, but I think we can do with fewer exams in between.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we are serious about redefining success, then it can start by redefining what exams mean.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must create a culture of appreciating the joy of learning and the challenges such a journey presents, be it easy or difficult, whether we get success or failure and accepting that there are multiple paths to achieve success.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In removing the minor exams, we can nurture an optimal lifelong learning concept and this, in turn and hopefully, result in a better mental health environment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We have done well to create multiple pathways.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: There are now numerous courses that a student can enrol in that matches their interests.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, one lesson we learnt from the pandemic was the inability of some of our fresh graduates to be agile in a volatile job environment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Who could have predicted that certain sectors can be so affected by the pandemic?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my previous speeches, I emphasised the need to give our graduates broad skills that can be generalised across other disciplines.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will put them in a better footing and give them the confidence to apply their skills across other sectors.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I would now go a step further and ask if we could allow greater flexibility to allow students to choose modules outside their main course and pursue side interests.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I could be a sports scientist with a good foundation in entrepreneurship.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Polytechnic students, for example, have three years to complete the course.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my previous adjournment motions, I highlighted several suggestions to destigmatise mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These include a push for mental health and social media literacy in schools and workplaces, improving accessibility at community touchpoints, providing regular mental health screening and introducing time-outs for individuals to recharge, re-organise and come back stronger to school or work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I also called for the Government to expand our mental healthcare infrastructure, expand community support network and to make mental healthcare and support affordable.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond Parliament, with support from other PAP Members, as well as the Young PAP, we drove the #452TooMany campaign and conducted dialogues to bring community partners like Total Wellness Initiative, ItAllStartsHere.sg, IMH, the Muslim Healthcare Professionals Association and many more, as well as volunteers and residents together.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Within my constituency, we have also organised workshops for grassroots leaders so that they can better support our residents.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is why I am very happy to hear our Finance Minister laying out broad plans to enhance and integrate mental health and social services in the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The setting up of the Inter-agency Task Force shows that the Government is committed to taking action towards mental health stigmatisation and supporting the needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Here, I would like to call upon three groups to play their part.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I spoke previously about the need to be more compassionate to our workers and provide them with periods to recharge, therefore I urge employers once again to review their mental wellness programmes, encourage regular health screening, both physical and mental and consider using time-outs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Like some say, a happy employee is a productive employee, but most importantly, an even happier employer.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While I am grateful that our mental healthcare infrastructure is robust and sound, it is sad that many of us are still not stepping forward to receive help.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some are obvious, others are silent and almost unnoticeable.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It would be unwise for one to generalise.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, a strong support system of family and friends play a key role in helping a loved one.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, the need for mental health literacy for everyone remains important to eradicate stigmatisation and create a more caring support system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With Singapore having one of the highest internet penetration rates globally, almost every adult and youth are connected to the internet and social media.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Cyberbullying, the woke culture and online shaming are becoming more rampant and have a detrimental effect on the mental health of those affected.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, it starts with us, not the Government alone or social media platforms, it begins with us – the community – to set a good online and offline code of conduct to create a more caring and inclusive home for all of us.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   I was happy to see this caring and inclusive Budget delivered by the Minister of Finance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I support his call to renew and strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my English speech earlier, I spoke about three issues.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, comprehensive support for workers; second, education; and third, mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, I urge that we provide a more comprehensive support for workers, especially healthcare sector workers and teachers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I call on the Government and employers to review their workload and job scope to ensure a quality Work-Life balance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This includes setting clear guidelines on working hours and introduce time-outs for workers to come back stronger to their workplace.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It underlines a strong commitment to tackle inequality as early as possible and ensures that every child is given the opportunity to fulfil their potential.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my previous speeches in Parliament, I highlighted several suggestions to eradicate stigmatisation and increase support for mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond Parliament, other PAP MPs and I have organised campaigns on social media and discussions to raise awareness about mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, I am heartened to hear the Minister laying out broad plans to enhance support for mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I urge employers and everyone from all walks of life to join us in this endeavour.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, in conclusion, I can only say that change in the only constant and if we, as Singaporeans, are committed to creating a caring and inclusive Singapore for our generation and the generations ahead, we need to continue to take decisive actions and remain agile in a dynamic, volatile landscape.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With the Government reiterating its commitment and the community stepping forward to co-curate these solutions, I am confident that we can be the shining light for other countries to emulate as we "chart a new way forward for Singapore together".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We welcome the further tightening of foreign manpower, the increased focus on re-distribution through the introduction of higher income tax rates at the top tiers and higher taxes on properties and luxury cars.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We think that more can be done but are happy with the direction we are taking.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we object to the raising of GST.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans are concerned about the rising cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Additional worries are on the horizon over the inflation outlook.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Federal Reserve Chairman and the European Central Bank's President articulated their expectations of high inflation this year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Oil prices rose by 50% in 2021 and the war in Ukraine is likely to worsen the picture.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: According to Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), food prices rose by 28% in 2021 and in December 2021, fertiliser prices rose to more than double the price from a year ago.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is expected to put further inflationary pressure on food prices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Closer at home, MAS has revised their inflation expectations upwards.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Bus, train and taxi fares have been raised.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Electricity tariffs has been rising steadily every quarter since the first quarter of 2021.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While for the time being, the rebates given out is more than the expected additional GST to be collected, it is only a matter of time before most Singaporeans have to pay more in GST; for that is the whole purpose of raising GST – to raise additional revenue.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fact that the Government is giving out rebates in excess of the expected additional GST to be collected over the next few years underlines the fact that we currently do not need the additional revenue now.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If raising GST is to fund the additional healthcare and other social spending in future, how much would we have to raise GST by?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is an alarming prospect which brings us to our second point: we need to look at other ways of raising revenue.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: GST was introduced to enable Singapore to cut corporate income tax and personal income tax rates to make Singapore a more attractive investment destination.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: GST started at 3% in 1994 and gradually increased to the current 7%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the same period, corporate income tax rate was gradually cut from 27% to 17% and personal income tax rate was gradually cut from 30% to 20%, before being raised to 22% in 2016.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This tax development benefited the rich more than the poor and middle class.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) initiative, not only will we lose tax revenue, using low corporate tax as a tool to attract investment will also become less effective.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is, therefore, time to review our previous approach of raising GST to cut corporate and personal income taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Income taxes are progressive while GST is regressive.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The pandemic has also worsened inequality by hitting the poor more than the rich.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In light of new tax developments and the current environment, we should reverse our earlier moves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of raising GST for additional revenue, we should look at raising corporate and personal income taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are happy to note that the personal income tax rate for the highest tax brackets will be raised, but we believe there is room for more.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While our corporate tax rate is 17%, there are tax incentives that lower the effective tax rate of many companies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even if we were to raise our corporate tax rate to 20%, it would still be low compared to the region.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some sectors suffered, others weathered it better, while some sectors actually benefited from the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Corporate tax is applied only on profitable companies and hence is a more discerning way of raising revenue.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Loss making companies will not be affected by an increase in corporate tax rate but some will be hit with increased cost due to a GST hike.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, many companies have benefited from the generous COVID-19 packages offered by the Government, including companies that remained profitable throughout the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is only fair that they now pay a higher corporate tax.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I will talk about land sale proceeds.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, land sale proceeds are not treated as revenue, but are put into reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government considers this just a change in the form of the asset – from land to money – not an income.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the land is sold on a freehold basis – once sold forever gone – then I would agree that this approach makes sense.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it would be a different matter if land is sold on a leasehold basis.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The issue of using land sale proceeds as revenue is not new.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague Mr Leong also mentioned this yesterday, but we are aware of the Government’s long-standing position on this matter.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, PSP would like to suggest an alternative way of treating land sale proceeds.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, the Government typically sells industrial land on 20- or 30-year leases, and residential land on 99-year leases.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After the requisite number of years, the land returns to Government and it can be sold again.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The land sale proceeds are, therefore, more akin to rental income over the length of the lease.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In other words, if a piece of land is sold on a 99-year lease, then the sale proceeds should be taken as revenue spread over 99 years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Take for example industrial land sold on a 20-year lease.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Suppose the sale proceeds were treated as revenue over 20 years, then each year, the revenue would be 5% of the sale proceeds for the next 20 years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In year 1, the revenue would be 5% of the sale proceeds in year 1.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In year 2, the revenue would be 5% of the sale proceeds in year 1 plus 5% of the sale proceeds in year 2.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In year 3, the revenue would be 5% of the sale proceeds in year 1 plus 5% of the sale proceeds in year 2 plus 5% of the sale proceeds in year 3.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: For the sake of simplicity in illustration, if we were to assume that land sale proceeds remain constant over the next 20 years, by year 20, the revenue amount would be equivalent to 100% of the land sale proceeds for that year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This is illustrated in the form of a table in the handout.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The same principle applies to land sold on 30- or 99-year leases.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The revenue stream is cumulative and builds up to a significant amount.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: PSP, therefore, contends that treating land sale proceeds as revenue over the term of the lease does not compromise on financial prudence and is also a significant revenue stream.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Thirdly, we need to look into cutting expenditure.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: We should not have this thinking that when cost increase, we just increase revenue to pay for it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: If expenditure increases in one area, let us first look for ways to cut costs in other areas.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This is how most individuals and businesses deal with cost increases Finance Minister Lawrence Wong shared that since FY2017 the budgets of all Ministries have been cut by 2% and, from FY2023, a further 1% cut will be implemented.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: However, a look at the actual Government expenditures from FY2017 to FY2019 showed them to be higher than the figures in FY2016.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Can the Finance Minister explain how this is a budget cut?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: If the race brings economic benefits, should the private sector not be paying for it?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Why do we need to raise revenue to subsidise F1?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: If SPH had not been restructured, the losses from its news operations could have been covered by the profits from its property operations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: With the restructuring, taxpayers end up with a $900 million bill!

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: These are instances where we feel that our tax revenue is not being used judiciously.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: We disagree with such voluntary wealth transfers from the Government to commercial entities.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: They result in the costs being paid by taxpayers and the commercial benefits kept by the commercial entities.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This internal transfer amongst different parts of the Government is treated as an expenditure on one end, but not as revenue on the other end.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This means that we need to raise tax revenue to fund this transfer of land from SLA to HDB.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: While the land was most probably acquired under the Land Acquisition Act back in the 1960s to 1980s at low prices in the name of national development, the transaction between HDB and SLA is made based on current land prices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In other words, even though Government had acquired the land at low prices using tax revenue in the past, taxpayers have to now pay for that land again at current prices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This state of affair does not seem reasonable to us and further strengthens the point that land sale proceeds ought to be treated as revenue over the lease period.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: We do not currently need the revenue and when we do, we have other revenue sources and we should cut expenditure first.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The delay and staggering of the GST hike and the slew of subsidies to soften the blow on most of the population are a relief.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Now, I wish to touch on three topics today.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I call it PCR, namely P for Principles of stewardship; C for Cost of doing business; and R for Resourcing of charities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Budget 2022 is a clear articulation of the principles of how Singapore stewards its resources.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Former US President Dwight Eisenhower once said, "A people that values its privileges above its principles soon loses both." What are the principles that undergirds the Budget of 2022 and by this Government.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It explains the conservative and cautious stand by which Government builds up and draws down its reserves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We spend within and sometimes below our means.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We do not easily borrow nor freely tap on past reserves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We save for the future; for rainy days such as that during the Lehman Brothers collapse and the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And when we draw down on resources, we will return it back promptly when we are able to for the use of future generations and for future rainy days – the principle of Prudence.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This Government invests highly in the education and training of our people through initiatives – proactive initiatives – such as SkillsFuture and capability building schemes for businesses across the private, people and public sectors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We are ready and able to defend ourselves so as to prevent ourselves from landing in a position such as the ongoing Ukraine-Russia war.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This Government no intent to leave anyone behind and intentionally develop measures and programmes to uplift the low-wage workers, households and the vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, these three principles of Prudence, Preparedness and Inclusiveness.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The extent that we as a people agree on these principles is the extent of how united we are to forge ahead.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The next is "C", the Cost of doing business.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Like all things, Budget 2022 is never perfect, though the undergirding principles of this Government are clear.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Matters of cost of living and cost of doing business are not new topics, raised in and outside Parliament.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But it is still noteworthy to hear out the local enterprises who are struggling, despite doing their best, especially in such a time as this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One case in point is rise in energy cost.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: She is a supplier of container packaging to industries ranging from food to paints to solvents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: She told me her struggles arising from not only supply chain disruptions during the pandemic but also high global energy costs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A loyal Singapore PowerGrid customer for a long time, her business was subject to fluctuations in electricity rates since last September, from 14 cents to 75 cents per kilowatt.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Alas, utility supplier after supplier turned down Mdm Tan's application citing full subscription and to try in July 2022.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: She certainly has no intent to close her business, this being a family business and doing quite okay for a long time.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have discussed the matter with Minister Tan See Leng in his MTI role and I know that he too – and he is a very earnest Minister – is mulling over the issue.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Still on "C", cost of doing business, the rise in qualifying salaries of the foreign workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Another major input heard from SMEs concerns the well-intended increased qualifying salaries of S Pass and E Pass holders.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The policy intent is this: to bring in the right calibre of imported talents and to make it more attractive for companies to employ Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The anecdotes I heard from the ground caused me to wonder if Government has been too blunt in this approach and if the policy intent, in this instance, has been achieved.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some employers claim that the increase in qualifying S Pass and E Pass salaries have pushed up not only the salaries of the foreign talents, but also local staff as well and, hence, cost of business.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not that bad but there is also this nagging issue that even if firms choose to hire local staff, some candidates are simply difficult to come by.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am referring to candidates for jobs such as preschool Chinese Language teachers, educators, speech and occupational therapists, even cybersecurity and IT professionals who are also in high demand by multinational firms setting up business in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, PCR, and lastly, "R", on Resourcing of charities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I wish to end off with suggestions on how Government can play a more effective role in resourcing charities to build a more caring and inclusive society – one of the strategic thrusts of Budget 2022.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Singapore Government has long adopted a "Many Helping Hands" approach to deliver a range of social services and assistance programmes, primarily, to work with partners who know the ground better.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: About 200 of these are large charities with more than $10 million in receipts.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Larger charities often fill important gaps where Government and the rest of society have not stepped in sufficiently.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are gaps which are also well-known and highlighted time and again in this House.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Government should play an active role in resourcing charities that provide essential services that Government would otherwise have to undertake.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Resourcing, of course, can be facilitated in three ways.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, by providing grants, hopefully sufficient grants, to the partnering charity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, by strengthening the nexus between top needs and potential top donors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can local multinationals such as DBS, Singtel, and so on, be persuaded by Government to take ownership or adopt some identified, and maybe unfilled, top needs agreed upon by Government and its charity partners?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Three, Government can help by simplifying or facilitating fundraising requirements to help charities help themselves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Because of the way the programme is currently designed, charities large and small, their behaviour is shaped by how the programme is designed, they are largely driven now to organise, for example, to meet the rule, maximum five campaigns a year, up to $100 per campaign.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Another way that Government can facilitate is also to help social enterprises, especially those which are owned by charities themselves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The proceeds do not go to any private pockets, it is back to the charities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If social enterprises owned by charities can be allowed to qualify for fundraising, and then being the arms of job creation and service creation, that will really help as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I really hope Government will help to look at the ways by which charities can be resourced, so that these charities can partner Government even more effectively.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I seek the Minister’s favourable consideration for my suggestions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It acts as a steer and a benchmark for Singaporeans to understand where we are going and how we intend to get there.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: History has shown us that societies tend to stratify as they develop.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With development comes a difference in wants, needs and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If left unaddressed, some of these differences may ultimately cause irreconcilable tensions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We see this happening all over the world and how we negotiate these differences in Singapore is imperative to our collective progress.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we cannot completely fight it, we can try to stave off the undesirable outcomes that it can bring, by ensuring that people, regardless of background, have a seat at the table to share in inclusive economic growth.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While there is much in Budget 2022 to talk about, I will focus on two areas for my English speech: support for mental health and social integration, and a stake for our youth.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From our frontliners to students, healthcare workers to teachers, seniors to caregivers, battling COVID-19 has taken its toll on Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More than half said they felt like they have lost control over their future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For seniors, we saw the highest number of suicides since 1991.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unlike physical health, the effects of poor mental health often go undiagnosed until too late, it starts to interfere in significant ways with one’s life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even if diagnosed, there is still a lack of social understanding on how a person who on the outside might seem okay, is not able to function because of what is going on in their minds.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is easier to see the difficulty someone faces in climbing a set of stairs, for example, if their leg is broken, but it is not as easy to understand that the same or even seemingly simpler tasks like getting out of bed, also can present a challenge for someone with mental health challenges, much less keeping up with the pace of life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is it no wonder, that many hide their conditions away?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On their own, already they may feel like they are a burden, without society’s reminders that they are not where they want to be in life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mental health challenges do not fit in a neat little box.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The implications of being diagnosed or having a loved one who is diagnosed with a serious mental health condition spans financial, familial and social considerations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, I am glad that the Government in 2021 announced the formation of the inter-agency task force and I certainly look forward to hearing more about the next actionable steps and plans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides the Government, it is really civic society and ground-up groups who have made great strides in promoting mental health awareness to reach different pockets of society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Awareness and education is but the first step towards destigmatisation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From Campus Psy to Silver Ribbon Singapore, Over the Rainbow to Hayaa’ Network and Samaritans of Singapore, youth, volunteers, suicide survivors and even religious teachers are telling stories of the complex realities which those who face mental health challenges are going through.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I am deeply appreciative of their work.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In particular, increasing access and affordability for people seeking mental health treatment and working towards better protections and integration of life for people with mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, patients seeking mental health treatments can lean, to a certain extent, on MediSave and Government grants.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We know that other than stigma and shame, cost can often be a prohibitive reason why people do not seek help.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, mental health challenges can be recurring and, unfortunately, the road to recovery is not always linear.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Options in the private sector for insurance coverage are few.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A CNA article in September 2021 notes that there is rising interest in mental health insurance, but options remain inadequate.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other than reviewing the withdrawal limits, will the Government consider working with the private sector to incentivise more options for the provision of mental health insurance coverage?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must go beyond mental health awareness and towards integration and acceptance of people with mental health conditions, including skilling, literacy and a more inclusive workforce.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As an example, how do we ensure that people suffering from mental health conditions are given a fair shot and not turned away simply because of their conditions at a job interview?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we also ensure that the caregivers may apply for discretional time-off to take care of emergencies that may arise.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having to rely on informal processes and the grace of colleagues to secure the foregoing can be extremely stressful.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many people living with a mental health illness do want to work and can contribute to the workforce if they are adequately supported.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For those who are not able to work, would we be willing to explore how social assistance can be more nuanced to tide over different demographics of people during difficult times?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are complex issues with many considerations but it is an important step for us to take sooner, rather than later.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my chats with youth on Zoom, via Instagram DM and in-person, many share their worries for the future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A commentary piece written by final year University student, Natalie Tan, was published in January 2022.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She notes how the pandemic has short-changed young people in financial, professional and social ways.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Natalie’s words, “For graduating cohorts last year, the absence of in-person graduation ceremonies was like a nail in the coffin.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It felt like we ran the race, won the prize but we are not there to collect the medal and hug family and batchmates. "It’s also tough to transit from attending classes on Zoom to searching for jobs in this floundering economy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With limited doors open, we went about in circles trying to figure out the next stage of our lives.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Those of us who managed to find jobs had to contend with a lonely onboarding experience.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Others weren’t so lucky.” Incentivising employment is something the Government has done.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From employers to employees, many appreciate these efforts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will our youth be supported through this package?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The lack of internships and in-person opportunities have made it difficult for some to even figure out what they want to do.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And there is little we can do to replace those years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also know of youths who have turned to the gig economy as a means of generating an income.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some now consider this to be their full-time job, while others use their freelancing skills as a side hustle for the time being.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As more turn to these roles as viable options, how can we work with companies to ensure better protections for these workers in the long  run?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Artists, musicians, dancers, actors, physical trainers and many others have been unable to generate an income at different points of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of them have been able to return to work in a limited capacity, others not so much.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While frequent testing is important, ART kits also come at a cost from already reduced incomes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One hard hit group includes live musicians such as bands and DJs who previously held residencies at nightlife institutions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since March 2020, many have not been able to continue their residencies and some hotspots have shuttered.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Like many others who have seen the large bulk of their incomes slashed, many have tried to pivot, some have taken their skills online and others have transitioned into other careers, but they remain hopeful that they will able to earn a living once again by doing what they know and love best.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Workplaces such as gyms have been able to operate with restrictions for some time now, in an attempt to mitigate the risk of transmission.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there ways in which we can limit the risks of transmission of performing on stage at an eatery that serves food and drinks, so that live music can return?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Government consider introducing balanced measures that enable this?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With watchful eye on Omicron, as measures relax in stages, can the Government give some clarity, what are some sort of circumstances and conditions we will need to see before members of this community will be able to return to work?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This increase was driven by increases in the prices of food, electricity and gas.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a small country, Singapore cannot escape geopolitical shocks and incidents that occur globally.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although our economy is still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, this year's Budget has demonstrated the Government's concern to continue supporting and enhancing the capabilities of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, COVID-19 and the rising cost of living have presented even more challenges for our community, particularly in terms of access & opportunities to prepare for an uncertain future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last year, the Population Census report stated that the number of Malay families living in 1-room and 2-room rental flats had more than doubled over the past decade.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And this is due to several factors such as the increase in the number of rental homes that are provided especially for families that need it.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They usually need help from various quarters, and we have to look for a holistic strategy and way.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I am glad that efforts such as the Commlink and the DIAN@M3 project are available, in which the Government, agencies and volunteers can coordinate efforts to reach out to residents living in rental houses and help them achieve their dreams and a brighter future for the next generation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Social service agencies such as the South Central FSC have provided innovative and holistic approaches such as the Keystart Home Ownership where they offer assistance which includes housing mortgages and the cost of shifting to a new home.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This pandemic has also reminded us that with time and changes in technology, it is possible that the jobs we have now will no longer be relevant in the future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should definitely encourage more people within our community, especially women, to venture into STEM and the growth industries.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Government can open up more channels and opportunities so that our community can participate in these fields.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we want to chart a new direction for Singapore, let us uphold our pledge to progress together, and emerge even stronger so that each generation can benefit from our nation’s progress.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, it is a precarious balancing act, managing the needs, wants, ideals and aspirations of citizens.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore is no stranger to cater to these differences, while at the same time rallying our people towards common goals and purpose.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Decades ago, the idea of a multiracial, multi-religious society, was thought to be impossible given the times and our geographical context.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In many ways, even today it remains an anomaly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the words of our talented artists, Linying and Evan Low in last year’s NDP song, and do not worry, I will not scare you by singing, "Come whatever on the road ahead; We did it before, and we'll do it again."

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Minister for Finance has put out a comprehensive suite of measures in his Budget Statement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, I would like to speak mainly on three issues.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The first is on Workfare Income Supplement, the second, to assure our business community, especially the small and medium enterprises (SMEs), of the direction and the pace of our foreign workforce policy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Earlier in this debate, the Leader of the Opposition Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Gerald Giam and Ms Jessica Tan, raised concerns about the $500 minimum income criterion for Workfare.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Leader of the Opposition has estimated that the number of affected recipients is 46,600 by referencing the number of employed residents aged 15 and above earning below $500 in 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Not all of these 46,600 qualify for Workfare due to criteria such as age, spousal assessable income and the annual value of their place of residence.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, in other words, nothing to do with the salary that they earn.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some would be students earning extra pocket money while they study or some of them are actually from higher income households.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They are not the intended targets of Workfare.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Furthermore, 46,600 is based on 2021 data and does not take into account the expected wage growth from the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) expansion.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And also, the new Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) requirements that would uplift many employees beyond the $500 threshold.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Should any of these 20,000 workers subsequently work more and earn more than $500 per month, they will automatically re-qualify for Workfare.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, the $500 per month is a reasonable and achievable wage for most regular workers under our Progressive Wage Model approach.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At this wage, a part-time worker only needs to work about two working days a week to meet the $500 minimum income criterion.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, we also recognise that there may be some workers who want to work more, but are unable to earn $500 per month, due to their personal circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Hence, if Ms Jessica Tan's resident requires additional financial assistance, she can apply for ComCare and if she qualifies she will receive concessionary Workfare as well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In short, for workers who are earning less than $500, the best way to help them is to help them find a job of the appropriate quality and quantity of working hours to earn at least $500.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Then, Workfare can come in to provide an additional boost to help such workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have a whole suite of employment facilitation programmes and initiatives, ready to assist.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Moving onto my second point that I would like to raise and that is on the foreign workforce policies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will speak more when MOM’s budget is debated in a few days' time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, let me touch on and elaborate on our thinking behind these moves, and how we will walk with businesses through these changes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Businesses, especially our SMEs, have expressed concern about rising costs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I want to assure SMEs that we understand these concerns and we have taken great care when designing the timing of our moves.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are well aware that if businesses do not succeed, there will not be good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Besides SMEs, foreign companies are also quietly observing our moves.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even foreign publications have been speculating that Singapore is now less welcoming to talent.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members of the House, we must not allow such perceptions or such misperceptions to take root, because this will be very damaging for us.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Hence, I want to be very clear that the changes we announce are to ensure that Singapore remains open to foreigners who can complement our workforce, so that our businesses can assemble the best team of locals and foreigners to compete on the global stage.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Indeed, this strategy was affirmed by the House last year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We recognise that having foreigners working alongside us and living amongst us can cause discomfort, even some tension, amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: My assurance is that we will be vigilant in managing the social frictions that may arise from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also guard against anti-foreigner and xenophobic sentiments.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Singapore has always been a multicultural society and we intend to keep it so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our foreign workforce policies will have to balance the needs of businesses and workers, and this has been MOM's core guiding principle.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The announced changes to the qualifying salaries for Employment Pass (EP) and S Pass are part of this series of adjustments to maintain a balance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The wages of our local workers have risen over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This reflects the growth of our economy and the deepening of skills in our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This also means that the quality of the EP and S Pass holders that we bring into Singapore must go up.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is why our EP and S Pass qualifying salaries are adjusted regularly to keep pace with local wages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If we do not do so, firms may choose to hire foreigners simply because they are cheaper than locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There will not be a level playing field.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our efforts to upskill our workforce and sharpen our business competitiveness will, therefore, be diluted.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We know that businesses would want more lead time to adjust before these changes take effect and this is exactly we have done.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We announced the moves early but incorporated a long runway between the announcement and implementation dates of all of these moves.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are being transparent so that businesses have ample time to adjust and certainty to plan ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The renewals will also not all happen at the same time in September 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will take another two to three years, so, up to 2026, before the last S Pass employee on the old qualifying salaries comes up for renewal.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, in reality, businesses will have a minimum of 18 months' notice.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But it could take up to four and a half years before all existing S Pass holders have to be renewed under the new rules.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And that is around three and a half years before the changes take effect fully.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I know these adjustments, they take effort, and change is never easy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But at the same time, it is only through continuous innovation and improvement that our businesses can and will grow from strength to strength.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Rest assured that we will walk this journey with our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am particularly mindful of the many SMEs in our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SMEs account for more than 70% of employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is a very significant proportion of employment, and they are a very important contributor to our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I personally know and I have also met with many SME business owners and have heard their concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some are worried that they may be hit more than the multinational companies (MNCs) because they have more financial constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They find it more difficult to compete for workers and they are concerned that higher costs for foreign and local manpower will just mean higher business costs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: How can our SMEs make the necessary adjustments and emerge stronger?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have been regularly and progressively making updates to our framework.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Each time when we made these adjustments, SMEs have taken advantage of the support schemes that we have available to transform, to pivot and to adapt.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The result is that our firms have a more sustainable and robust business model – they continue to thrive and they continue to be able to tap the labour market for their manpower needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With this round of changes, we will continue to support businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They can look into redesigning jobs to make jobs more productive and attractive for employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
