text: Businesses can tap on schemes, such as the Support for Job Redesign under the Productivity Solutions Grant (PSG-JR) for job redesign consultancy support to complement and drive business and workforce transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In addition, businesses can expand local hiring and upskill their local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The extended SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package and the Jobs Growth Incentive will continue to provide a significant boost to the hiring of locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Together with the tripartite partners, we will make sure that SMEs which are prepared to transform their businesses and increase local hiring will receive the support they need.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some business owners told me that it is hard to find manpower even with the support, given that our unemployment is so low and that our labour market is tight.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They say they need manpower across all levels, from the Professionals, Managers, Executives and Technicians (PMET) level to the Rank-and-File (RnF) levels.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is something that we are happy and very glad for.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One such group is women outside the workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are vacancies across all occupational levels with varied qualifications and needs which could potentially be filled by this group.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In order to tap on this segment of our population, businesses will need to consider how the jobs they offer can be more flexible and attractive to locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As flexible work arrangements can come in various forms and some may be more relevant for certain jobs than others, businesses can adopt the most suitable flexible work arrangements that suit their organisations' as well as their employees' needs, including for those in frontline or shift work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some businesses are already doing so and we should press ahead as best and as fast as we can.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some SMEs also tell me that they wish to hire at the Work Permit level to manage their manpower needs but are unable to do so because of the rules, such as source country restrictions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we can find a way to offer some flexibility.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is something that MOM has been working on.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will address this at the upcoming MOM's Committee of Supply (COS) in a few days' time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And I think it will be good news.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Lastly, as we continue to refine our policy levers, we will ensure that there will not be a disproportionate impact on SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, there have been suggestions for the Government to look beyond qualifying salary in our Employment Pass (EP) framework, which may be a blunt tool.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have considered and taken the feedback very seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will elaborate further in MOM's COS debate about how our refinements of the EP framework have taken into account the size of the firm.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They are exploring various options to transform to adjust to the changes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We know that border controls have made things more challenging.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But with our border reopening in a calibrated manner, some of this pressure will be relieved.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But SMEs and businesses alike need to start to plan ahead on what works best for their business model and their workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, I hope that our businesses will take a longer view on this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To support businesses in their planning, we have laid out our foreign workforce policy moves for the next few years so that businesses have greater certainty, predictability and time to adjust.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They oppose the Budget because of the GST increase.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But they agree with the moves we are making to shore up the social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In fact, they would like us to spend even more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I believe their position is – agree with all the good and nice things that we propose and then say, "not enough, ask for more".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But what they oppose is how we intend to do the difficult thing and, that is, to raise the revenues to pay for all the good things that they like so much that they want even more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They say, "put a heavier load on some Singaporeans" so that we do not have to have a GST increase.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It sounds very simple and attractive but ask yourselves – is it really doable?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This Government's approach is that the rich should carry a heavier load.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are raising income taxes on the top earners, property taxes on higher value properties and the additional registration fee (ARF) for luxury cars.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That was the mantra in my colleague, the Minister for Finance's Budget speech this year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The well-off will pay more and receive less, and the less well-off will receive more and pay less.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The well-off will pay more and receive less and the less well-off will receive more and pay less.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Amongst the revenue options proposed by the Workers' Party, they have suggested increasing personal income tax and property tax even more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If we were to do that, we will have to raise the tax rates on income and property even more substantially and we have to make more people, including middle-income earners pay more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, the consequence is that we will have to raise income taxes for not just those at the very top but it will percolate down to our middle, our upper-middle income, including those who have benefited from our educational system, our years of social mobility, those who have toiled, who have laboured, who have worked very hard all through the years to move up from more modest circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will have to apply higher property taxes to a larger base of properties, not just your landed properties, your Good Class Bungalows, your semi-Ds, your terrace houses, your luxury condos – which will already, by the way, see a significant increase – but it will also go to all condos, perhaps Executive Condominiums (ECs) and, perhaps, even eventually even larger HDB flats.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Residents from across the country, the whole island, my residents in Marine Parade, residents in the nearby East Coast, Joo Chiat, Bukit Timah, Thomson, Upper Thomson, Bishan – you name it – Upper Bukit Timah, including even in Sengkang, in Aljunied, too.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These are the people who may have to make up the difference.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, this year, this debate, the impression I took away of what the Workers' Party want is two things.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One, they said loud and clear; the other may not be so loud or, perhaps, it is hidden somewhat and, perhaps, they could clarify.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Loud and clear: "I like all the nice and good things you are proposing but more will be better." But what they are not saying, and I am baffled and, as a consequence is, "I like it that you are raising taxes on the wealthy and more of such taxes would be better".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, have they considered the burden would inevitably have to be borne and applied to a wider group and variety of Singaporeans and taxpayers?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, the first "more", they shout from the rooftops; the second "more", relatively muted, hoping that, perhaps, people would not notice that inevitably, that could be a consequence of what they are proposing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Deputy Speaker, we fundamentally disagree with what the Workers' Party's proposal will imply for our society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will ultimately result in a system where our approach to revenue is just to squeeze anyone who does well from the middle-income upwards, potentially; where we tell Singaporeans, "Look, there is someone better off who can afford to take on all of the burden, you don't have to put in your share, or you don't have to put in your fair share." That is not good nor is it sustainable for our social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: All of us have a stake in our society and we benefit from public services and from progressive policies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To conclude, Mdm Deputy Speaker, it is not an easy task ahead for all of us.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are difficult things that we must do together.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But as long as all of us – workers, unions, businesses, fellow citizens and Government – are prepared to play a part and work closely together with the long-term interest of Singapore and Singaporeans at heart, I believe we will continue to live long and prosper.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I take his point with regard to the number of workers who could be affected by the changes to the Workfare Income Supplement that a more accurate number would be 20,000, as he suggested.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He said, "I will introduce a minimum income criteria for Workfare at $500 a month to encourage part-timers and casual workers to take up regular full-time work".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, that seems to be the policy intent to move them into regular full-time work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I clarify from the Minister, even for these individuals who may continue to earn less than $500, going forward, can the Minister confirm that they still will not qualify for the Workfare Income Supplement?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is that a lesser amount of Workfare for these individuals who cannot do full-time work, which is the policy intent as it would appear from the Minister for Finance's speech, that he wants to transit these people into full-time work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the Minister not agree that there are individuals who just cannot do full-time work for a variety of reasons?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Minister then moved on to some other subjects and in the course of moving on to those subjects, he was drinking some water and he wet his shirt.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I do not know whether that was in anticipation of some of the points he was going to make.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There were some words that were used: like the Workers' Party wants to put a heavier load on Singaporeans, a fairer, a more punitive load.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think the point of our suggestions really is a more equitable load.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How do you balance things in a manner which is more equitable for society, going forward, for a more fairer, more sustainable and more inclusive society?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is the thrust of what the Workers' Party had put forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And to just make the point Minister spoke about a number of taxes, for example, property taxes, alluding to residents in various parts of Singapore who would suffer with raised property taxes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But does the Minister not agree that there were a number of proposals put forward by the Workers' Party?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And on a Monday, yesterday, a Business Times article made the point in a different way – that the OECD Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) is unlikely to hurt competitiveness and may net Singapore gains in tax revenue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I think in the spirit of seeking a more equitable tax distribution, amongst various segments of society, I think the Workers' Party is fully entitled to raise alternate forms of revenue, which we have.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I also cannot understand why he is baffled because it would be in the course of this debate that the Workers' Party would propose alternate revenue sources.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And you have cherry-picked some and criticised them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But if you look at the proposals holistically, you would understand that the Workers' Party has put up alternatives for a rise in GST.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It was actually because of the fact that it is a new flask, I did not figure out exactly how to press the right buttons yet.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: He has put up a series of questions, some of them, we will cover, for example, Workfare, in the upcoming debate under the MOM COS so I do not want to give too much of a preamble.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are also help groups available to try to understand where the bottlenecks are in terms of them being able to get a higher income or even get to that $500 mark.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Suffice to say, the whole policy construct is to encourage, to nudge our local able-bodied Singaporeans towards gainful employment and also a higher sense of achievement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And, eventually, for us to sustain it, consequentially, this would end up percolating or pervading down to the upper middle-income and eventually affecting the middle-income as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am pretty sure the Minister for Finance in his round-up speech will cover more aspects of it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the moment, I want to assure that our policies take a very measured and a very calibrated approach, designed for most people to be able to adjust and also be able to absorb some of these measures.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Indeed, Minister has accurately stated the policy purpose.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am sorry he did not accurately say it; you added something more to it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: You said the policy construct is to nudge able-bodied Singaporeans towards gainful employment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What I am suggesting is that part-timers may well be able-bodied, casual workers may also be able-bodied, but for various reasons, they cannot take up full-time work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And if we can help this small number of workers and why should we not?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think that Mr Singh missed my point.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That may be a whole myriad of reasons why able-bodied Singaporeans cannot or are not prepared to commit to just two days of work a week.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we have already started the Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also gotten some of the other measures to help to uplift the lower-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And many of these schemes will take effect over the coming months.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When that rising tide comes up, we will certainly see where this group of Singaporeans, who are still not affected, would fall into.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think that we can then review the policy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you look at the last few years, we have been constantly reviewing, improving and uplifting the framework.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will invite Senior Minister of State Mr Zaqy to further add to it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: On the minimum income criterion, I just want to say quickly that: one, it is not meant to discount any of our lower-wage workers from receiving Workfare.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: When Minister Tan spoke about concessionary Workfare, what it means is that: if you are receiving ComCare, or if you qualify for ComCare, then automatically you will get Workfare as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Even if you are a part-time worker, earning less than $500.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This is because with the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) coming into play, the number that Mr Pritam Singh cited will certainly reduce, because the hourly rates will go up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Like the example that Deputy Speaker raised, for someone like that, if they are truly low income, if they are on ComCare, they will automatically get Workfare.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can I just confirm if they are not on ComCare, they would not get the WIS?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, as I shared, if you are on ComCare, means you are low income and most likely, if you are earning less than $500, part-timer, you will get it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And that extends to all our persons with disabilities too, to ensure that no one gets left behind.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This separates our truly low-income part-time workers who may be constrained for whatever reason, whether caregiving or other constraints, that they are still provided assistance, not just from ComCare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I just wanted to clarify a few points.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And I understand that by peppering Minister Tan with more questions, we might end up making him yet more thirsty, but it is important, I think, to get some of the points that we made right.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will start off by pointing out that I wonder whether he could clarify where he thinks there is such a large philosophical difference between our particular approach of raising revenue relative to that of the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, for the corporate taxation lever, when we made that proposal about raising the rate of corporate taxation to what would be compliant with the OECD Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) agreement, we also made very clear that the target of that would be the multinational firms and not the small and medium enterprises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Keeping with that particular scenario, we would have kept the corporate taxation rate on them at the effective rate of 3% or so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The reason why I think it is important to clarify that we are not philosophically seeking a very narrow tax base.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We are, in fact, seeking alternative revenue levers that subscribe to the general principles of public finance, which are, as much as possible, to spread the revenue schemes in as broad a manner as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But at the same time, recognising the importance, as suggested by Minister Wong in his speech, of a certain degree of fairness and equity, and that is precisely why we have some components, in fact, one third of one of our four levers, where we do include wealth taxation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I hope that clarifies and perhaps Minister Tan can clarify a little more.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Again, I thank Prof Lim as well as the Leader of the Opposition for their concerns.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am fine to take any number of questions and happy to engage because it is also good to clarify the points.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have shared earlier on, in my speech, what the impression that we have taken in terms of where you have decided to load this is on the wealth tax portion, which seems to put a huge burden on a certain very small group of Singaporeans, and I question its sustainability.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And hence, if you noticed that in my speech, I said consequentially, this will eventually end up having to be more spread out, in terms of having to be borne by more people.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In terms of the philosophical differences, therefore my point to perhaps Assoc Prof Lim and the Workers' Party is that: do they now, having heard our explanation, decide that they support the GST hike and support the Budget.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The other point is that Minister Wong will address a number of your points in his round-up speech tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How did it arrive at the conclusion that imposing a $500 minimum income would encourage, rather than discourage, them from working?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Because to me, it seems to fly against the logic of the WIS which is the whole purpose of the WIS is to supplement the income of low-wage workers, so that they would be encouraged to work more.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, why would you have a cut-off such that the lowest income workers are not encouraged in that way to work more.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And if the Government is still intent on keeping this $500 dollar minimum, can I get an assurance from the Minister that the Government will adopt a more flexible approach to take into account the various constraints faced by workers that prevent them from earning more than $500 dollars.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, some may have caregiving responsibilities who just cannot spare the time to work, to earn more than $500 dollars a month, or to work more than two days a week.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, to some extent, I hope that clarifies and responds to the Member's question.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I am sorry, Senior Minister of State, I do not quite understand how those who earn less than $500 will get Workfare still.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And also, from some of those who are doing vacation jobs and so forth, this puts a differentiation and puts our focus on our social compact that you are low-income, and you need the money, you would not be left behind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just a quick one, it is not a clarification.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just to confirm with the Minister, the understanding that he had of the WP's alternate proposals are incorrect.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And we will clarify in the course of Minister's wrap-up speech, depending of what Minister for Finance says.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is just important for me to put that on the record, because otherwise the media may interpret your interpretations of what we are proposing to be correct.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I just want to put it on record that it is not correct.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This increasing inflation rate is contributed in no small part by the cost of food, electricity and gas in our country brought about by supply chain disruptions caused by the worldwide COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Now, with the Russian invasion of Ukraine causing the prices of oil and natural gas to skyrocket, as well as imminent threat of further global supply chains disruptions occurring down the road, Singaporeans are no doubt worried that the cost of living will continue to increase to a level greater than they can grapple with.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This worry has also trickled down to the youths: "Will I be able to earn enough in future to keep up with these increases?", "Am I reskilling or upskilling enough so I can earn better wages?", "Can I support my family?" These are just some questions that the youths ask.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And lastly, "how do we ensure those more vulnerable are not left behind?" This Budget's theme, "Charting Our New Way Forward Together", demonstrates that everyone has a part to play for us to progress as a country.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget is noteworthy, because it tries to uphold the values of care and inclusivity.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget introduces measures to ensure that those with more contribute more, to help build a more balanced society.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, I am highly encouraged by the recent moves to increase the personal income tax, property tax and luxury car tax levied on the more well-off in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It sends a strong signal that Singapore wants to re-distribute its wealth and reduce wealth inequality.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly, it sends a signal that Singapore priorities efforts to ensure that our social mobility framework remains agile.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is a good start and one that I am sure was only made after careful research and calibration.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: While the wealthy should not be made to shoulder the entire of the society's tax burden, at the same time, it is only equitable for those with more to also contribute greater to the society they have benefited from.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I do hope these measures are but the beginnings of a more progressive tax system in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As the Minister stated in his Budget speech, "Everyone chips in and contributes to a vibrant economy and strengthened social compact, but those with greater means contribute a larger share." The COVID-19 pandemic has already affected low-income families in rental housing disproportionately compared to the rest of the population.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Longitudinal Early Development Study, published in November 2021, found that lower-income families were hit the hardest by the pandemic due to the economic impact, job losses, struggles with adapting to work-from-home and home-based learning as well as social distancing measures, affecting them physically and mentally.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The combination of rising costs driven by this period of heightened inflation and the newly announced GST increase will hit the low-income families hard.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I am therefore heartened to see that this Budget has boosted social support for Singaporeans, especially those from the low-income.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to enquire if the Government will be prepared to reconsider how it awards the GSTV.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, GSTV is only awarded after review of both assessable income and the annual value of recipients' property.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is also only awarded to Singapore citizens aged 21 years and above.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This ignores the fact that residents of houses with identical annual values may have vastly different financial needs and require greater rebates based on the number of household members and children under 21, who maybe residents.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In the same vein, would the Government also be relooking at the eligibility criteria of each social welfare scheme, especially in the backdrop of rising costs?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: If it is assessed that it is not the time for such a review, then would there be clearer guidance of when the Government will decide to review the eligibility criteria and amount of benefits under each social welfare scheme?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: When there is more, everyone will get more, when there is less, everyone will get less.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Scaffolding vulnerable groups are something youths also feel strongly about.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The National Youth Council's regular sentiment polling showed that in the area of supporting vulnerable populations, the top issues youths feel need to be addressed include the empowerment and social safety nets for lower-income communities; the rights, treatment and policies for migrant workers; and capability development and empowerment of persons-with-disabilities.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The GST increase will affect them from the onset and at the same time, they will not be able to qualify for the GST Vouchers.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They are also less able to adapt to these increases due to their low wages and debt.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The migrant workers have been integral in our nation-building.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Our streets, houses and skyscrapers are built by them.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Government have any plans on reviewing the social support schemes to ensure that their well-being is also looked after?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For the persons-with-disabilities, I am pleased that we are launching the Enabling Masterplan 2030 and am looking forward to hearing more details about it.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In this Budget, Singapore has taken a bold move forward and it is something I support.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, green technologies are more expensive in the short-term.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As Minister Fu answered in my Parliamentary Question in the last sitting, and I quote, "Green products and services may cost a bit more.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: But in a competitive market, businesses will compete to provide consumers with the most value-for-money products and services.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As sustainable products and services become more mainstream, economies of scale could bring down costs." This means, however, that, in the meantime, costs will trickle down to consumers.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be monitoring on how the costs are trickling down to consumers, similar to the safeguards and monitoring that will take place by the Committee against Profiteering for the GST hikes?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The rising cost of living may lead to greater mental anxiety and strain among Singaporeans about the future.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is exacerbated with the impact of the pandemic on mental health.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: A new study by BMJ suggests that catching the COVID-19 virus increases the risk of developing mental health problems such as anxiety, depression, stress and adjustment and substance use disorders.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As you know, as significant proportion of our population is infected with the virus.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is significant that a Minister mentioned mental health and the inter-agency task force for mental health in the Budget.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It signals the seriousness of the Government to tackle the issue and its recognition that all segments of the society have mental health needs.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Our SG Mental Health Matters, which is a community of mental health policy advocates, comprising individuals who also have lived experiences of mental health challenges, recently advocated for a whole-of-Government approach to mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I agree with this approach as it would consolidate all efforts between Ministries, public agencies, social service agencies and ground-up initiatives to plan for the short, medium and long term more effectively.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The youths may be especially worried about their future.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Even before the pandemic, Singapore youths were already concerned about job prospects, the climate crisis, inequality and mental health.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The World Economic Forum Global Risks Report 2021 also showed a worsening of mental health since the start of the pandemic, leaving youths vulnerable to depression, anxiety and disillusionment.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In China, we have the "lying flat" movement.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Though I do not think Singaporean youths are at this stage yet, how do we prevent this from happening and wearing out the potential of our youths?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Especially when bad news seems to come from all sides?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the youths can find comfort that this Budget demonstrates how the Government places importance on improving social mobility and reducing inequality in the rapidly changing global economy.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Hope and optimism that together as one Singapore, when we make the effort to look out for one another, regardless of our differences, we can make sure that no one gets left behind.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There is a common Malay Saying, "Berat sama dipikul, ringan sama dijinjing".

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It means when we face challenges, we surmount them together, because together we are stronger.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Together, even the greatest of challenges make light work.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is exemplified by a "pantun" written by then 12-year-old Iman Solihin Bin Mohamad Fariq which won an SG50 poetry competition.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   The first quatrain (pantun) refers to the student himself, who, when asked where he was from, he replied proudly that he was from Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In the second quatrain, he describes Singapore as a peaceful and prosperous country, where all the communities get along with one another.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The final quatrain is a declaration of his love for his motherland and his readiness to sacrifice everything for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Therefore in these times of uncertainty, I would like to say to the youths, have courage.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As it takes courage of heart, will, mind and spirit to face the headwinds of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I am glad to hear the Finance Minister say that this year's Budget is "a first step in renewing and strengthening our social compact".  "Renewing and strengthening our social compact", precise choice of operative words and a profoundly important aspiration.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And today, I wish to offer three key reflections.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, a renewed and strengthened social compact must be about the state playing an even more activist role in healthcare, to ensure quality and affordability for all.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And we have to find a way to fund this.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Over the years, we have invested billions in our public healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because we have decided early on, that quality and affordable healthcare would be a key pillar in our social compact in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And because we cannot rely only on the free market to achieve this, the Government has been playing an activist role.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To have kept that commitment and stayed the course, investing billion after billion, year after year, this is something that should not be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, as we look ahead, we need to do even more.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is because our future healthcare challenges will be different and amidst these challenges, Singapore must continue to be a nation where all Singaporeans can aspire to take good care of their parents while providing the best for their children and where every Singaporean can have basic peace of mind for him or herself.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: More advanced diagnostics and therapeutics are becoming what we call standard care.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These can drastically improve quality of life, as patients who have actually gone through TKRs would know.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And TKRs are indeed becoming more and more common.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But the real cost of a TKR is thousands of dollars.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The question is, how can we help all Singaporeans who need a TKR and opt for one in future to afford it?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In my House Visits, I have met many residents, either in remission, or even on active treatment and management.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They show that it is now possible to live well with cancer, because of incredible advances in cancer care.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But again, there is a real and high cost.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How can we help all Singaporeans and their caregivers and their loved ones, afford such life-giving care, if cancer finds them one day?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Inevitably, with many more seniors with advances in standard care.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the years ahead, we must spend much more on healthcare.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so based on that scale of what is needed, some levers of revenue generation, on their own, are simply not going to be enough.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Realistically, two key levers that can meet our needs come to mind: one, GST; and two, the contribution of returns from investing our reserves, or what we call NIRC.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A higher NIRC means we take more of the investment returns to spend today and plough less of these returns back into future investments for future returns to benefit future generations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This was a specific suggestion by Mr Louis Chua yesterday, who by the way, I think made a very good and insightful speech.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, increase NIRC to 60%, rather than raise GST.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I have heard a compelling argument for this.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It goes like this: "The younger generation wants to earn its own keep and is capable of earning its own keep.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so the money available today, let the older generation spend it and make full use of it, today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: No need for the older generation to leave anything behind." Many kids today would tell their parents the same.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But parents will want to leave something behind for their children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is a basic instinct, a basic desire.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Parents want to gift a legacy for their children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And, in my view, it should be the same for a country's finances.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Each generation must want to leave something behind for generations that follow.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Our forefathers have left much behind for us.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, all of them contribute to most of the GST.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We then take some of this to return back to most other Singaporeans a portion, if not all, of the GST that they pay and, whatever GST revenue is left for the Government in this way, the net GST revenue, we spend on healthcare for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, if we look beyond the theoretical nature of consumption tax as being regressive and an undue burden to the middle- and low-income, if we look at the specific design of GST here, where non-Singaporeans and a small portion of Singaporeans, some high-spending Singaporeans, pay most of the tax that we then use to benefit all Singaporeans and, when we return the GST paid by the middle- and lower-income to make the tax effectively progressive, if we look beyond the theory and recognise the uniquely Singapore design of GST here, in practice, we can conclude that it actually works for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, we should really be looking at our GST system as a lever of first resort in our fiscal toolkit, rather than a lever of last resort, as it is being framed, I think, from time to time in this House.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To be clear, I am not saying that we cannot and should not do more on other levers like personal and corporate income taxes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Mr Louis Chua has also raised salient points about these and I agree with him.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We can do more and I do hope that the Government will do more in good time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But my basic point is to let us look at all our revenue levers as a whole mix and recognise that we are already moving on property and personal income taxes as part of this mix but, at the same time, higher GST must also be an essential part of the same mix.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, because of the way in which we have designed it, GST should be a lever of first rather than last resort in the mix.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Getting this consensus right is important for our renewed and strengthened social compact.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   In this year's Budget, what attracted the most attention is the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If we were to analyse the pros and cons of this move, we must first understand the fundamentals of our unique GST system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Under this system, many of those who pay GST are foreigners and tourists.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: GST collected from them are also a big chunk of the total tax revenue.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Hence, our GST system is a two-pronged one.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, it gets substantial tax revenue from non-Singaporeans; second, they are spent on Singaporeans, especially in healthcare.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, our GST system is on the side of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Coupled with the Government's support measures, the impact on lower- and middle-income Singaporeans will be minimised.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In English): Madam, my second reflection is that in this social compact, those with more will be contributing even more to support those with less even more strongly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The higher taxes on property, luxury vehicles and top individual earners send a strong signal that, in our social compact going forward, those with more will contribute even more.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, those with less will get even stronger support than before.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In terms of cushioning the impact of GST, this Budget provides both transitional and permanent support which, when added up, amounts to a very significant level of support, perhaps, the most in our fiscal history.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If we include enhancements to the GST Voucher scheme, which is permanent and permanently helps Singaporeans with higher GST, then, for the same period from 2022 to 2026 alone, the couple will receive an additional $1,800 in GST Voucher cash.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Actually, the absolute cash amount is more than $1,800 but the incremental alone is $1,800, thanks to enhancements to the scheme.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Another example – an elderly couple, retired, in a 3-room flat.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Workfare is effectively a negative income tax for those at the bottom.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It makes our personal income tax regime highly progressive and what this Budget does is to enhance Workfare to make the overall regime even more progressive.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These are major advancements for those with less.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, coupled with the Progressive Wage Model, which, essentially, is about getting the whole of society to chip in to supplement and uplift wages at the bottom, when this Progressive Wage Model works alongside Workfare by the Government, the combined boost in gross wages for our lowest-wage workers will be almost $1,000 every month by 2025.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is, in my view, an overdue but nonetheless decisive move that will profoundly transform jobs and lives at the bottom and form a key part of our renewed social compact.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On this note, I also urge the Government to consider raising the chargeable income ceiling for the zero-rated personal income tax bracket from $20,000 today to $30,000 in a future Budget to ensure that our tax regime continues to keep pace with wage developments and stay progressive.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It cannot be about "what can you give to me" because all of us, we, are in this together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, while those with more will contribute even more in future, we must be careful not to take it to the extreme.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We will have a very different ethos if we devolve into a state of "what can or should you do for me".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Hence, everyone pays GST and we put in place large transfers to achieve net effects but the same GST rate applies to everyone in the first instance rather than a tiered system or a system of exemptions by segments, by categories, at the outset.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think it sends an essential signal that, in the first instance, we are all in this together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But the reality is there are many other forces, apart from GST, pushing prices up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, there are many businesses as well who are trying their best to absorb what they can even as they have no choice but to pass on some of the costs to consumers by charging higher prices.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I hope that, on cost of living concerns, all of us – consumers, businesses, workers, the Government – can recognise the part that everyone else is playing to help address the problem.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I urge the Government to continue monitoring the situation closely and provide decisive support, as necessary, even beyond this Budget.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Actually, on further reflection, another key phrase by the Finance Minister struck me and, that is, that this Budget is the "first step".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, it means there are more steps to come.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Well, it may be future policy moves in the same direction.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But I believe that a key step or, indeed, steps going forward, must be the discourse that we have on these very important issues.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The discourse, the process, beyond policy pronouncements, are key steps ahead in renewing and strengthening our social compact.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As fellow Members have said, it will show who we are and what we value.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To this end, I hope our discourse ahead can be based on facts where we explain and correct misconceptions where we must, instead of propagating and reinforcing these.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I hope our discourse ahead will recognise and be rooted in our own local context where examples of other countries are thoughtfully analysed and interpreted.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Above all, I hope our discourse ahead will seek to elevate us collectively to an ever more mature, more inclusive democracy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Raising taxes is one of the hardest things to do for any Government.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And that, I think, will make for a truly renewed and strengthened social compact that all Singaporeans can be proud of.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I just wanted to ask a clarification on one point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, in other words, I am just asking is there anything magical, is there some special methodology that leads us to say that 50% is the Goldilocks zone, that it is exactly right, but 60% is irresponsible or 65% is irresponsible and so on.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I will keep this short in the interest of time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I listened to Prof Hoon Hian Teck yesterday and he spoke about every society having to find its own judgement about where is the sweet spot.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Through the Budget, we seek to achieve a more equitable distribution of finite resources we have so that those who need more help, get the assistance they need; and those who can afford to spare some help, do so.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Enough has been said about how, in Singapore, our people are our only resource.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: While I applaud the focus on strengthening our social compact, we can do much more for our young people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And this applies equally to youths who are on the fringes of social norms and the law, many of whom would come from the more vulnerable segments of our society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: What drives our young people to commit these offences?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: A 2015 study of 168 male youth sex offenders provided glimpses to better understand the motivations behind youth sexual offending in Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The study notes that the most common motivation behind youth sexual offending in Singapore appeared to be attempts at “seeking pleasure”.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: While there are no surprises here, given adolescence is often associated with exploration, sensation-seeking and impulse activity, we need to better understand the potential triggers behind such offences.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: All in all, the devil is in the details.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: There are plenty we do not yet comprehend.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: What are other contributing factors that feed the youth’s impulse to commit a sexual offence?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For instance, how does the consumption of pornographic material impact our youths' behaviours?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Being digital natives who navigate the virtual world with perhaps much more ease than those amongst us who are digital migrants, the risks and dangers that our youths face are real.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: A recent study by Google found that at eight years of age, the Singaporean child is among the youngest in the world to receive his or her own first Internet device.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Couple that with a study by social service agency, Touch Cyber Wellness, which found in a recent survey of over 800 youths aged 13 to 15 that as many as 50% of those surveyed have watched or read sexually explicit materials, and some were as young as seven when they were first exposed to such materials.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: On a related note, how many amongst us Asian parents have the courage to start the conversation with our children about the birds and the bees?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Members will agree that, for many parents, the butterflies that such conversations bring to our stomachs, probably means that many will choose to shun it completely.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our youths' interactions with sexually explicit materials and how families choose to deal with this awkward issue are but only a couple of slices in what is a complex, multi-dimensional but, unfortunately, little understood issue.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And we will need to invest much more to better understand this nascent trend, so that we can better design appropriate upstream interventions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our youths’ liberal attitude towards drugs is also a cause for concern.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Between 2016 and 2020, a noticeable uptrend in the total number of youth drug abusers was observed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This number rose from 277 in 2016 to 376 in 2019.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The dip observed for 2020 to 305 could have been a function of border closures and movement restrictions brought about by the pandemic and that could have impacted supply and demand.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Anecdotally, my conversations with both youths and youth workers have been alarming, as many shared how "soft" or recreation drugs were being pushed in venues familiar to our youths.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: A 2015/2016 survey by the National Council Against Drug Abuse (NCADA) also found that, over the years, youths were increasingly permissive when it came to drugs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Such a trend, though concerning, should perhaps not come as a surprise.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Globally, attitudes towards drug use have been shifting.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our digitally savvy youths consume a vast amount of what they know about the world through social networking sites.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: A 2017 Youth and Public Perception survey by NCADA found that, amongst youths aged 13 to 21, 16% “were open to trying drugs for a new experience, if they are overseas or if it does not affect their daily routine”.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Clearly, youth attitudes towards drugs appear to be slowly but steadily liberalising.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: There is nothing soft about soft drugs like methamphetamine, otherwise known as ice, glass, crystal or cannabis, otherwise known as marijuana, pot, grass, weed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: These substances are not less addictive, nor are they less harmful, as many young abusers misunderstand.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The Central Narcotics Bureau’s preventive drug education programmes have reached out to youths both within and outside of schools.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Despite our best efforts, how else can we drive home the message amongst youths of the harms that drug abuse brings?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This is, hence, a second area of concern for which, I propose, we will need to resource more heavily in the coming year, so that we do not lose our younger generations to the scourge of drugs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To ensure that our young ones do not fall prey to the perils of drugs and sexual offending, our response must be one that involves a much deeper understanding and appreciation of our youths’ psyche, a coordinated and deliberate movement across society to combat these ills afflicting our future generations and an openness in evolving our approaches to engage and empower our young people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Notwithstanding the points I had raised above, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Several parts of the Budget deal with developing our manpower resources to ensure we remain competitive, as well as how we can uplift our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My speech will centre on two key themes: first, ensuring that our workforce remains motivated and enterprising, and making sure we level up the working conditions of and opportunities for our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There has been an inexorable global drive by employees to seek work-life harmony.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Employees, especially new job entrants and younger workers, are drawn to workplaces that offer flexible work arrangements, like work-from-home and compressed work weeks, and that can guarantee freedom from work considerations outside of contracted working hours.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It has even been suggested in this House that we consider implementing a four-day work week and the right to disconnect.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This move to find workplaces that are more accommodative of workers’ personal pursuits and aspirations has been called the “Great Resignation” or the “Great Re-alignment”.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Although the statistics bear out that this may not have happened yet, it appears that the trends underlying the Great Re-alignment are likely to become the new norm.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: To give effect to such aspirations, the Government has, amongst other things, introduced the Tripartite Advisory for Work-Life Harmony and instituted an Alliance for Action for Work-Life Harmony.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is, however, easier for larger corporations and those with deeper pockets to put in place work-life harmony initiatives.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs may need to be more creative since – and this is something that Minister Tan See Leng mentioned earlier – they have less resources and could do with experts assisting them to design and implement such measures.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, employees’ expectations are to find a workplace that offers both work-life balance and an attractive salary and benefits.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is, of course, aspirational and, on the face of it, it is a good aspiration.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: However, there will always be workers who wish to do more, to go the extra mile, who take additional pride in their work and desire to do a good job.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, this may take them beyond their working hours.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I refer to these people, Madam, as “dedicated workers”.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are also workers who upend and buck the trend of work-life harmony, who are willing to forgo their benefits and their rights.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They are ambitious, driven and committed to achieve and surpass their organisation’s goals.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They want to do more because they want more.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They are hungry and their professional goals have become their personal goals.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I refer to these people, borrowing a phrase from professional sports, as “elite performers”.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Both these types of workers go beyond their contractual obligations and they do so not because they are asked to or because they are pressured to.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They do it out of a sense of responsibility and commitment to their job roles.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They still feel that they have work-life harmony, just perhaps a different form, because work-life harmony means different things to different people.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As we move towards balanced workplaces, we need to make sure that, inadvertently, these dedicated workers and elite performers are not discouraged from wanting to be the best and, if they wish to forgo their rights and benefits, we should not judge them, dissuade them or, even worse, ridicule them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, we must not allow a culture to develop that is against hard work and hard workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A case in point is the varied reception that Twitter's new CEO Parag Agrawal received when he announced that he would be taking "a few weeks of paternal leave" after the birth of his second child.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Many applauded him, seeing his move as helping to normalise the taking of paternal leave.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But there were some who questioned why he had taken only a few weeks and not the full 20 weeks he was entitled to; and others yet who criticised him when he said he would still be taking meetings while he was on leave and keeping up with the company's business.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is almost as if the responsibility and dedication to his work was being vilified.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Now to be clear, I am not saying that everyone should strive to be an elite performer.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A recent article on Rice Media titled "Everyone's Progressing, but I Lack Ambition.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Is That So Wrong?", carried a quote as follows: "Just because I'm not ambitious doesn't mean I'm lazy or lagging behind.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I don't need a big house, for example.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I don't need to travel the world too.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If I'm earning enough and happy, it's my choice".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And this is equally so for elite performers and dedicated workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But the difference may be felt ultimately in promotions and increments, and employees who decide to enjoy the fullness of their benefits should temper their expectations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is not because they are being punished – it is because it is fair, just and equitable to reward dedicated workers and to reward elite performers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The hard truth is that those who do more, especially if it exceeds expectations or contractual obligations, will get more.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And yes, this will inevitably spark others who also want to get ahead to go the extra mile.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: What is important is for employers to put in place mechanisms to prevent their elite employers and dedicated workers from burning out or suffering from mental health issues arising from work.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But employers and peers should never hold them back.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As regards to elite performers, we must make special effort to identify, nurture and promote them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They pull their organisations forward; in the private sector, they drive profit and growth, attract and keep clients, and they help to create more jobs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They include business leaders, entrepreneurs, admin service officers in the Government, senior counsels.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They include Razer CEO Tan Min-Liang, Singapore's youngest self-made billionaire, who recounted at a Singapore Management University commencement ceremony that he was spurred on by his parents who told him that he needed to just go get what he wanted out of life through hard work, attention to detail and responsibility.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They include Carousell CEO Quek Siu Rui who has said that he had not taken a holiday in years due to his obsession with his work and with doing things well and good.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For a country that has nothing but people as our resources, we need these captains of performance to continue to be motivated, to continue to push the boundaries and ultimately to expect, see and feel the rewards of their hard work.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And while we raise awareness about the importance of balance and mental health, an extremely critical endeavour, we should not forget to concomitantly celebrate our elite performers, to fortify them and to recognise them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is because their successes are the successes of their organisations and ultimately, of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While striving for work-life harmony, we should not lose our culture of meritocracy and our system of meritorious rewards.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I am happy to hear Minister Wong’s announcement of the new Singapore Global Executive Programme and I trust that our elite performers will be identified to be involved in it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, I call on the Action for Alliance for Work-Life Harmony and TAFEP to consider how to make sure that even as we adopt work-life harmony principles as norms at our workplaces, we do not at the same time unwittingly discourage elite performers and dedicated workers from putting in hard work and effort, and rising above the rest nor should we allow a culture of complacency and adversity to work to foster, because Singapore cannot afford it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I will now move on, Madam, to my next points on lower-wage workers, before which I declare my interest as President of the Security Association Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The narrative on work-life harmony is weighted towards flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is more suited to office workers and those whose work can be done remotely.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We need to consider the work-life harmony of employees who are in jobs that require them to be at their workplace, many of whom are essential workers like nurses, or in lower paying jobs like bus captains, cleaners and security officers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I raised this last year, but I feel compelled to raise it again this year.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Security agencies, who are the employers of security officer, can only do so much to change the norm of 12-hour work shifts, because as an outsourced service, supply follows demand.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, if a buyer stipulates 12-hour work shifts, that is all that an agency can bid for.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Most security contracts in both the private and public sector are based on 12-hour shifts.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We need to seriously think about whether this pattern of work is reasonable.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If we cater one and a half hours for her to wash up, have her breakfast and commute to work, it means she has to wake up at 6.30 am.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: By the time she gets home, it is 9.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If she has young children, she has barely an hour or less of time with them before they go to sleep.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: After she has her dinner, spent time with her family and done some chores, she goes to bed at 12.00 am.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If she needs more time for these things, she sleeps later.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This routine then continues, Madam, for the next six days before she has one day off and this day off may well be a weekday.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, Madam, amidst all this hullaballoo about work-life harmony, where is the work-life harmony for this security officer?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, more than 50,000 if we consider ad hoc workers and many of them, Madam, older workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, the private sector will take some convincing to move away from 12-hour shifts because it involves costs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Achieving work-life harmony for our lower-wage workers means challenging and changing their working conditions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I plead, Madam, that as we take steps towards achieving better work-life harmony generally, that our security officers, low-wage workers and older workers are not left behind.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Another group that may be left out in this drive to improve working conditions and work-life harmony are workers in outsourced services.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These are sectors where workers do not work at their employer's premises, but at third party sites that their employers are contracted to supply manpower.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
