text: As such, these employers do not have much control over their employees' physical working conditions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Working conditions and how these outsourced workers are treated are dictated by the service contracts between their employers and the service buyers, not the employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Outsourced workers are not even parties to these contracts and have no say in how they will be treated at their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Pursuant to the service agreements, they often face the threat of summary immediate removal from their workplaces or discrimination.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And they have no recourse nor protections under the law.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This issue must be addressed urgently as it affects a large proportion of our outsourced lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is similar to the Workplace Safety and Health Act, which imposes obligations on building owners and managing agents.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: However, prices in the PWM outsourced sectors continue to lag wages, as Minister Wong noted in his Budget speech and the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS) has been introduced to support businesses in the short term.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But the PWCS may operate ultimately as a crutch, in which service providers use it as leverage to bid lower in upcoming tenders.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The net effect is that these companies will find themselves in a similar position when the PWCS tapers off: that is, providing services at a rate that is unsustainable vis-à-vis the PWM wage increases.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, in order for companies in these sectors to meaningfully transform, including implementing work-life harmony schemes and adopting technology, they will need to earn enough to afford these measures.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If prices continue to lag wages, SMEs will invariably forego transformation initiatives for day-to-day operational needs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this connection, I would like to ask how the Competition Act applies to the PWM outsourced sectors, given that in the outsourced services sectors, fixing wages is essentially fixing the cost of supply.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On a related note, will the Government consider working with the tripartite partners to set out reasonable prices that service buyers can expect to pay for each of the PWM outsourced sectors, derived from objective costs, for example, insurance and costs of replacements, so that prices can keep in tandem with wage increases.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is because the PWM prescribes not only wage increases but also a skills and progression path.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In-house and outsourced workers in these sectors do identical work and differentiated wage ladders based on who their employers are, in my view, does not make sense.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On a related note, the current PWM sectors tend to have a fairly large number of ad hoc or part-time workers who choose to be ad hoc workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, many of them work every day, often with the same employer but do not take up full employment.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This would appear to be antithetical to the PWM, which provides a career progression path with concomitant skills upgrading.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, efforts should be made to encourage workers in these sectors to be employed full-time, instead of doing jobs on an ad hoc basis.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Some skills and professions, like that of gaffers, artists, technical crew, woodworkers and hawkers are best acquired through a period of apprenticeship.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This will first be implemented for the security industry but we will very soon then make it available for other industries as well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: To conclude, Sir, I support this Budget and all it will do to help our businesses and workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But despite our best efforts, some may still fall through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I have sought to identify some of these areas and have made suggestions as to what we could do.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Together with the cooperation of the tripartite partners, I have no doubt that we will not only chart a new way forward together but that we will also leave no one behind.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Singaporeans adjust to the new norms and with borders opening up progressively, our economy has also gradually improved, and the outlook is optimistic.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last year, I rose to speak about safeguarding and improving the welfare of three vulnerable segments of our population – persons with disabilities, women who are caregivers, and seniors living alone or with their spouse only.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given the 2022 Budget's focus on charting a new way forward together, I intend to highlight three areas where I feel there are long-term implications to pay more attention to as our nation moves forward to living with COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These three areas are: (a) social mobility amidst COVID-19, economic restructuring and digitalisation; (b) managing long-term healthcare needs; and (c) fulfilling the housing aspiration of our younger generation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, I would like to raise the issue of social mobility amidst economic restructuring and digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: COVID-19 has exacerbated the need for economic transformation and digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We know that this is important as we strive to thrive in a volatile, unpredictable and fast changing world.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet this may also bear a considerable impact on vulnerable groups including the lower-wage workers, middle-aged workers, persons with disabilities and their families.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While Singapore's overall unemployment rate saw a decline from 3% in 2020 to 2.6% in 2021, we know the recovery in the labour market remains uneven, especially for those that are more impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Families with members in these sectors would likely have experienced a greater loss of income or job insecurity and their children may face a host of obstacles in their social mobility.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A study in the UK assessing the social mobility implications of COVID-19 has shown that a fall in earnings can reduce the options available to displaced workers as they have less resources to finance reskilling and to lean on while they search for re-employment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For their children and young who are still in education, a fall in parental income or job loss has been shown to reduce attainment in school and through this, have long-run impacts on future earnings.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am thus really glad to hear in the Minister for Finance's Budget speech that we will continue to invest and upskill our workers and encourage companies to do so through skills development initiatives, increase in support for continued training and SkillsFuture Career Transition Programmes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These will certainly go towards helping our people remain employed and to transit into new growing industries and the digital economy.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Programmes such as the Fresh Start Housing Scheme, KidSTART, UPLIFT Community Pilot and scaling up of ComLink are also helpful in ensuring that our children in disadvantaged and low-income families have opportunities to improve their lives.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I note that many of these schemes will take years before they can reap their full benefits.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would thus like to ask how will the Government monitor and ensure that the families these schemes are targeted to help are making the transitions in these few years of rapid and intense changes?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also observe that families, for example, with parents who are trying to upskill, find new employment and manage their transition into new jobs while raising young children all at the same time would be struggling in juggling multiple demands.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The second topic that is close to my heart is the issue of managing the long-term healthcare needs of our ageing population.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic showed us the importance of building a resilient healthcare system.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singaporeans, healthcare and frontline workers have rallied together and through the cooperation and efforts of everyone, we have avoided overwhelming our hospitals.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I take this opportunity to salute all our hardworking healthcare workers and frontline workers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to continue to strengthen our healthcare systems and build capabilities to ensure that our frontline workers would remain adaptable in responding to future crises.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides being able to be prepared for future pandemics, a resilient healthcare system should also meet new challenges and changing healthcare needs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, the National Population Health Survey 2020 highlighted that diabetes prevalence increased with age where more than 20% of adults aged 60 and above are diabetic.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although the crude prevalence was partly attributable to population ageing, it is nonetheless important to know that more than one in every five older adults aged 60 to 75 are diabetic.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, the age-standardised prevalence also showed an increasing trend from 21.9% in 2017 to 31.7% in 2019 to 2020.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This data shows that we must do much more to manage chronic diseases in an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my Committee of Supply cuts for health, I will also elaborate on my suggestions on activating more primary care general practitioner's (GP) clinics as well as the use of technologies to help our population manage chronic diseases.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to hearing from the Ministry of Health their overall plan for managing population health.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, I would like to speak about helping to fulfil the aspirations of our younger adults and the challenges that they are facing in building a home and a family.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, it is definitely important for us to engage Singaporeans more, especially during these few years where housing remains an issue for many of the young couples who want to settle down.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we strengthen our resilience from the shadows of COVID-19, my hope is that the Singapore Dream – where opportunities and care continue to be available to all and aspirations of all Singaporeans can become real – will remain alive in the many years to come.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Allie – not her real name – is a girl who used to live in my constituency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When I first met her in 2016, she was just eight years old.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She was like a big sister to my daughter Ella, and they used to play together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her family had little and lived in a rental flat, but she gave what she could.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She patted Ella on her back whenever she coughed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One could not wish for a sweeter, kinder child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But all this changed when in about a year later, Allie was sent to live in a place of safety – to protect her and to help her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it also made her a completely different person.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Torn from her friends, her family and her home, she shrunk into her shell.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When I visited her, she barely spoke a word.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She just sat in the room and stared into space.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This was not the lively child I once knew, and it was heartbreaking to see how much she was affected and how she had her childhood ripped from her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is hard to blame the social workers at the place of safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They tried their best with the limited resources they had.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When I was there, I saw a little boy climbing the fence and the barb wires, trying to escape.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The social worker was trying so hard and so gently to calm him down.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Children like Allie need all the help they can get.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spent a lot of time thinking about what we can do to help children like her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I raised questions in Parliament about places of safety and about intergenerational incarceration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I thought, surely, we can launch new programmes, more programmes, to help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But as we deep dived into the issues, I realised we have plenty of programmes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The issue might be that social workers had too much on their plate and many were burned out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Over the past year, I talked with many social workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke to senior social workers and junior social workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke to those in the frontlines and those who have left the profession.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke to those from family service centres (FSCs) and from other voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also carried out a public survey and reached out to over 120 social workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I listened to their concerns, their worries and most of all, their deep passion in wanting to help others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But Sir, they too need help, especially during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The study also found that social workers in FSCs faced higher depression rates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These findings mirror what I was hearing from social workers in my dialogues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One after another, social workers described their heavy caseloads and exhaustion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I heard the same requests over and over again: requests for more time, more resources and more help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I want to focus on social workers at our FSCs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: FSCs are often the first port of call for those in need.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many see them as a clearing house for all social services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They advise and support families with financial, housing, employment, social and emotional resources.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I have three recommendations to give our social workers the time, resources and support they need.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first recommendation is to set a cap on the number of cases that each social worker can take on at any given time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, too many social workers are forced to juggle an excessive caseload.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If 22 cases was the maximum, that might be fine.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Maybe they are outliers but their views are important too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Social workers have told me that excessive caseloads directly hurt their ability to do a good job.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A FSC social worker shared with me that they feel that they are shortchanging their clients who so desperately need help and they feel bad.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another social worker shared this quote with me to explain how they feel, "If you ever wanna know what a social worker's mind feels like, imagine a browser with 2,857 tabs open.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All the time." With a huge caseload, they obviously have to give less attention to each case.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Often, they end up doing what they call "firefighting", which means tackling only the most urgent problems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This firefighting makes it hard for them to give 100% to each case.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It also denies them time to attend courses, mentor junior staff and create community programmes, equally important tasks that build organisational capacity, transfer knowledge and support communities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Elizabeth Quek, a community social worker, shared about "the helplessness social workers feel when we don't have the time or resources for someone who needs more support." This is not a sustainable solution and many social workers are reaching or have reached their breaking point.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to have a cap on the number of cases that social workers can take on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In many industries, caps are set to ensure service quality remains high.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Schools, for example, limit the number of students in each class so teachers can dedicate more attention to each student.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Quek, whose quote I shared earlier, said that reducing caseloads will improve social workers' capacity to help their clients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know this cannot happen overnight and it is not easy to implement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will require changes in FSC human resources (HR) practices but this cap is absolutely necessary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The actual number of the cap should also be decided in consultation with social workers from across the profession and take into consideration the wide spectrum of cases – Group 2, Group 3 and Group 4 cases – a social worker handles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Social workers told me they spend a significant part of their work entering data from their cases into the Social Service Net, or SSNet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This might sound like a miserable task but many social workers I spoke to talked about SSNet as a treasure trove of data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They think the rich information stored on SSNet could provide useful insights on the communities they serve.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some social workers have spent their personal time, after work hours, to trawl through and crunch the data in search of insights.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One enthused to me about how it would be possible to run a sentiment analysis by applying natural language processing techniques to the data, to surface trends across cases in the same community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Their graduates emerge with research and technical skills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be a waste for them to let these skills atrophy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I have mentioned, the only barrier is that FSCs often do not allocate time or staff to do research.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The same social workers who beamed about unlocking the insights held in the SSNet data were also the ones frustrated by how they never had the time or support to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: About half of the social workers that I surveyed shared that their FSCs do not have dedicated manpower for research work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: About 85% wanted Government funding for headcounts dedicated to research.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know MSF is trying to help and recognises the importance of research work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It does provide FSCs with data from SSNet whenever a social worker request for it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we can cut the administrative workload of social workers making these constant requests by having in-house researchers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With funding support and dedicated headcounts, our FSCs can arm themselves with data about the vulnerable families and communities they serve and they can go upstream to solve these issues within the community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That brings me to my third and final recommendation today – to increase the time, resources and headcount for community work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke earlier about how social workers do not have the time to do things like create community programmes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, when I met them, some social workers described community work as their CCA, as something secondary to case work, something they dabble in during their spare time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it is something they feel is crucial.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It enables FSCs to reach at-risk families not yet clients of theirs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This improves outcomes as the families can receive support before their problems worsen significantly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Easier to put out small fires than raging infernos, after all.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: No man or woman is an island, and everyone needs a robust social network to succeed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Often, families working with FSCs lack friends and neighbours they can count on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Through community work, FSCs can link their clients with others in the same community and enable them to provide mutual support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This reduces the family’s reliance on institutions such as FSCs, helps them succeed in a sustainable way and also offers a way for families themselves to support others around them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Community work will also help to slow the inflow of new cases which will give social workers the space and time they need.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It might help to break the vicious cycle some social workers are in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are other NGOs that do community work and, indeed, many do excellent work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But why not empower FSCs to do the same?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: FSCs are located in the heart of the community and they have their finger on the pulse of their community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: FSCs are already working with many of the people in the community, already meeting with them regularly and have the data on the trends and needs on the ground that many other NGOs do not have.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There might be worries about duplication of work but there is so much to be done.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should be concerned but I think we hardly need to fear the duplication of work currently.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: About half of the FSC social workers I surveyed said their FSCs do not have dedicated manpower and resources for community work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But there is a lot more we need to do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, social workers need to know there is existing funding for this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During my consultations with social workers, many were surprised to hear that funding for this headcount existed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, we need to increase the funding available.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many social workers shared that funding for two headcounts is hardly sufficient.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, MSF needs to work closely with FSCs and ensure they use this funding available to them and hire the headcounts required to focus on community work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She has been released from the Place of Safety and I brought her out for a meal and a day at the arcade with my daughter recently.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that one day Allie will be able to lead a stable and fulfilling life within the community in spite of everything she has gone through.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope no other child has to go through what Allie went through.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To do this, we need to help our social workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate the important work that MSF is doing and I could feel the passion in the room when they spoke about how they were helping FSCs and social workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That really is what some social workers are feeling.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Social workers want to be the social safety trampoline that Senior Minister Tharman spoke about.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can and we must do more to help our social workers and empower them to help make Singapore a better place and more inclusive place for all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I think, so far, from yesterday to today, we have heard many hon parliamentarians in this Chamber talk about this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This impact is especially salient for middle- and lower-income households, both financially and psychologically.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Household income growth barely matched the CPI growth in the same period for these households, as median monthly household income from work grew by 3.6% in nominal terms from 2020 to 2021.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, at first glance, middle- and low-income households may feel pressured that their incomes are only barely matching the rise in prices.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But after taking into account Government transfers, middle- and low-income households would have seen higher real income growth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I am glad that the Government has multiples schemes, such as the CDC vouchers, education accounts top-ups and enhanced U-Save rebates, in place to support these households.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, we must not undermine the psychological factor of the public, even if income is still outpacing inflation in reality.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is not always immediately obvious how Government transfers have buffered the impact.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It takes multiple steps to calculate the net impact.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, there remains much uncertainty in how costs can fluctuate in the future and, therefore, how families can or cannot cope.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The psychology of uncertainty, if left unaddressed, can severely affect one’s well-being but, more importantly, threaten our nation’s ability to stay together, overcome crisis together and progress together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Rising global demands for the same products that we demand with the arrival of COVID-19 vaccines, oil and gas supply crunch made worse by geopolitical turmoil, and global supply chain woes are driving costs up.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Clearly, these are macro factors beyond our control.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, the sudden spike in energy price forced a few of the open energy market operators out of operations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Customers are transferred back to grid operator SP Group.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Or, they could choose other private operators that survived.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Regardless, energy prices have increased significantly across the board.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During a house visit in January this year, I met a MacPherson resident who runs a small shop and she shared her frustration and anxiety with me.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She had subscribed to Best Electric, one of the open energy market operators that went bust last year.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For small operators with a modest margin, such a shocking increase drives them into the red.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Needless to say, these small operators, many of whom are Singaporeans with families, will see their household disposable income being affected as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could the Government have stepped in more strongly in such extraordinary instances to help mitigate the increase?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Perhaps, to put a cap to the amount of increment for these affected small businesses and household in such instances where the impact or the increase was not of their own doing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In another example, an elderly couple in MacPherson in their 70s live on their CPF payouts and allowance of a couple of hundreds of dollars per month from their three children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They are typical middle-income Singaporeans who have retired and are living in a flat of their own.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One may argue that this is not too bad and they certainly receive subsidies and benefits from various Government schemes as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But both elderly have chronic medical conditions that incur recurring medical costs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: MediSave savings are also fast depleting for them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They tried and are still trying to be self-reliant but rising food, groceries, utilities and public transport costs in recent times are really testing for them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While Singaporeans understand that some factors are beyond Singapore’s immediate control, and that self-efforts are important, the pressure from fast rising costs stress them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Successive news or observations of price increases in a short time frame are unsettling.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I sincerely appreciate Government’s efforts in introducing various support packages to help households and retirees cope with living costs, as well as uplifting workers to uplift wages.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The latest measures announced in Budget 2022, along with those introduced in the past, will help to push down the “bottomline” costs and push up “topline” income for households.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Government transfers through various help schemes help to offer buffer, but households are uncertain how much the costs will rise further, how long might they be eligible for Government subsidies or assistance and whether the assistance is even enough for them to cope.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For retirees who no longer have active income, this worry intensifies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What happens if the oil price spikes again or if the oil price and, therefore, the electricity bill stays high?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singaporeans must not feel that they are left to deal with the pressures alone as this can erode our sense of togetherness and undermine the social compact in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, our Government must continue to assure Singaporeans of its support through words and deeds.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Next, I would like to speak on the national reserves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Again, I am thankful that our past and present leaders have been judicious in managing our reserves, painstakingly saving up for "storms" like this COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Money drawn from our past reserves has been put to good use as we battle the crisis and provide tangible support for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My question now is – from this point, what is the Government’s plan for our national reserves?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our Pioneers took more than 50 years to save up this pot of gold because they want to protect their children and future generations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Similarly, we have a duty to use this pot of gold wisely and make sure that we put back what we took once we can, so that our children and their children can continue to have this asset to fall back on when they face the crisis of their generation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Lest I get misunderstood, let me state that I believe it was necessary for us to draw on our reserves to help Singapore and Singaporeans get through this COVID-19 storm.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I also believe that at this juncture when Singaporeans are struggling with escalating cost of living, now is not the right time to put money back into the reserves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My next point is on building up for the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many of the problems we face today are not novel.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We probably already have the solutions to these old problems and we need to accelerate the implementation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For instance, our energy needs are over-reliant on oil and gas that we import.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We benefit from processing these imported natural resources but our electricity prices are almost totally dependent on the prices set by oil export countries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One solution is to diversify to use clean energy so as to dilute the impact of oil prices on our own energy cost, and I believe this topic has been very passionately debated by fellow colleagues yesterday and today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And I am also aware that the Energy Market Authority is also actively exploring these solutions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Another possible solution is to actively deploy smart technology that allow us to move from reactive to predictive maintenance, so that we can save energy and reduce waste.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This also includes other types of green technology as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The upfront CAPEX could be costlier, but the longer-term savings could be worth it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, the problem is not without a solution, but could we hasten it?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to build future-ready infrastructure that can last.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When others are looking at 5G, we must look at 6G.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When others are looking at Web 3.0, we must start imagining Web 4.0.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The current S-curve is already saturated, we need to get onto the next.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And to do so, of course, we need good people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I am definitely also very supportive of the plans to invest in our people throughout the stages of their lives, from when they are young and in school to when they have entered the workforce and can benefit from mentorship to when they reach mid-career and to when they have become mature workers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It used to be that one’s career is a straight-line progression, hardly changing jobs or industry.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But it will increasingly be commonplace for one to change path multiple times in his/her working lifespan.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, by investing in our people, we not only help Singaporeans to achieve their many aspirations but also recognise them as our nation’s key asset.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I will also speak more on this during the Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By building up for the future, we can better take advantage of the opportunities and rise comfortably above the challenges that we now face.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To move away from quibbling over small margins but changing games altogether.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From focusing on survival as a nation in the 1960s to the 1980s, to the "Many Helping Hands" approach that encouraged a greater sense of collective responsibility, and that was from the 1990s to the mid 2000s, to now recognising that Government and the community need to play a bigger role to complement individual and family efforts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we look ahead, the world is getting chaotic again, Singapore’s society is also getting more complex with more sophisticated needs and issues.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are still many challenges and uncertainties ahead.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, to continue keeping our people and Singapore together, we must have sufficient guardrails, sufficient support and very importantly, mutual trust that we will be there for each other in good times and bad.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore will definitely emerge much stronger with every generation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is because IHLs need to keep pace with industry changes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: A candidate applying for an IT support position in his 50s did not have any diploma in IT or a degree in IT.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, the HR department did not think he was fit to join as an executive using the conventional wisdom.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But this candidate had a lot of work experience in running an IT infrastructure and support business.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: He self-learned over the years and was competent in IT support.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Eventually, the IT head decided to hire him, and he performed very well thereafter.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This episode reflects the need for continuous training and lifelong learning and IHLs need to play this role.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When my son was about to complete his full-time National Service last year, he was searching for a temporary job before commencing university this August.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While serving his National Service, he started diving into the rabbit hole of blockchain, cryptocurrencies, decentralised finance and stablecoins.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With his deep knowledge about cryptocurrency, he managed to land a temporary job with a cryptocurrency firm as an analyst despite having no official training.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: All things related to cryptocurrency is developing very fast and is hard to imagine how the subject can be taught in the university with sufficient currency.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: After working for a few months, he wants to defer his university education to pursue his interest and continue working in the same field.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: He does not want to miss the swift developments in the cryptocurrency industry.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I am old school and very much believe in the notion of having a university degree to fall back on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But taking a step back, I am amazed that these days, young people without a university degree can do very well in certain industries especially in technology and make a very decent living.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: These days, even without a university degree, skill sets, personal experiences and knowledge can take a person very far.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Young people may have their own ideas about their professional development.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Taking this into account, our universities need to evolve to remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Unlike my time in the university, the main pillar of the curriculum was to impart knowledge and learn how to search for information in the library.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But today, knowledge is abundant with the help of the Internet.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The demise of print encyclopaedia reflects this reality.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: What is important about university education is to learn how to search information, verify the information and organise the information to present in a coherent, concise and simple manner.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: University education is also about sharpening the presentation skills, collaboration skills, social skills and other soft skills through project works, through tutorial seminars and internship, both locally and overseas.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, do we still need a four-year full degree course?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Should we have extended and more purposeful internships as part of transformation of IHLs that Minister for Education is thinking about?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: How do we involve industry leaders in shaping the curriculum of the IHL education so that the professors and students are more in touch with the industry’s needs and development?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Can we have the flexibility of converting the second half of the full-time degree course into a part-time degree should the students want to extend his internship or even start work earlier?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Above are food for thoughts as we transform our IHLs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is always evolving, and we cannot be static.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: People with tech skills are high in demand.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Or will it burst just like the dot.com bubble did 20 years ago?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Given the trend of how digital technology has disrupted many industries, there is a high chance that this technology craze will continue for quite a while.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In fact, every company has to be tech company to survive.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Even the media companies that are reporting our speeches in Parliament have to be tech driven as declared by the chairman of the newly formed SPH Media Limited.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I know of a family where the daughter, a fresh graduate of computer science, is earning close to the pay of her mother who has been a teacher with MOE for more than 30 years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, we have many recent Polytechnic and University graduates that cannot find jobs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There are also many mid-career PMETs who have lost their jobs and aspire to earn the starting pay of the recent IT graduates.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I had the privilege of visiting Tata Consulting Services (TCS) SG United Program with Minister Iswaran about two years ago.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I also recently had lunch with the Asia Pacific Head of TCS.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I understand that the trainees go through foundational and specialised training courses in areas like cloud adoption, artificial intelligence, machine learning, coding and getting on-the-job training by working on projects with TCS clients.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If we believe in the notion that every company has to be a tech company to survive, then almost all key personnel in the company, ranging from HR, customer service, marketing, procurement, all have to be IT savvy and be able to adopt technology that can make their work more efficient and effective.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: That being the case, the IHLs have the urgent need to incorporate tech components in almost every course in the university.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: More importantly, the IHLs have the mission to provide continuous training to existing professionals to equip them with technology and skills so that they can keep up with the industry trends.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If we take a step back, we may need to examine if we need to put a time stamp on the degree conferred by universities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: One radical idea is to put it as a requirement that the graduates have to attend upgrading courses every five years or so.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If you do not upgrade, your degree will fade over time and you no longer can claim the degree as your credential after a while.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It may not and should not happen overnight.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But, we have to start to transform our IHLs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Budget debate over the past two days has seen two consensus and one difference.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The first consensus is that the Members of Parliament all agree that the country's spending needs to be increased, especially the budget for MOH.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is because our population is ageing, healthcare costs will go up year by year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The second consensus is that so far, no Member of Parliament has suggested cutting our defence spending to pay for the increase in healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Because of the war in Ukraine, many people realised the importance of national defence.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If we cannot ensure our territorial integrity, there is no need to debate this Budget here.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Therefore, I am heartened that Members of Parliament who have questioned why defence spending is so high in the past, or have asked the Government to freeze or even cut defence spending, are no longer making the same request.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, the biggest difference now is that several Members of Parliament have called for using more Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Currently, half of NIRC is spent on Government spending and the other half is used for topping up our reserves to increase investment capitals, thus increasing the returns on our net investment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Without this $43 billion, the NIRC will also be reduced.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, the Finance Minister has also said that it is difficult to plug this big hole with current Government revenue, especially taxes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Without the trees planted by our forefathers, we would not have the reserves to help Singaporeans to cope with the impact of COVID-19 in the past two years.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: With COVID-19, the mental health of care workers, caregivers – and I shall refer to them as "carers" – has deteriorated significantly in the past two years.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many news articles have come out recently, documenting the stress that they have come under due to the disruptions brought about by the pandemic, whether they were social workers, teachers, healthcare workers, mental health workers or informal caregivers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As my colleague, hon Member Mr Louis Ng, mentioned in his speech last evening, 56% of social workers had mild to severe anxiety during the past two years.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Burnout occurs when people feel overburdened and depleted of emotional and physical energy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Some effects of burnout include loss of motivation, negativity, a sense of failure, self-doubt and a cynical attitude towards others, as well as a loss of empathy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Empathy is the bedrock of caring professions and it runs short when people feel burnt out.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What quality of care can we reasonably expect when those who toil in our care professions and social services are stretched too thin?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In charting a new way forward together, we need to protect the well-being of those who take on the work of caring for others, because people can only provide quality care to others when they themselves are well physically, mentally and emotionally.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Two things are vital to ensure quality care: adequate capacity and adequate recognition.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need to provide sufficient resources and support to carers so that no one burns out.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We also need adequate recognition through reasonable compensation and opportunities for advancement to boost morale and motivation and ensure that the care industry remains sustainable in the long term.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Most people who chose the care professions are motivated by a strong desire to care for others and very few are calculative about monetary contributions and compensation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: However, we should still take good care of them and ensure that they have the means to sustain themselves.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many caregivers shared with me in focus groups last year that they struggled to pay for outpatient expenses that are inadequately covered under MediSave.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Such costs add to a family's financial burden, especially for those who had little choice but to give up their jobs and income to care for ageing parents, special needs children or mentally-afflicted family members.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The pandemic also made caregiving responsibilities and expenses heavier because care resources, like daycare centres and domestic workers, were short in supply, as shown in a survey done by the Singapore Alliance for Women in Ageing (SAWA) in 2020.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Care recipients who require assistance with more activities of daily living (ADLs) can and should be supported with higher amounts of HCG.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many caregivers who had to quit their jobs suffer a loss of self-identity, decreased self-worth and emotional stress.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Often, the family members who are not personally involved in care work fail to understand how demanding it is.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Carefare is one way we can provide crucial financial relief and offer recognition to informal caregivers for the labour of caregiving.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I will now speak a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   I recommend that the Government enhance financial support for informal caregivers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I urge the Government to increase the quantum of the Home Caregiving Grant for informal caregivers and implement "Carefare".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many caregivers shared that they faced various challenges, including not being able to pay for outpatient expenses that are inadequately covered under MediSave.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Such costs add to a family's financial burden, especially those who had little choice but to give up their jobs and income to care for their ageing parents, special needs children or mentally-inflicted family members.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: According to a survey done by the Singapore Alliance for Women in Ageing in 2020, the pandemic made care resources like daycare centres and domestic workers short in supply, aggravating the financial burden and pressures faced by caregivers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Because finances are the most significant source of stress for caregivers, improving the Home Caregiving Grant will go a long way to lighten their load.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Carefare is what I propose as a scheme similar to Workfare, but for lower-income individuals who provide full-time care to their loved ones, not by choice, but by circumstance.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many caregivers who had to quit their jobs suffer a loss of self-identity, decreased self-worth and emotional stress.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Family members who are not involved in the actual care work also often fail to understand how demanding it is.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Carefare is a way to provide crucial financial relief and offer recognition for the labour of caregiving.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Second, we need to ensure adequate national resourcing for social work, social services, healthcare and mental health care to be adequately staffed and well-protected from work hazards.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond salaries, we can do more to enable them in their work and support them in their well-being.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: More preventive steps need to be taken to ensure that healthcare workers remain safe and supported at work.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond just improving salaries, we need to ensure safety, support and adequate staffing, to retain and develop individuals in the care sector for as long as possible to adequately meet the needs of our ageing population.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, we need to protect our teachers from burnout.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The role and workload of teachers have expanded drastically over the years.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, teachers face more challenges as well as increased expectations of them, with home-based learning and the rising concern over our youths' mental health.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In October last year, there was a letter written from a Mr Ng Wei Yang to The Straits Times and his plea went, "My wife's a teacher.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Can I have her back with my family please?" I have spoken about this before in Parliament and I caution again about putting dual responsibility on teachers to double up as counsellors amidst an already overwhelming workload.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Although teacher-counsellors will have a reduced teaching load, I am concerned about whether they will have sufficient bandwidth and emotional capacity to do both effectively while maintaining their own mental health.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Some teachers shared with me that providing students with some form of basic counselling is already part of their role and they do it quite organically.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: However, I am concerned that formalising this role could create even more expectations by parents and the public towards teachers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The mental health of our teachers is next on the line if we continue to load them with too many expectations.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I hope MOE will augment its efforts in this area with effective stakeholder communication towards parents.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: On top of that, other than being trained in youth psychology, the Ministry could consider adding on training in family therapy for school counsellors.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: School counsellors need to be well-versed in the everyday struggles faced by youths, including those they may encounter within their families.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Other skills, such as mediation, could be helpful to foster and bridge relationships between students and their parents, especially during the difficult adolescent years.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Within the wider community, I urge MOE, MSF and MOH to jointly resource and enable the training of mental health responders and volunteers from the grassroots to be empathic listeners.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Our People's Association (PA) grassroots network has been a formidable and dependable way to reach out to residents in times of need, from mask distribution to mobilisation for vaccination and, in pre-COVID-19 times, organising activities to bring people together.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can tap on this network further, provide targeted training to suitable members and build their capabilities in one-to-one care support to residents.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Social Service Agencies (SSAs) can partner PA to train and equip volunteers as befrienders in the community for anyone who needs a non-judgemental listening ear and guidance on further resources for help.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Someone facing mental health struggles may not need to see a counsellor if they feel listened to early on in their difficulties.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Those who require more attention and expertise can be advised by the befrienders on where to get more support.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This pool of volunteers serve to help distribute and mitigate the care load from the limited number of existing professional counsellors until we can train more to handle the needs in the system.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am piloting this in Nee Soon South with the support of Yishun Health and HPB this year, and I look forward to share our learnings to help build this care network model in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, we need to enable SSAs to improve their capacity-building capabilities.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We should use such support to encourage private philanthropists and corporate donors to finance capacity-building in Singapore's SSAs for roles and headcounts, such as volunteer management, marketing and communications and fundraising.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to the implementation details and hope it will be a simple process for SSAs in its execution.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need to help redistribute their care load.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   A mentally healthy nation is a strong nation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: If we could provide better care for our caregivers, they will be able to better look after more people.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: If we take better care of our carers, they can care better for many more.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding the above that begs further attention, I fully support the Budget.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many look out for what the Government is planning to do to address day-to-day cost of living issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some look out for whether the Government will do more to address their areas of concern and the matters they champion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For the Members of this House, the Budget debate and the Committee of Supply debate provide the opportunity for us to talk about issues that are close to our hearts and to highlight areas for the Government to look at more deeply.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For me, it is also an opportunity to share about everyday heroes who advocate for important issues in the community, who quietly work hard to improve their lives and those of others and, in their own ways, contribute to nation-building.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are two people I would like to speak about today.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I want to first introduce you to Dr Chen Shiling.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Dr Chen is a medical doctor trained in internal medicine and who has special interests in dementia and intellectual disability (ID).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: When she was in Junior College, she had the opportunity to volunteer at MINDS, to provide support to individuals with ID.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She shared candidly that, in the beginning, the experience was daunting and, after her first session, she was not certain if she would do it again.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Despite her reservations, she continued to help out at MINDS over the years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: After graduating from medical school and becoming a doctor, she volunteered in her free time to give medical care to patients with ID.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is challenging because, typically, patients with ID also have multiple medical issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Aside from that, what Dr Chen came to realise was that it was also necessary to track the health and well-being of their parents and caregivers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Patients with ID depend on their caregivers for many things, including, but not limited to, compliance with medication, nutrition and therapies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Their health, largely, depends on the ability of their caregivers to manage their care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This means that the health and well-being of the caregivers also needed to be addressed, especially as they age.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is a fairly niche area relating to healthcare and, although seemingly illogical, it is a refreshing and efficient approach to the issue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Only someone in the sector and familiar with working with such families would appreciate the specific challenges they face and curate the appropriate solutions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe this area of work is very important.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have heard, in recent times, the call to provide more support for families with children with special needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I will touch more on this in my speeches for the COS debate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, Minister Chan Chun Sing’s and Minister Masagos Zulkifli’s replies to recent Parliamentary Questions gave assurance that the Government will continue to strengthen efforts and will work with the community to provide this support and build an inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Dr Chen has been championing this cause of caring for patients with ID and their caregivers as a family unit for many years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She has been working with Government agencies to see how this effort can be made accessible to more in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a parent of a child with ID, I am heartened and glad that there are people like Dr Chen, who looks out for the needs of those with special needs and their caregivers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They do not only volunteer their time but seek to find solutions to make things better for others, especially for those who are vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Dr Chen shows how it is so important to walk the talk.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She does not just give comments and expect the Government to come up with the solutions, but she has come up with substantive and constructive plans, tirelessly working with partners and taking effort to implement the ideas.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The other person I would like to talk about today is Mr Hafiz Kasman.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Mr Hafiz is a graduate from Singapore Management University (SMU), who co-founded Kinobi Asia.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Mr Hafiz was a consultant, and Kinobi initially started as a movement during COVID-19 to help prepare students for the working world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Mr Hafiz and his friends-turned-partners started conducting webinars on career role models and tips on how to get into different industries.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Mr Hafiz realised from there that there is a big under-served market of students preparing for jobs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe this is also an area that the Government is keenly aware of.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The pandemic has reshaped the economy, made some sectors less desirable but also created new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Those who were about to enter the workforce had to adjust, like everyone else, and prepare for this new world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For several years, even before the pandemic, the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) had developed their career guidance framework.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There were efforts by NYC and Young NTUC to provide resources for the youths to learn about growth sectors and how to prepare themselves for the working world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For example, the YouthTech Programme launched by NYC for youths to gain work insights in the increasingly important area of technology and digitalisation, creates pathways for young people to learn new skills and gain tangible experiences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Another example is the career symposium entitled LIT DISCOvery organised by Young NTUC as part of the SkillsFuture month in July last year.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There were online webinars, workshops as well as virtual mentoring and masterclasses to equip youths and young working adults with the necessary technology and soft skills to pivot into new and evolving job roles in the growth sectors.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think the provision of support for our youths remains acute and necessary.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Aside from career guidance, mentoring should also be an area that the Government continues to develop.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In fact, Mr Hafiz, whom I was speaking about, is, himself, a champion of mentoring.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He is the co-Chairman of the Mentoring AfA and also oversees Mara Mentoring, one of the M3 programmes, which aims to accelerate the career and personal progression of high-potential Malay/Muslim undergraduates, by connecting them to a dedicated community of successful early career professionals.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Mr Hafiz has also managed to turn his passion into a business opportunity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Kinobi sees itself as the technology partner for university career services, driving a systemic change.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They create, replace and augment the institution’s career platforms, enabling career services staff to do more to serve their student population.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Mr Hafiz said that Kinobi is thriving with the support of the Government and the Singapore ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: His alma mater, SMU, has supported them via their incubator, by connecting them to the alumni based in Indonesia and by partnering with Kinobi across initiatives like SMU Fintech Symposium.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Dr Chen Shiling and Mr Hafiz Kasman, our people, are pieces of the puzzle in realising our vision of a fairer, more inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In renewing and strengthening our social compact, the Government needs to address areas of concern, especially of groups which are vulnerable and have been most affected by the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But part of the deal must be that of active participation of our people in augmenting Government efforts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The needs are acute and varied and we need the Government to provide the framework for whole of society to come on board in this journey of making our society more inclusive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is value in enhancing the resolution of this support through developing the framework for mentoring.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many of us have had the good fortune of meeting someone in our lives who has guided us, shown us what is possible and brought us to a completely different trajectory in our lives.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Not everyone, or every young person, is as fortunate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should build an ecosystem of support, a culture of mentoring, so that every young person, regardless of his or her background, has the chance to be guided to find and seize all the opportunities that come their way.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, aside from the Government's efforts, Singaporeans also need to play their part.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many Members of this House have spoken about this, too.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government needs to be responsible for providing the fiscal framework for the economy to thrive and provide the infrastructure for many dimensions of support for different demographics in the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, there are many opportunities for all of us to fill in the gaps and propel our community forward.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   In renewing and strengthening our social compact between the Government and society, the Government has the responsibility to address the issues faced by those who are in need or have been most affected by the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, all of us also have a role to participate actively in all efforts to help uplift the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My hope is that, firstly, the Government continues to channel funds to increase support for families with children who have special needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Their needs are varied and we need the Government to provide a framework for the whole of society to work hand in hand to build a more inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Second, the Government should continue to provide opportunities for our young people to explore career opportunities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It would be good to build on efforts to create a mentoring ecosystem, so that every young person gets the support they need to succeed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Third, every Singaporean must participate in efforts to build the nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government needs to think of ways to ensure that our economy continues to progress and provide support for various groups in society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, there is much we can do to uplift our community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: All of us have to play a part.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, to me, the Budget goes beyond just fiscal considerations but reflects our priorities and shapes what we become as a nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A Budget channels funds, creates opportunities and empowers individuals.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, it is not the be-all and end-all and should not be so.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope we can find solace in the strength and unity of our people, to share the load and take advantage of the opportunities before us.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Though these can offset the GST increases for up to 10 years for the lowest income group, we should continue to look out for those among us who need more support.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, faced with higher costs in their daily expenses, from the prices of food and drinks to other grocery bills, Singaporeans are feeling the pinch constantly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every day, when people have to pay the extra 20 cents or 30 cents more for their beverages and 50 cents more for their food, they feel squeezed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The elderly and retired feel such financial pressures especially keenly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, that adds an additional layer of stress and anxiety to their lives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is, therefore, important to remind worried Singaporeans that there is a package to help offset these increases, through this package, as well as other support schemes that are in place.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, it will be especially helpful to provide some reassurance that the Government is watching the inflation rate very closely and will consider additional support measures when necessary.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As for our elderly residents living in private estates, I have also received some feedback that they do not receive as much assistance.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Yes, they do receive assistance but, understandably, it will be less than HDB dwellers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge MOF to consider highlighting the various payouts to all residents in both public and private housing estates through a letter or email to them or a mode of communication that they are comfortable with.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Though this might alleviate some stress, I would still appeal for more consideration of some cases, as they do have genuine circumstances that do warrant more support.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singaporeans in the middle-income group have always felt that they are “sandwiched” as their incomes are not rising as fast as the inflation rate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, they are not receiving as much help as the lower-income groups and, yet, they are contributing taxes and also have to grapple with increased prices.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They feel strongly that the incremental revenue needs to come from the affluent and not the middle-income sandwich class, considering that our taxes are still low, compared to countries we are competing against.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some have suggested taxing capital gains and dividends and increasing them progressively.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I know that we are not taking that route today as it will not help to attract investors and companies coming to set up shop in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I do sincerely hope that the Government watches this space carefully so that the sandwich class does not feel squeezed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the Employment Pass issue, I have also received feedback from some residents that foreigners’ salaries seem to be going up faster than local salaries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is actually a misunderstanding of our EP policy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, this change is, in fact, a higher barrier to foreigners and to get employers to hire locals for job functions at this salary level instead of foreigners.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some Singaporeans have misunderstood this to be pushing employers of new EP applicants to give them a salary increment, instead of the intent of this change, which is to put up a higher barrier.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that MOM can continue to watch out for such employment trends in the months to come and to be ready to take firm action if employers are found to be abusing the system at the expense of local staff.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Turning to hawker trade heritage, a topic very close to many of us and our hearts, affordable food in our hawker centres has helped to keep the cost of living manageable.
