speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These delicious dishes are loved by all income groups.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, many of our hawkers do not have successors for their trade.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their children are not interested, as many have jobs which do not require long hours on their feet over a hot stove.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The compensation sum should reflect the value of the heritage recipe and technique.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In turn, the apprentice could be bonded to the stall for a period of, say, three years, for example; if I may say so, similar to a Government scholarship with a bond.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will help to keep our hawker trade alive and ensure that our hawker culture stays on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should also start reviewing how we can transform the hawker trade.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we improve the work conditions so as to attract more younger hawkers?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is it possible to improve productivity in the hawker trade, ensure fair prices, rest and medical care?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have already seen some hawkers adopting machines to automate their cooking or other processes and we have seen how most of our hawkers have now adopted digital payments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We will, therefore, need to review all aspects and think out of the box to keep our hawker traditions alive.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore will, definitely, not be the same without our hawkers and we have to put in greater efforts to support the hardworking men and women who labour every day to fill our stomachs with delicious and affordable meals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Our hawker centres offer delicious and affordable dishes, which are loved by all the people from all income groups.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will help to keep our hawker traditions alive and ensure that our hawker culture will be preserved under the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Sir, I conclude with my support for the Budget.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I echo Minister Vivian Balakrishnan’s sentiments that Singapore cannot accept the unjustified attack by one country on another.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This was a clear violation of the Olympic Truce.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Hearing the Ukrainian athletes and what Ukraine is going through is truly heartbreaking.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The sporting world is aligned with the Minister’s position that the sovereignty, political independence and territorial integrity of countries, big and small, must be respected.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: My thoughts and prayers are with the citizens of Ukraine today.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I now turn to speak on the Budget.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I rise in support of this today and I consider that the Budget is a sensible one that balances the long- and short-term needs of the country.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It also focuses on national development in a sustainable manner that addresses the challenges posed by climate change.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As some of you know, yesterday was Founders’ Day and as our motto goes, “The best is yet to be”.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: So, today, in keeping with this motto, I shall raise three issues which I believe can bring our society to new heights.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: One, how do we, as a society, manage the rising cost of living?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Two, how do we ensure a safe and sensible reopening of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And, three, as we look forward into the future, how do we create a better and more conducive space for the development of the sports in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I speak, first, about managing the rising cost of living in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This is a concern which many hon Members and colleagues have raised, in particular, the effects of rising costs felt, primarily, by the sandwich class and youths in Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Although the cushioning measures are generous, the rising cost of living is a concern and I raise three issues in this regard.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Given additionally that the rising tensions in Europe are expected to bring an increase in energy prices, I am concerned daily living expenses will increase significantly.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Second, on manpower, I am also concerned about the adjustments to the foreign worker policies, in particular, the rise in minimum qualifying salaries for S-Pass holders and the impact of these adjustments on the hospitality, F&B and construction industries.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Would such measures increase the costs of labour which would, ultimately, be borne by the end consumer?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The cost of living in Singapore will also impact Singapore’s competitiveness in being able to attract talent from overseas.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We need to keep a close eye on this.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I wholeheartedly support a review of the programming at IHLs to not only provide quality continuing education and training, but also to prepare Singaporeans with skills to take up job opportunities in the market.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: But we must not forget our seniors and persons with disabilities (PWDs) in this endeavour.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: How would we enable PWDs to access job opportunities?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Is there more that we can do in this endeavour?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that addressing these concerns will not only lay the foundation for the successful implementation of these measures but also create a liveable and affordable Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I now move on to talk about my second point – ensuring a safe and sensible reopening of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore takes a positive posture to reopening and leans on the possibilities of a COVID-19-endemic world, I would like to take a moment to thank our frontliners and immigration officers for their hard work and dedication over the past two years in ensuring the health and safety of Singaporeans and its visitors.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Our airports, seaports and causeways are the first and last experience Singaporeans and tourists have of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: With events returning to Singapore, such as the Singapore Rugby 7s in April, the Singapore Grand Prix in October and many other MICE events on the calendar, I hope the MTF will consider not only safe management measures (SMMs) that balance the safety of participants, officials and spectators, but also the viability, practicality and experience of these events.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The SMMs did not allow for food and drinks to be consumed at the venue.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Many of the international events require minimum spectator numbers and ticket sales to break even.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Enabling food and drinks to be consumed at these venues is also part of the experience of watching a live event.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It would be good if distinctive SMMs as well as the administration of these SMMs can be considered for such events organised at venues, such as the Singapore Sports Hub.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The sports industry has been hit hard since the start of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Productivity has been low because of the nature of the industry.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Things are picking up; things are getting better.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: One group I would like to focus on are the operators that service children who are unvaccinated.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Because of the SMMs, they are unable to operate productively.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: These operators perform an important function – introducing physical skills to toddlers and tweens.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: If we do not help them, we will see the effects in our competitive sport pipeline in the future.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The fitness industry has also been affected since the start of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I am thankful for Minister Lawrence Wong’s continued support for the sports and arts sectors.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The Sports and Arts Resilience Grants have helped the sector with some relief and I hope they will continue to be available for organisations that are still affected by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: On my third point, I would like the Ministry to encourage the growth of sports in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Before I move on to this point, I would like to declare that I am the Chairman of the SNOC Athletes’ Commission, a coach at the Singapore Disabilities Sports Council and a Director of the Global Esports Federation.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The year 2021 has been a terrific year for Singapore sports.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We were all inspired by the fantastic performances of our athletes in Tokyo and sang the Majullah Singapura twice at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As an Olympian, I am very thankful to the Members of this House who supported the Motion to recognise Team Singapore’s performances at these Olympics and Paralympics.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As Yip Pin Xiu’s coach, I am thankful that Pin Xiu’s achievements were recognised and she was awarded the President’s Award for Inspiring Achievement by President Halimah just two weeks ago.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore had several athletes become world champions last year.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Aloysius Yapp became Singapore's first number-one-ranked pool billiard player.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In bowling, Shayna Ng won gold at the IBF Super World Championships.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In e-sports, Singapore's DOTA-2 Women's Team comprising Sheng Ying "KazeL" Ho, Hui Chun "Merody" Tay, Amanda "bings" Lim, Joanne "Minkiey" Lim and Paula "xiaoma" Teo clinched the gold medal in a close final against Team Great Britain at the Global Esports Games.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: To cap off a fantastic year, shuttler Loh Kean Yew did us all proud by winning the 2021 Badminton World Federation World Championships title.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: These performances inspire us, ignite the competitive fire within us and redefine our definition of what is possible.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This, as well as the various world and regional championships and qualifiers our athletes compete in.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Behind every athlete is an entourage that comprises our sports scientists, coaches and sports administrators.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As many of our Team Singapore athletes are also National Servicemen, I would like to encourage greater collaboration between MINDEF and MCCY to enable our Team Singapore athletes to continue fulfilling their National Service obligations and requirements, whilst being able to train, compete and bring glory to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: National Sports Associations (NSAs), like many of our charities, were not able to conduct events.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This will, no doubt, affect the national team performances downstream.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Essentially, many of our youth and development athletes have lost two years of physical literacy and competitive experience.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Hosting and organising events are another vehicle for the sports industry to grow and develop.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: With the support of SportSG, Singapore Tourism Board and the National Youth Council and many others, the event was able to showcase Singapore as an e-sports and gaming hub and proved that Singapore had the capability to host such properties and do it well.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The GEG21 showcased how gaming and entertainment in the metaverse could look like as we look towards the future.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: When I speak of the metaverse, I mean the seamless merging of our physical and digital worlds.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: During GEG21, we also saw local technology firm, Refract, showcase "active e-sport" which it co-created with traditional sports body, World Taekwondo Federation.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: If you are wondering what e-sport is, it is using the entire body as a controller competing in virtual reality.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This breaks down physical limitations, such as age, gender and physical size.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Because I think they will go a long way towards enhancing and cultivating the uniqueness and strength of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I urge you to consider them with an open mind and imagination.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to more conversations on these topics to best position Singapore to continue leading and innovating globally.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I raise these issues because they will contribute towards enhancing and cultivating the fabric of Singapore's society.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I believe the best is yet to be and I am excited about the possibilities in these aspects, strengthening our Singapore Core and identity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Ms Liyana's memoir traces her journey as a young mother sleeping rough in "crazy rich" Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: She, eventually, got back on track with the tenacity to fight stigma, with support from social workers and a spot of luck with generous friends.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are many people in Singapore like Liyana who have pulled themselves up to thrive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But, Sir, my Budget speech this year is not about individual actions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is about ensuring our policies are designed to substantially reduce poverty and decisively break the poverty cycle for all children born into poor families.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, I will argue that we need to substantially improve access to support in three ways.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First, access to support for the well-being and dignity of the poor.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Second, access to programmes that give a leg-up to children in poor homes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And third, access to employability support for those at risk of being stuck in low-income jobs or long-term unemployment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such support should be provided in a holistic, results-oriented way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: NGOs, volunteers and ground-up charitable initiatives all have a role to play.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But they should not be doing the heavy lifting when it comes to funding action against the root causes of poverty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They should be providing the "heartware" to help those who need it, while we maintain a strong baseline of state support, on top of which, NGOs and the community can layer personalised effort, expertise and passion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As a country, we have stood up to national challenges like the threat to our water supply and the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A major effort to wage war on poverty is not just something we can afford – it is something we must do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our pledge to build a society based on "justice and equality" calls on us to act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But beyond that, investing in additional anti-poverty and early intervention action for poor children may reduce the incidence of persons needing social welfare support in future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such investments may unlock talent for our economy, which would raise GDP and the tax base.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In this sense, investing in anti-poverty action is like making adult vaccines free – it may more than pay for itself in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Last and most importantly of all, a war on poverty would strengthen the foundations of social solidarity in our nation and help realise the promise that we truly have everyone's back.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One response to what I have said thus far would be – well, we are already waging a war on poverty, we are already doing it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We have programmes like ComCare, KidSTART, Workfare, Silver Support, the work of bodies like MENDAKI, CDAC, SINDA and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But let us take a look at some of the objective evidence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Two in five experienced it at least once a month.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do meet some Singaporeans who experience food insecurity when we engage constituents, as, I am sure, do other Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In a Parliamentary Question reply, I was told that even as Safe and Sound Sleeping Places run by community partners were scaled up in 2021, their utilisation rate was 93%.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a rate our hotels would be envious of.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I estimate that this means that the average living space per child in such flats is just 10 square metres, 60% less than the average living space per person in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Yet, 100,000 people in our local workforce earn a gross income of less than $1,300 per month.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not have a figure for the families of four or more earning less than $6,400 per month but it must be significant.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The last Household Expenditure survey shows that, on average, households in the bottom 20% spent more than they earned.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On social mobility, the available data shows a worrying trend.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A 2019 MOF study of intergenerational income mobility found a high degree of mobility for those aged 44 to 53 today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, this generation came of age at a time of rapid expansion of the economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Younger Singaporeans today face a completely different set of challenges, such as high housing prices and high income and wealth inequality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One study by Prof Irene Ng, based on a 2002 survey dataset, concluded that 58% of the income advantage of Singapore parents was being handed down to their children, a level similar to the USA at that time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2015, the Principal of Raffles Institution said that the school enrolment was exhibiting a class skew that it did not have in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some baby boomers made a windfall from property and this shows in our parallel problem of wealth inequality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My colleague, Sengkang Member of Parliament Mr Louis Chua has spoken about wealth inequality and cited quite a few data points which I would not repeat here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But we also need to look beyond statistics to the lived experiences of Singaporeans to fully understand why this matters.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A 2018 CNA survey found that it was class and not race or religion that was the most divisive factor in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It also found that those identified as upper class were more likely to feel a greater sense of belonging and national pride than those identified as lower class.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I begin, to set some context, the assistance that is provided to the poor is not always channelled through a one-stop shop.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Assistance schemes and ad hoc help are available from different agencies and the process of navigating this ecosystem can be stressful and daunting.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the Government's "kueh lapis" approach of multiple lines of assistance may, in fact, levy an unnecessary bandwidth tax on the poor when they seek help. "Bandwidth tax" refers to the additional cognitive burden they face.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To get support from multiple schemes, they personally have to fill up paperwork, produce documents, attend meetings and meet deadlines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And because they struggle, their cognitive functioning is impacted and they may make what many others see as "poor" decisions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As a result, they become entangled even more deeply in the poverty cycle.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Poor families would benefit from having one window for state support and also to have that support scaled up and follow more of a results-driven, account management approach.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I will suggest four ways to do this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The first involves us currently having too many financial assistance schemes that confuse and overwhelm their applicants.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These include CDC vouchers of various kinds, ComCare and the Pioneer Disability Fund, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should aim instead to minimise the number of scheme distributors and not have applicants being referred from one organisation to the next.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What I propose is that all state schemes be funnelled through a central account manager, with one such manager paired to each poor family.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Social workers at Family Service Centres (FSCs) seem to me to be best placed to play this role.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These account managers should be empowered to channel and administer all state schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They should also have visibility on schemes that are automatically administered, like Silver Support and Workfare, so that they can also address issues or errors there and so that they can take a more holistic view of the family's situation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To mirror the one account manager for social welfare support, each poor family and low-income worker should have one account manager in charge of employability at WSG.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That manager should be empowered and mandated to coach the worker to access the large array of work and training schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Their mandate should not merely be process-driven, meaning they should not be limited to training them on CV-writing techniques or asking them to sign up to passive job alerts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But they should also proactively work with their beneficiaries to assess different opportunities and find the right one, like a consultant and coach would do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have spoken in this House previously on how some state employability counsellors in some other countries take a results-driven approach.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An employability account manager for the disadvantaged would also be in a position to nudge their beneficiaries to upskill or reskill to move out of "at-risk" jobs before they are made obsolete.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This recommendation is linked to my earlier call to expand the supply of such training and conversion places.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The second issue involves the current process of applying for financial assistance being too complex and exhausting.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, the interviewing of family members by agencies, in some cases, is unnecessary.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some applicants are deterred from pursuing their Financial Assistance applications because of the humiliation that they would feel if agencies call their relatives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I repeat my call for Financial Assistance to be provided based on declarations as to whether family support is being obtained, without the need for interviewing family members, and with strong disincentives associated with making false statements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There should be a certain runway where the Financial Assistance continues after such events to enable the beneficiary to settle debts, to adapt to the new income structure and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Applicants are sometimes asked to produce various documents that they may no longer have.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some are asked to hold physical meetings at the SSO office, which can be very hard for them if they are taking care of young children or working.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can social workers visit beneficiaries more frequently at their homes, which would help them to better assess their living conditions?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And this is a topic that I have raised before.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can we convince more beneficiaries also to grant the agency direct access to past records residing with banks or Government agencies so that the absence of documents does not become the impediment it often is?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, let me address how we can increase the quantum of Financial Assistance available based on the beneficiary committing to positive actions that would help them and their family.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: More financial assistance can be provided beyond the current scheme caps, but tied to various conditions about which the welfare account manager is best placed to decide.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These may include, firstly, commitment to ensure attendance of children at early intervention programmes, such as KidSTART, or attendance at school for families where absenteeism is an issue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This follows the Bolsa Família principle of conditional cash transfers to poor families, which has had some success globally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And I note that in a Parliamentary Question reply that just came in, 2% of Secondary school students are tied up with absenteeism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, commitment to healthy behaviour, such as going for health screening and adult vaccination.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, commitment to attend personal life skills courses, for example, related to financial literacy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, some of the increased Financial Assistance can come in the form of digital currency that can only be spent on healthier food.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At the Committee of Supply (COS), I shall elaborate on this and on child early intervention programmes to break the poverty cycle.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: More can be given, with part of it being conditional, as I have argued.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And not every person who is vulnerable accesses multiple schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am sure other Members of this House have had the same experience as I often have, where persons approach me to plead for Financial Assistance and the case is referred to the SSO.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A letter from the SSO sometimes follows, which states that, in their conversation, the residents agreed that they were receiving certain state benefits already and, hence, they have agreed to withdraw their application for Financial Assistance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, the fact that they initially came to the Member of Parliament underlines that there is a difference of perspective on how much is enough.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In citing this, I want to be absolutely clear that our social workers and SSOs, generally, do their very best and do good work, but they operate within the policy parameters prescribed for them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should address the issue of poverty in a results-oriented fashion and in way that takes into consideration new research when it becomes available.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To be sure, I am not suggesting that welfare assistance should be unlimited and unconditional in all cases, or that the levels should be so high as to make it unattractive to work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But as we apply progressive wage laddering, the quantum that makes work unattractive will rise and this should be reflected in our welfare schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The financial services industry is, currently, not set up to do this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many poor Singaporeans I know are willing to work hard and may have a passion or talent for something that could become a source of stable income, pride and self-esteem.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Micro-entrepreneurship, particularly among women, whom research has shown are more likely to share financial gains with their children, unfortunately, is a pathway to poverty alleviation that attracts a great deal of multilateral funding in other countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This could provide opportunities for the low-income and ex-offenders to pursue their aspiration to set up a hawker stall with subsidised rents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, I would like to touch on the social work profession.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Social workers are at the core phase of dealing with poverty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many I have spoken to feel that many of our social workers feel overworked.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And this was my sense, too, when I was an FSC volunteer in the 1990s.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a subject that has been discussed in this House a number of times.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need to invest in more manpower and we need to ensure that compensation is well matched to the rigours of the job, which can be intellectually, socially and emotionally draining.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We can do more to set benchmarks for caseloads and increase headcount when these benchmarks are breached.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Social workers will find it hard to help others if they are looking for help themselves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Social workers with sufficient capacity are the best people to provide advice and support on more complex issues and not just disburse money.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They could be like venture capitalists, investing in people and also providing them with critical advice and coaching to help realise a return on that investment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In short, social workers can help people thrive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The last subject I would like to address in my speech is to call for the release of better data to tackle the issues of poverty and social mobility.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Better data helps public debate and helps us figure out what works and what does not.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And in tackling a problem that is as complex and resistant to simple solutions as poverty is, such data is critical for performance management for the goals we have set.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One head of an FSC who had been in the field for over 20 years told me that he was receiving cases of young families that were the children of cases he had handled as a young social worker.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a poverty cycle we must break.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, I would like to call for in-depth studies to be done, directed, especially, at younger poor Singaporeans, to do deep root cause analysis of the reasons for poverty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, we should aim to release more data by socioeconomic status, including on health outcomes, educational attainment, new business formation and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Any relevant public survey of studies that relate to this should, by default, be published.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, my colleagues, Members of Parliament Gerald Giam and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, have tirelessly spoken about minimum wages in this House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Member of Parliament Louis Chua moved an Adjournment Motion about expanding the supply of rental housing, while Member of Parliament Faisal Manap did the same on motorcycle COEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Workers' Party chair Ms Sylvia Lim has spoken passionately on social mobility.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A 28% hike refers to the increase in GST rate from 7% to 9% – that is, a 28% increase.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is spending more and investing more effort in fighting poverty and breaking the poverty cycle really worth it?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I understand that changing our mindset and paying to tackle poverty costs money.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There will be returns from investing in a war on poverty and breaking the poverty cycle.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If the help is provided in a results-oriented, holistic way, with sufficient dollars, there is every reason to believe that that spending will diminish over time and yield broader social and economic and even sociopolitical benefits, as more people improve themselves in terms of health, life skills, employability and – that most precious commodity of all – self-belief and confidence in themselves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must not judge our success solely on how much GDP growth we have achieved each year, but also by how much poverty we have eliminated.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In recent years, it is unclear if we are making success on this front, with no real downtrend in demand for ComCare, rental flats and other assistance schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must break this cycle and make a substantial dent on poverty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Then, and only then, can we truly claim to be living in a First World Country.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Only then can we say that we live in a society that has everyone’s back.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will deal with three matters in my speech: first, the war in Ukraine and its implications for Singapore; second, our response to COVID-19; third, I have some suggestions in relation to public housing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This war broke out after the Budget Statement, but before this debate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There remain risks that this conflict may escalate further.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The eruption of conflict has already created turbulence in financial and commodity markets.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is anticipated that, in the long term, various commodities may rise in prices, adding to inflation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I support the principled position that Singapore has taken in relation to this dispute.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While we are not against any country, we stand firmly against this invasion as a violation of Ukraine’s territorial sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As at the time of this speech, it remains the case that despite the violation of international law, Ukraine is largely fighting alone against Russia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, the international community has been swift in taking action, including tough economic sanctions, against Russia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This raises a number of related issues for us to consider.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While I expect we will have more details on the defence spending in MINDEF’s Committee of Supply – I have filed several cuts on that – I think we need to remain committed to defence spending and national defence even during times of peace.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There will be many demands on our spending in the coming years and it is always tempting to say we should cut defence spending in times of peace.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second is we must continue to maintain and build good and deep relations as well as mutually beneficial economic ties with as many countries as possible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We hope never to go to war, but the stronger and deeper our ties with the world around us, the better our chances of avoiding war and also of getting support from the international community in the event we are drawn into a war.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is always a big ask for others to join our conflict, but they may help in other ways, which will be vital.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second topic – and now coming to home more directly – is our response to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has done an excellent job of handling this crisis.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have taken a generally cautious, science- and evidence-led approach that has enabled us to achieve a high vaccination rate amongst the population and kept fatalities at a relatively low rate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The main price we have paid is living with social restrictions, which have taken a toll both on the economy and on the mental health of some of our people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over the last few months, with Omicron spreading, COVID-19 has been affecting even many in our highly-vaccinated population.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I, myself, came down with COVID-19 in December when I was with my family in the UK.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The UK's approach to COVID-19 was quite different from Singapore's and, while there were some restrictions in place, including requirements to wear masks indoors, many activities had resumed when we were there.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These included football matches, dining at restaurants and eateries and watching plays and performances.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, this is probably part of the reason I came down with COVID-19, as did my daughter.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, for both of us, the experience was not particularly bad.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Although we had mild symptoms for a few days, we did not test positive until our pre-departure test, where my daughter and I tested positive.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thereafter, we isolated ourselves, in line with the UK's guidelines at the time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, within about two days, we were testing negative again and our symptoms were relatively mild.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my case, just a slight sore throat and runny nose.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As we spoke to more people, we realised that almost everyone knew someone or had family or friends who had come down with COVID-19 and some had come down with it themselves.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For most, it was not debilitating and life could go on.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, this is not to trivialise the COVID-19 experience.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My wife and I had three shots of the vaccine and this, probably, helped us in resisting and overcoming the virus.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, from what we understand, the immunocompromised and those with pre-existing ailments remain vulnerable to serious complications.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, there are studies in the UK pointing to a group of people who suffer symptoms called "long COVID", which means they have different after-effects following a COVID-19 infection, some of which can be serious and debilitating.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We need to reiterate the message that, for those with COVID-19 who are either asymptomatic or who have mild symptoms, there is no need to visit the doctor or the hospital.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If necessary, sceptical employers who are asking for medical certificates can ask employees to send photographs of their current ART test results for human resource (HR) record purposes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I understand that even with the relatively large number of COVID-19 cases that are emerging every day, our hospitals remain able to cope with those who need urgent assistance.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our population is amongst the best vaccinated in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think we are ready to open up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The third topic I wish to discuss, quite different from the earlier two, relates to housing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my Meet-the-People session (MPS) cases, appeals in relation to housing are one of the common ones that come up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Housing affordability and availability are a concern for many residents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the curious issues that has arisen during the pandemic is that the housing market has heated up, both in the public and private sector.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think this is a combination of both increased demand and tightening supply.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the demand side, as more people are at home, the more people seek more personal space for themselves and family members.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thus, in large extended families, various members may wish to move out into houses of their own.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: New couples getting married want their own place as it may be difficult to move in with either of the parents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Appeals for new flats emerge regularly in my MPS.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, the resale market has been limited by the imposition of minimum occupation periods, or MOPs, for both resale and new flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was actually the state of affairs for many years before MOP was extended to resale flats as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even without MOP, there are other disincentives to flipping flats, including the seller's stamp duty, which is higher if a flat is sold within a shorter holding period.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A new flat is both brand new and has a fresh lease, and it comes at a lower price.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, as a result of this, there is almost no logical reason for anyone to buy a resale flat unless they feel they have no choice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, people who buy resale flats also get a feeling they are getting a raw deal and are envious of those who get new flats at a lower price.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This exaggerates the "lottery effect" of new flats and those who are eligible for it vis-a-vis those who are not or who are lower on the priority list start feeling more resentful.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My humble suggestion would be to take away the MOP for resale flats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This would, at least, create a greater supply of resale flats, which should ease their prices.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I also do not expect this to be a one-off effect because, if a resale flat is bought, it could still be put on the market again if needed, whereas now, if a resale flat is bought, it would be out of the market for at least five years, hence, constraining supply.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, in that sense, every transaction constrains the resale market further.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It would also give resale flat buyers the benefit of flexibility – at least, one tangible benefit for the huge premium they would otherwise be paying.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Currently, the two most common HDB appeals I get are either for new flats or to reduce the MOP because families need to change their living arrangements as a result of changing circumstances.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe that if more buyers are prepared to go to the resale market to buy their flats and the resale market is accessible, this would reduce the heavy demand we have for BTO flats at the moment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if this disparity falls enough, such that Government grants would make buying resale flats as attractive as new flats even for those who are house hunting, I think this would also further reduce the current pent-up demand for BTOs and the lottery effect people are feeling from this.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, while the Government provides direct monetary aid to our citizens, I believe that we can go even further by ensuring that all Singaporeans have the knowledge and the tools to become financially self-sustainable.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the saying goes, "Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime." One suggestion is that various Ministries should consider working with the People's Association to organise financial literacy workshops in the community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These workshops would cover essential topics, such as budgeting for necessities, planning for big ticket item purchases and the basics of investing, which can also include sharing of useful tips on scam prevention.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can also pair these workshops along with estate planning and law awareness talks, which are also an extension of managing household finances.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The law awareness talks should involve multiple agencies, including the Office of Public Guardian (OPG), the CPF Board and MinLaw to work hand in hand together with the Law Society of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This would be a welcome relief for parents, especially single parents and families with special needs children, as this pandemic has caused many of our little ones to miss school for extended periods of time without compensation.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the same note, I also hope that more support can be provided to families with autistic children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: All of these expenses are subject to GST.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These 5Rs will not just enable us, as a community, to work towards our Singapore Green Plan 2030 but will also help fellow Singaporeans to reduce their day-to-day expenses.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To that end, the Government can contribute towards improving the "software" and the "hardware".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In terms of the "software", a few of my suggestions include setting up workshops in the community, sharing useful tips to practise the 5Rs and empowering residents with the knowledge to conserve water and energy as well as to reduce food waste.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One example would be the Singapore Institute of Building Limited (SIBL)'s ongoing SG Eco Fund project in Woodgrove aimed at raising awareness on environmental issues and encouraging more residents to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle through community and education programmes, sustainable markets and an app with interactive games.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another suggestion would be in relation to developing new TV programmes to educate our younger generations about the 5Rs in an engaging manner.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Captain Green, an iconic green frog mascot was first introduced in the 1990s to encourage Singaporeans to adopt a clean and green lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In recent years, Captain Green has ventured into storybooks and quick teach cards used in preschools to inculcate our children with the habit of taking responsibility for their actions and to reflect on their choices towards a clean and green environment.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe these teachings can be further enhanced through a collaboration with Mediacorp to introduce a cartoon series involving mascots like Captain Green, Water Wally as well as the recently launched Bloobin, using rhythmic content akin to the popular "Baby Shark" song to attract our children and to encourage them to be our young budding green champions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To tackle the "hardware" part of the equation, quite a number of my Woodgrove residents have expressed during our regular Green Living sustainability dialogues that the present design of the blue recycle bins poses many challenges for the community to recycle effectively.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While we note that NEA has been stepping up efforts to educate the public on how to recycle correctly, all we need is one irresponsible user to deposit food waste into the blue recycling bin to cause the rest of the recyclable items in the bin to become fully contaminated and attract rodents unnecessarily.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We should, therefore, not merely provide one bulk container for people to dispose all types of recyclables and waste.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There needs to be more innovative solutions to encourage or incentivise single-type recyclables, such as having one specifically or specially for batteries, plastic bottles, paper or cans and so on.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In relation to the energy- and water-saving component, HDB can assist by considering green features in future housing projects and upgrading existing ones through Home Improvement Programme (HIP), such as adopting sustainable materials and designs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of our existing HDB flats incorporate full glass windows that emit a considerable amount of heat during the late afternoon.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As an example, HDB can consider installing low heat transfer windows, such as double-glazed windows, as a solution.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Finding a suitable greener alternative that helps cool down our HDB flats will translate to less reliance on fans and air-conditioning, indirectly contributing towards reducing residents' utility bill costs each month.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has also introduced several assistance packages, providing reassurance to Singaporeans whose livelihoods have been affected by the pandemic, and easing their financial burden.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While these assistance packages are substantial, responses vary from household to household.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some residents from low-income families expressed their gratitude to the Government, while others told me that they hoped the Government could have given more.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the long run, we should not rely too much on Government assistance to sustain our livelihood.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Instead, we should carefully plan for our future and build our own financial foundations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Like our reserves, if we plan ahead and manage our finances and expenses well, we will be prepared for rainy days.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not only was this Budget set against the backdrop of a COVID-19 year three, it was also set against rising global energy prices, increasing core inflation, the rising cost of living and Europe on the brink of open conflict between Russia and Ukraine, which, by now, has become a grim and sober reality.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And added to all these, of course, was the impending increase in GST.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The issue of the GST increase has been debated quite extensively in this House and I understand that Members have opposing views on whether the GST should or should not be increased.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe it is fair to say that almost all Members, if not all Members of the House, would agree that more can and should be done for the less privileged in society and those with more should contribute more.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The fundamental question is, of course, how that more should be funded.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should we continue to draw more from the reserves?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should we significantly raise income tax and corporate tax?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should we base property taxes on property values?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should we tax the wealthy based on the value of their wealth portfolio?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should we use more of the NIRC and, if so, how much more – 60%, 70% and so on?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These might very well be decisions that could be taken by either this Government or governments of the future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I would like to urge those governments to exercise caution because such decisions have to be part of a holistic, balanced and diversified taxation policy that strikes a careful balance by considering the impact on all the various groups and stakeholders in our society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us not use a sledgehammer and swing away wildly when perhaps a discerning use of a chisel might be more appropriate.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With these schemes, the net transference from the Government to lower-income families and those who need it will increase from the current sum and the impact of GST increase on lower-income families will not be felt for many years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that this transference and these schemes are really quite seamless and the effort for many of those who need it is quite minimal to access these schemes and that would significantly thus reduce the impact of any bandwidth tax that was mentioned earlier by our colleague, Mr Leon Perera, in his speech.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The revisions in the rate of these progressive taxes will help to ensure that the overall tax regime in Singapore remains resilient, with those with more means contributing more than those with less.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notice I have said "those with more", not "those with a lot".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, as long as I have more than you, I should be happy and willing to contribute to you.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This has been raised before by other Members in this House.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has changed the way we utilise spaces, interact with one another and how we build social relationships.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The stress of having to live with the pandemic, the need to face medical unknowns related to the disease, the increase in contestation for living and working spaces, job and income insecurity, and having to constantly navigate the ever-changing COVID-19 management measures, have left many of us physically exhausted, emotionally spent and mentally drained.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When we think about mental wellness, we have to understand that different groups of people have different mental wellness needs as they can be affected by the same stressors differently.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We recognise this, of course, if we look at mental wellness for the youths, mental wellness that affects seniors, postpartum depression when it comes to women who have just given birth and so on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, rather than to treat mental wellness as a collective term, it will thus be beneficial for us to recognise that, just like these other different segments of society, men are also affected very differently by stresses.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In many societies today, some patriarchal beliefs continue to be commonly held by the majority of the population and there are corresponding societal expectations of how men should behave in social settings.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Men are still expected to be the head of the family, the dominant breadwinner, to have the "eye of the tiger" by demonstrating strength and confidence and to stare adversity in the face and to "man-up", take the fall when things go wrong.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These expectations have, inadvertently, caused men to experience stressors that are different from those from other segments of our society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ms Porsche Poh is one of the leading mental advocates for mental health, having founded Silver Ribbon way back in 2006.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have to promote mental health among men more so that they feel comfortable to speak up about their struggles." And I thank Ms Poh for her valuable inputs in my speech.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that we should go upstream to educate men about the importance of mental wellness and let them know that there are sources available to them when they need help.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could MINDEF consider running programmes educating our NSFs and soldiers about the importance of mental wellness and promote the idea that it is okay to seek help?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To help them move away from the stereotype that you should shed blood and not tears because "real men don't cry?" I believe that having such mental wellness programmes and demolishing archaic male stereotypes are not incompatible with training our soldiers to be tough and resilient.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Making our young men better soldiers by making them more aware of their mental wellness also prepares them to be better men for the rest of their lives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also hope that the Government can devote some resources to having more community-based platforms that specifically cater to men who are presently struggling with mental wellness.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, one could start with mental well-being activities in community clubs and centres that cater to men and perhaps this could evolve into dedicated structured support group sessions that men could attend.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The ultimate aim of this would be to destigmatise help-seeking behaviour from men as signs of weakness by creating a more gender-neutral society and providing platforms where men, and women, feel comfortable to discuss mental wellness issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But to use that term is to draw lines of divisions between just "what or who" is rich and "what or who" is poor and dishes out unhelpful labels that can only be divisive in our society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rather than reducing it to a blunt tool about simply taking from one group and giving to another, I see this Budget more as reinforcing a uniquely Singaporean version of "noblesse oblige" where those who are in positions of relative privilege and wealth – and I use the word, "relative" again, Mr Speaker – have the social duty and obligation to take care of those who have less.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, it is not just about implementing a particular fiscal policy; it is about strengthening a societal philosophy.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be wonderful if this philosophy could permeate into every single Singaporean social consciousness, whereby, regardless of our income levels, we are willing to contribute not just our money, but also our time to those who need our help and assistance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because that is what a family does, Mr Speaker: those who are stronger, take care of those who are not as strong; those who can, help those who are trying; those who have more, help those who have less.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And it is only by staying strong as one united Singaporean family that we are going to get through the economic and societal challenges of the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And with that, I end my speech in firm support of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 1.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 1.15 pm until 1.40 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many suggestions have been raised and I cannot cover all of them in this round-up speech, but I assure everyone that we have listened to every view and will study your suggestions carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Members have also raised many specific questions related to the programmes of the Ministries and these will be addressed at the Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are charting our way forward together – towards a fairer, greener and more inclusive society.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: From what I have heard during the debate, there is strong support for these key thrusts of the Budget and I thank everyone for the support.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The key issues raised during the debate can be summarised in three broad questions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Are we doing enough to sustain our recovery and position Singapore well for the future?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Why do we need more revenues and, in particular, why raise GST and are there alternatives to this?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And is the Budget fair to all Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will address these three issues in turn.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ensuring a strong and vibrant economy is of critical importance because it raises our standard of living, provides good jobs and opportunities for Singaporeans and generates revenues, so that we have the resources to do more, especially for the more vulnerable groups.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In my Budget speech, I shared our outlook for the year and some of the risks on the horizon, including the tensions in Eastern Europe.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Minister for Trade and Industry has provided an update of the economic outlook.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singapore’s direct trade linkages with Russia and Ukraine are relatively small.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But the conflict will impact the global economy and global energy markets, which will, in turn, affect us.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we are taking actions to enhance the resilience of our energy supplies.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are coordinating actions across the whole-of-society as some Members have suggested.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are getting businesses to offer more value-for-money house brands to consumers so that consumers can stretch their dollars.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are extending Price Kaki to help consumers make better, more informed purchasing decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we are standing up the Committee Against Profiteering to take action against unfair price hikes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Where inflation risks are concerned, MAS had taken the pre-emptive step to tighten monetary policy in January.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The appreciating exchange rate will moderate the impact of higher global inflation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MAS will continue to assess the appropriate steps to ensure medium-term stability.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are monitoring the external situation and the risks for our economy closely.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Risks in terms of both growth and inflation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If the situation worsens, we will not hesitate to take further actions to protect jobs and to help households and businesses deal with increased costs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Notwithstanding these near-term uncertainties in the external environment, our overall prospects are good.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are operating from a position of strength and that is why we can make bold moves now, which will position us well to seize the opportunities ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One decisive step is to accelerate the decarbonisation of our economy and achieve net-zero by or around the mid-century.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All of us will have to adjust to the new levels of carbon tax to facilitate this green transition.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But moving decisively will bring many benefits and open up new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As we attract more of such green investments, we will also step up training efforts to equip Singaporeans with the right skills to take on these new green jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As several Members, including Ms Poh Li San, Prof Koh Lian Pin and Ms Hany Soh highlighted, this will take a whole-of-society effort to achieve our climate ambition.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will, certainly, move forward in that direction.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, we will continue our R&D efforts in emerging technologies, such as carbon capture and hydrogen, as suggested by Dr Tan Wu Meng.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All of these moves will enhance and strengthen Singapore's position as a choice destination for new investments in the green economy and, ultimately, create many more good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members, I think Mr Seah Kian Peng and Ms Denise Phua, worry that we are making too many changes at the same time – foreign worker adjustments, progressive wages, CPF, carbon tax and so on – and that all these will add to cost pressures for businesses at a time when demand is still weak for certain segments of the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why we are continuing to provide significant support to the harder-hit sectors, including through the Small Business Recovery Grant.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are also phasing in the new requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the carbon tax increase will be staggered over three phases from 2024 to 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The changes to the S Pass minimum qualifying salary will be implemented over three steps from this year to 2025.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What we are doing is to be upfront, clear and transparent to businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are announcing these moves well ahead of time so that businesses can plan ahead and make the necessary adjustments.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even as we make these policy moves over the coming years, we continue to pay very close attention to our SMEs, something which many Members spoke about.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to help our SMEs upgrade and maintain a vibrant SME sector in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This includes our heartland enterprises, as mentioned by Mr Melvin Yong.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, our support and grant schemes for companies are designed to benefit SMEs the most.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Prior to COVID-19, smaller firms were receiving about 12 times more grants from the Government on a grant per dollar of revenue basis, compared to larger firms.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Twelve times more grants from the Government on a grant per dollar of revenue basis.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And throughout the past two years, SMEs continued to receive significant help through schemes like the Jobs Support Scheme, rental relief and financing schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Of course, not every SME will get the same support.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is because our strategy favours SMEs which are actively training their workers and increasing their productivity.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If the SME is prepared to make the effort, it will enjoy very generous co-funding.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Under the Productivity Solutions Grant (PSG), firms that undertake productivity solutions this year will receive significant funding support.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit (SFEC), eligible firms can get additional funding for up to 90% of out-of-pocket expenses for their supported programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Derrick Goh, Mr Edward Chia and several Members who have spoken passionately about SMEs will be heartened to know that we will intensify our outreach efforts to the SMEs to let them know about the support schemes and how to take advantage of them.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will proactively reach out to our SMEs through our Trade Associations and Chambers (TACs) and Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, we are making it easier for SMEs to access information on schemes and available support through the GoBusiness portal and SME Centres.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I recognise that the operating environment in Singapore can be challenging for businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are no longer competing based on being a low-cost business location.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Where we can, the Government will manage the pace of cost increases and make it easier to do business.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, through GoBusiness Licensing, we have streamlined the number of regulatory touchpoints for food business owners from 14 to one.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This reduces the number of licence applications that firms have to fill up and saves up to 14 days of turnaround time.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Janet Ang and Mr Edward Chia shared concerns from the business community on the availability of manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is a key concern for many businesses and I fully understand.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The current shortage of Work Permit holders is partly due to our border restrictions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, firms should continue to take full advantage of the various schemes that support job redesign and improve productivity to become more manpower-efficient.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the near term, the Government will also help to offset some of the cost increases.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, we have the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme to help co-fund wage increases for low-wage workers.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we cannot offset wage and cost increases perpetually as that will not be viable nor desirable.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Keeping the cost of employing foreigners low would also mean depressing the wages of local workers over time.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our focus, therefore, is not to hold down labour costs indefinitely but to support efforts by our firms to be more productive and innovative so that they can be competitive and successful even as labour costs gradually increase.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why we are redoubling our efforts to invest in new capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng asked about support for our TACs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are already doing this through the Local Enterprise and Association Development (LEAD) Programme, which provides funding support for TACs to drive capability development and internationalisation projects.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, as Mr Shawn Huang noted, we are continuing to invest heavily in R&D and technology to strengthen the overall competitiveness of our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked why we appear to be lagging behind in some of these knowledge and technology outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, we have been doing better over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They take time to bear fruit but we are seeing positive results.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am confident we will continue to see more positive results in the years ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As I shared in my Budget speech, one area of focus is to strengthen the linkage between research institutes and industry so that companies can readily access frontier technology and high-quality research.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are also paying closer attention to the more promising SMEs to help them scale up faster and expand overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Take the example of Cheng Yew Heng, a food manufacturer and food ingredients supplier.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It started out as a small family business in 1947, producing candies and preserved fruits.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is now run by the third generation and has embarked on a journey of production innovation, automation and has expanded into overseas markets.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, it is a leading sugar manufacturer and ingredients supplier and operates its own e-commerce platform.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They include many household names like BreadTalk, Koufu and SK Jewellery.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With all of these efforts, we look forward to celebrating many more homegrown success stories in the years to come.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another critical aspect of competitiveness is to stay open and connected to the world, something which many Members like Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat, Mr Cheng Hsing Yao and Mr Patrick Tay have emphasised.
