speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must never let anti-foreigner sentiments take root here or give the impression that we are becoming more inward-looking.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I caution some in the House who have been shrill on this subject.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Take a look at some of the articles that have appeared in the international media recently, wondering if Singapore is closing itself and Singaporeans are becoming less welcoming of foreigners.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If global investors conclude that this is so, Singapore will become less attractive to them and it will be ordinary Singaporeans who suffer the most.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: My colleague, Dr Tan See Leng, the Minister for Manpower, had also sounded a similar warning yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this Budget, we are adjusting some aspects of our foreign worker policies.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is not a sudden change in policy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We made our intentions very clear in the Economic Strategies Committee report in 2010.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Since then, we have been making careful, calibrated adjustments to our foreign worker policies.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We recognise that tightening too quickly will hurt our SMEs, but moving too slowly will lessen the incentive for firms to upgrade.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, it is really about maintaining that careful balance.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are, and will remain, integral to our economy and our competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are a valuable complement to our Singaporean Core at all levels of the workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We continue to welcome all who contribute to us having the strongest teams here, to give Singaporeans, ourselves, the best chance of success amidst intense global competition.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we welcome those with the capabilities and the commitment, who share our values and our way of life, to stay on and help us build the next phase of our Singapore story.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I also recognise that certain segments of the economy may need more help.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And Members have provided many useful suggestions in this debate.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, Mr Don Wee and Ms Yeo Wan Ling spoke about self-employed persons (SEPs) who are vulnerable and in need of support.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government has rolled out several schemes to support self-employed persons through this difficult period.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have also set up the Advisory Committee on Platform Workers, which comprises multiple stakeholders, including our tripartite representatives.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Committee is deliberating on ways to further strengthen protections for these gig workers and will give an update when they are ready.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: More generally, we will continue to review our social safety nets to ensure that they meet the needs of our workers in a rapidly changing economy and labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As I mentioned in the Budget, this is a multi-year agenda.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This Budget is just one step among many that we have taken before and will take in the future to renew and strengthen our social compact for a post-pandemic world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this regard, I am heartened by the various suggestions of Members in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They include Mr Cheng Hsing Yao, Mr Henry Kwek, Mr Patrick Tay, Ms Denise Phua, Mr Louis Ng and, just now, Mr Leon Pereira, around social workers and our social safety support schemes, all suggesting for us to do more and to do better for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to study these suggestions carefully and review all of our schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But to do more, we will also need to ensure that we have sufficient revenue.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is what I will move on to very shortly.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some have suggested that before we raise revenues, we should put in more effort to slow down expenditure growth.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Government spending is about 18% of GDP today.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We already run an extremely tight and lean ship, compared to other developed economies, and yet, we have been able to achieve consistently good outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, by making these cuts and reallocating to new initiatives, we are able to moderate the increase in our spending.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am glad that several Members, like Mr Yip Hon Weng, recognise that Government spending and revenue are two sides of the same coin.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But in every Parliamentary session, I must say that I hear many requests for the Government to do more and much fewer requests for the Government to do less.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because we are raising revenues now, I think Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa say we should cut back spending further, but they have conveniently neglected to mention that they and the PSP have made requests on multiple other occasions for the Government to spend more, for example, funding of insurance premiums for MediShield Life and CareShield Life; hiring more teachers, reducing class sizes, all of which cost a lot of money.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we want the Government to do more, then let us be upfront and explain to Singaporeans why additional revenues and tax increases are needed.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In many countries, the tendency is for politicians to focus only on the spending side, because it is inconvenient to talk about taxes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a result, these governments spend beyond their means.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They run up unfunded obligations and debt, and they kick the fiscal can down the road.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some of the increase in Government spending is necessary and unavoidable.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, healthcare spending will be the main driver of the increase in social spending.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And the key reason why healthcare spending will rise is our rapidly ageing population, as everyone in this House understands.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Take the number of people who are aged 90 and above.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Or take the number of centenarians, aged 100 and above.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: By 2030, the numbers will increase much more.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our seniors will require more medical services – they are more likely to be hospitalised and their length of stay in hospital tends to be longer, compared to younger folks.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They also need elective procedures like cataract operations that help them lead more fulfilling lives.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, just the demographic effect of having more seniors alone will already push up healthcare spending significantly.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Further increases will happen as better and more costly treatments become available and with the medical inflation that is inevitable, even with the best organised healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another reason for more spending is that our social needs are getting more complex, something which several Members have recognised and highlighted, including Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How, Mr Desmond Choo, Dr Wan Rizal and Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These issues are not so easy to resolve through standardised schemes alone.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Often, we will need to customise approaches to suit the circumstances and needs of individuals and families facing complex and multiple challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also need strong coordination, which our agencies are continuing to do, not just across public sector agencies, but with social service agencies on the ground, to take a family-centred approach.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And to do this well, we need trained counsellors and social workers to befriend, mentor and journey along, handhold the individuals and families and journey along with them, like what we are doing with ComLink and KidSTART.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is important work, it likely to produce better outcomes, but it is also highly resource-intensive and will, invariably, cost more.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This was mainly due to higher spending on healthcare, public transport and significant enhancements to Workfare and the introduction of Silver Support, to name a few.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All meritorious programmes, but all requiring significant funding.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Now, if we are able to keep Government expenditures at 20% of GDP in 2030 – so, from 15% to 18% over the last decade, but in 2030, if we can keep it to 20% of GDP – that would already mean a slowing of the rate of increase, compared to a decade ago.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I think that would be a good achievement.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government will do its part by using its fiscal resources prudently and judiciously and ensuring value-for-money in public spending.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to streamline coordination across the whole-of-Government to reap synergies, as Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim suggested.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But there is only so much the Government can do on its own.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also require cooperation from all parties, as Miss Cheryl Chan rightly said – to moderate our own expectations for the Government to keep doing more and to consider how community groups and individuals can also come together to contribute solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And I am glad that there are, indeed, many ground-up initiatives taking off, like the #EastCoastBeachPlan started by Ms Samantha Thian.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: She started cleaning the beach herself when she noticed large amounts of trash piling up there.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Then, she started a Telegram group for like-minded individuals to join and undertake clean-ups together.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Now the group has grown to 3,300 members and they have conducted more than 400 beach clean-ups.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are many more ground-up projects all over Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They self-organise to tackle issues and solve problems, sometimes even before the Government gets a chance to respond.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to support and encourage such initiatives and find new ways to partner them and work in collaboration together.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will reinforce the spirit of mutual support in our community and will go a long way in strengthening our social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Both the WP and PSP have suggested spending more from reserves to meet our rising expenditure.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is tempting to turn to our reserves each time we need more funds.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But is this the right thing to do?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Leader of the Opposition, Mr Pritam Singh, has highlighted that the reserves' rules were amended in the past, so, we can easily amend them again now, for example, to adjust the percentage we use from the NIRC.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As we have explained before, we last amended the Net Investment Returns (NIR) framework in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That would not be the responsible thing to do.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some argue that they have insufficient information about the reserves or about our fiscal projections to make an informed decision about our fiscal options.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, there is already a lot of information published, on the reserves, for example.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What we do not disclose is the size of funds managed by GIC, so as not to reveal the full size of our financial reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is not in our national interest to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our reserves are our strategic defence against threats.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we disclose this information, we will be making it easier for potential adversaries to use it against us.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Where fiscal projections are concerned, the Government will continue to put out as much information as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have released data on our key expenditure drivers, I have mentioned several times our demographic projections and explained why our healthcare and social spending will increase in the coming years as a percentage of GDP and included the expenditure growth figures.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On taxes, we expect them to keep pace broadly with GDP, so, there is clearly a structural funding gap as our spending needs rise.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have shared extensively about our needs and plans and will continue to put out more information, where necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But I cannot help but feel that the persistent requests for more information are red herrings – they are distractions from the key problem at hand.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At some point, we need to make decisions, including difficult and critical ones, like what we have done in this Budget, to better prepare Singapore for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the question is whether all Members are prepared to come back to the real issue – on the need to strengthen our revenues through our various tax measures, to meet the structural growth in our expenditure in the coming years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Unfortunately, both the WP and PSP paint a false, distorted and misleading picture about our reserves, that these are being accumulated at the expense of the current generation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They have assumed that the present rules result in an accumulation of more reserves than is necessary, but that is not the case.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that going forward, we expect this NIRC stream to continue to keep pace with economic growth.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even to achieve that is, by no means, a sure thing.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We would have done very well if we can do so, given that our investment returns are subject to significant headwinds in the global investment environment, for example, due to ageing populations in the developed countries, lacklustre productivity growth, rising government debt levels and geopolitical tensions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Both the WP and PSP have also suggested different ways to spend from our land sale proceeds.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are variations of what they have put out before and they still do not recognise that land is a scarce asset that is protected as Past Reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have said it before and we will say it again, when we sell land, we are not creating new wealth.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are merely converting the land from a physical to a financial asset.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Therefore, we invest the land sale proceeds back with the rest of the reserves and we spend 50% of the expected long-term real return through the NIR framework.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this way, our land sale proceeds provide a stable and sustainable stream of income for our Budget over time.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, to be clear, that means we are already spending from our land sale proceeds.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But our approach avoids the pitfalls that we will face if we were to spend on land sale proceeds more directly.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, land prices will move in cycles and can be volatile.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We know that, for a fact, there are property market cycles.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It will not be a static "$100", as Ms Hazel Poa has assumed in her proposal.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we do not want Government revenues to fluctuate with the market because it makes Government spending itself procyclical and creates too much uncertainty for the Government to plan long term.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, once a government gets used to relying on land sales to fund spending, it will have a vested interest to keep land prices high to maximise revenues.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will, ultimately, hurt the economy and will hurt Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the more prudent approach is to treat our land as a finite asset, as what we have done today.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We sell the land that we need for urban development and invest the proceeds, as we are doing, to generate a steady income over time.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is a sound approach and it has served us well.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Ms Tin Pei Ling asked about returning the sums drawn from our reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But if there continues to be an extraordinary need, we will have to go through the due process of seeking the President's agreement to a Budget that results in a draw on Past Reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is an appropriate move for managing shocks, as Prof Hoon Hian Teck has noted, and that is how our framework is designed.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms He Ting Ru suggested that by saving for the future, we are discounting the needs of the current generation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our fiscal policy, including our Reserves Protection Framework, keeps faith with all generations – current and future.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have drawn on Past Reserves to protect the lives and livelihoods of the current generation, throughout crises.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are also tapping on the NIRC to fund many programmes for the current generation, from the young to the old and, especially for the Merdeka and Pioneer Generations.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, we need to consider the needs of the future generation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Do we really want to leave our next generation with fewer resources in a more uncertain and volatile world?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Furthermore, no one can tell what the world will be like in 30 years' time.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it is very likely to be a more dangerous world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our children and the generations after them will have more, not fewer, emergencies to contend with.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The recent conflict in Ukraine reminds us that we are living in an increasingly divided and troubled world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will encounter more episodes, where size matters, where might is assumed to be right even though that is not a stand we can accept, and where international rules are blatantly ignored by major powers.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is a world that will be less hospitable for small countries, let alone a small city-state like Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will always be at the mercy of these external forces and we must ensure we have sufficient resources to defend and protect ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And in the years to come, we will need to deal with many other major and pressing challenges, including global warming and rising sea levels, as well as future public health emergencies, which public health experts are predicting will happen with increasing frequency.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are all thankful that our forefathers did not take the easy way out.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Instead, they were disciplined, they considered our needs and chose to keep faith with future generations, meaning us today.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we benefit from the reserves that they have built up painstakingly.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They cared for their future generations, which is us.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I say we continue to husband our reserves, keep faith with the generations after us and ensure that they, too, will always have access to this "rainy days" fund to meet any emergencies and, importantly, a steady stream of income for their future needs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: My biggest concern with these requests to use more of the reserves is that it reflects a certain cavalier mindset, one of spending whatever we can today and not caring sufficiently about tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we see this happening throughout history and around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As countries become more affluent, they feel they have arrived and they get tempted by easy money.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It begins with something small – allow standards to slide a little; just tweak the parameters a little.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But, over time, these small things add up.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Then, it becomes politically very challenging to roll back any benefit and to raise taxes, or even to talk about it, and the country ends up quickly in a downward fiscal spiral.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Very few countries are in the same position as us.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, intergenerational equity is better preserved in our system than in other places.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we must never take what we have for granted, for it can unravel very quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I strongly appeal to all Members in this House, let us all do our part to uphold the ethos of fiscal responsibility, discipline and stewardship that is so vital to our success.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, let me turn to other revenue options.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They asked if we could do more on other revenue options, especially income and wealth taxes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And, in particular, the Workers' Party offered a range of revenue options as alternatives to the GST increase.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is how we ensure that our revenue base remains diversified and resilient, while achieving its objectives of being fair and progressive.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, all jurisdictions rely on these three forms of taxation and the OECD jurisdictions have much higher VAT rates or, our GST, than Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But let me go through the revenue options one by one.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As I Have said in the Budget speech, it is hard to be definitive at this juncture about the overall tax revenue impact from both Pillars 1 and 2 of BEPS 2.0.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: International discussions are still ongoing on the reallocation formula for Pillar 1.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But before we have reached an agreement, Mr Louis Chua has already concluded that the impact of Pillar 1 will be limited, because it only covers 100 multinational enterprise groups, or MNE groups.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I must clarify that although the number of in-scope MNEs affected is small, these are the largest and most profitable MNEs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Any reallocation of profits away from Singapore will have a significant impact.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Louis Chua then projected that the CIT revenue could be as high as $71.5 billion.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Louis Chua should have paused at this huge number for a reality check.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But he should have said it is wishful thinking.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Seventy-one-and-a-half billion dollars, that is the total amount of revenue we collect from all taxes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Does Mr Chua really believe that CIT revenue from the profitable non-SMEs, the larger companies, will jump by seven times, from $10 billion to $70 billion?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Will the implementation of the Minimum Effective Tax Rate, or METR, bring us more tax revenue?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mathematically, it has to be so, if nothing else changes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The eventual impact cannot be ascertained by a simple static analysis, as it also depends on how governments and companies will respond, post-BEPS 2.0.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: BEPS 2.0 represents a fundamental change in the competitive environment for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But this is no longer as effective, post-BEPS 2.0.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Companies will review their existing and new investments.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Governments will also seek to compete via non-tax investment promotion in order to recover from the pandemic and to make up for what they can no longer do through tax incentives.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our engagement with investors is already revealing this.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, likewise, Singapore will need to find other ways to stay competitive, from investing even more in our workers to building new infrastructure and incentivising R&D.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, even if we can generate additional revenue from Pillars 1 and 2, these will have to be reinvested towards ensuring Singapore remains competitive and attracts our fair share of investments to create good jobs for our people.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I would, therefore, caution against jumping to conclusions or believing wild guesses on how much more revenue we can get from changes in global tax rules and use that as a reason to avoid raising the GST.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, the top 10% of taxpayers who pay PIT already account for about 80% of our total PIT revenue.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With the top marginal personal income tax rate at 24%, we will be higher than the 17% top tax rate of Hong Kong and closer to the Asian average top marginal personal income tax rate of 28%.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is a limit to how much we can increase PIT rates for the top income brackets, without touching the PIT rates for the income brackets below it.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that would apply to everyone with chargeable income of at least $320,000 or more.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is assuming the tax base remains unchanged.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we all know this sharp increase is untenable and will badly damage our competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Investments and jobs for everyone, including lower- and middle-income earners, will be impacted, not just taxes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, to raise the same amount as a GST increase through higher PIT, in reality, we would have to raise the PIT rates for a broader group of income earners, including the middle- and upper-middle income earners.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that was what Dr Tan See Leng was trying to explain yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, Prof Hoon Hian Teck had correctly observed that as our economy matures and population ages, a bigger share of the population will become economically inactive.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will, in turn, shrink the tax base for income-based taxation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we cannot rely only on income-based taxes alone, if we want to maintain a resilient and future-proof revenue base.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I have covered corporate and personal income taxes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Louis Chua also said we should do more on this front, especially on property taxes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On the other hand, several Members, like Mr Chong Kee Hiong, raised concerns that increased property taxes will impact many retirees and senior owners of private residential properties.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, again, we have to find the balance.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, the changes we have made to property taxes this time around, are not insignificant at all.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we have structured it in a highly progressive manner.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For the owner-occupied residential properties, the increased tax rates affect only those with Annual Value (AV) above $30,000.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That means that all owner-occupied HDB flats are not affected.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Two-thirds of private residential properties, like condominiums in the suburban areas and lower-value landed properties, are also not affected.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The remaining one-third of private residential properties which are affected are higher-end condominiums, as well as most landed properties.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And then, all non-owner-occupied residential properties will also face higher property taxes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The tax rates for these are higher because these properties include second homes and those held for investment.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And the increases are also more significant for the higher-end non-owner-occupied residential properties.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we want to raise enough tax revenue from property tax to eliminate the need for a GST rate increase, what would we have to do?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Well, we would have to tax all non-owner-occupied residential properties at a significantly higher rate.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Let us, say, we taxed all non-owner-occupied residential properties at a flat 36%.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This would still not be enough, because the number of non-owner-occupied residential properties is considerably less than that of owner-occupied residential properties.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we would need to raise property tax rates significantly for owner-occupied residential properties, including for HDB flats. ﻿In fact, I am somewhat surprised that Mr Louis Chua characterised our moves on property tax rates as tokenism.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Three hundred and eighty million dollars more per year; and he says it is tokenism.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I suppose that is what the Workers' Party is proposing.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, Mr Saktiandi Supaat suggested estate duty.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We did away with this in 2008 because it did not achieve the social equity outcomes we had hoped for.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the end, middle- and upper-middle-income individuals were disproportionately affected by estate duties, compared to the wealthy, who were able to find ways to avoid through tax planning.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides us, the jurisdictions that have repealed their estate duties, like Hong Kong, Malaysia and New Zealand, have not reinstated it either.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There were also suggestions to tax capital gains or dividend income.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But remember, jurisdictions in the region do not tax capital gains or dividends.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And if we were to do so, that can very easily hurt our competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As much as we would like to tax the net wealth of individuals in theory, I have explained, it is very challenging to do this in practice.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What happened with estate duties could very well happen here.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And as long as there are differences in wealth taxes across jurisdictions, wealth can and will move.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why many jurisdictions have already abolished their net wealth taxes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, only three OECD jurisdictions now have a net wealth tax.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to study the experiences of other jurisdictions and explore other options to tax wealth effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also welcome feedback on how to make a suggested net wealth tax work in practice in our context, when almost all our competitors in this region and worldwide do not levy such a tax.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Then, what about the so-called “externalities taxes”, such as sin taxes and carbon tax, as suggested by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am surprised that he raised this, in the first place, as a means of generating revenue.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Tobacco taxes, for example, are a regressive tax – the lower-income groups pay a bigger share of it.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Workers' Party had expressed such strong concerns about the regressivity of the GST, but does not appear to be the least concerned about regressivity here.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In any case, we do not levy sin taxes for purposes of generating revenue, but for deterring consumption, and we will review and adjust these taxes from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For carbon tax, as I have already highlighted, we will channel the revenue to help with the green transition.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this will not help to meet our structural funding gap.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I have explained how we cannot rely on reserves or these different revenue options to close the funding gap.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But let me now address the key issues pertaining to GST.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I had considered this matter very carefully, before deciding to start on 1 January 2023, to delay the start and to stagger the increase over two steps.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some ask: what happens if inflation turns out to be more persistent or higher?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Would it not be better to wait until we are sure that inflation has come down before raising GST?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As I have mentioned before, I fully understand the concerns about inflation and cost of living, but we cannot keep delaying the GST increase, given our pressing revenue needs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If inflation turns out to be persistent and higher than expected, we will deal with this separately through other tools, like I mentioned at the start of my speech.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides managing inflation, we also share the concerns raised by Mr Chong Kee Hiong and Mr Saktiandi Supaat, which is that we want to see local wages rising faster than prices.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, we have done well on this front in the last 10 years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Median Singaporean wages, in real terms, have risen by about 3% per year, faster than many other developed jurisdictions, such as the US, the UK, Japan and Hong Kong.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to work hard to ensure such real wage increases are sustained in the coming years across all segments of our workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Meanwhile, we are helping Singaporeans with the Household Support Package this year and we are cushioning the impact of the GST through the enhanced Assurance Package and the permanent GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The enhanced Assurance Package and GST Voucher will be rolled out together, starting from this year, even before the GST rate goes up.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Combining the two, households will receive a very significant package of benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But before I proceed, I should say that I have noted Ms Sylvia Lim's suggestions on our household archetypes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We do, in fact, take into account different household formations in studying the effects of our policies and we adjust our policies where necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And I am conscious, personally, that there are other kinds of household formations besides the traditional, and we will bear Ms Sylvia Lim's points in mind in our future illustrations.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But for now, take the example of a family with two young children, earning about $2,500 a month and living in a 3-room flat.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, over the next five years, most low-income families will receive more benefits than what they will pay in GST.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Middle-income families have not been left out and will also enjoy significant benefits from the Assurance Package and the GST Voucher.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We know that some are caring for both elderly and young dependents.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why we have designed our measures to help them.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Again, take the example of a household of five persons living in a 5-room flat, but, this time, with two young children and a retired grandparent, and they have a combined monthly income of $9,000.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Over the next five years, they will receive, on average, around $1,300 per year from the enhanced Assurance Package and around $1,100 per year from the enhanced GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Again, altogether, $2,400 per year of benefits over the five-year period.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Not a small sum at all, and this is for a three-generation household with a combined income of $9,000 a month.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Dr Shahira Abdullah and Mr Dennis Tan have commented on the criteria we use for our GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have used Assessable Income combined with Annual Value as a measure of an individual’s means and access to family support.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are not perfect, but I think they are quite reasonable.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to review and see if there are better criteria for our schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Meanwhile, where there are challenging or unique circumstances, we will carefully consider the appeals.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms He Ting Ru asked if we can make the GST less regressive, such as through a multi-tiered GST system for different items, or if we can exempt certain essential items from GST.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: From the outset, the Government has always cushioned the impact of the GST on the less well-off Singaporean families.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is how we have been implementing the GST since 1994, with offset packages and, eventually, the permanent GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The question is: what is the fairest and most effective way to achieve this objective?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Exempting or lowering the GST on a basket of essential goods sounds like a good idea.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The first is that a multi-rated GST system leads, in practice, to highly arbitrary distinctions between products and lots of creative effort by businesses to get their products classified into the lower tiers.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is administratively costly and onerous to implement.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms He Ting Ru said that these costs can be easily overcomed.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But that has not been the experience of other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we were to go down this path, it will significantly and unnecessarily complicate the GST system.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But the second and bigger problem with this suggestion is that, in fact, it does not effectively target support to those with greater needs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, aside from the administration of it, it is not effective.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, such an exemption for a basket of goods tends to benefit the well-to-do, because they spend more on everything, not just luxury items, but basic necessities as well.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We looked at four categories of items: uncooked food; basic food serving services that include hawker centres, food courts and coffee shops; telecommunication services; and utilities.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this is ineffective as a redistributive tool to make our system fairer.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is not just MOF's conclusion, mind you.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This chart shows the existing effective GST rate, across different income deciles, after subtracting the GST-V and the GST that is absorbed for publicly-subsidised healthcare and education.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And you can see that the lower-income households pay a much lower effective GST rate than the higher-income households.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For the second decile, the effective rate is very low.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even for the middle-income households, the effective rate is well below the headline 7% rate, because of how their GST expenses are being offset on a continuing basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Essentially, we already have a highly-tiered GST system in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it is not tiered by the different types of goods or services, which Ms He Ting Ru had asked for.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Instead, it is tiered by the impact of our GST, such that the well-to-do pay more GST and the lower-income are impacted the least.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is a fairer and far more effective way of taxing consumption.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Many Members of the Opposition – in fact, both the Workers' Party and the Progress Singapore Party – object to the very idea of raising GST, claiming that the payouts are temporary and that the GST is regressive and disproportionately impacts the poor.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, again, such misguided claims ignore the way we have implemented GST in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What happens when the GST rate is raised to 9%?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, for them, the enhanced permanent GST Voucher neutralises the impact of the increase in GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is not true that the GST increase hurts the poor.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Not in the way we have designed it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even for the middle-income, you can see they continue to pay an effective rate which is well below the headline 9% rate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is another effect of the GST which causes it to bear more heavily on the well-off.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A consumption tax also allows us to tax those who may not be earning income in Singapore but are, in fact, well-off.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They may be investors or persons of means.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They may not be paying much in income tax today even though they have the means to contribute because their income is not easily ascertained.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That could be, for example, if they are self-employed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But they will certainly be consuming more and the GST ensures that such people, those with greater means, will contribute their fair share of taxes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai had made some calculations and he concluded that the middle-income will bear a disproportionate burden of the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For the middle 20% of households, they will pay a slightly smaller share of GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I appreciate that the Workers' Party offered suggestions on alternatives to the GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, we have studied every tax option even before the Budget in order to design what we have put together as part of a package of tax changes in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have looked at all the options again.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I have explained, there are limitations to all these different proposals and, in some cases, the sums just do not add up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Every tax move we make is carefully considered so that we have, in the end, a balanced, effective and fair set of tax measures in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: More importantly, a progressive fiscal system does not and should not mean that each and every tax is progressive, let alone highly progressive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What ultimately matters is the overall system of taxes and transfers, to ensure that the overall system is progressive, and that is what we have done.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If we were to take a revenue-by-revenue approach, we will end up with less revenues and you will also undermine the broader need for everyone to contribute, as part of a durable social compact.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In this regard, I should say that there is a fundamental difference between the measures we have put forward in the Budget and the Workers' Party's alternative proposals or, for that matter, the position taken by the Progress Singapore Party.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: From what I have heard in this debate, the basic position of the Workers' Party and the Progress Singapore Party is that we can close the funding gap without having to raise the GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Anything but GST increase – even though I have already explained the GST increase in Singapore does not hurt the poor.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I can understand why they think these alternatives are politically more attractive options to offer, but I am afraid they are too simplistic and divisive and will end up creating more problems for our society.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The bottom line is that we cannot sustain a tax system where the bulk or all of the burden is borne by a small group of people at the top end.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It will not be possible to hold our society together if only a small group of people is required to pay more taxes all the time, while the rest simply get to piggy-back on their contributions to enjoy more benefits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why having a broad-based tax like the GST is so vital.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It makes a direct link between our demands as voters and our responsibilities as citizens.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Break that link and we encourage irresponsible lobbying and playing to the gallery.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Someone else will pay for the good things in life.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is how we have designed our system – on the principle of collective responsibility.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Everyone contributes towards the cost of delivering services and everyone benefits from these services, but to different degrees.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Those with greater means bear a higher burden and they draw less on Government support but they still enjoy some benefits from the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Those with fewer means carry a lighter share but they still contribute something and, in return, they receive more benefits from the Government – more than they put in and more than the better-off.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In this way, we all do our part to help ourselves and one another and we strengthen the trust that binds us together as a society.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We should also remember that the well-to-do contribute in many other ways and not just through income or wealth taxes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, many have set up businesses in Singapore, creating good jobs for Singaporeans and helping to develop new capabilities in our economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While these individuals are here in Singapore, they consume more and pay more in GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some also set up philanthropic foundations, contributing to our charities and other worthy causes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Ms Denise Phua spoke about this, about enhancing our framework for philanthropy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I want to make it very clear, too, that we have no issue with people doing well, earning more and achieving success in their careers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our tax system must never discourage hard work, effort and enterprise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, we want to avoid in Singapore the emergence of stark income inequalities or social stratifications, which will undermine social cohesion and pull us apart.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will continually review and update our system of taxes and transfers to achieve this balance: to reward enterprise, innovation and work and to mitigate the pressures of social inequalities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue to ensure a fairer and more resilient fiscal structure to underpin our social compact and to strengthen our social solidarity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Many Members in this House – Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Miss Rachel Ong, Mr Xie Yao Quan – have affirmed this and I thank everyone for your strong support.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is designed to provide opportunities for all to succeed – the young and the old, the lower-income, the middle-income and even the higher-income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, a significant part of our social spending goes towards ensuring broad access to affordable and quality housing, healthcare, education and lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are important social provisions and they support the aspirations of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we have also been careful to design our schemes so that those who come from less well-off backgrounds will get more support.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I assure Members like Dr Shahira Binte Abdullah and Mr Abdul Samad that we will continue to review our eligibility criteria and schemes so that support is sufficient and targeted towards those in need.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are continuing with this emphasis in the Budget to provide, generally, for all but to tilt the support towards those who need them more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Over the last decade, our policy moves have helped to reduce income inequalities and steadily brought down the Gini coefficient.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas said, we are determined to continue reducing wage disparities despite the global economic pressures that are pulling incomes apart and making it harder to hold our society together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we are setting aside significant resources in this Budget for both Progressive Wage and Workfare.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This reflects our shared commitment for a fairer and more equal Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I assure everyone that we are moving as fast as we can to uplift the wages of these lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The new Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) will take effect soon, from 1 April this year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will work with our tripartite partners to get the employers to come on board quickly, even before the mandatory progressive wage requirements kick in.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Overall, our system of taxes and benefits continues to be fair and highly progressive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I will show a chart to reflect this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It depicts the overall net benefits, including grants and subsidies, that Singaporeans receive in a year from the Government, after subtracting the taxes they pay.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You can see here our seniors are well taken care of.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is a significant and tangible form of support.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Of course, as incomes go up, the net benefits are correspondingly reduced.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The higher-income are net contributors – they contribute more than they receive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They benefit from the political stability, social cohesion and overall environment that we provide in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some Members have asked if we are doing enough for the sandwich middle-income group.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you look at the chart, for those in the 40th to 60th percentiles of household income, they continue to receive more benefits than the taxes they pay.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For those in the 60th to 90th percentiles of household incomes, they pay some taxes, after netting off the subsidies and transfers they receive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I understand the pressures faced by this group.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some are caregivers who bear a heavy burden financially and emotionally, even physically.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is why we have been mindful to make sure we expand our suite of broad-based support in areas like education and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have also increased healthcare and caregiving-related subsidies and support to relieve the load on these families, especially for those who care for young ones and elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Importantly, we have taken extra care to keep the tax burden for this group low.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, their tax burden is significantly lower than what it is for their equivalent in most other cities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For the relatively low amount of taxes paid, they enjoy many benefits in Singapore: affordable public housing and healthcare, beautiful parks, excellent infrastructure, quality preschools, schools and tertiary institutions with highly-subsidised fees.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, when you put it altogether, this is how we have designed our fiscal system: one, a fair revenue structure with everyone contributing, but those with greater means contribute more; two, a fair system of subsidies and transfers where all benefit but those who are less well-off benefit more; three, a system where we keep taxes on middle-income households low by targeting our social safety nets at the more vulnerable households who really need the support, while ensuring universal access to high-quality public housing, education and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When you put all three together, we have a highly progressive system of taxes and transfers where the better-off contribute more and receive less in tax-funded benefits while the less well-off still contribute, but a smaller amount, and receive much more in benefits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is reflected in our benefit-to-tax ratios, something which many Members are familiar with but which is worth reiterating.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These ratios that we have achieved for the lower- and middle-income households are no mean feat at all.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will have to continue working hard to maintain this in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in that sense, I have been through many Budgets, even though this is my first time delivering one.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Over the years, I have had the chance to study the fiscal systems of many other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I can confidently say that Singapore is unique in having such a highly progressive system of taxes and transfers, while keeping the overall tax burden low for everyone and especially for the middle-income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have a system that is fair, progressive and effective.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It reflects our values: what we stand for and who we are as a people, and it provides a strong foundation for us to build our economy and our society.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That does not mean that we have a perfect system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are continually adapting and adjusting our approach, as circumstances change and as our society evolves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Typically, after a Budget, we get two types of responses: "too much" and "too little".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the one hand, some say that the Government is doing too much – making costs higher for SMEs and for consumers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the other hand, there are voices that say we are doing too little – not enough taxes for certain groups, more is better.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: After 25 years of public service, I know it is almost impossible for the Government to do anything that pleases everyone all of the time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I want to assure everyone that every move we make is considered very carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We weigh the costs and benefits and the implications.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We discuss extensively with all stakeholders, especially our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is what the team and I in MOF have worked very hard to do in this Budget – to ensure a balanced and fair package of measures, adjusting what is necessary to meet our evolving needs, while bearing in mind our economic and social imperatives and, above all, upholding the principles of fiscal prudence and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is the approach we will continue to take in reviewing and updating our policies – never compromising on our principles and values, and always doing what is in the best interests of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: (In Mandarin):   The Budget has something for everyone and will provide opportunities for all to succeed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I know many are concerned about the impact of the Ukraine crisis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I assure you that we will do more to help Singaporeans and businesses cope with cost of living and business costs should the situation worsen.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some are worried that even with the delay and staggering of GST, there will still be an impact on prices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we have the enhanced Assurance Package (AP) and the GST Vouchers (GSTV) to offset the GST expenses of households.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Both will be implemented starting from later this year before the GST increase takes effect.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Combining the two, households will receive significant benefits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This should more than cover their GST expenses during this period.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have also not forgotten the middle-income or "sandwich" group who are taking care of both old and young.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They, too, will enjoy significant benefits from the AP and GSTV.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The GST system that we have here in Singapore is unique.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Low-income families pay less GST than high-income families.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we are doing this in a way that is fair and progressive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The less well-off contribute a smaller amount of taxes and receive much more in benefits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the other hand, the well-to-do contribute more in taxes and receive less in benefits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But that would mean leaving behind less and less for our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If we keep doing this, one day, we will deplete our reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Like our forefathers, we must exercise stewardship and responsibility over our hard-earned money.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We must not only be fiscally prudent, but also plan for the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is how we ensure that Singapore’s wealth can pass down the generations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I believe the changes to the tax structure we introduced this Budget will help to strengthen our social compact and social cohesion because we are all chipping in and doing our part to tackle our challenges and build a better Singapore together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ultimately, that is how we can build a fairer and more inclusive society, where no one gets left behind and all can enjoy the fruits of Singapore’s success.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, in every Budget, we discuss and debate the design of policy parameters or schemes in monetary terms.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the Budget is much more than that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It reflects something deeper: our ethos and our values.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is an expression of our shared compact to tackle our challenges together, to never stop thinking of tomorrow and to never cease building a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All this boils down to trust, something the Prime Minister spoke about recently in this House – trust between the Government and the people; the trust we have in one another and trust across the generations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It takes effort and time to build up, but it can be destroyed very quickly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When there is trust, we can achieve great things together, we can make the impossible possible.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But when we lose faith in one another, even simple things become impossible.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, whatever views we may have about the Budget, whatever differences we may have on policy issues, let us always work to strengthen trust in our institutions and in one another.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That means debating the issues based on facts and not biased soundbites, or worse, half-truths and lies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It means being honest and upfront with Singaporeans about what we need to do together; not sugar-coating realities or pretending that there are quick and painless remedies available.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In this Budget, I have set out plainly the challenges and also the opportunities ahead of us and explained why we need to move on difficult measures like the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not the popular thing for me to do: certainly, not for my first Budget as Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I have a responsibility to do what is right and what is in the best interests of all Singaporeans; not what is politically expedient now but will store up problems for the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am convinced that the measures in the Budget are necessary and will put us in a stronger position to strengthen the self-reinforcing system of trust we now have and to ensure that every citizen contributes their fair share to building our common enterprise, which is Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A lot has been said about the redistributive aspects of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, in fact, to deepen the trust in one another, we must also engage the human spirit and involve every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We must strengthen the culture of responsibility for one another, so we all feel a renewed sense of duty towards one another and not just a right to the benefits of citizenship.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Singapore must always remain an open and egalitarian society, one without rigid hierarchies and class distinctions, but with a big heart and a generosity of spirit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do not begrudge those who do well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Instead, we celebrate them and we take pride in their achievements.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, for those who have succeeded, there is no need to flaunt one’s wealth or be ostentatious about it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Instead, keep a modest and unassuming approach and do your part to give back to society, so that wealth can be recycled and invested back into society to expand opportunities for others.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They can decipher whether the Budget reflects our shared vision of a fair and just society, whether this Government is one they can trust to manage our resources in a way that is in line with our values and whether this Government is keeping faith with them and their children.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the weekend immediately after the Budget, I had several engagement sessions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As someone shared with me, his wife asked him: "Why are you so happy to pay more taxes?" This is by no means a well-to-do individual, just an ordinary person.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to thank the Finance Minister, particularly for the acknowledgement towards the Workers' Party for coming up with alternative revenue proposals for the Government's consideration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think the prices of goods and services are not a point I need to repeat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Minister would know, thanks to CPI information from MAS and MTI, that price pressures will impact Singaporeans, particularly at the low- and middle-income levels.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is even as the question is important with respect to raising the GST at this time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister made some brief points about it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But I think the question remains: is this a reasonable thing to do in these circumstances?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I think the point arises more acutely when you take into account what market watchers have said about the OECD Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) 2.0, which may well result in corporate tax revenue gains for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I think this is a point that has been raised at the start of the week, coinciding with this Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Surely, MOF would have prepared itself for these various scenarios.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And can I confirm that MOF does not have these various scenarios planned out?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This really brings up the other point the Minister raised about red herrings, that, somehow, when the Opposition asks for revenue and expenditure projections, these are red herrings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because, as I have mentioned in my Budget speech, it is something that many jurisdictions do.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: You are projecting into the future, so, it cannot be perfect and I think people will give the Government buffer and leeway for that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But that is incredibly important and that is precisely why the Workers' Party put forward different revenue streams.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister rounded off at the end about the importance of information, facts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But would not this approach not to make a call for information, characterising it as a red herring, but actually just producing that information lead to the outcome that the Minister himself speaks of and reduces the prospect of individuals mischaracterising positions which, one could argue, has also been done in the course of this debate?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think there were arguments made in the extreme which were not put forward by Workers' Party (WP) Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I do not think anybody suggested raising personal income tax for the upper tier up to 42% to make up for the GST hole.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But it was, nonetheless, characterised as an Opposition idea.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I think it is a case of what is good for the goose must be good for the gander.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And this is something I hope can actually be alleviated through more projections of what the Government needs, how much it is going to collect, because this will result in a more fruitful debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the course of my Budget speech, I did make a point about the revenue that the carbon tax will bring in.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He said it in the beginning, when he opened the debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He does not expect carbon tax to bring in new sources of revenue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But still a debate has to be had.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Particularly, when you look at utility prices, utility bills for average Singaporeans, which the Minister says in his speech are going up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But if you follow it in a linear fashion, that is $12 by 2030 – an increase.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, those numbers should really be brought forward by the Government so that we can debate these and talk about how people, both at the lower- and middle-income levels, can be supported in a better way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think the Minister raised a number of other points.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The other WP Members, of course, will chip in and make those clarifications with the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But Mr Louis Chua is not here today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He will be happy to come into this debate, I can assure you, but he is self-isolating, just to be on the safe side.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think he was COVID-19-positive yesterday but it was a false positive.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I think better for him to stay away.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But he will definitely come back to this in the course of what happens with BEPS and actually what are those projections that the Government is working with vis-a-vis its impact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A number of other points, like I said, I will let the other WP Members come in.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But I think there is a useful question to ask about the reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We have had this exchange in this House a number of times on our position on the reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I do not think it is an accurate reflection to say that, first instance, you look at and turn to the reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And we have really made the Government's own approach informed in this House as to how it also takes a certain approach to change how it deals with the reserves mechanism, at quite short intervals – 2008, 2015.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We are entering a decade where circumstances are changing quite significantly.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Pritam Singh, this part is really for clarification.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I will allow preamble and, as Leader of Opposition, I am prepared to allow you some leeway.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And before I end, just a reminder to the rest of the Members, this is meant for clarification.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And he made the point that this really was not answered and he put the question to Finance Minister Lawrence Wong.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I suppose Mr Singh's point is that even that is not enough.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
