text: And I can understand that some people might feel and be concerned that even that delay and that staggering are not sufficient to address concerns, especially in light of the recent developments in the external environment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why I mentioned just now that the best way to deal with this is: firstly, if, indeed, inflation turns out to be more persistent and higher than expected – which may happen – we will deal with that decisively and separately, and we have the tools and resources to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Well, we have monetary policy to deal with inflation; secondly, we are able to take a series of actions to better secure our energy supplies; and, thirdly, we can help households and businesses directly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, if the need arises, we will not hesitate to take all of these actions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is the first assurance we have for everyone.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The second assurance is that, even setting aside additional measures and actions, we have already done a lot.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I have been trying to explain that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Look at the significant help that is on the table today: household support package this year, plus Assurance Package and the GST Vouchers, both of which have been enhanced, combined together, and both being rolled out this year before the GST goes up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the two, taken together, I think should assure everyone that we are not doing this in a cavalier manner at all.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We considered it very, very carefully before we decided to proceed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And making sure that we are taking all the necessary actions and steps and have contingency measures in place to take care of the concerns of every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, on projections, numbers and data, I accept Mr Singh's point.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I was not attempting to characterise it unfairly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I was sharing my feelings about these repeated requests for information as perhaps distracting us from the real issues.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I accept Mr Singh's clarification and I assure him that he has my commitment that we will continue to put out more information, as much as possible, in order to provide for more informed debates.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I hope he also takes what he said seriously, that the Opposition will also exercise leeway in recognising that these projections in the outer years are inherently fraught with a great deal of uncertainty, especially for a small, little, open economy like Singapore, where so many external events can never be predicted with any degree of certainty.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, very often, we do not even project GDP beyond the year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, when you talk about outer year projections for the economy, for fiscal projections, there will be a very high cone of uncertainty around these numbers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we, therefore, want to make sure that if we were to provide any figures, we do not inadvertently mislead people, cause people to have the wrong impression.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I seek the Leader of the Opposition's understanding, too, that, in putting out such figures in the future, we may very well get it wrong, because there is a lot of uncertainty when we project into the outer years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But he has my commitment that we will continue to see how we can improve the data and information that we put out.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Third, on the reserves, I have explained our position and why changes in the rules, done hastily, we think, are not wise, are not prudent and will come at the detriment of the next generation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If we have to change any rules, we will have to seriously consider them very, very carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if we make any tweaks in parameters – more land sales, more NIRC – what it basically means at the end of the day is that our future generations will be the ones to have to carry the burden.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They will have to pay more in taxes in the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And they will have that much less to deal with any future emergencies, which we all know, will come at a more frequent rate in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, all I say is, let us have a care about this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I do not think it is prudent to make this change now, in place of raising the GST or other tax changes, which we can and should do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As for the quantum of reserves, I have actually mentioned that in my speech.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We would not be able to tell you what the actual figure is, for the reasons I have explained.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But as I have said in my speech, our reserves are growing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But our economy, our needs, the complexity of our needs and the magnitude of the challenges we face are growing even faster.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What is more important when you drill it down is, are we accumulating more than necessary?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: How do we know that this is the case?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because our NIRC, as I mentioned before, we project will continue to grow at a rate that keeps pace with economic growth.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is how we know that we are not over-accumulating.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And as I mentioned in my speech, even that, we cannot be sure that we can achieve that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if we are able to do so, it will already be a significant achievement because of all the headwinds that we are facing in the global investment environment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think I have answered all the questions from Mr Singh, Sir.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For BEPS, again, this is one of those things.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, as I mentioned just now on Pillar 1, the rules are still being finetuned.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yes, there is the pronouncement of 2023, but I do not know for a fact that this will happen in 2023 because many details are still being worked out.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would say it would range from neutral to perhaps some increase, but we will have to look at the figures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will provide some figures, hopefully, to help everyone get a better sense of what it might be.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because the reality is competition for investments is not going to go away just because of BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think it just reinforces the point that I have been trying to make about the alternative revenue streams that the Workers' Party came up with in the course of this debate, knowing that there are quite fundamental changes taking place worldwide where we need a better fix on what the revenue situation will be.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the Minister missed out one question that I also put in my speech about the carbon tax and the estimates that the Government has with its increase at the tiers up to 2030.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Even though I take Minister's point, as I mentioned in my earlier clarification, that he does not foresee this to be a revenue generator, if I can put it that way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I think this is something that we should have a debate about, in good time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We will not be having such a difficult debate, if Singaporeans, especially the middle-class Singaporeans are not asked to pay more taxes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Speaker will allow me to ask all the six questions, but let me ask two questions first.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have given a number of the tax burden of the GST on the middle class to be $1.2 billion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Take away all the compensating packages that you are going to give them, divide the taxpayers into three groups.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Top 20%, the middle class who will not get permanent vouchers, and those taxpayers who will get permanent vouchers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How is the $3 billion or $3.5 billion additional GST going to spread over these three groups?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Question two: PSP has not been talking a lot about alternative sources of revenue because we think there is a lot of justification to make use of the unutilised revenues.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if you look at alternative avenues, actually, it is very easy from our point of view.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second question: if you have to choose between a 2% GST hike and a 3% to 4% personal income tax hike on the top 10%, they will yield about the same amount of revenue, would you still choose the GST 2% hike?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The sums do not add up, Mr Leong.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, we are already raising the personal income tax rates in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will get some money from it, but it is not enough and that is why the GST increase is needed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But as I have repeatedly said, the objections to GST on the basis that it hurts the poor are completely unfounded.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But do not use that as a reason for disagreeing with GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is no basis for that in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, stop pretending that this is the reason.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the first question, impact on the middle class.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I know what you are trying to do with your computations, but I have shown in my chart and in my speech a different way of showing it, which is the share of GST paid by the different groups.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And you can see from that, the chart is self-explanatory, the middle 20%, the share burden that they pay for GST, the increase in GST comes down.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is exactly how we have designed the system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is that group that will bear the burden of the GST increase, while the rest of the population pay the GST rate, but the impact of GST expenses is offset on a continuing basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why we can have the confidence of implementing a consumption tax in Singapore that is fair, effective and does not hurt the poor.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think the Minister did not answer my question.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: After all, someone has to pay for the $3 billion or $3.5 billion GST.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I am asking the Minister what is the tax burden on the different groups of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You cannot say there is no increase in tax burden.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I can tell you that a 3% increase in the income tax on the top 10% will yield $3 billion.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I do not intend to get into a debate on figures with him.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If he thinks that me and all my MOF officers know less about revenues than him, he is entitled to take that view.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I do not wish to entertain or continue the debate further when we are not even able to — if the Member is unable to accept facts which I have put out and says that that is wrong, I do not know how to debate any further.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Member is unable even to accept an authoritative fact from the Minister for Finance and say it is wrong, so, what is the point of continuing the debate on facts and data if the Member does not accept the figures which I have put out on personal income tax?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I have already explained that it does not yield that figure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Just look at the revenue generated from the tax change we have just introduced in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is nowhere in the region of billions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I can only say the facts that the Member has are wrong and it should not form the basis for public policy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the first question, I have, in fact, answered it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I did not say that there is no increase in burden.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I said the burden is borne by the upper-middle and top-end.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And it is reflected in the chart and we will be able to circulate the chart after this, put it out on the website and Mr Leong Mun Wai can have all the time in the world to analyse the figures and internalise them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have three clarification questions with regard to three separate areas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first has to do with corporate taxation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And the question is whether the Government plans to subscribe to the spirit of the BEPS agreement as a signatory and to roll out, broadly speaking, the framework as prescribed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I mentioned this, in part, because the Workers' Party's proposal for corporate taxation is quite different from the hypothetical.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, if we can just keep it to largely clarifications.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sure, I will allow some preamble, but not another speech again.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My second question has to do with wealth taxation and the question is whether the Minister believes that the modest increase in wealth taxation that is set forth in our proposal, which is broadly consistent with – in fact, it significantly is lower than some other neutral analysts have had, our estimate is $1.2 billion – whether he thinks that this modest increase in wealth taxation will be such that it will make Singapore so unattractive that high net worth individuals would relocate and be footloose in that sense.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My third question has to do with land sales.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I accept the position that this Government has that they treat land sales as part of reserves, but then I am wondering if the Minister is able to reconcile the treatment of land sales that are less than 10 years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will do so while ensuring that this is, indeed, implemented around the world.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because our bigger concern is that it must be a level playing field.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It cannot be that some countries do it and others do not; and then, there are revenue leakages that will undermine Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But countries have to go through their own domestic processes to roll out BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not a certainty that this will get through their respective parliaments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Signing the declaration is one thing; 2023, but will it get through all the countries' parliaments, legislation and implemented in law?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we do want to make sure that there is a level playing field and we will do our part as a signatory, as a responsible member of the international community, to likewise implement, when there is that global consensus and global implementation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I have explained that, yes, in theory, you could design a scheme like that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But in practice, it will be much more complicated and it is not just about the fears of people leaving, but the fact that there are so many ways for high net worth individuals to circumvent whatever taxation rules you have in place and to plan away the burden of the wealth tax on themselves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The ones who do, are usually the ones with better means and higher wealth.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And this is why, even in Switzerland, for example, if you look at the net wealth tax they have there, the burden of tax falls on a much broader base of the population.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The so-called "net wealth tax" in Switzerland is not a wealth tax for the top-end only.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Many middle-class, many middle-income people pay for that net wealth tax.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This was our experience in estate duty, mind you.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I mentioned, the top-end, the very wealthy, knew how to plan it away.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the burden ended up falling on the middle-income and the upper middle-income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is our bigger concern, on top of the concern that, yes, there will be some competitiveness reasons.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why we have to study this very carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have to think through, look at the experiences of other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Not very many left to study because, as I have said, many of them have dropped the idea of doing a net wealth tax.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will have to consider what is suitable for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But at this stage, we do not have something that we are confident can be effectively implemented, suited to Singapore's circumstances.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We could have said everything, regardless of the duration of the lease.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we have worked out what we think is a reasonable balance and that has been decided and agreed with the President's Office.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But would he not agree that more taxes on tobacco and gambling are acceptable, if they can help discourage that behaviour because the effects of that behaviour have far higher health and family costs on the lower-income and, therefore, are more regressive?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: That was what he said just now in his speech.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He said this makes a fair and inclusive system and he repeated that point in his Chinese speech as well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And he just said just now that the burden is all borne by the upper-middle and the top deciles of income earners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And to be clear, Workers' Party is not against the lower-income getting back more, if this is, indeed, the case.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But can the Minister clarify whether or not the GST hike will make the lower- and middle-income pay more in net taxes over a 20- or 30-year period?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I was simply highlighting that the Workers' Party made a big issue of regressivity in one case, but not in another case.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I did not understand why there was inconsistency there.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we have never made a big issue of it and, in fact, we do not look at fiscal systems like that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I have said, it is not appropriate to consider item by item.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yes, it generates some but not a lot.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But really more for curbing consumption, which we think is necessary.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why we will continue to review these taxes from time to time, as we have been doing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the second point, the burden of GST increase and how our system works, I think Mr Gerald Giam is saying, well, you want everyone to contribute, but, with GST, the low-income do not end up paying.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With the GST, yes, they may get back something in terms of continuing offsets, but they do pay.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If there were no price to pay, we will not be having this debate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Everyone will happily say, "GST goes up and there is no opposition to it".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I think the Workers' Party and the PSP know that this is something not very popular on the ground and, therefore, they are objecting to it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But because people have to pay for it, then they feel that they are contributing to the system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Therefore, we have confidence to say that, on a continuing basis, the charts that I have described, how we can offset the impact on the low-income groups.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is something we can do, not just today and not just five years, but on a continuing basis.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You do know that we have a Committee of Supply coming up, where the specific and technical questions can be asked.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, if we could keep our focus on the overall fiscal policy of the Government.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Before that, just a very short sort of response or preamble.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think the Minister talked about how much the personal income tax and property tax would have to rise to fill the hole if GST was not hiked.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I want to clarify that when my colleague Assoc Prof Jamus Lim outlined different proposals for revenue generation, there was never the intent that the entire burden of plugging that hole falls onto personal income tax or property tax.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, with respect, Sir, I think the view that we are putting forth proposals that soak the rich is a mischaracterisation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In fact, it is a caricaturisation of what we have put forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The bulk of revenue generation in those proposals actually fell on the changes to the land sales, the changes to NIRC and also the net effect on corporate tax's take from compliance with the BEPS regime.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Not a discretionary increase in corporate tax, but how that would impact the overall corporate tax taken.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think our point there is that —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leon Perera, if you can come to your clarifications and questions, please.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I asked the Minister at that time what would be a reasonable time interval when we review these rules governing the reserves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: They were amended in 2008, they were amended again in 2015.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Are we saying that it is set in stone and we will never amend it?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And the hon Minister's reply to me at that time was, "you never say never" and these things do have to be reviewed at a certain point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, my question is, what does the Minister think is a reasonable point in time when we review these rules, as we have suggested?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: On that note, would it be the case that the Minister rejects altogether any notion that there is an optimal level of reserves and we keep adding to the reserves, ad infinitum, without any regard to the absolute level and its relation to GDP?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The last clarification is, the Minister alluded to the fact that when we make suggestions about the reserves, land sales, NIRC, there is a certain cavalier mindset involved in doing so.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And if that was not cavalier, why is it cavalier when the Workers' Party now suggests doing that?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the first, I recognise that the Workers' Party's suggestions for revenue alternatives could entail mix and matches as they have highlighted, a bit from here, a bit from there.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I still say, as I have highlighted, the sums will not add up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is what it comes down to.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The future generations would mean land sales and NIRC, these sorts of changes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I have explained why we do not think it is financially prudent to make those changes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is contingent on the evolving rules around BEPS 2.0 and, even if we were to get some additional revenue, we are very likely to have to reinvest back to strengthen our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This leaves me with the third group – the wealthy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why I highlighted the sums still do not add up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I appreciate and I take these in good faith that there are these different options that the Workers' Party has offered as alternatives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have studied all of them before the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: During the Budget debate, when these options were raised, we went into them again with my team, but we still are not able to make the sums add up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The next two questions I will take them together – when is the next reasonable interval when we might review our reserves' rules and is there an optimal level of reserves?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is very hard to answer these questions, because I do not have a crystal ball.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Really, who knows what will happen to the world in the next 30 years or more?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think it will have to be something really very disruptive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Not just once off, but on a permanent basis, and we will have to study the options very, very carefully at that point in time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because there are deep, deep implications if we were to change anything on the reserves' rules.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Deep implications for intergenerational equity, essentially, resulting in our next generation having to pay more taxes, as I have said, and having less to deal with any emergencies in the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why I would say not something we will do today because we have other options.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have the GST, which we can implement in a fair way.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is the reason why I ask, well, I wonder, maybe this is taking it a little bit too lightly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because why turn to the Reserves when we have all these options and why make the GST into the last resort?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Future generations – never mind, let us do it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Especially when the way we have implemented the GST is not the way the Workers' Party has characterised it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not, and you know it, too.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have explained it before multiple times and we have reiterated our explanation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, if you understand this, then why are your proposals anything but GST increase?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even Reserves can be touched, but not GST increase.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Workers' Party cites that the GST will hurt the poor.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And on that basis, they cannot support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Do you know what you are saying then?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You do not want to support all the things we have in this Budget?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: To uplift the wages of lower-income workers, Workfare, progressive wages, to help vulnerable families with KidSTART.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I find it hard to understand, frankly, on the misguided view that GST hurts the poor, which it does not.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I can only, therefore, ask whether you are taking things too lightly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Or whether you are raising opposition because of other reasons, political reasons?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As opposed to seriously looking at the facts and doing what is right for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Workers' Party is entitled to their views and to not supporting the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it will not stop me as the Minister for Finance from doing what is right and it will not stop this Government from continuing with all our efforts to build a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There is time for one clarification from you.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just now, the Minister for Finance responded to my question about the Budget cut.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I did not just ask about the 1% cut, which is meant to start next year but also the 2% Budget cut that was supposed to have been implemented from FY2017.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I take it that the same reason applies?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That it was not really a cut but was reallocated to new initiatives and that therefore this is a reallocation, not strictly a Budget cut?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do the new initiatives, therefore, include subsidies to F1 as well as the transfer to SPH Media Trust?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, therefore, this allows us to reallocate expenditure from existing to new, without having to just top up more monies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In this way, we can moderate the increases in expenditures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On how or what are the areas these reallocated monies go to and whether the SPH Media Trust and F1 are part of it, I think we can discuss all these in the respective Ministries' Committee of Supply debates when they come up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Workers' Party would like to record its dissent.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Members who would like to record dissent, please stand up for record.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, we are taking a record of the dissent.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you have other clarifications, you can raise them during the Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Our Chair Ms Sylvia Lim, Members of Parliament He Ting Ru and Louis Chua are not here because they are self-isolating.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party agrees with this important direction in pathfinding the way forward for our little red dot.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Workers' Party Chair and Member of Parliament for Aljunied GRC, Ms Sylvia Lim, will speak further on this, with inputs on inclusivity and innovation in her Budget debate speech tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will outline the Workers' Party's position on the GST and briefly introduce the areas that Workers' Party Members of Parliament will speak on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Then, I will share my views on the main prongs of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the GST hike was anticipated, it comes at a difficult time for our people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Inflation is on the upswing and prices are high.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Supply chain disruptions are having an outsized impact on people's purses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is real concern on the ground that the announcement to raise the GST will lead to price rises across the board.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, some price rises have already occurred, with speculation that these were in anticipation of a GST hike.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A Straits Times column last month discussed the urgency of rebuilding public finances in the face of Budget deficits and the drawdown of reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The GST was held up as being one of the largest and most stable revenue sources, difficult to replace with any other kind of tax.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The impression created by the article and similar arguments was that raising the GST is the only viable option for financing offset packages for the needy and healthcare, and to balance the Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We disagree that there are no other options.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party has previously raised several proposals in this House, both on taxes, as well as adjustments to the reserves framework.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These options do not constitute a raiding of the reserves, as the PAP enthusiastically and inaccurately portrays.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We have supported the call for fiscal prudence as a principle of governance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But we also believe that the judicious use of progressive tax measures can achieve wider societal goals in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Within this term of Parliament, we have proposed a wealth tax and raised the prospect of more progressive corporate tax policies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government, for its part, has not rejected further wealth taxes outright but spoke of the difficulties of implementing some of these tax measures.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These will have to be proactively explored, particularly in view of the limited impact of some measures announced in the Budget, which had been characterised as a tax on wealth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, on the additional registration fee, or ARF tier, for luxury cars announced by the Minister for Finance, a senior manager of a large car dealership which includes luxury vehicles in its stable, was asked if the higher ARF would curb spending on high-end cars.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He was quoted in The Business Times as saying: "It is possible, but I think there's still enough wealth going around".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the Government continues to explore wealth taxes, the Workers' Party's view is that a distinction needs to be made between different types of wealth taxes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We should recognise the legitimate accumulation of wealth through effort and tangible business activity, especially that which creates jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even as there remains scope for wealth taxes, the values of entrepreneurship and equitable reward for hard work can, nonetheless, be recognised and even promoted through tax rebates or relief for such individuals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, wealth accumulated through capital appreciation should be dealt with differently and taxed accordingly in the name of a fairer and more inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government has disagreed with these reasonable suggestions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2001, then-Prime Minister Goh referred to the reserves as a golden goose.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party remains of the mind that we can continue to grow the golden goose, but at a slower rate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The impending population bulge for our seniors portends stress lines for our healthcare needs and our welfare system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But, the fact is that our population is getting older and living longer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While it is responsible to ensure that wastage is minimised as far as possible, our healthcare needs will likely be on an upward trajectory.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the very Singaporeans whose energies contributed to the reserves and who have played their part to fatten the golden goose, spending for them in their golden years and at their time of need should not even be a question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Moderating the growth of the reserves also improves intergenerational equity and accounts for the changing needs of Singapore and its people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It must be noted that the Government has shown, over time, that they are of a similar mind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the 2001 National Day Rally, then-Prime Minister Goh said that the reserves must be protected and fattened.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, changes to the reserves scheme have been implemented by subsequent PAP Governments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is despite the fact that the Government's adjustments have slowed the rate at which the reserves grow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Here, I ask that the Government not rule out changes to our Budget framework.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just as we should not kill the golden goose, we should also not fatten the golden goose at the expense of the people's well-being.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the necessity of a GST hike, the Workers' Party has also made the point that the Government should lay out its revenue and expenditure projections for the rest of the decade.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is so that the necessity of a GST hike can be considered properly and with greater introspection.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We note that the Government has resisted the publication of such revenue and expenditure projections, but the publication of such information is not unusual in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just last week, on 23 February, the Hong Kong government issued its budget statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At Appendix A, the Hong Kong budget includes a medium range forecast of its revenue and expenditure positions for each subsequent year up to fiscal year 2026 to 2027, with assumptions laid out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And, more specifically, does MOF have such projections at least up to five years in the future?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And what is the hesitation in publishing these projections?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Doing so would allow the public to have an in-depth insight as to the need to raise GST and the sustainability of public finances in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The question of projections with respect to public finances must also be considered in the context of the absolute necessity of raising the GST at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, a Business Times article today advanced the view held by market watchers that Singapore could potentially make a net gain in terms of revenue from the global move to introduce a standardised minimum corporate tax rate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even so, it is of little doubt that the GST has been put to good use by the Government to finance spending.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But after more than two decades, its drawbacks remain.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The GST is a regressive tax that hits lower-income earners harder.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And this fact has been recognised since the GST was introduced in the early 1990s.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleague, Sengkang GRC Member of Parliament, Ms He Ting Ru, will speak more about the GST.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Like now, the concerns back in the 1990s were about the average Singaporean worker who was vulnerable to increases in the prices of necessities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, with offset packages targeting low- and middle-income Singaporeans, it is the middle-class that is particularly anxious.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In spite of the headline-grabbing GST offset package announced at this Budget, there is an anxiety as to how much prices will rise in future over the period the offset package would cover.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition to the concerns about spikes for specific Consumer Price Index (CPI) items, there are also concerns about minor price hikes across the board that will hurt cumulatively, not too different from the analogy of the frog in a pot of gradually boiling water.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As Singaporeans well know, no offset package lasts forever.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government expects that, in time, Singaporeans will internalise the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At this Budget debate, the Workers' Party will raise additional alternative proposals to raise revenue so as to stave off the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In particular, Sengkang GRC Members of Parliament, Louis Chua and Jamus Lim, would explore other levers for revenue generation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Apart from the reserves' framework, the alternatives proposed are not inconsistent with the principle that recurrent expenditures should be backed by recurrent revenues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What continues to weigh heavily on Singaporeans today is the rising cost of living, including for the middle-income or "sandwiched" class.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Cost increases in electricity, gas and transport were thrust upon Singaporeans last year and over the last few months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The enthusiasm with which the Government spoke of the electricity retail market in 2018 as a means to manage the cost of living has become decidedly more muted with the exit of multiple retail players.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In December, the electricity tariff for households was raised by 0.6% and there was a recent revision of household refuse collection fees which took effect last month after a previous hike in 2017.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A TODAY article from late October last year quoted the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) predicting that food, preschool and healthcare costs may go up this year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the current economic outlook, it is safe to say that this is a foregone conclusion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: According to data released by the MAS and MTI last week, the headline CPI remains at what it was last December at 4%.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Lower-income Singaporeans, working Singaporeans and middle-class Singaporeans are all being hit very, very hard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is also a pattern of increasing public transport fares over the last three years, as shown in information from the Public Transport Council.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While measured in cents, these increases are by no means small to many who have to incur these costs every day – not as a luxury or as discretionary spending, but as an unavoidable expense simply to get to work and back.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: About three weeks ago, ComfortDelGro Taxi announced an increase in fares by 8%.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just last Friday, all the other taxi companies announced that they would follow suit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: All these and the other inevitable price hikes to come over the next five to 10 years will blunt the impact of the GST Assurance Package, to say nothing of the psychological impact of the package's reduced effectiveness against a backdrop of rising prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party's position on the GST notwithstanding, I welcome the announcement of the formation of a Committee Against Profiteering to address concerns that some businesses could use GST as a cover to raise prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, in order for this Committee to be effective, the public should be clearly informed as to what evidence they would need to file a complaint with the Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Otherwise, it would be a case of the word of a person against that of a business.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, at a time when inflation due to the supply chain crunch is a real concern, some businesses may have good reason to raise prices, or a legitimate reason to raise prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, because of the rising price of raw materials and not under the pretext of the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This may cause misunderstanding amongst the public about resorting to the Committee to investigate the price hikes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But if rising business costs are due to supply chain woes, then prices should correct in time and even fall as the supply chain crunch eases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If they do not, then it would be legitimate for the Committee to inquire why this is the case.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Third, the Committee should look into the businesses that move to raise prices before the GST hike is introduced.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It should not rule out looking into complaints of such pre-emptive price rises that try to bypass the Committee's terms of reference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: SMEs, hawkers and sole proprietors should be allowed to respond to the Committee if they have been falsely or unfairly accused of raising prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Minister of State Ms Low Yen Ling has written to me to nominate one Member from the Opposition benches to sit on this Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have extended this invitation to our Parliamentary colleagues from the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) and Non-Constituency Member of Parliament Ms Hazel Poa has agreed to sit on the Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party is of the view that the Budget is broad-based in providing assistance to individuals and businesses to address both immediate as well as short to medium term concerns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, it provides a useful transitional support such as the Small Business Recovery Grant to businesses in eligible sectors that have been hit hard by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One input we have is to ask the Government to actively consider appeals from businesses that fall outside the eligibility criteria on a more flexible and case-by-case basis as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We also support CPF transition offsets to help phase in the raising of employer and employee CPF contribution rates for senior workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This raising of rates is vitally important in supporting the retirement adequacy of senior workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What was not fleshed out in significant detail was the Minister's commitment that the Government intends to refine how Employment Pass (EP) applications are assessed to increase certainty and transparency for businesses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even while it is a given that Singapore will always be open to foreign talent, we must always prioritise Singaporean talent who represent the Singapore Core.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If a Singaporean can do the job or be trained to do the job, the Government should not inadvertently make it easier or more convenient to resort to hiring foreigners.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope Minister will share more details of the Government's thinking on the new EP framework in his wrap-up speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Budget also renders important support to businesses to ensure that our workers at the lower end of the salary spectrum will see meaningful salary increments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the PWM Credit Scheme as announced by this Budget, I would argue that this can be achieved forthwith instead of waiting for all PWM sectors to be rolled out incrementally before the low-wage situation for these workers is addressed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government is persuaded to move quickly on this even as discussions on PWM sectors are ongoing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As they already earn very low salaries, these 32,000 workers can and should be supported with higher wages immediately.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A second intervention I would suggest for low-income workers amongst us concerns the changes to the Workfare Income Supplement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There was no such criterion in the past.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister has said that the policy intent of this is to encourage part-timers and casual workers to take up regular full-time work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, this new criterion will penalise part-timers and casual workers significantly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are legitimate reasons why Singaporeans take up part time or casual work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some may be caregivers who do not have the flexibility to take up the full-time work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Others may not be able to stand for eight hours a day, for example, in a food and beverage setting for various reasons, including their advanced years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For some individuals, full-time work can be gruelling; for others, retraining is easier said than done.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet some others simply cannot find full-time work in the limited areas they are qualified for and take what part-time or casual work they can find.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would urge the Minister for Finance to remove this criterion so that our most financially vulnerable workers can benefit from Workfare.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party believes that the Government can move the needle for these low-income earning Singaporeans in a decisive way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be consistent with the philosophy of this Budget: "Charting our way towards a fairer, more sustainable and more inclusive society" to alleviate the financial stress of our most vulnerable Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his Budget speech, Aljunied GRC Member of Parliament, Mr Faisal Manap, will speak on other segments of Singaporeans who continue to be left behind because their plight has not been adequately addressed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's net carbon emission goal, as part of our green transition, recognises the important shifts that are taking place across the globe.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Hougang Single Member Constituency Member of Parliament, Mr Dennis Tan, will focus on Singapore's transition to the green economy in his Budget speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More generally, Workers' Party Members of Parliament have made several interventions and suggestions during the debate on the climate Motion in this House last month, covering subjects such as greenwashing, just transition and accelerating electric vehicles (EVs) adoption, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note the Finance Minister's commitment to provide U-save rebates to the cushion the impact of the carbon tax on households from 2023.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Going by the Government's own calculations taken in a linear way, it would follow that a carbon tax of about $ 75 per tonne could potentially increase utility bills by $2 a month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, unlike the new tiers for personal income tax, the upper end property taxes and ARF hikes for luxury cars announced at the Budget, the Minister did not reveal the absolute quantum of revenue the carbon tax is projected to bring in up to 2030.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is not only for the purpose of showing how the carbon tax revenue would be utilised to support decarbonisation, this information will allow meaningful debate to take place on the funding for these decarbonisation measures and whether and how cost of living pressures for the average Singaporean could be further alleviated through the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before concluding, I am reminded that in Singapore, "A"s are not usually given for effort, but for outcomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With this Budget position as a first step in renewing and strengthening Singapore's social compact, the Government should reveal how it reports on initiatives that were previously announced and whether they met their goals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The new social compact ought to require a report card that goes into far greater detail than the bi-yearly Singapore Public Sector Outcomes Review.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A transition is taking place from the original ITM to ITM 2.0, which is now dubbed the ITM 2025.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I wish to ask if there is it is a report card of what has been achieved by the initial ITM, especially for deliverables where Singaporean workers are supposed to benefit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In previous exchanges in this House, notably in 2020, we received assurances that Singaporeans are benefiting and are prioritised in such efforts to generate quality jobs so there was no need to worry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To date, however, we do not have a detailed data set, sector-by-sector of how many jobs were generated by ITM 1.0 since its inception in 2016, 2017, and how many of those jobs went to Singaporeans and at what wage levels?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The ITM 1.0 roadmap set out to develop new and redesigned jobs with better wages provide more overseas opportunities and more strongly support Singaporean workers' upgrading and skills deepening.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Without numbers, however, it is hard to tell whether these broad and lofty goals were achieved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The overall picture maybe rosy with rising wages and low unemployment maintained.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the precise deliverables of the ITM have to be followed up upon, to know whether outcomes have been meaningful or whether alternative approaches to improve outcomes should be considered.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A significant goal of the ITM was to further the interests of Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the timely reporting of ITM 2025 outcomes should be made a key objective of this Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When I asked for specific figures for the first ITM outcomes and what it has achieved for Singaporean workers, MOM stated that more time was needed before we could obtain the full data.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Surely, enough time has passed for such data to be available, as the planning for ITM 2025 is well underway?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If such data is released, it can ameliorate the persistent angst surrounding competition between Singaporeans and foreigners over job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Further, making such information accessible will help Singaporeans better understand the overall economic landscape so that they can develop their skills in specific industries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is really about empowering the Singaporean worker to make informed choices surrounding their economic future in line with the nation's.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, the announcement of further adjustments to foreign manpower policies announced by the Finance Minister is instructive.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The value proposition for businesses to hire Singaporean workers ought to become more compelling, given the anticipated increases of S Pass qualifying salaries and separately, foreign worker levy hikes announced in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Businesses will also benefit from this information as they can be incentivised to redesign jobs to attract Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The outcomes of such initiatives should be a major feature of the new post-pandemic social compact where the Government seeks to renew between citizens and the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleague, Aljunied Member of Parliament Mr Leon Perera will explore the national goals the Government should focus on aggressively, including poverty alleviation, inequality and social mobility.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ready access to data on outcomes of Government initiatives, including multi-year ones will greatly support all three prongs that Mr Perera will advance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To conclude, COVID-19 was and remains a generational crisis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But it has also proven to be a priceless opportunity to reflect on the robustness of our social compact and the live reality of Singaporeans, particularly at the lower- and lower to middle-income levels.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is also an opportunity to reflect on our values as a people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How much do we value the efforts and contributions of those around us, regardless of social economic class or nationality?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How does the Singapore system recognise the effort and labour of those who work with their hands like our conservancy and landscape workers, or those who invest their lives in looking after the needs of others or nurturing future generations of Singaporeans, such as our teachers and our nurses?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And what about the foreign workers in our midst?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Their living and working conditions must be a priority for not just their well-being, but our well-being too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I say for our well-being too because caring for others establishes the standards that we set for ourselves on the type of people we wish to be.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While COVID-19 has been debilitating for the economy and for many families, from a community perspective, it reminded us of the nurse, the teacher, the cleaner, the security guard, the bus captain and so many others who continue working to keep Singapore on an even keel.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The efforts of these Singaporeans make my colleagues in the Workers' Party and I proud to the Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These times have shown the resilience of our people, a subject my colleague, Aljunied GRC Member of Parliament, Mr Gerald Giam, will peg his Budget speech upon.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I echo the statement by the Foreign Affairs Minister that we are shocked and appalled by the blatant aggression and are saddened by the loss of lives and destruction there.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It once again reminded us of the importance of our own ability and our will to defend our sovereignty and our independence.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must expect no one else but ourselves to defend what is ours.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Social compact is not a new concept to us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It has always been the underpinning core values of the Government, manifested in many of our policy formulations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is a vision that galvanises us as a nation and unites us in our commitment to care for each other.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Yet, after listening to the Finance Minister's Budget Statement speech, the meaning of social compact took on a refreshed and more tangible feel and operationalised versions of sorts or more realisable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the last decade, countries and democracies around the world including Singapore, have been grappling with three deep-seated issues.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How do we manage the pace and the trade-off to pivot to a low or net-zero carbon society?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Budget 2022 will stand out for how we have made decisive and bold moves to tackle these issues head-on and to build a fair, inclusive and sustainable society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But it helps to steepen the overall progressivity of our tax structure and towards a fairer system.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Corporate tax changes are also expected to come next.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The two-percentage point increase in GST will happen in 2023 and 2024, by one-percentage point step each.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The GST increase and the upsized Assurance Package put together, actually further enhance the overall progressivity of our tax structure.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is because the Assurance Package will have more than adequate payouts and rebates to cover at least five years of additional GST expenses for the majority of Singaporean households and about 10 years for the lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The existing permanent GST Voucher scheme will also be enhanced to provide continuing offsets for the GST expenses of the lower- to middle-income household and the retirees' household.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the other hand, the higher income and the wealthier will pay more GST, especially with the two-percentage point increase, as they tend to be higher spenders, bigger consumers and hence, will contribute more to GST.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Taken together, it attested to the system of social compact that we have always wanted where the better-off contribute more and those with less contribute less and will receive more benefits and support to help them cope with life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In recent years, as income and wealth disparities continue to widen, the view that the better-off should contribute more in taxes has gained traction and it is heartening that in Singapore, we are also hearing calls from the high-income earners and those who are wealthy themselves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This reflects our values and mutual responsibility amongst ourselves as a society and as a nation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, there is often this argument that rising income or wealth taxes may diminish our competitiveness, or that wealth is mobile and can be easily moved to a jurisdiction with no or low taxes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Yes, we have to be watchful of this possibility but we should also not underprice ourselves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore has its very compelling proposition as a triple-A rated global hub, excellent infrastructures, deep and diverse talent pool, trusted and enforceable legal and regulatory structure, strong and stable Government, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are rated among the best place to live in the world and we are a nation that is always passionate about excelling ourselves and constantly charting ahead and investing for a better future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We cannot just count on low taxes or lower costs as a way to attract investments and talent.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The significant moves on tax structure in Budget 2022 demonstrates our confidence and also our self-assuredness as to what Singapore can offer.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have to keep working on strengthening each of these fundamental propositions and not only safeguard but also keep growing the value of this premium.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In a globally connected and knowledge-driven world, those equipped with in-demand skills and know-how tend to be duly compensated for their expertise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Salaries of the top earners have seen their income rise at much faster pace.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the other hand, the incomes of our lower-wage workers continue to stay stagnant or not keeping up with the rise in cost to live a better life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are concerned with this widening income inequality and that is why we have Workfare and other skills upgrading programmes, among others, to intervene and uplift the wages of low-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government will co-fund the wage increase of low-wage workers through the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Those earning between $2,500 and $3,000 will also receive support, but at a lower co-funding ratio.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And to complement the Progressive Wages move, the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) will also be significantly enhanced.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, fiscal interventions alone cannot be the only way to uplift wages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Businesses and consumers will also have to contribute their share to help raise the income of our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And we should continue to encourage and support our lower-wage workers to upskill, so that they can also move up the wage ladder.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On decarbonising Singapore, I applaud the bold moves by the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is thick enough to bite or hurt and can nudge and change behaviours and business practices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The sharp carbon tax increases demonstrates the Government's resolve to achieve net-zero emission by around mid-century.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Since our founding, we have always kept long-term environmental sustainability in mind and, in fact, have been ahead of the curve.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the 1970s, we have already scaled up the greening of our island by sustained tree-planting programmes and safeguarding our nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We mounted ambitious efforts to clean up our rivers, build comprehensive sewage, waste infrastructure, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But this coming series of carbon tax increases will be our most ambitious move.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It will have significant cost implications to businesses and households.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, without transitory support, some businesses may not be able to cope and some may exit.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I welcome the clarification by the Finance Minister that the Government does not expect to derive additional revenue from the carbon tax levy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The carbon tax raise will be used to cushion the impact to households and businesses, as well as make decisive investments in new, low-carbon, more energy-efficient solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should leverage on this major decarbonisation effort to catalyse the development of the green economy and to entrench ourselves in this global green transition and to create jobs, create opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I have raised this concern in earlier Parliament Sittings, including whether we can delay the increase of GST, given the cost pressures at the moment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the recent spate of price increases is a cause for great concern for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Whether it is electricity, food or transport, we can feel the overall trend of inflation and the pressure of rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Most of the goods we consume are imported, so any rise in international inflation, especially energy prices, will have a direct impact on domestic consumer prices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While we have comprehensive measures to cope with the inflation, such as using a strong Singapore dollar to offset rising prices of imported goods, expanding and diversifying our sources of imports, and a slew of packages to help the low-income group, they do not fully offset external inflationary pressures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fortunately, in this year's Budget, the Finance Minister has added a $560 million Household Support Package to help Singaporeans cope with rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The package offers up to $285 worth of U-Save rebate per household living in HDB flats, an additional $200 top-up to every child and student's Edusave account and another $100 CDC voucher which is very popular among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the international situation and global supply chains continue to be unstable, I hope the Government will continue to pay close attention to consumer price fluctuations, especially utilities, and expand the package when necessary to help Singaporeans cope and tide over this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: He has postponed the timetable to next year and the following year and will raise the GST one-percentage point per year in two years' time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many Singaporeans feel that while GST increase is inevitable, it is better later than early.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is better to raise it in two tranches than two-percentage points in one go.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Most importantly, we will have a $6.6 billion enhanced Assurance Package to help most Singaporeans offset the impact of higher GST.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, under this package, each adult Singaporean will receive a cash grant of between $700 and $1,600.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government will also give out $600 to $900 in GST vouchers to lower-income elderly Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Other subsidies include a U-Save rebate of up to $570, and $200 worth of CDC Vouchers for each household next year and the following year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The total amount of these rebates is substantial and will be sufficient to offset the increased GST amount that most Singaporeans will have to pay over the next five years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For low-income families, the increased GST amount can be offset over the next 10 years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In other words, the subsidy that this family will receive is more than 10 times the additional GST they need to pay.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Retirees living in 4-room flats will receive subsidies that can fully offset the extra GST they have to pay.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The tax changes this time round further strengthen this characteristic by raising the income tax and wealth taxes for high-income earners on one hand and expanding the assistance and subsidies for lower- and middle-income families on the other hand.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Those with better incomes or wealth can afford higher taxes because of their better economic conditions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Most of them are also consumers who spend more, so their GST contributions are also higher than those of the lower-income groups.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The middle 20 percentile will receive a $2 subsidy for every $1 of tax paid.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: High-income earners will receive a subsidy of $0.30 for every $1 of tax paid.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These figures demonstrate vividly that our tax and grant system is really focused on taking care of lower-middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I think this is a fair tax system that we aspire to.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This year's Budget reflects our pursuit of the spirit of social cohesion and joint advancement of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In English): Sir, Budget 2022 to charge the new wave forward to realise our vision as a fairer, greener and more inclusive society, we want to level up our society, secure the well-being of our people and at the same time, we need to grow our economy, create exciting future opportunities to build our best home.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Every of the above that we want to do for the good of Singapore and for the good of people require financial resources.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is meaningless to have big plans and big ideas, but does not come with sound and sustainable financial plan to fund them.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to have a clear mind how we intend to charge the way forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But at the same time, we also need to have a clear mind how we can find the means to pay for these new ways.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Budget 2022 strengthens the foundations of our long-term funding plan, which is sustainable and fair, and it opens up further exciting possibility ahead for Singaporeans and Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This move by the Finance Minister brought some relief to concerns amidst rising prices.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We all know that it would have been more expedient for the Government to effect the total increase in one go and the earlier the better for the Government.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But we appreciate the sensitivity shown to delay it and do it in two separate steps.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Taken by itself, this amount may not appear large.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, property-related taxes such as Additional Buyer Stamp Duty (ABSD) have in fact contributed significantly to our revenue base over the years.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: ABSD was further increased just a few months ago in December across all categories except for first-time local home buyers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The ABSD rate for foreign buyers now sits at 30%.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As ABSD targets mainly property investors, this has effectively become a form of wealth tax, apart from acting as a policy measure to cool the property market.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst I know the Government may not consider this as a stable form of revenue base for the Government, I think investors should not hold out much hope for the ABSD to be lifted, as it is now a significant part of Government revenue.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In fact, we should expect more to come on the property front, including the low hanging fruit of injecting further progressivity to the basic buyer's stamp duty from the current 4% for properties valued at $1 million and above, for higher tiers to apply to more luxury homes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It was only recently in 2017, when the top tier personal income tax bracket was increased to 22%.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Yet, this Budget proposes to increase it again, further to 24% from 2024.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In Singapore, top 10% income earners who pay Personal Income Tax already foot approximately 80% of total personal income tax collected.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have seen a steady decline in our Gini coefficient from 0.45 in 2010 to 0.38 in 2020, after transfers and taxes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Another $9.5 billion over five years is being set aside to support the Progressive Wage Model and Workfare Income Supplement scheme, benefiting 94% of full-time low-income workers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our system is designed such that for every dollar of tax paid, the bottom 20% of our residents receive about $4 of benefits back, the middle-income residents get about $2 and the top 20% receive about 30 cents of benefits.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I think we have all understood how it works, my colleague mentioned this earlier too.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The principle of helping those with less inherent in our system of taxes and transfers has gone some way to moderate the vagaries of globalisation and inequality.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Globally, increasing numbers of wealthy individuals are engaging in philanthropy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: A "Global Philanthropy Report" by Harvard identifies some 260,000 foundations with total assets of more than US$1.5 trillion.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In Singapore, we have also seen more privileged individuals "giving back", including the setting up of private charity funds with $200,000 and more.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: More and more family offices are setting up in Singapore, with strong mandates to do good and to give back to society.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should therefore enhance our philanthropic policy framework to accommodate new forms of giving and encourage the establishment of more foundations, of greater sophistication.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
