text: Currently, our policies are geared towards straightforward forms of giving.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But wealthy families aspire to make significant contributions beyond plain chequebook giving.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They hope to tap their financial resources, unique capabilities and networks, in creative ways to make an impact.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They want their gifts to be transformational and so do we.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Enhancing our policies around philanthropy can help establish Singapore as a philanthropic hub – a pillar of excellence to build alongside our hub status for finance and sustainability.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This intent to promote Singapore as a philanthropic hub is not new.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Several changes to taxation and regulatory framework were indeed made by then-Second Minister for Finance, Tharman Shanmugaratnam, in Budget 2007.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, the concept of philanthropy has evolved rapidly over the years.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Wealthy families and philanthropists are keen to explore new models such as social impact bonds, impact investing, venture philanthropy and so on.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Have our current policies kept up with the times?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In its early days, Singapore benefited in similar ways from generous giving by visionary philanthropists and organisations, such as Tan Kah Kee, Govindasamy Pillai and Ngee Ann Kongsi, to build our communities, our schools and our hospitals.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Today, we have a window of opportunity to work alongside a new generation of philanthropists, using modern, innovative and creative ideas, so that their contributions can be a fulfilling experience for both the donor and the beneficiary.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Finance Minister announced Singapore's commitment to sustainability by bringing forward the timeline for the country to attain net-zero carbon emissions by and around mid-century.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The higher carbon taxes will accelerate our drive towards a greener economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should aspire to be the leading location in Asia for expertise in carbon services and be the trusted regional marketplace for carbon credits.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, we need to carefully navigate this journey to go green, to avoid dislocating our industries or losing our attractiveness as an investment destination.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We will need to take an ecosystem approach for the transition, laying clear frameworks, standards, roadmaps and sector-based solutions to build green capabilities and collaborations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We will need to champion green financing and be the preferred issuer of green bonds to enable sustainable investments across sectors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We will need incentives – incentives to green our buildings and step up investments in sustainable development and renewable energy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is especially so for the manufacturing sector with utilities making up to around 9% to 10% of their operating costs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I urge the Government to ensure transition measures will be in place to cushion the increase in electricity costs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With the tight labour market, employers shared that the $500 dollar increase in work pass qualifying salaries will likely translate to just "forced" salary increases for their foreign workforce, as there are few alternatives in the foreseeable future.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: A points system which considers a range of non-salary factors will make the work pass system more transparent and economical.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The higher work pass thresholds have triggered international firms to review the sustainability of their operations in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many businesses worry about how they may weather the storm in the coming years.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Increase in taxes, higher carbon and energy prices, as well as higher local and foreign manpower costs are the main challenges.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Companies need urgent help to fast track digitalisation, reskilling of local workers as well as job matching to aid their transformation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They are also screaming for the Government to calibrate the timing, the timing of new policies to provide some breathing space for the transitions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: More economists are predicting that given the externally driven inflation catalysts, they expect inflation will be sustained at high levels for up to two years.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst I do agree with the expansionary policy to ensure that recovery will be sustained, so I support the Budget, it is equally important that we do not lose sight of the fiscal prudence that has defined Singapore's approach to budgeting.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government commonly accumulates surpluses in the early years of its term to ensure that the constitutional requirement to achieve a balanced Budget is achieved.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: If I may start with a quote from Martin Luther King, who once said: "The ultimate measure of a man is not where he stands in moments of comfort and convenience, but where he stands at times of challenge and controversy." I believe that men and women, we all are standing at times of challenge and controversy right now.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is amongst one of the most inoculated against COVID-19 with, I believe, 86.1% of population vaccinated and with low casualties.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Still, we see how the Omicron strain, while fortunately not as deadly as Delta, is causing stress in our healthcare system and a slow-down in our easing of safe management measures and opening up of borders.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our muscle for alertness and resilience has been developed and put to the test time and again over the past two years, and we must continue to keep it well-oiled and ready for action, but at the same time, not be paralysed by fear.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, gratitude to everyone from the Multi-Ministry Task Force, to our healthcare workers and essential workers on the front lines who have helped keep the lights on and the rest of us safe.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A big thank you, from all of us, to all of you.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Whether Budget 2022 delivers on its design now depends on how well Team Singapore executes.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Nearly half, about 47%, of businesses are confident that the economy will improve in 2022, compared to 31% of businesses in the previous survey.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I must add that the survey was pre-Russia-Ukraine situation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses adopt a cautious outlook towards global and regional economic climate.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In the survey, businesses reported that manpower cost and availability are key challenges that they face, along with demand uncertainty, travel restrictions and changing regulatory environment.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: However, 2022 will expect to see more job openings and better compensations as businesses look to build up their human capital.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Companies are focusing on digitalisation, re-engineering of work processes and diversifying supply chains as key areas of business transformation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Even though most firms are aware of the importance for digitalisation, many lack manpower and resources to transform their businesses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses need Government support in technology adoption and development of human capital as they push towards a more digitalised future.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, assistance with digitalisation remains the top area of support reported by businesses, with 43% desiring Government help in this aspect.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Support towards human capital development rose to be among the top three areas of business support needed in 2022, with 37% of businesses reporting a need for such assistance.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The level of business internationalisation remains consistent with 2020.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is another area that they are counting on Government and the whole-of-society's support.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is no evident drop-off even in the face of travel restrictions.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: China, Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia continue to be the popular destinations for expansion.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Meanwhile, geopolitical risks including the US-China continued trade tensions, the acceleration of inflationary risks, the escalating costs of energy and the recent Russian-Ukraine military conflict will dampen the optimism going forward.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Still, we need to focus on what we can influence and keep moving forward.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For the purpose of my speech today, I would like to speak on four issues and put forward some ideas which have come up in my discussions with industry leaders and trade associations and chambers (TACs).

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We hope the Government can support and help to address these.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The business community in general is concerned with manpower availability and costs as it is.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Some sectors in particular, F&B and construction, are very concerned with the adjustment to Foreign Worker Policies (FWP) in this year's Budget.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These industries are local industries, and their manpower cannot be offshored.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our restaurants and our BTO flats depend on them being able to have the workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is hoped that the Government can look into sectorial differentiation when implementing the changes to the FWP at least for the foreseeable short- to medium-term.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Some manufacturing companies which are more labour intensive are concerned that there may be a hollowing out of manufacturing to lower-cost locations.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, we might have to accept that outcome as inevitable considering Singapore's scarce labour resources.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Meanwhile, I would like to suggest that Government and industry could get together to review the costs across the entire supply chain of our key industries and consider our strategic competitiveness end-to-end.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This will also help identify supply chain risks and identify actions to mitigate supply chain disruptions which we have experienced during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is also a suggestion by TACs for an Alliance for Action (AfA) to be set up to look into manpower issues for overlapping industries.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Next point – SMEs need capital and credit, talent and network.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has had an aspiration to grow global champions from amongst our local enterprises.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Temasek-linked companies have done Singapore proud in putting Singapore on the map, whether it be DBS or SIA, pre-COVID-19, or Keppel or Singtel.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Outside of tech companies like SEA or Grab or Carousell and other tech companies, the question is why our Singapore medium-sized companies do not get the same lift?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It boils down to a lack of capital, talent and network.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I did suggest for the support be extended beyond the large local enterprises (LLEs) to include our local SMEs, or at least, the medium-sized companies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we have promising mid-size companies which may be "stuck" due to a lack of capital, lack of access to tools and networks especially for going beyond Singapore, and lack of leadership and expert capabilities needed to break out and stand out.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With some support by way of talent, capital and network, we give ourselves a better pipeline of global champions in-the-making.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The first story is the story of the M&A journey of a Singapore mid-size company.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: When they were looking for partners, they received 40-over NDAs signed by companies from all over the world but none from Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The next story starts off well with how the Government's Temporary Bridging Loans (TBLs) and Enterprise Financing Scheme (EFS) were going to help our local companies tide over the difficult COVID-19 times.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, the relief was short-lived as the companies found their commercial credit lines with their banks terminated and transferred to the Temporary Bridging Loans (TBLs) and Enterprise Financing Scheme (EFS) offered by the Government.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure these are sound credit risk decisions made by the bankers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But for the SMEs, they are in a tight spot.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps there are misunderstandings in the implementation of TBL and EFS that needs both sides to dialogue and move forward.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This experience will, in fact, equip them with the empathy they will need when crafting policies for the country and sharing the talented resources with our SMEs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Leveraging IP is also an exciting opportunity for our companies but our local enterprises who have attempted to do so, share that IP filing and registration need deep pockets.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Some of the TACs have requested for Government to consider providing funding support to guide and enable businesses to actively leverage on intangible assets as a competitive advantage.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This would include leveraging on overseas IP owned by Singapore companies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that MinLaw and IPOS are already supporting but perhaps SMEs can be made more aware.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our businesses have woken up to the Singapore Green Plan 2030 vision as a call to action for today.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is no longer something to think about tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The carbon tax rate increase and the roadmap ahead are a clear conviction that sustainability is a matter of importance and of immediate action.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: COP26 targets are not just the Government's business.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Financial support for green transition is critical for businesses as they map out their net-zero plans.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I will speak more about what is needed during my cut with MSE.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For now, suffice to say that the "Made-in-Singapore" brand needs to soon carry a new mark of global sustainable standard.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: My fourth point, investing in our people for the future.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To navigate a tight labour market, businesses are turning towards building a strong local core through enhancing recruitment efforts and offering competitive wages.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses will continue to upgrade their team's skills and upgrade their expertise and knowledge, and the support by Government via the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credits, the newly set-up NTUC administered grant for transformation plans and other programmes, for example: schemes to support ICT, will all go a long way.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Minister for Education Chan Chun Seng has in recent speeches called out the key role that the IHLs – ITE, Polytechnics and Universities – can play in partnering our enterprises to skill up and transform.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I declare that I am the Chairman of Singapore Polytechnic (SP) and so, pardon me if my examples are from SP.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The first example is how industry can proactively work with IHLs on their curriculum to enable the students to be work-ready, job-ready when they graduate.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The SP faculty at the School of Chemical and Life Sciences developed an opportunity for deeper linkage with industry via the Diploma in Perfumery and Cosmetic Science.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The School co-created the Industry Now Curriculum (INC) with industry experts like IFF-Lucas Meyer Cosmetics and Johnson & Johnson Pte Ltd.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The innovation involves three semesters of learning in class and lab, one semester of a co-supervised "live" industry projects sponsored by industry partners including start-up companies like NUSMETICS Pte Ltd.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The students then go on to complete their final two semesters in a year-long internship with an industry partner.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The second example is a bold eco-system collaboration.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: SP designed and setup an Advanced Manufacturing Centre in collaboration with 16 industry partners including experts like TÜV SÜD Digital Service, ASTech Pte Ltd, Bosch Rexroth, Delta Electronics and Onn Wah Tech Pte Ltd, and others.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Together, they curated the "Advanced Manufacturing Learning Journey" curriculum focused on enabling companies to re-imagine and re-think manufacturing processes.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There are many initiatives which all the IHLs have rolled out to support industry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The call to action is for all our Singapore companies to accelerate the reskilling of their workforce for transformation and for the Singapore workers to seize the day and get re-skilled to stay relevant in the dynamic, fast-moving workplace.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has put their money squarely on investing in our people to be ready for the future.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: If it can happen to Ukraine, can it happen to us?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans must not think it could never happen.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What are the lessons for us to draw on?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One thing for sure is that our total defence and diplomatic corps cannot be over-emphasised.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans cannot take our existence as a nation for granted.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our founding fathers, Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his old-guard colleagues wrote our Singapore story.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They had the courage to dream big, to create a "First World oasis in a Third World region".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Their rallying cry was for this "mudflat to become a metropolis".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We were poor then, but we were certainly rich in spirit.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Many were the Work Permit holders, Employment Pass (EP) holders and S Pass holders of their time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Some may have come as workers, others as merchants and traders from afar.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Yet others came as missionaries, as teachers and nurses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I will wait for Mediacorp screenwriters to tell that story!

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Whatever the reasons that brought them here to our shores, they had the grit to defy all odds and in spite of the diversity of race, cultures, language, religions, our forefathers and mothers, uncles and aunties bonded together behind that big dream.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And so, here we are today, having inherited a Singapore that is one of the world's globally recognised city state with strong governance, high trust, smart, innovative and hardworking people, though a little "kiasu" or risk adverse at times.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Through the COVID-19 crisis, we saw how well we could ride the rolling waves of the pandemic with our reserves and the resilience of our people; the reserves that have been built over years of prudent fiscal discipline and strong monetary and economic excellence.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In the wake of the pandemic, we saw the hearts and minds of Singapore citizens and residents reflect the care, the generosity, the empathy and the love for neighbour – whether our essential workers or our migrant communities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Building back up is where we are now, and we must not fall into potholes of narcissism, discouragement and pessimism.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that Singaporeans at the core have a strong sense of integrity and a deep sense of responsibility to our work, to our family, to each other, to our country.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As we learn to live with COVID-19, we must learn fast to tackle this next pandemic of climate change that is already upon us.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We must take responsibility for the development of our own skills, leveraging the support that the Government is providing.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Together, let us not wait for the fish to be handed to us but let us learn to fish for ourselves, our family and our neighbours, and live the dream that our forefathers could only imagine.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I will not sing for you, but here are the words: "There were times we were uncertain, But we just kept walking on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Hear this anthem, it's the voices of our friends.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Come whatever on the road ahead, We did it before, and we’ll do it again." With this I conclude with my support for the Budget 2022.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unemployment also plunged to 3.2%, close to pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And exports, the traditional engine of growth for our economy, expanded by around 12%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With growth, employment and trade figures strong, there is some justification for a renewed sense of confidence as we emerge from the pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the economic picture is not all peaches and roses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Higher prices have been exacerbated by an overall increase in the cost of living in the city, which has already been rated as one of the most expensive in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And tailwinds from the generous fiscal stimulus as well as the favourable external environment will fade further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Growth, accordingly, is expected to fall to around half that of last year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It therefore strikes me as premature to be contemplating any form of tightening in the stance of fiscal policy at this time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the removal of wage support for all but the most hard-hit sectors of the economy was prudent and economically sound, going in the other direction of making fiscal policies more contractionary takes a sensible argument to an absurd conclusion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Doing so would introduce unnecessary frictions into what is still a nascent recovery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It runs the risk of shooting ourselves in the foot, of scoring an own goal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this is precisely what will occur with an increase in our Goods and Services Tax (GST).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Japan applied consumption tax hikes – their equivalent of the GST – three times in recent history: first in 1997, then in 2014 and subsequently in 2019.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first two times, GDP collapsed and the economy promptly went into a recession.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is worst, the subsequent collapse in output meant that the tax increase itself failed to produce sufficient revenue to justify its increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The most recent time was also accompanied by a recession, although this time, the effects were exacerbated by the onset of COVID-19.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the most recent Omicron variant has turned out to be less detrimental to economic performance than earlier ones, this episode is a reminder to us that a GST hike would rob us of the precious opportunity to revive support for the economy if, knock on wood, some unforeseen Pi or Rho variant – and I understand I am showing off my very limited knowledge of the Greek alphabet here – were to emerge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, we last hiked GST in 2007.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This did not trigger a recession the following year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The economy eked out a 1.1% growth rate in 2008.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it nevertheless represented a sharp drop in activity compared to 7.8% the year before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Back then, we were helped by the fact that on both years, global growth remained in positive territory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This time round, the global environment may be less favourable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus, global growth will be slowing just as the burden of an increase GST will be kicking in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A hike in GST is unarguably a contractionary fiscal policy that could offset what had hitherto been a very healthy consumption and investment growth over 2021.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The private sector, by anticipating the anticipated tax changes and the need to save more, could further scale back on spending today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A GST hike is also particularly ill-timed because it holds the potential to stoke already elevated inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the direction of inflation in the future is anybody's guess – and economists have a particularly dismal track record of predicting price dynamics, one that would make a weather forecaster blush – it would not be surprising if inflation remains elevated through till year end.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Supply chain constraints have not resolved as quickly as previously anticipated; energy prices are high and could rise more in response to geopolitical tensions and the likelihood of global sanctions; labour markets are tightening, spurred by the global great resignation and lying flat movements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, this state of affairs may even become a more lasting fixture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is a risk that inflation expectations have become unmoored from the traditional 2% health by advanced economies worldwide and is now permanently higher by up to half a percentage point, compared to prior the pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if this turns out to be the reality, then rolling out a GST hike at this time will only add fuel to the inflation flame, which is already starting to burn uncomfortably hot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is for this reason that any delay of the hike, were it to occur, is critical, as opposed to the historical pattern of rolling out increases in July.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Doing so in a staggered fashion – 1% in 2023 and another in 2024 – will certainly cushion the impact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And this measured approach is echoed by economists and observers, and SMEs have also expressed their relief about the delay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the key question, Mr Speaker, here that remains is this: will the Government stand ready to potentially re-examine the timing with a view toward an even more significant delay should macroeconomic conditions remain unfavourable for a tax hike come 2023 and 2024?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Should the Government proceed with a tax hike at the pre-announced dates, will they complement the hike with a justification based on the contemporaneous economic situation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The reason provided by MOF is that our revenue needs have risen, especially with regard to providing healthcare for a rapidly ageing population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is no doubt that we should do more to take care of the elderly among us – the Merdeka and Pioneer Generations that have contributed so much to bringing Singapore to where it is today, as well as generations that will enter their twilight years in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My concern, Mr Speaker, is whether GST is the ideal instrument for doing so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On its face, GST fulfills many of the criteria economists traditionally look for, in optimal public finance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is efficient because taxing all of consumption usually does not distort spending behaviour compared to taxing income or other taxes specific to certain goods and services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is broad-based, meaning that it can raise significant revenue across a large population and it is simple.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unlike income, we do not need to futz around with appropriate measurements and exemptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: You just pay a fixed fraction of what you buy, period.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this is precisely why we do not rely on GST alone to raise income, there are also some problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is generally sound to diversify the Government's revenue stream as opposed to relying on narrow forms of taxation, more recent research has questioned whether consumption taxes are truly more efficient, especially if we relax some of the standard assumptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But perhaps, most importantly, most people believe that it is actually easier to ensure that income taxes are progressive, that is, those who are better able to afford a higher tax burden, pay more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In and of itself, it is, therefore, regressive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government's solution to addressing regressivity has been to pair GST with a voucher system, where cash rebates of a certain amount albeit not matched directly to actual spending, are issued to lower-income households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This transfer can indeed be progressive and it may be the case that the overall tax system, even after raising GST, will remain progressive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, the earnings of lower-income groups have been eroded comparatively more as a result of the pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Prices are rising everywhere and furthermore, support payments via the COVID-19 Recovery Grants will expire by year end.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have focused much of my remarks on the importance of supporting the less fortunate, not just because of some heightened notion of equity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many studies have pointed out pandemic-induced changes will have lasting effects on incomes, savings, educational attainment and other socio-economic outcomes for poorer households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a society, we can ill afford to have them fall further behind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It will be an affront to our sense of equality, of opportunity and genuine meritocracy as well as a stain on the morals and values we hold as a society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While cut-offs have to occur somewhere, it is worth remembering that many households in this income bracket are also in the "sandwiched generation", who face expenses of supporting their aged and retired parents, as well as their young, school-going children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One alternative – but admittedly more complicated – scheme for enhancing the progressivity of the GST is to consider GST where progressivity is built right in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means the purchase of goods and services that the wealthy are much more likely to purchase – fancy cars, high-end properties, first class tickets and luxury experiences – be subject to a higher rate of taxation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government has in this Budget and over the past year taken some significant steps in this direction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: An increase in the Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD) by 5% and 10% for the second and third properties is welcome, if a little blunt, since it does not entail any associated minimum value, and PR and foreign purchasers confront even steeper rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Budget further sharply increases property taxes for homes with annual value exceeding $30,000.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It remains to be evaluated whether these additional taxes successfully target the wealthy, or whether much like the ill-fated estate tax, they end up affecting mainly upper-middle and marginally higher-income households while the ultra-rich retained their ability to shield themselves from progressive taxation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It will also be valuable to revisit in a few years' time whether such taxes move the needle, in terms of freezing and reversing the rising income and wealth inequality in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The other question that inevitably arises is, are there no alternatives to a GST hike?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One lever which we call, say, "the corporate tax lever", accepts the broad premise of the OECD-led effort to implement a global minimum corporate tax rate of 15% known as BEPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We assume a reasonable loss of corporate and personal income taxes arising from the agreement of 20% and 10% respectively and full compliance of the corporate tax rate to the new global minimum for multinational corporations, which amounts to about the two-thirds increase in the effective rate from current levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, we allow small and medium enterprises to retain their current 3% effective rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another lever which we call "the wealth tax lever" puts asset taxation at the front and centre of revenue generation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We adopt the Government's current threshold of 10 years required for land leases to be classified as permanent, above which land sales receipt must be fully channelled into reserves and extract just the first nine years for recurrent expenditure, while redirecting the remainder into reserves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We also incorporate the Government's proposed property tax changes expected to generate an additional $380 million.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And finally, we follow the net wealth tiers that had been previously proposed in this House to derive revenue from this channel under very modest recovery assumptions and this could generate $3.7 billion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A third lever, which is the reserves' contribution lever, the Workers' Party had spoken at length about this possibility before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To reiterate, we can reduce the share of reserves interest income that we send straight back to reserves currently held at 50%, to a lower but absolutely still respectable 40%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, this does not constitute a draw on the reserves stock.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The final lever, which we call "the externalities lever", entails increasing so-called sin taxes – those levied on gambling, alcohol and tobacco – as well as carbon-generating activities for which we apply an increase to $80 a tonne but channel only half the revenues towards mitigating the transition and encouraging the adoption of green technologies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, I would be the first to admit that the Government, with its army of Ministry analysts and superior access to data and information, would be able to fault some or all of the assumptions underlying these scenarios.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What then is the purpose of this exercise?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, we will also show that even when we mix and match among the proposals to craft a revenue mix that we can accept – after all, the math suggests that any single one of the levers will be sufficient to fill the GST hole, much less alternative permutations and combinations of them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And third, and perhaps most importantly, is to underscore our desire to engage in good faith debate on whether there are genuine options available to us in meeting the revenue hole, other than raising GST.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The most thing for us is to cease stating "I wish", but to start stating "I will".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We must instead consider nothing impossible and treat possibilities as probabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to end with a few quick reflections on several aspects of this year's Budget.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In last year's Committee of Supply debate, I flagged the importance of elevating our national R&D expenditures to a share closer to that of most innovative nations in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, more can be done given how we still lag the OECD average for total R&D spending; although, of course, we need to ensure that our outcomes match our inputs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, we should ideally direct this towards downstream activities that the part of R&D, and hence, the stated goal of elevating local firm R&D is the right one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And third, the guiding principles of the BEPS agreement means that one acceptable way to lower the effective tax rate for our SMEs and to continue attracting foreign investment is to do so through R&D tax credits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am, likewise, heartened to hear of the continued efforts to improve the lot of our low-wage workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party has repeatedly called for a roll-out of the minimum wage for Singaporeans and the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) effectively institutes such a floor for a significant majority of Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Progressive Wage Model (PWM) is being rolled out to additional sectors, but I am left to wonder if the Ministry has evaluated how many workers would still remain uncovered by either the LQS or PWM stipulations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If there is room to increase the LQS to an amount of $1,600, which roughly corresponds to a take-home salary of $1,300.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Simplifying the qualification process for this application, however, would surely be welcome.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But stubborn reliance on raising the GST in spite of alternative, more progressive forms of revenue generation is the fundamental reason why I cannot lend my support.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can have all the right fiscal policies in place and the mettle to see them through, notwithstanding the pain and pinch, but what we have not sorted out is political succession.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has the unique capability to plan decades in advance across many policies – manpower, trade, climate change, defence, to name a few.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we must ensure that we have successive generations of leaders to see those policies to fruition and, Mr Speaker, I say that political succession planning is key in this regard.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just last year, I stood here to talk about what I had hoped to see in our 5G Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That race should not matter, that he or she should be able to lead the leaders into 2040 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I focused on 5G because at the time it looked as if the 4G Prime Minister was secured – Deputy Prime Minister Heng.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yet just a few weeks later, the bombshell came.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I respect the Deputy Prime Minister for that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It was an act of selflessness in the face of a force majeure, being the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That he, meaning the Deputy Prime Minister, was not getting any younger and the pandemic was still getting longer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, Singapore was at the heart of Deputy Prime Minister's decision.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I respect that but it does not solve the issue of succession.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A recently published book by Shashi Jayakumar entitled "A History of the People's Action Party, 1985-2021" was launched by the Prime Minister late last year.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Dr Jayakumar is not one to mince his words.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He had to be as accurate in his analysis as he could be because many of the people that he wrote about are still alive.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What was a central focus of his book?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I was at the book launch and should at this point, declare that I have known Dr Shashi Jayakumar for 20 years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We were University mates and I count him as a close friend.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But putting personal affiliations aside, there were several themes that struck me as I listened to the three speeches given at the book launch.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first speech was given by Peter Schoppert, Director of NUS Press, the publisher.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is what Schoppert said, and I quote: "It's a brave historian who writes a contemporary history.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That historian is brave on at least two fronts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, the contemporary historian writes about people who are very much with us.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: You will see in the book that interviews form a very important source for the book and, of course, interviewees have their own views and they can read what you said about them, they can answer back.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They might even be in the room when you launch the book.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They might even be invited to launch the book for you.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What he chose to focus on was insightful and piercing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I quote: "There are many themes and ideas in this book and I do not have time to enumerate on all of them, but I did briefly want to highlight two points.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first is renewal – this is felt to be an urgent imperative.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From the very beginning, Party files showed that Mr Lee Kuan Yew was thinking about the issue at an extraordinarily early point, from the early 1960s in fact.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this area of renewal, things that would see fruition much later, time and again, would be thought of by Mr Lee and others within the Party from a very early stage." Prime Minister was invited to launch the book and Prime Minister, too, picked up on the importance of renewal.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I quote Prime Minister: "A pivotal general election had just taken place in December 1984.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In that election, many of the PAP old guards either retired from politics or stepped down from leadership roles.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the new Cabinet, from the founding generation – only Mr Lee Kuan Yew, Mr S Rajaratnam and Mr EW Barker remained.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After the election, the younger Ministers chose Mr Goh Chok Tong to be the leader and he became the first Deputy Prime Minister." Two Opposition candidates were elected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr JB Jeyaretnam in Anson re-elected and Mr Chiam See Tong in Potong Pasir for the first time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the post-election press conference, Mr Lee interpreted the election results using a biblical reference.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He described it as the inevitable transition from the Independence generation to a new generation of voters who knew not Joseph.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Prime Minister went on to say, "The Party's early years, pre-1985, were full of drama and excitement, whereas the post-1985 story has been one of relative calm and stability.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Year after year, Singapore continued to sustain its strong growth and rapid transformation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We carried out two leadership transitions smoothly – from the 1G to the 2G, and then from the 2G to the 3G.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has been a story of stability and progress.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Before I go into the meat of my speech, let me respectfully ask a few questions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What if Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean were 15 years younger?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What if Senior Minister Tharman were 15 years younger?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They would be ideal candidates for the 4G Prime Minister-ship.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Or what if Minister K Shanmugam, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan or Dr Ng Eng Hen were just 10 years younger?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They, too, would be ideal candidates for the 4G Prime Minister-ship.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The point I am getting at is that I can appreciate that there are many constraints in choosing a leader – age, years in politics, circumstances beyond one's control.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To get my point across, let me share what leadership means to me.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And here, I offer a very humble parallel through the lens of sports.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In secondary school, Junior College (JC) and in the club leagues, I was asked to captain hockey teams.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Was I the best hockey player on the team?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In every team I captained, there were three or four players better than me.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Maybe because I could read the game; maybe because I had deep friendships with everyone on the team; maybe because I was able to decipher what our potential as a team was and worked our guts out to materialise that potential.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Whatever the reason, I gave it my best shot and the players better than me also became part of the team's cause.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When I moved on to play for Singapore in the men's national hockey team, we chose the best person for the captaincy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There were four or five of my teammates who were better players than the captain who was chosen.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because he could read the game better than any one of us.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He could gel a team better than any one of us and he understood his opponents and their tactics well.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The point I am getting at is that we cared less about who the captain was.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We were more concerned about how Singapore was faring on the scoreboard and, when we played in Malaysia and India, the matches could get very tense.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sure, choosing the right teammate to wear the captain's armband is important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But what mattered more was the whole team's performance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What mattered in any stadium we played in, whether on home soil or internationally, was what was on the scoreboard.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What do we need to do better for our performance as a team?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For Singapore and the Singapore flag we wore over our chest.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: You have in your ranks hon Members – Chan Chun Sing, Lawrence Wong, Ong Ye Kung, Tan Chuan-Jin, Desmond Lee, Edwin Tong, Tan See Leng, Indranee Rajah and many others.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There was Ng Chee Meng but we had sadly lost him in Sengkang.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Among the 5G, you have hon Members Sim Ann, Chee Hong Tat, Zaqy Mohamad, Janil Puthucheary, Alvin Tan, Desmond Lee, Sun Xueling and many others, first among equals – primus inter pares – team effort.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We lost Amrin Amin and Lam Pin Min who would have been key members of the 5G team.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I, for one, have no ambition whatsoever to be Prime Minister, in case that is already not obvious.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If I did not mention a Member's name in the speech, please do not read anything into it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I only have 20 minutes to give the speech and I do not want to breach the time limit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We do not need to think variant-to-variant, day-by-day, month-by-month; rather, Singapore plans decade-by-decade.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The manifestation of such far-sightedness is our leadership renewal.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must get it right and we must make the world aware of the succession plan.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do I think we have the best man as Prime Minister now?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Around the dinner table, when we meet over a meal, my father and mother would say to me, "Is Prime Minister alright?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is Teo Chee Hean alright?" These questions come up, especially when Singapore is going through tough times and tough spells.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My response to my parents is that: "Prime Minister and Senior Minister are fighting fit but that the load is heavy to carry." Please do not misinterpret me.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Again, so as not to be misunderstood, I would hope that even when the 4G is in place and holding the reins, Prime Minister, Senior Minister Teo, Senior Minister Tharman and the seniors in Cabinet will stay on as Senior Ministers or Coordinating Ministers to shepherd the new team.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me to move to a different but somewhat related point.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me to share some private-sector perspective on this.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am a lawyer at Lee & Lee.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My clients, including MNCs, look very carefully at political predictability when making decisions as regards which country to invest in.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Time and again, my clients have shared that Singapore's predictable political environment gives them confidence to invest their business, human capital and infrastructure long term in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Germane to that is their understanding of Singapore's political succession planning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And, here, I am talking about political succession planning within the PAP.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is this a speech better suited for a Party conference or a speech in Parliament?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would say it is an appropriate and relevant speech to be made in Parliament because the PAP and its succession planning have been organic to Singapore's success story.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This reminds me of a conversation I had with hon Member Sitoh Yih Pin in Morocco.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We were there to learn counterterrorism measures and whether Morocco's counterterror tactics could be deployed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In between the busy schedule, Sitoh and I spoke about political succession among the 4G.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because we like to play political chess games?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The backbenchers discuss these things between themselves because we want to see Singapore succeed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I make this speech with no personal agenda.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, in this Chamber, I have, for years, been pushing for causes and policy changes under the steady hands of four Speakers and under the watchful eyes of five Whips.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Members, please know, in articulating these views, I have Singapore at heart.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Let us show the world what Singapore is made of.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That shows the world that we have mettle.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That shows the world our ballast in a time of crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That shows the world our deep reservoir of resolve and our steely determination to persevere and fight on.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It was the worst of times as we watched the early outbreak in the dormitories unfold, together with reports of terrible living conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It was the spring of hope, as we opened up to Phase Three at the end of 2020.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It was the winter of despair as, in particular, our key workers and restaurants suffered many reverses and took many steps back in our path towards reopening.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Old certainties have been shaken, the script had to be torn up multiple times and many a time, we have been left wondering – and perhaps still are – if the light at the end of the tunnel was actually that of an oncoming train.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And today, even as we struggle to stay afloat amid what feels like endless price increases, we are also faced with understandable anxiety over climate change, the situation in the Ukraine, as we wonder whether we are witnessing the birth of the great conflict of our times.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Today, more than ever, we have seen that the way we react when we are threatened, the actions we take when we are under pressure, are the most accurate reflection of our characters, of who we are as individuals, organisations and as a society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The various peaks and troughs which we have experienced since COVID-19 hit us have been exhausting and there will be more to come still.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our path to living with COVID-19 is a long one and the fatigue experienced by many of us – from our frontline care workers, young parents, teachers, business owners – is real.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also troubling to hear pleas, both online and offline, for our leaders and policy-makers to "come down from the ivory towers" to see what the situation is on the ground.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should adopt a reflective approach on the possible drivers for this feeling amongst the public and work together to overcome it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Budget this year is entitled "Charting Our New Way Forward Together".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It acknowledges that a "New Way Forward" is required and that we, in this House, have a duty to ensure that we do so together and that we do not leave anyone behind.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is something we can all get behind.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the Workers' Party's 2020 Election manifesto's preamble is entitled "A Singapore For All".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But the key is to ensure that the formulation of our policies and their effects on the ground move us decisively towards achieving this aim.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As a society, we need to decide together how best to invest in our people, how we should spend our tax dollars.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are real-life scenarios that all of us have seen our residents tackle.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And while it is true that many helping hands are available, we are often told that much time, energy and stress is involved in navigating the support system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While these systems are in place to prevent abuse – and quite rightly so – we must also ask ourselves and continue to ask ourselves important questions: who we are as a people and what values do we stand for?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Do we want our policies to empower Singaporeans to be our best selves or do we restrict Singaporeans from being our worst selves?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As we think about our new way forward together, it is still a key principle that Singaporeans must be self-reliant and we must be responsible.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Is this consistent with our laws and policies that are formulated with the assumption that everyone is out there to game the system, on the lookout for unfair advantage for themselves to the detriment of others?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Does this approach not build a culture of Singaporeans trying to figure out what is legal or allowed, rather than applying their own mind to what make sense and is reasonable for both themselves and their fellow citizens?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Another clear example is the current debate surrounding our medical certificate (MC) culture.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The requirement for many employers for the doctor's note for any absences from the workplace due to medical reasons stands in stark contrast to my experience in my first job in the city of London.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Workers are asked to self-certify if they are sick for less than seven days.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In fact, it was not unheard of for employers to offer "duvet days" to their employees: days off not because they are ill, but because employees sometimes just need some time to rest.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are often structured in a way that works best for their firm or industry, and have been shown to actually increase productivity and the mental and physical well-being of workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am not advocating a wholesale copying of these approaches, but I believe it is worth looking at our own labour market to see what positive changes we can make by studying these examples.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To those who worry that these practices may result in people taking advantage, I observed that these practices appeared to work well in a highly dynamic, profitable and productive environment, as the common understanding was that people were serious about their jobs and were willing to work hard in order to progress in their careers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, we cannot discount that the financial services coming out of London remain world-leading and innovative.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If the argument that these are the things that could not work for Singapore, then we should take a long hard look at ourselves and ask: "why not?", followed by "how do we get there?".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How do we move to a society where people are empowered to exercise good judgement and be truly responsible?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How do we ensure that people do not succumb to the temptation to indulge in corrupt practices because it is the right thing to do, and not because they have a high salary preventing them from being tempted?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Against this backdrop, I would like to turn to the most pressing problems and issues facing Singaporeans as we emerge from the COVID-19 years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In particular, our residents in Sengkang keenly feel the press of having to deal with lasting financial and social effects of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many of them are members of both the "sandwich" class and also the "sandwich generation", and rising prices have and will continue to hit them hard while they struggle to provide for both the elderly and the very young in their families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For these Singaporeans, the concept of inter-generational equity, or intergenerational solidarity, is extremely important in ensuring that one generation does not unduly bear the brunt of paying for expenditure of either a future or previous generation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My colleagues have and will continue to touch on these issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But while this concept may appear to be remote in Singapore at the moment, I would also note that as we restructure our economy and society, we should be wary of allowing a situation to develop where political outcomes and opinions are, or are seen to be divided strongly along intergenerational lines.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This has been seen in the West in the phenomenon of "Boomer blaming" for everything – from Brexit to toxic work environments that degrade mental health, and only serves to exacerbate generational grievances.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And we need to tackle this matter in a holistic way, ranging from creating more opportunities and spaces for the generations to learn from and support each other, and to ensure that our fiscal policies do not, and do not get interpreted as unfairly favouring one generation to the detriment of other generations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Coming back to the issues surrounding the here and now, the ever-increasing cost of living is a topic that we hear feedback about time and again.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They have also noted that there have already been price increases prior to the tax hike taking effect.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, global brands such as Nestle have also sounded the alarm and announced that they will increase prices of their products – and these increments will not be captured by any GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I fear that the cascading and knock-on effect that such cost increases will be devastating on households already on a knife edge.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, the war in the Ukraine, which has finally come to a head last week, will only lead to more supply chain disruptions and global price rises, and if it proves to be prolonged, it may end up having a far larger effect than predicted or catered for.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Food prices will not be spared, as Russia and the Ukraine are major exporters of agricultural products, and Russia is one of the largest exporters of fertiliser globally – any drop in supply would lead to an increase in costs, which means farmers will pay more and have to pass it down to the end consumer.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Russia is also a major supplier of natural gas, which has implications for us in Singapore, as around 95% of our energy needs are still powered by natural gas.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will only add to the woes currently experienced by our households and the businesses already grappling with huge increases in their energy bills.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Notably, politicians in Germany are already advocating a natural gas reserve to shelter consumers from price shocks in the wake of the conflict.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet we also acknowledge that there are long-term pressures on our public purse strings, as we search for a shift towards long-term sustainability on all fronts, be it environmental, demographic or economic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, the world cannot keep growing endlessly, a fact illustrated by figures released in November last year which have shown that India's fertility rate has dropped to below replacement rate for the first time ever.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In view of this, we also believe there is room to make our GST system less regressive beyond the current approach to further ease the burden on the lower-income groups.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is why we have to consider if our GST can start allowing for exemptions on certain essential items – treatment that is often seen in the case of other economies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The list of items should be kept to essentials such as food supplies, healthcare and care services, including childcare.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is what economies, such as the UK, Australia and Japan, currently do and their experiences should inform us as we come up with our own list of exemptions that would be most beneficial to more vulnerable Singaporeans, and to avoid the pitfalls some countries have come across while deciding which items should be exempt and which not.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Exempting items such as healthcare, infant care and childcare will also help to ease current and future cost pressures in industries that struggle to fill their manpower requirements with local workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And I note there are stark implications for those industries with the foreign worker policies which are being tightened by the measures just announced in this Budget.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, I note that exemptions applying to children's products and childcare would surely be welcome relief for parents or prospective parents and go towards addressing our low total fertility rate (TFR), as financial concerns are often cited as one of the key reasons why people delay having children or decide not to have them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I need hardly add that raising our TFR is an existential problem for us that we have been unsuccessfully trying to solve for decades.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, while it is true that higher-income earners also benefit from such exemptions, these items, being essential in nature, should result in any derived benefits being self-limiting – after all, how much more rice can a rich person eat?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Another argument is that it is too expensive to implement these exemptions and that this will increase compliance costs for businesses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, with the advent of AI and advances in technology, these costs should be much lower compared with when GST was first introduced and any upgrades to accounting or associated software should be a one-time cost for both Government and businesses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, compliance costs will likely be of far greater concern to smaller enterprises, and I note too that small businesses with turnovers of less than $1,000,000 are not required to register for GST.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How can it be that a country such as Singapore, which has long-prided itself ourselves on having targeted, efficient – even convoluted at times – policymaking, could shy away from implementing a system of GST-exempt items by saying that it is too much effort?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Turning now to how we measure our spending and our progress, I repeat previous calls made in this House to rethink the long-term sustainability of how we measure our progress.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Since its adoption in 1944 at the Bretton Woods Conference as the formal measure of a country's economy, gross domestic product (GDP) has proved to be a useful measure of the progress made by a country.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And Singapore has done extremely well from our difficult beginnings.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, in recent years, there has been a sense amongst many of us that GDP does not tell the full picture by any means.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In particular, healthy GDP figures in 2021 and 2022, especially compared against the depressed bases in 2020, leave out the entire story of our country.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is a growing acknowledgement that beyond economic growth and survival, we should also thrive as a society and be mindful of the impact that we have on our planet.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: GDP measurements alone fail to address these shifting values in our current world.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: GDP alone also does not capture the full picture of how we care for our people.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To illustrate this point, many may not realise that GDP does not measure things, such as planting a tree, and that it does not measure the unpaid household and care labour undertaken by so many of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, one would be hard-pressed to argue that these do not matter in how we measure our progress as a society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How do we, therefore, determine whether enough has been done to address concerns about, for example, mental health and well-being?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, it is clear that there is much work to be done in Singapore, judging by the number of registered psychologists and psychiatrists in Singapore, especially in the public sector.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There are also long waits to see counsellors in schools and tertiary education institutes, and concerns have been raised about the quality of support received.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are but some examples of what should matter to us as we measure our society and how we measure our holistic progress.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many economists have been advocating for years that countries start developing a dashboard which contains a variety of other measures for how well an economy and society has been doing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yes, GDP matters, but it does not do well in measuring our human, social and natural assets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The dashboard should also contain measurements of the impact that we have on our environment and planetary health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Lessons can be learned from the introduction and abandonment of the "Green GDP" by China in the early part of the century.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This means that while we aim for zero waste in terms of material use and energy resources, we also need to ensure we do not waste wealth, technology and knowledge, have a thriving knowledge commons and a strong culture of philanthropy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The last point in particular is something I note that this Budget aims to promote through various tweaks to tax incentives and co-funding measures.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To know how successful the increase in spending has been, philanthropic indicators on the dashboard could include details such as trends relating to donations and the nature of who is donating.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As little is currently known about how a circular economy or society can promote better social equity, more research is certainly needed – particularly in the local context.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Narratives of a circular society can and should be developed, as the long-term sustainability of our country and planet is at stake.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must stop assuming that infinite economic growth is possible and start shifting towards formally measuring our progress on other things that matter.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Headwinds will be strong and frequent in the years to come, and our people will need to demonstrate grit and fortitude to survive and thrive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are still dealing with the pandemic and it has been challenging for business and individuals.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need to continue to support those still impacted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But we must position Singapore for the future and we must grow our economy to provide opportunities and quality of life for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
