text: Beyond growth, we must also ensure that Singaporeans and Singapore have the capability to seize these opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I will focus on three topics in my speech today.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Three, inclusion and ensuring that no one is left behind.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the Budget debate last year, I spoke about the need for Singapore to grow and to step up the momentum for businesses and individuals to build capability to seize opportunities when the economy opens up.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One year on, this call is more urgent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While COVID-19 is still with us, Singapore continues to attract investments in electronics and biomedical manufacturing, as well as new investments across sectors such as agri-food, chemicals and materials.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many of these new jobs are PMET jobs and require relevant skills and competencies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But to be able to seize these opportunities, our businesses and workforce must have the relevant capabilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The pace of digitalisation has accelerated as businesses were propelled to go digital to adapt in order to be able to operate in the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many are still in the midst of their digital transformation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Now, with climate change, high global energy prices and the Ukraine situation, there is a pressing need for businesses to become more sustainable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We have seen that companies that had invested in digital were better able to pivot and do business in the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For companies to become greener, it will require not only funding but more importantly know-how, rethinking of how work is done, how goods are produced and services delivered.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Processes and, more importantly, behaviours need to change.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We do not want to have to wait for another crisis for our businesses to become more sustainable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Digital can also help with more sustainable business practices.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How can we ensure that we do not leave our small businesses behind?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the new carbon tax, if businesses do not transition and invest in clean technologies, they will definitely find it hard to survive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Businesses tend to see sustainability as the need for compliance and cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What can be done to help businesses understand the benefits, competitive advantage and growth opportunities?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the joint study that was done by Economic Development Board (EDB) and Enterprise Singapore (ESG), it outlined the role that Singapore can play to become a key carbon service hub.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Carbon services can generate new businesses and jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What can we do to help our businesses build the capabilities to participate in these opportunities and more importantly, to thrive?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The feedback from companies across industries is the difficulty to meet their manpower needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These range from tech talent to roles across different segments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is impacting their ability to operate effectively.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The impact of the pandemic on manpower and the level of Omicron infections has made the situation even more pressing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As business picks up, the situation will not allow our businesses to address demand and will impact their ability to grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What targeted support can be given to allow viable businesses to address these current manpower constraints to transform and more importantly, to grow?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister Wong in his Budget Statement stressed the need to "redouble our efforts to invest in new capabilities".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Technology and digitalisation have picked up pace across all sectors in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Workers even in non-tech jobs need to understand and know how to use technology in order to do their work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is not just about how to use the latest technologies and devices as they will continually change.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These skills are not about having deep technology skills in artificial intelligence, data analytics, or any future technologies but rather how to work with these new and ever-changing technologies to be able to do their work and thrive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the greater reliance on digital, the security and resilience of our digital infrastructures are crucial.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need to continually invest and strengthen our digital infrastructures.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister shared that broadband access speeds will be increased and investments made in future technologies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can Minister Wong also share what investments will be made to strengthen the reliability and the security of our digital infrastructures?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is demonstrated in the components of the Assurance Package of Cash Payout, Additional GST U-Save Vouchers, GST Cash Vouchers for seniors in the Senior Bonus, Medisave Top-ups; and the Community Development Council (CDC) Vouchers to address essential expenditure of families in areas of utilities, groceries, education and health.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A subtle but important point to note is that the cash payout eligibility is on assessable income and property ownership, rather than the annual value of residence.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Annual value (AV) of the property is used as the main criterion for means testing and eligibility for many support schemes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While I do not disagree that the value of the property reflects one's means, it does not always mean that all who live in these properties have the means or have more.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A point that I have raised previously is the application of the AV criterion for those who live with their extended families in properties with annual value above $21,000.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These persons could be elderly parents or siblings who live with relatives as they need care or cannot afford housing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In some of these cases, they do not have means but because of their residential address, they do not qualify for any support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the trend of smaller families and people marrying later, we do have more couples who have to provide for both their young children and senior parents or relatives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do have such families in my constituency who live in private properties with annual value between $21,000 and $30,000.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the spirit of renewing and strengthening the social compact, Minister Wong has said: "we want every Singaporean to know and feel that he or she has a stake in our society, and that they will not be left to fend for themselves when times are down".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am not asking for the AV to be removed but rather can it be refined to apply to home ownership rather than residence for extended family members or higher AV for the "sandwiched generation".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we look to the Government to continue to provide and support Singaporeans when they need it, as part of the social compact, we too, need to do our part and balance that with what each of us can do.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, as we talk about cost pressures and one of the biggest cost pressures that is now facing us is fuel cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As a taker, I do also say that individuals and businesses, apart from asking for support – and I will continue to ask for support for businesses and individuals, we all need to do our part to also finds ways to conserve, to be greener.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Otherwise, it is just addressing cost but not finding better ways to do things; otherwise, it is not sustainable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am talking about being able to fund this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Those above 55 years of age make up 25.7% of the workforce in 2020.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As part of PAP.sg efforts to better understand senior employability, in the last quarter of 2021, we conducted an online survey with seniors aged 50 years and older; 934 people responded to the survey and 98% of respondents are Singaporeans, 60% are currently working and almost 60% of them have post-Secondary education.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We have a balance of male and female respondents.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The respondents are from a variety of industries, working in a diverse range of occupations; 98% liked the work they are doing, citing meaningful work and having relevant experience; 60% of respondents who are working face challenges at work, with about one-fifth of them citing challenges like needing to learn new skills, dealing with changes and new norms.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Amid the challenge of learning new things, the most commonly cited skills-gap is in learning new digital skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With digitalisation and the drive for sustainability, can we rethink how we prepare and enable matured and senior workers – who want and can work – to actively participate in quality jobs in the growth sectors in the post-COVID-19 economy?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I welcome the enhanced announcement in Budget 2022 for the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS).

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will impact older low-waged workers or those who are caregivers and need to the flexibility of part-time work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For this group of workers, while they can and do want to work, part-time work may be more suitable for them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: She is 69 years of age and works as a relief programme coordinator at an eldercare centre.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: She covers the duties of staff who are on leave or medical leave.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Her estimated monthly income ranges from $200 to a little over $500 a month.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: She is currently eligible for WIS and is appreciative of the support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, with the minimum income criterion, Mdm Lee is concerned as she will not be eligible for WIS.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Economic success is necessary, but on its own, it is not sufficient for Singaporeans to make Singapore home.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we focus only on economic growth, our people will just leave Singapore and go where the economic opportunities present themselves.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Last year, I spoke about Singapore's burning platform, a world on fire with COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: With natural habitats being destroyed, we must expect more pandemics, some worse than COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But climate change is a graver challenge than any disease.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we need to stress-test our assumptions, test our plans for the future before the future tests us.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we need to move quickly and boldly.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: An earlier generation spoke of mudflats to metropolis in one generation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And now we face a new ambition, again, born of necessity and survival.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: From what is unsustainable to what is sustainable within one generation?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because that is the implication of reaching carbon net-zero by the middle of this century.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is not much time and we need to be seriously bold because the climate crisis is about Singapore's survival, whether we stay above water.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In 2019, a research paper in the journal, Nature Communications, showed very vividly, with maps, how hundreds of millions of people around the world would be underwater by the end of this century and that is just assuming a low-carbon emissions scenario.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In a world where carbon border adjustment taxes are being talked about; in a world where consumers choose what to buy, where to work, how to invest based on sustainability; in a world where narratives can shift from free trade to sustainable trade.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We need to be ready and it means Singapore needs to raise our ambition to stay above water, to survive and to thrive.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can only do this fast enough, within one generation, by moving boldly and ahead of the market.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: All these link up with our Total Defence because, if Singapore is underwater, if we cannot keep the lights on, we are not even going to be at the starting line in a challenge.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If we are laid low by a pandemic or our people are splintered and divided, we are not going to be able to deal with whatever threats come our way, kinetic or otherwise.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I spoke on pandemic security during last year's Budget.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have spoken on social security over the years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, I will focus on our energy security.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not just keeping the lights on in our hospitals, in our homes.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It keeps our NEWater plants, our desalination plants going.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our water security depends on our energy security.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We know what it means if Singapore's water supply is ever called into question.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And we need to think about energy security that way too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Supplies by pipeline, also LNG terminal, but it is still almost all natural gas – 95%.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some would say it is a serious concentration of risk.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Recent events around the world, market shifts, events in Eastern Europe, are a reminder of this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Electric vehicles (EVs) will further concentrate this risk because EVs also draw energy from the electricity grid.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is a price for "just in case".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is a cost to preparing in advance for danger and for crisis.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But by strengthening social support in a progressive way, we can help Singaporean families even as Singapore proceeds through a necessary transition, a just transition.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Solar is part of the solution, but Singapore is small, we are solar-constrained.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even with solar photovoltaic panels on every building's rooftop, on every external surface of every building, solar alone would not be enough.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Regional power grids can be useful, but they do have limitations.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When there is an energy crunch, some regional grids will come under the same market pressures as our own.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even if you use an undersea cable, a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission line, that line is still one underwater dredging accident or incident away from being unplugged.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we need to look at other options, too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In July 2021, I had asked in Parliament about Singapore's potential as a hydrogen hub, in particular, low-carbon hydrogen, and whether we should move ahead of existing market conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We already have established capabilities in the energy and chemicals sector and in transshipment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Their green hydrogen, when exported, will need to be shipped to destination markets.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, the question is, which cities in Southeast Asia have the potential to be a hydrogen hub in the hydrogen economy?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And, if so, do we want to be first mover, second mover or too late to move?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Moving ahead of the market will help Singapore build capabilities, reduce the risk that we will be left behind.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Starting up hydrogen-based electricity generation and fuel-cell capability will help us build the experience to scale up when we need to.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because the most difficult step is going from no capability to having some hydrogen capability.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On other developments, Mr Speaker, we should also keep a very close watch on developments in nuclear energy, both fission as well as fusion.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For nuclear fusion, it is still early days, but promising prospects.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, you look at the Keeling Curve, the CO2 concentration is 420 ppm.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In last year's Budget debate, I said: "…we must also ask ourselves beyond what is possible today, what is necessary for tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Necessary dreams as we face up to necessary realities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Lines which I find to be quite apt to describe the situation we find ourselves in today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Two years into the pandemic, we are still battling the latest wave of infections brought about by the Omicron variant, with many of our healthcare workers struggling to cope with the stressful working conditions today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: COVID-19 fatigue has also meant that many of us cannot help but feel overwhelmed at times even as we try so valiantly to live with endemic COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the economic front, it seems that economic growth is starting to pick up again.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the rosy headline numbers belies the risk to the fragile global and local economic recovery, not least because of geopolitical tensions and rising concerns over inflation, among others, and one cannot rule out the tail risk of a recession in the near future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Inflation and the rising cost of living, in particular, have been of grave concern to policy-makers globally and the man-on-the-street alike.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As shared in one of my speeches in November last year, it was unclear if the current inflationary pressures in the market are transitory or permanent, though the US Federal Reserve has since then dropped the term "transitory" in its description of inflation and with concerns about stagflation now appearing in the market lexicon instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Locally, the MAS has been concerned enough about inflation to surprise the market with a tightening of monetary policy in October, given that external and domestic cost pressures are accumulating.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And soon after its first tightening in three years, MAS acted again in its second tightening in three months, given upside risk of inflation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even if what Minister of State Low Yen Ling shared in this House ensues and that inflation is expected to ease in the later part of this year, it does not mean prices are going to come down.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It just means that prices will still rise but not jump and still continue to eat into the real incomes of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Who can forget the slew of price increase signs being put up at coffeeshops since the start of the year and the more than 30% increase in fuel prices or the 23% increase in electricity prices since a year ago?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the context of rising inflation and an uncertain global economic recovery, a GST hike, while delayed, would still be counterproductive, given the potential drag on private incomes, consumption and, ultimately, our GDP.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As my fellow Workers' Party colleagues have shared earlier, there are alternative revenue sources that can and should be considered beyond the regressive tax that is GST, with options to use more of Singapore's existing physical headroom, for example, having the added benefit of minimising the impact to our local households and economy alike.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My speech will thus focus on three main areas which warrant urgent consideration.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Minister Wong made adjustments to residential property taxes and the Additional Registration Fees (ARF) for cars as part of Singapore's answer to wealth taxes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When viewed from a glass half-full perspective, it is a step in the right direction when it comes to tackling wealth inequality and strengthening our social fabric – albeit a small step.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, when viewed from a glass half-empty perspective, the measures are a tokenism rather than a meaningful attempt at wealth taxes in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is significantly below what some academics have put forth as possibilities in our conservative estimates of what the net wealth tax could bring at about $1.2 billion annually.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Consider the case of property taxes which, as the Minister said, is currently Singapore's principal means of taxing wealth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As what Business Times' correspondent Ben Paul shared in his article, "As an owner/occupier of a modest apartment in the core central region, property tax is not a particularly big expense for me.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, it is nothing, compared to the maintenance fees and costs of general upkeep for my unit." While the increase in the headline marginal property tax rates appear high, the actual impact on the households involved are unlikely to be material.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The corresponding numbers for non-owner-occupied properties are $1,004 and $19,200 respectively.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Based on my analysis, a centrally located condominium in Cairnhill that is being leased out as an investment property, only raised rents by 2% to offset the higher property tax rates while that of a luxury development located on Nassim Road commanding monthly rentals of almost $20,000 a month need only raise rents by 7% to offset the higher property taxes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To put into context, rents in 2021 for a private residential property already rose by 10%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The other tax change is that of introducing a new ARF tier for cars.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For a Bentley Flying Spur, which retails for almost $900,000 without COE, the new ARF tier is expected to increase ARF by about $59,000, a fairly large number in itself but represents just about 6%-7% of the cost of the car.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For someone who is prepared to pay almost $1 million for an asset that depreciates rapidly over 10 years, is it even meaningful in the grand scheme of things for this person?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Thirdly, higher personal income tax rates are not wealth taxes per se.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But I do agree with the principle that those who earn more should contribute more and it is a fine example of what progressive taxes look like.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the increase appears to be very modest once again, once you work through the mathematics.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Also bearing in mind that from 2015 to 2019, that is, the latest available year on SingStat, the number of individuals with assessed income of more than $300,000 has increased by 22% within this timespan as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that the Government will continue to study the experiences of other countries and explore options to tax wealth effectively.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And I sincerely hope that more meaningful efforts to change our tax system and raise wealth taxes can be made sooner than later.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yes, I agree that taxing wealth has its challenges.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But consider a hypothetical case of a multi-billionaire tech founder who made a windfall after his start-up's IPO and has retired from the firm.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From time to time, he collects dividends as his income while continuing to hold shares in the listed company, which accounts for the vast majority of his wealth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, he is renting multiple luxury apartments instead of owning just one place of residence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And does our tax system adequately capture the wealth of what could be one of Singapore's richest?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would this person even be paying income or wealth taxes at all?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we think about the Forbes' 50 richest list in Singapore, just how much of their wealth is in their residential addresses or the cars that they drive?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As highlighted by a 2018 OECD report on the role and design of net wealth taxes, which provide for certain tax design recommendations, in countries where capital gains are not taxed, there may be a stronger justification for levying a net-wealth tax.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A similar argument can be made for countries that do not levy taxes on inheritances.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must guard against only going through the motions when we move towards addressing wealth inequality, while still leaving the least fortunate among us still pleading, "Please, Sir, I want some more".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Corporate income taxes have consistently been the largest contributor to the Government's operating revenues and 2022 is no different, at an estimated $18 billion, or 22% of operating revenues.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, while part of the goals of this Budget is to build a fairer and more resilient tax system where those with greater means contribute a larger share, could there be more scope for certain corporates to pay their fairer share of taxes, especially against the context of a looming GST hike, which ultimately, is borne by the end-consumer and not the corporates?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, I fully recognise that many local SMEs and small businesses, especially those in the retail and F&B scene, have been struggling to make ends meet amidst the pandemic and the changing safe management measures (SMMs) rules over the past two years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And I applaud efforts by the Government to strengthen our local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, it is interesting to note that while more than $29 billion of Job Support Scheme (JSS) funding was provided to corporates in the last two years, it appears that corporate profitability, as a whole, did not fare too badly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In FY2020, while the Government expected cooperate income tax (CIT) revenues to fall by 18% year-on-year or around $3 billion to $13.7 billion in FY 2020, the actual CIT revenue turned out to be $16 billion, not too far from FY2019 levels.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This brings me to my key point on BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge the Minister's comments that the Government needs more time to study these issues thoroughly and will announce changes in the corporate tax system when we are ready.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, if things go according to plan, BEPS 2.0 is already on the horizon, with the implementation of the two-pillar solution targeted to start in 2023 next year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While Minister Lawrence Wong noted that pillar one will result in a negative revenue impact to Singapore, this is, firstly, limited in scope, as it is expected to apply only to global MNEs with a global turnover of more than €20 billion, with just around 100 of such companies globally.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And, thirdly, I do not believe that profits are being artificially inflated here in Singapore, given rigorous transfer pricing rules.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the other hand, for pillar two – this applies to a much larger group of MNEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Any company with over €750 of annual revenue would now be subject to a global minimum corporate tax.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore alone, the Government shared that there are over 1,800 such multinational enterprise (MNE) groups operating here that are unlikely to be affected.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have shared in this House last year, I hope that the Government will view the global minimum tax reforms as an opportunity rather than a threat, given Singapore's strong non-tax advantages and attractiveness to MNEs, bearing in mind the current average effective corporate tax rate is closer to 3% in YA2019.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we look at the subset of non-SMEs or those with revenues exceeding $100 million and making an accounting profit, then in YA2019, the average effective corporate tax rate is even lower, at 2%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Profitable non-SMEs contributed $10.4 billion or 64% of total CIT paid by all companies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Of course, this is purely hypothetical, since obviously, not all companies will be scoped into the rules and there could be some slippage from both pillar one and pillar two rules and the actual impact will be much lower.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But the point remains that, technically, even a small shift towards the proposed global minimum rate of 15% could result in significantly higher corporate tax receipts for the Government.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Beyond the dollars and cents, the more important conceptual point to me is this: if a global MNE is already operating in Singapore, what incentive would it have to incur additional relocation costs, when the minimum corporate tax rate of 15% would be normalised globally?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And with tax considerations out of the way, why would not a global MNE keen to tap on the attractive growth prospects in Asia, base their headquarters here in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The World Bank has consistently placed Singapore as among the best places in the world to do business and I am confident that our competitive strengths and strong non-tax advantages will continue to provide a competitive edge to companies seeking a place of business.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It was previously said that we have drawn on our reserves equivalent to over 20 years of past Budget surpluses.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We have used a generation's worth of savings to combat a crisis of a generation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I asked Deputy Prime Minister Heng during last year's Budget debate, after accounting from the draw, where would our reserves be, compared to five years ago and 10 years ago, though I do not think there was a direct answer to the question.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, I would like to ask Minister Lawrence Wong, after considering the $43 million drawn on our past reserves, are our reserves today higher or lower, compared to five years ago?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I ask this because it is important to put into context the growth in our reserves as we debate the source of funding for our future expenditures, even if the Government continues to be guarded over disclosing the absolute size of the reserves itself.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Temasek's net portfolio value as of March 2021 stands at $381 billion, up to $75 billion or 25%, compared to a year ago.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And I believe GIC would have grown its portfolio as well, given generally supportive market conditions in the last two years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yes, I understand that the design of the NIRC framework is to provide a stable, sustainable source of income to our Budget, smoothed out over market cycles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But it is also helpful to remind Members of this House that our financial reserves grow not just from the balance 50% of NIRC not utilised, but also from inflows directly into the reserves, such as from land sales which averaged around $13 billion a year in the past 10 years and from MAS interventions in the foreign exchange market to dampen appreciation pressures, given Singapore's excess of domestic savings, over investments and persistent capital inflow.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If the goal of this Budget is to ensure a fairer revenue structured, that means everyone chips in and contributes to a vibrant economy and strengthen the social compact, but those with great means contribute a larger share.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If so, should we not revisit the contribution of our investment returns as opposed to the individual Singaporean who is grappling with the rising cost of living?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If the assumption is that Government spending is at 18% of GDP today, but expected to go to more than 20% of GDP by 2030, could we not raise the contributions from the NIRC to the Budget and raise its share of GDP too?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope that Minister Wong will agree with me that raising the NIRC contribution rate will not result in a drawdown of the reserves and will, in fact, still allow us to continue building our reserves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, to belabour with the point, this will not mean that we will not get a steady stream of income from the reserves to benefit today's generation of Singaporeans and our children and our grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the contrary, as Minister Wong has said, it is about being able to invest even more in our people and social infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is to me about ensuring that we invest not only in financial assets overseas but in our people, Singaporeans, who to me are the most important resource of this country.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is simply about sustaining the value of our financial reserves and sustaining the lives and livelihoods of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   We are still in the amidst of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instead of raising GST, Workers' Party Members of Parliament suggest that alternative sources of government revenue be considered.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Budget 2022, the Finance Minister will adjust the Additional Registration Fee for luxury cars and the property tax as a way to collect wealth tax.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I welcome these changes, I also feel that there is much room for improvement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has strong non-tax advantages and appeals to MNCs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, the Government should view the tax reform on global minimum tax rate as an opportunity, not a threat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This will not reduce our reserves; instead, we can continue to grow our reserves steadily while ensuring that we use our national resources more effectively to help sustain Singaporeans' livelihood.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.04 pm until 4.30 pm.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: That prompts the question: "why raise taxes?" This is a fundamental question in political economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: I think that we can offer three answers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: First, we raise taxes to create the fiscal capacity to support a well-functioning society.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we raise taxes to achieve economic inclusion.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Third, and particularly relevant in the Singapore context, we raise taxes to pay for recurrent spending so that we can prioritise the use of our national reserves to manage external shocks as we remain integrated with the global economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: We can take a cross-country perspective and an intertemporal perspective.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: When a country's income per capita is low, the need to raise taxes is great so that the country has the resources to provide public goods like national defence, law and order as well as relief for the poor.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the viable tax base is small because the tax administration and enforcement ability is low at this stage of economic development.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Historically, countries that are starting on the path of development turn to trade taxes in order to generate government revenue to pay for their expenditure.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Trade taxes have tended to make up a larger share of total revenue at the early stages of economic development because it is relatively easy to keep track of the flow of goods at major shipping ports.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: These countries then shifted to greater reliance on direct taxation of income which happened late in the 19th century and broad-based consumption taxes which happened from the middle of the 20th century.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is a sense in which the way the tax revenues are spent, notably on education which has been a priority in the very early Budgets.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is a form of investment in building fiscal capacity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Spending on public schooling generates a virtuous cycle.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As the human capital base is expanded, the size of the economic pie grows so the tax base correspondingly increases.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: At this stage of our development, boosting innovative activities will play a bigger role in growing the economy and thus, the tax base in the post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The support given in Budget 2022 to further strengthen the collaboration in engaging in R&D projects between SMEs and our Polytechnics and ITEs ultimately expands our fiscal capacity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The initiative dubbed "Singapore Global Enterprises" provides fiscal support for our large local enterprises (LLEs) to break into overseas markets.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As our LLEs expand into overseas markets and become bigger and more productive, they become more profitable and can afford to pay their workers more.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is a statistical and practical fact that larger firms doing the same business, tend to pay their workers more, because they are more productive and they tend to break into overseas markets.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, there are there are also factors acting to contract our fiscal capacity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: One is the demographic transition and increased life expectancy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: With a bigger share of the population becoming economically inactive, the tax base becomes relatively smaller.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: That is a fact well recognised by many.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Another factor that can reduce our fiscal capacity comes from the harm that is caused by climate change, a point that many Members have alluded to.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed schedule of increases in carbon taxes introduced in Budget 2022 can be justified on the basis of helping businesses internalise the negative externalities caused by emission of greenhouse gases.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike a tax on labour income, as an example, which reduces economic efficiency because people respond by working fewer hours when their take-home pay is reduced.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A carbon tax, nevertheless, increases efficiency because it reduces activities that society wants to reduce.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Roughly speaking, an efficient outcome is for the carbon tax on firms to be set equal to the amount of external damage caused by the greenhouse gas emission.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Another point is that a carbon tax also has the effect of giving incentives for upstream firms to develop green technology by discouraging downstream firms from using devices that embody environmentally unfriendly technology.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is a classic trade-off between equity and efficiency when we use fiscal tools to achieve economic inclusion.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: While this narrows the income gap, there are microeconomic distortions caused by such tax increases, also called excess burden.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is a standard concept in public finance.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The idea is that the quantity of an economic activity, such as labour supply decreases when there is an increase in income tax rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In designing an optimal tax policy, the Government has to take into account the fact that raising the tax rate has consequences for the tax base because if the income tax on income earners goes up, as an example, they work less, the tax base shrinks, so there is an efficiency loss.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, despite the loss in efficiency, every society has still got to choose a point on the equity efficiency frontier, sacrificing some efficiency in order to attain a desired level of equity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Since the excess burden of a given tax rate increase rises more than proportionately, it is optimal to broaden the tax mix from this perspective, such as relying also on other tax instruments, like raising consumption taxes and wealth taxes to pay for higher social spending.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: That argument calls for some diversification of tax instruments rather than a dependence on a very narrow particular tax.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Since the beginning of the 20th century and especially in the post-war period, in international cross-sections of countries there has not been a clear negative relationship between the level or growth of tax-based social spending and GDP per capita.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, looking historically – particularly over the last century and across countries as a whole, broadly, the message is that the social cost of financing higher social spending through taxes does not appear to be especially high, although obviously, to achieve a certain point on the equity efficiency frontier, there is an efficiency loss and society has to make its own calculation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Being engaged in work confers non-pecuniary, that is non-monetary benefits that go beyond receiving wages.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: For me, it is significant that the WIS Scheme will be extended to younger workers aged 30 to 34.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Another point, investment in children from low-income families facilitates upward social mobility and, in that way, boosts future fiscal capacity when these children, having received help to overcome the initial disadvantages, take up good careers and pay taxes when they become adults.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Health spending, as a share of total Government expenditure, is expected to rise with the demographic transition.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Enabling our senior citizens to live healthily adds to the country stock of social capital.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It can be argued that even the younger segment of the current population may want the Government to raise taxes to pay for health spending going to the elderly so as to lighten the financial burden of providing care to their parents.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Third, and my final point, prioritising use of national reserves to manage external shocks, particularly negative external shocks.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Remaining integrated with a global economy presents Singapore with the opportunity to grow.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is undeniable that much of our catchup from third world to first world was facilitated by international integration, but the earliest stage was very much about technology transfer.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the next stage, we will have to generate innovative activities.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: But in order to have a steady contribution to growth of the economy, our firms will have to be integrated into the global economy, selling not only domestically but into the region and into the world as well.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: But remaining integrated with the global economy will come at a cost of sometimes sharp recessionary shocks.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Responding to the global financial crisis from 2007 to 2009 and currently in the last two years, the COVID-19 health shock, if we were to respond to these negative shocks by raising taxes to finance the national efforts to save jobs, that would be tantamount to incurring huge excess burden on taxpayers – recall that the excess burden rises more than proportionately by every unit increase in the tax rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, being able to draw down our reserves to fund these schemes to save jobs and especially in coping the global financial crisis for the Government to share some financial risk, allows us to smoothen the tax rate across business cycles.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: When the economy has recovered, it would be necessary to tax finance recurrent spending in order to keep our reserves for rainy days.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The fact that our social security system, the Central Provident Fund (CPF), is a fully funded rather than a pay-as-you-go old age retirement scheme contributes to our national savings and thus, adds to the stock of reserves.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: One context in which there is justification for the Government to borrow rather than tax finance is raising taxes for infrastructure investment which serves to mitigate the adverse effects of climate change, such as sea walls and dykes.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The emphasis in that last statement is on the words "individual" and "society".

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Much of real life is not well represented by the story of Robinson Crusoe, a story that we tend to use in teaching international trade in the classroom.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: He was, of course, a castaway who lived alone on a deserted island for many years.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As entertaining as the novel by Daniel Defoe is, Budget 2022 is built on the premise that we can build a dynamic economy, although more mature now, we have transited from third world to first world, the challenges are bigger and we need now to generate our own indigenous innovation to propel the productivity growth that we will continue to need in order to grow the economy, in order that our citizens will flourish.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: But such an economy with social collaboration results in creating a surplus.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, the economy is not an individual living on an island trading with another, although that helps.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: But within the society, we each have different capacities, we each have different strengths.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On top of that, many Singaporeans living in private properties who are asset rich but cash strapped, will bear a significant part of the $380 million property tax increase per year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Budget is a feeble attempt to increase the taxes on the rich after three decades of favourable tax policy towards them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The additional personal income tax raised is only $170 million per year, which many Singaporeans cynically pointed out, was not enough to pay for the $180 million per year funding for SPH Media Trust.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Additional Registration Fee increases for luxury cars is not really a burden to the rich, because the fee is transferable to future owners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not enough has been done on foreign manpower policy too.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The increase in the minimum qualifying salary for Employment Pass (EP) holders is too little to be effective.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am also surprised that S Pass holders are needed in the finance industry where many Singaporeans are hoping to work.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The more effective way to manage the quality of our EP holders is to ensure fair competition between the EPs and Singaporeans through imposing a standard wage levy on all EPs who do not make CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As global inflation is on an upcycle, we will have to do more to help Singaporeans to cope with the rising cost of living and asset inflation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the best timing to share with Singaporeans a small part of the huge windfall profits chalked up by GIC, MAS and Temasek last year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, not only did the Government not do that, it also increased the tax burden on Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government used healthcare costs as the main rationale for raising taxes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, Singaporeans have paid and are still paying dearly for healthcare.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it fair to ask them to pay more taxes for healthcare again, especially in these challenging times?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Look at the facts: $100 billion of the Singaporeans' CPF funds are locked up in MediSave accounts, and Singaporeans contribute $10 billion to MediSave every year; $10 billion of reserves have been accumulated in MediShield and CareShield, while Singaporeans continue to pay $3 billion of CareShield premiums every year and the premiums are likely to rise every five years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans also pay billions of dollars in private healthcare insurance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore is actually in a very strong financial position.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have the resources to pay for even the large healthcare cost increases forecasted by the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is an indication of the size of our national reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our nation's financial assets are currently closer to $1.6 trillion, due to an increase of $200 billion of reserves over the last two years, despite and after the COVID-19 drawdowns.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Net investment income from these assets is now more than $40 billion a year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Half of the net investment return, or $20 billion, is recycled back into the reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can actually provide for our current generation while continuing to save for future generations at the same time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, the Government's argument for the future generation does not hold water.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The virtue of frugality preached by the Finance Minister is telling cash strapped Singaporeans to tighten their belts again while the Government is sitting on massive reserves and unutilitsed revenues.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, we cannot rest on our laurels and rely on our reserves and unused revenues all the time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I only want to stress that we have the buffer and time to make better long-term plans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those plans should include the Government focusing on fiscal efficiency and discipline.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the Government has been running Budget surpluses these years, public spending cuts have not been discussed openly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our Budget has increased by about 7% per year over the last two decades to about $100 billion for FY2022.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is, thus, ample room for us to cut down on existing spending.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Finance Minister has disclosed he is imposing a 3% cut on existing expenditure from next year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If he can achieve that every year, we will have a saving of $3 billion per year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Again, there is no need for the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can probably do more cuts than 3%.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We advocate setting clear socio-economic targets for each expenditure.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is the reason we supported the SINGA scheme, which will bring big infrastructural projects under stricter financial discipline.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, many Singaporeans are asking, what are the socio-economic targets for SPH Media Trust, to which the Government is committing $900 million over the next five years?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How about the billions of dollars of taxpayer money spent on local Universities that have relied heavily on foreign talent, but do not seem to be producing sufficient local skills and talent needed for our economy?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When public funds are used to support or rescue a commercial organisation, are there plans to claw back the funds when the commercial organisation starts to make money?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The clawed back funds could have been used to help many more Singaporeans who needed help.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, as the amount of resources at the disposal of the Government grow larger, we need to check on the expenditures more closely.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are also against the goody bag approach that is adopted by the Government to convince Singaporeans to accept the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Handing out short-term ad hoc goodies to Singaporeans instead of using permanent schemes, will not produce resilient Singaporeans but dependent Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have been recommending a minimum living wage of $1,800 per month in take-home pay for all Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This works out to about $2,250 in gross wage per month.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This may appear high, but if you add Workfare Supplement, GST Voucher (GSTV), U-Save rebate, CDC Voucher, and now, Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS), you could easily reach the $2,250 gross wage per month.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, instead of handing out drips and drabs to Singaporeans, the Government could have provided a lump sum to top up the average worker's gross wage to $2,250 per month.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A permanent monthly wage of $2,250 will give workers more clarity in making personal financial plans for himself and for his family.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is how we make Singaporeans more resilient.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   The PSP is against the GST hike and therefore does not support this Budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At a time when Singaporeans are still facing various difficulties, we should try to come up with better fiscal solutions to help them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why does the Government want Singaporeans to tighten their belt at this juncture when it is sitting on this gold mountain?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans have already spent a lot on their current and future medical needs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, our focus should first be on reducing rising healthcare costs, rather than adding to the burden of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Government expenditure has grown rapidly by 7% per annum over the past 20 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is time to see how we can reduce non-social and non-medical expenditures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of these, the Government's $100 billion Covid-19 relief package needs to be properly accounted for.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are looking for a new financial compact that distributes national resources more equitably and benefits all segments of society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai mentioned that the GST hike will result in $1.2 billion in tax burden on middle-class Singaporeans in the long run.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can he share with us how he got that $1.2 billion figure as I do not seem to be able to find it in published material?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, 40% to the bottom 80% and 60% to the top 20%.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, that is how I got my $1.2 billion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I just want to confirm that his calculations do not include those.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I presume that the GST Vouchers and all the compensation payments will only apply to the lower-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There are some applying to the middle-income, but the permanent GST Vouchers belong to only to the lower-income.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, at the end of the day, when the Government argues that this is not regressive, it is not true, because apart from the top 20%, who are the people who are there, the remaining 40% of the GST increase?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I hope that answers Mr Saktiandi Supaat's question.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The reason why I asked is that I just want to have an understanding.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The way I interpret the Budget booklet and the Statement that Minister Lawrence Wong highlighted is that the Assurance Package and the permanent GSTV in some ways neutralise the impact on the majority, including the middle-income as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It seeks to strike a fine balance between helping our businesses and people emerge from the pandemic and investing in our longer-term objectives by taking tough decisions today.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In my speech, I will start by addressing the concerns of Singaporeans namely the middle-income segment amid rising costs of living – including the GST increase, and one of the reasons why I sought clarifications from Mr Leong is because the middle-income segment is something that will be a theme in my speech, Mr Speaker – and the need to focus on real wage growth to combat rising costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I will then turn to the brave decisions we are taking to build a fair, inclusive and sustainable society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Thereafter, I will round up with some thoughts on maintaining Singapore's hub status.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As the economy recovers from COVID-19 both domestically and globally, we can expect inflationary pressures to drive prices up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Against this backdrop of rising costs of living, the GST increase has generated great public attention.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The GST was last raised to 7% in 2007, some 15 years ago.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: While the increase to 9% – announced as early as 2018 in light of our ageing population and increased healthcare and social spending – will still be lower than the GST or VAT in many other countries such as Australia and the UK, but it is still a very visible price increase for the average Singaporean and Singaporeans are understandably concerned.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: To help Singaporeans cope with rising costs of living in a sustained manner, we must focus on growing their wages.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Based on MOM's data, the real growth in our full-time employed resident's median gross monthly income has slowed down in the last five years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This looks at the income of a typical worker in the middle, after all workers are ranked by their income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The last two years have not been easy for everyone.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: While I am happy to hear that we will uplift lower-wage workers by extending the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) to security officers, drivers and workers in the retail and food services sector, what are we doing to boost the wages of our middle-income workers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: On that note, I have a few suggestions to make.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: One, as a start, and probably to nudge the public and private sectors, we could raise the salaries of our frontline workers, regardless of whether they are lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am mindful that it needs to be paid from somewhere.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This includes our wider range of healthcare workers and Adult Educators (AEs) who are private-sector individuals working across the Early Childhood, Student Care, Universities, Private Education Institutions and International Schools and who are represented by the NTUC-affiliated Education Services Union (ESU).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The nature of their occupation meant that these AEs, who are largely aged 35 and above, were one of the first to return to their workplaces as this pandemic dragged on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Increased remuneration would recognise their invaluable societal contributions in this pandemic and extend our appreciation to them like how we did for our nurses last year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Theoretically, this means that jobs which previously paid between the old and new salary thresholds – which could have gone to a foreign employee previously – will now have to filled by a local.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, will the Government consider further differentiation of sectors beyond just carving out the financial services sector?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Different sectors pay vastly different salary scales and the point at which they require foreign labour or expertise may vary significantly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Having a single uniform qualifying salary may also penalise sectors where Singaporeans are less interested in those jobs, while those employers cannot get pass holders to do the jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Third, another way to raise wages is to ensure that our workers can quickly and smoothly transition from their existing industry – which may be a sunset industry with stagnating wages – to emerging growth areas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In facilitating our current and future workers' transition and upskilling, why is there no further focus on the Professional Conversion Programme or the Capability Transfer Programme in this year's Budget?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Over the years, I see value in these programmes, especially as we face the risk of structural unemployment and an economy in transition and faced with global disruptions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How are these programmes going to sit alongside the new SkillsFuture Career Transition Programme announced by the Minister for Finance?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And I have mentioned this in many of my Budget debate speeches.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is like a broken record; I have been raising this point.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is as opposed to a preceding-year basis, this system can help taxpayers – a significant proportion being middle- and upper-middle income Singaporeans – so that they can better manage their cash flow by matching tax payments with contemporaneous income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Before the pandemic, the number of freelancers was already on the rise, reaching 8% of Singapore's working residents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Through the pandemic, I have heard from residents that they or their family members have turned to delivery and private hire driving "gigs".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The launch of apps to connect gig workers and clients have only accelerated the growth of freelancing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As an advisor to the NTUC-affiliated Education Services Union (ESU), one of the first groups of people that come to my mind are the private-sector individuals working across the Early Childhood, Student Care, Universities, Private Education Institutions and International Schools – otherwise known as AEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The nature of the sector lends itself to freelancing as training providers and institutions are increasingly reluctant to hire these individuals as employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Some AEs may even be compelled to start their own sole proprietor company and enter a business-to-business transaction just to get the job.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Common problems faced by freelancers include not getting paid on time, and onerous, unclear contractual provisions, such as those that unfairly appropriate the freelancer's materials or intellectual property.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Unlike employees who have some protections under employment law, freelancers often fall back on contractual terms that they agree with their clients.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: For AEs in particular, I understand that the ESU is currently working with SkillsFuture Singapore to formulate Tripartite Standards for freelance AEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: When that is done, I hope the Government can take the lead and require training providers to adopt the Tripartite Standards before they are eligible for SkillsFuture funding.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am proud that our Government is "walking the talk" when it comes to addressing inequality – with higher taxes targeting the top 1.2% of earners; luxury cars, investment properties and on the top 7% of most valuable homes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: A recent OECD report has observed estate duty can be a particularly efficient way of enhancing equity and raising revenue if the class of exempted assets are minimised and the tax base is kept broad.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Besides being a fair and inclusive society, we also want to be a sustainable community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Just last month, many Members, including myself, spoke on the Motion for an "inclusive transition" to a low-carbon society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am grateful that the Government has taken on board the suggestion to announce our carbon tax plans in advance, in order to give businesses the runway to plan ahead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: While the contemplated measures to help businesses – such as emissions allowances and support for green investments – are welcome, are we also looking at adjustment measures to prevent carbon leakage to other countries with "looser" requirements?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: For example, Indonesia's carbon tax is going to be set at US$2.10 per tonne, come April 2022.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: If businesses simply "offshore" their operations away from Singapore, not only do we lose jobs associated with such operations, we may also fall short of our goal to manage climate change.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In addition, further details would be useful to assuage concerns that exemptions to companies using LNG, diesel and petrol may undermine our efforts in this space.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Positioning ourselves at the forefront of sustainability trends by developing into a go-to regional marketplace for the trading of carbon credits is essential.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I had previously mentioned in the House that the global carbon credit market could be worth more than US$50 billion come 2030.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In our efforts to build a carbon trading ecosystem in Singapore, as we are in such early stages, I would suggest organising a dedicated inter-agency taskforce now to coordinate these efforts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The creation of a vibrant marketplace with many active participants depends on a range of issues that we will need our different agencies to work out.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I will be filing a cut on this during the Committee of Supply debate to address this in greater detail.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Second, on Singapore's overall attractiveness for foreign investments following the implementation of the agreed global tax reform, or BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Is it possible to repackage some of these tax incentives, so that agencies like the Economic Development Board (EDB) can still continue to have these "carrots" in the bag as they pitch to foreign investors?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What will happen to the investment tax credits with the changes?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The fairness of the global tax reform under BEPS 2.0, and the achievement of its stated aims, will depend on exactly how individual countries choose to implement the two pillars.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As we consider our own implementation steps, I hope we can adopt a "wait and see" approach – to consider how other countries are implementing BEPS 2.0 before tailoring our implementation steps in tandem, rather than pioneer an implementation model ahead of the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Operationally, supposedly 1,800 companies are going to be affected, but no indication which sectors and type of companies they are and how hard they will be hit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As you can see – and I have mentioned it earlier at the start of my speech and previous Budget speeches mentioned by Minister Lawrence and other Ministers for Finance, I have requested for more help to be given to the middle-income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I recalled in her response speech to an Adjournment Motion on "Taxation for a Dynamic and fair 21st Century Economy" just three months ago, Second Minister for Finance, Ms Indranee Rajah, clarified that over 60% of the net GST from households and individuals is estimated to be collected from the top 20% of resident households, foreigners residing in Singapore and tourists.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: That was not the first time this information has been given to the House.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This, effectively, neutralises the GST increase for these groups for those durations and, in some cases, for even longer; and not to mention the permanent GSTV scheme which will add on to that Assurance Package as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, to get a sense of how much the different households will receive, colleagues and Members, you may find it useful to refer to the infographics, and I have seen the infographics on MOF's website.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In addition to the middle- and lower-income, they will receive offsets under the permanent GSTV scheme, over and above the amounts under the Assurance Package.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, it is not right to say that the GST increase will be borne by the middle-income without taking into consideration some of these transfers and some of these longer-term and permanent transfers, which is quite unique for Singapore – the permanent GSTV scheme.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: (In Malay):   I am glad that the Government has listened to the people's concerns and delayed the GST increase start date and staggered it over two years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am also heartened that, under the Assurance Package, the majority of households will get five years' worth of offsets and the lower-income will get at least 10 years' worth of offsets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: For example, let us take a Singaporean couple with two young children, who live in a 4-room HDB flat and earn the combined household income of $8,000 per month.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is the middle-income group that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This does not include the permanent GSTV scheme which they will also receive for a longer period beyond that.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: If I can just summarise this using two Malay quatrains.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
