text: The first quatrain speaks about many segments of our society receiving extraordinary support.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The second quatrain states that the amount spent on the Budget is worth it because it makes us stronger and gives us hope.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, in the last two years, we have dipped into our reserves and Singaporeans have worked very hard to pull Singapore through the COVID-19 challenges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am glad to read that our collective efforts have paid off in buttressing the recession as well as resident unemployment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We must now turn our attention to middle- to long-term goals and uplift our citizens' well-being, as well as to continue to help Singaporeans out of the long shadow of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: On that note, I support Budget 2022 which aims to secure the welfare and the future of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2022 introduces measures that reflect the many challenges and opportunities that Singapore faces as we emerge from this pandemic.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget addresses important bread-and-butter issues by investing in immediate support for our businesses, our workforce and our households.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: These measures will help Singaporeans manage the cost of living, ensure we continue to track a strong and steady economic recovery and create new jobs and opportunities for all.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, the Budget also acknowledges several additional priorities, such as strengthening our social support system, transitioning to a greener economy and tackling climate change as a global emergency.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: These social, economic and environmental sustainability measures are hugely important, because they help build our resilience against present and future shocks to the well-being of our fellow Singaporeans, our economy and our natural environment.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Achieving these goals will not be easy and requires careful consideration of the many trade-offs, particularly when different priorities require common and limited resources, such as our land.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these new measures may also require businesses to acknowledge the environmental costs of their activities.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Faced with these challenges, it may be useful to look back at the most testing times in Singapore's history, for insights and inspiration that may guide us forward decisively and successfully.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In his speech to the Singapore Press Club in February 1972, former Senior Minister, the late Mr S Rajaratnam, noted that he once believed Singapore as a small city state – and I quote, "… without a natural hinterland, without a large domestic market and no raw materials to speak of, has a near-zero chance of survival politically, economically or militarily" – end quote.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: However, when Mr Rajaratnam made that speech, he immediately acknowledged that he had already been proven wrong.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore had, in fact, not only survived, but also begun to thrive.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The reason for that, as Mr Rajaratnam observed, is because we had been transforming ourselves into a new kind of city – the Global City.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We had begun to view ourselves, not as a self-contained city state, not as a regional city, but rather, as a world embracing Global City.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Fast forward to today, as we embark on our sustainability journey, we may wish to consider that Singapore can be a "Global City for Sustainability".

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In the same way that Singapore has had to transform ourselves when faced with an existential crisis half a century ago, we have to pivot ourselves yet again today as we face the existential crisis of climate change.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: By working with other Global Cities as our eager collaborators, our allies, our co-inventors of new knowledge, new technologies and new opportunities, we can leverage our respective strengths, overcome our individual weaknesses and amplify our capacity to meet our challenges.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: As a Global City for Sustainability, size matters not, because the world is our hinterland.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We can free ourselves from the shackles of our geographic limitations.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We can expand the canvass of our imagination through innovation.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: We can collaborate with other Global Cities to address the emerging sustainability challenges that the world faces.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore as a Global City for Sustainability is not just a thought experiment.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the programme will develop solutions for creating a more people-centric and pleasant living environment, by addressing the impacts of climate change in cities, while considering the social sentiments and needs of the people and communities.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: As Minister Desmond Lee noted during the Urban Sustainability R&D Symposia 2021, and I quote, "We aspire to build a city that not only meets our physical needs, but that also enables us to forge strong relationships and deep emotional connections with each other".

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The programme will also support our transformation into a City in Nature, by developing the necessary tools and techniques for enhancing biodiversity and our natural environment and implementing nature-based solutions to tackle climate change.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: These are timely and important goals that will undoubtedly deliver new insights and innovations to benefit Singapore.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, as a Global City for Sustainability, we may want to be even more ambitious, by not only developing solutions that cater to Singapore's needs, but also exporting the solutions we develop, to meet the needs of other cities around the world.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This requires our Universities and research institutes to work collaboratively with our public, private and people sectors towards a common vision of transforming Singapore into a Global City for Sustainability.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Another area that requires close collaboration between these different sectors, is education.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially true in our nascent but rapidly growing sustainability sector, where the need and demand for the upskilling of our workforce may prove to be the greatest.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Fortunately, our educational institutions have already been rising to the challenge.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these training programmes are taught by both academics and industry specialists, who are eager to share their perspectives, knowledge and experience in the field of sustainability.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: There is clearly more to be done, to build capacity on sustainability across different sectors and value chains.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: My recent discussions with stakeholders in Singapore, point to three main buckets of skills gap, as follows.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: First, the most basic and foundational knowledge on climate change and sustainability that every worker should possess.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Second, function-specific skillsets to ensure the capacity of corporate function departments to support the rest of the company in developing and deploying sustainability initiatives.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: And third, sector-specific competencies to enable the successful transition of key industries towards more sustainable business models and practices.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, as we continue to develop and deploy more training programmes to fill these gaps, we should also be cognisant of the needs of other cities.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: By helping other cities build their capacity for addressing climate change and sustainability challenges, Singapore may also become a sustainability academy for the world.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: With the bold and decisive announcements in this Budget of our net-zero ambition by or around mid-century, and our revised carbon tax policy, we are signalling to the world that Singapore is absolutely serious about taking concrete actions to tackle climate change.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: As Minister Grace Fu recently highlighted, our carbon tax increase sends a clear signal to companies, that emissions have an explicit environmental cost.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Companies must factor these costs in their business decisions.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: By putting an appropriate price on carbon, we are incentivising companies to transition to renewable energy, to improve their energy efficiencies and to invest in cleaner technologies.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly, as many of our Singapore-based companies have international value chains, these changes in corporate decision-making and behaviour can have far-reaching global impacts.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: But in my opinion, there is an even more important and impressive aspect of our revised carbon tax policy.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This is nothing short of visionary, as also noted by Mr Mikkel Larsen, CEO of Climate Impact X.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This measure will go a long way towards supporting the growth of a vibrant international carbon market to achieve climate impact at scale.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I am optimistic about the odds of our success, not least because our youth are bursting at the seams with an overwhelming sense of civic virtue, purpose and pride.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In more ways than one, they are the reason we are on this sustainability journey.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Ms Kate Yeo, born and raised in Singapore, is currently a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in the US.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Kate is deeply passionate about environmental and sustainability issues in Singapore and has been regularly posting her explainers and thoughts on Instagram as @byobottlesg.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: After hearing about the green transition initiatives on Budget Day, Kate posted the following on Instagram, and I quote, "Still lots of details to be released, and of course we will still have to see how these policies will work in practice.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: But on the whole, I am hopeful – simply because Singapore is sometimes painfully pragmatic, and we do not set targets we cannot hit.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: If the Government says net zero by or around 2050, I have faith we will get there".

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: They are putting their trust to do the right thing and to succeed.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: At the heart of cities are their people.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: While Singapore is uniquely challenged in several ways, we are also uniquely endowed in other ways, in particular, the indomitable spirit of our people has enabled us to survive and thrive throughout our history, despite all odds.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: As we emerge from yet another "crucible of fire", to borrow the Prime Minister's words, we will level up and emerge even stronger yet again.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore confronts climate change and other sustainability challenges, we have the opportunity to be part of something bigger than ourselves, to punch above our weight once more, to achieve happiness, prosperity and progress not just for our nation, but also the world, charting our new way forward together as a bright green spark, as a Global City for Sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And, in fact, I believe Assoc Prof Jamus Lim had asked a similar question on the broad impact of the GST and the GST Voucher (GSTV) changes as well as other text changes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, many Members would probably surface them in their subsequent speeches too.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But I just want to assure Members that I will give a full response to all of this when I deliver my round-up speech.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I know many residents who contracted Omicron or know someone who has.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If the experience of US and Europe is applicable, Singapore will be in better shape within weeks or months.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When COVID-19 first struck around Budget 2020's period of time, I asked the Government to hire many displaced Singaporeans, especially mid-careers Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There are others who made the same suggestion.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our Government wisely hired many Singaporeans to implement SMMs, to supplement our healthcare and social services, and to help our migrant workers cope.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With Omicron, the situation is now quite different.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A large part of our SMMs may no longer be as preventing the hyper-contagious Omicron and we have to learn to coexist with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And today, most of our industries are in a much better shape compared to 2020 and 2021.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In fact, some industries are experiencing a shortage of staff.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Also, MOF's spending has done an exceptional job in preventing economic scarring in the lives of our people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I believe it is also equally important that these Singaporeans I mention do not stay away from their respective industries for too long, which diminishes their skills in the long run.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And this is all the more important, because I believe our local labour supply will stop growing within a few years, even after the planned increase in retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To be clear, I am not suggesting transiting everybody transiting back to their private sector from this group of people involved in COVID-19 management.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The rest can transit back in phases, based on whether their previous industries are ready for them and whether they need to be reskilled before going to a different one.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: That brings me to my next point about reducing the cost and complexity for businesses through a decisive streamlining of safe management measures (SMMs), so as to fight rising inflation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our Multi-Ministry Task Force (MTF) chairs have done an excellent job simplifying our SMMs and healthcare protocols as the virus evolves.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Such clarity will help our civil servants achieve a quick, decisive but effective relaxation of SMMs when the time is right.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: My final point is about our SG Green Plan and our participations in climate change negotiations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Over the past few months, I have met a number of Singaporeans and international climate change groups and organisations, and recently many of them told me they were absolutely delighted to hear about our new net-zero pledge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Given that I have spoken on a number of occasions about the importance of carbon offsets and carbon trading, I am also heartened to hear that our Government was involved in the negotiation of Article 6 of COP26, because it unlocks the possibility for Singapore to fight climate change internationally, while having this contribution potentially recognised under our National Determined Contributions (NDCs).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Article 6, as it stands today, mentions bilateral negotiation, but based on my understanding, without mentioning a large number of details, if bilateral negotiations determine how two countries, the one that contributes to projects and the other where the project is based, splits contributions to their respective NDCs, then I hope our Government can start bilateral negotiation with a sizeable number of countries, some from our immediate region and some from beyond.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Doing so will ensure that our overseas climate contributions are not all in one single basket, so to speak and will not be disadvantaged in negotiations with any one country in the future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many people I spoke to were relieved to hear that the GST increase will be staggered and only starting in 2023, especially given where inflation is today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But many Singaporeans acknowledge our pressing and fast-growing needs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Just to name a few – it is not just increasing healthcare costs, it is not just paying for ageing infrastructure, it is not just investing for future capabilities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But, let us not also forget that there will be less Singaporeans working in the future to support more people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: By now, many Singaporeans are aware that our uniquely Singaporean GST model is progressive.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is, in fact, a tiered GST system where the well-to-do pays more.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: All these show that our Government has listened carefully to people from all walks of life, balanced our country's needs with the complex global situation and come up with practical ways to make Singapore better.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, I offer my strong support for this Budget.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Please allow me to speak on the impact the conflict in Ukraine has on Singapore's economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I will also respond to Members' comments on what we can do to help businesses and Singaporeans to cope with the rising inflation and the challenges ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, had earlier delivered a Ministerial Statement on the matter.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I will focus on its potential impact on Singapore's economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are closely monitoring the rapidly unfolding situation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore companies have a limited presence in Ukraine, and we do not import many essential supplies from Ukraine and the region.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have adopted a multi-prong strategy to manage supply chain risks, especially for essential goods which we had enhanced during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This includes diversifying our imports, stockpiling and producing locally where viable, and working with major importers and retailers to ramp up supply from alternative sources if necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Having said that, the conflict is still evolving and the situation could change very quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While Ukraine may seem very far away from Singapore, the conflict there will have real and significant impact on all of us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: With the sanctions being imposed on Russia by various countries and the disruption to supplies, global prices of energy and other products are set to rise in the coming weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These measures will certainly come at a cost to us too.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But I hope Singaporeans will understand why we need to make a clear stand, even if there is a price to pay, as Minister Balakrishnan has explained.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One key area we will be significantly impacted by the conflict in Ukraine is energy cost, as we import most of our energy needs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have already seen in recent months a spike in the global prices of oil and natural gas, which Russia is a major exporter of.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Brent Crude benchmark also surged past US$100 per barrel just a few days ago, compared to US$71 average we saw last year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Motorists must therefore expect pump prices for petrol and diesel here to rise in time.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Electricity rates for both businesses and households will also increase in tandem with escalating global energy costs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These will undoubtedly impact Singaporeans and further raise the cost of living here.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The crisis will also further strain global supply chains as Russia and Ukraine are major exporters of commodities such as wheat and metals like nickel and palladium.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Supply disruptions for these commodities will raise the prices of goods that use these commodities as intermediate input.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, a global disruption in the supply of nickel could affect the production of stainless steel used in manufacturing and construction sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Disruptions to palladium supply will affect the semiconductor industry and consequently, the wider technology goods market.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are working with our key companies to review their business continuity plans to minimise disruptions to their business operations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must also be prepared for the follow-on impact on trade and investment flows.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: A protracted conflict will affect business confidence and weigh on global economies and impact their recovery from the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Ukraine crisis has clouded our economic outlook.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The actual impact on Singapore's GDP growth and inflation is difficult to estimate at this stage, given significant uncertainties.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: A lot will depend on how the conflict unfolds, the global response to the situation, and the longer-term impact on the global economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, what is clear is that inflationary pressures are likely to rise further in the near-term, especially through an increase in the prices of oil-related items in the first instance.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The downside risks to our economy have also increased significantly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some may ask, can we shield Singapore from the impact of these external factors?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As an open economy, we will not be able to totally insulate Singapore from the impact of higher global costs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some ask whether we can help businesses and households.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Small Business Recovery Grant (SBRG) and the Household Support Package (HSP) we announced at the Budget will help our businesses and households, and I will talk about them shortly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will continue to monitor the situation closely and if necessary, introduce additional measures to help them cope with the challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: After two years of the pandemic, many have been looking forward to ride the wave of a strong recovery in the global economy this year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The conflict has added considerable volatility and stress on what is an already challenging business environment arising from supply chain disruptions, higher electricity and fuel prices, and a tight labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Households have been similarly affected by these inflationary pressures.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government understands the strains that businesses and households are under and we will do our best to help them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have put in place a multi-prong strategy to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, we will work with industries and firms to keep Singapore's economy competitive so that it can continue to sustain real wage growth for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, MAS on 25 January this year, raised the rate of appreciation of the trade-weighted Singapore dollar.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: A stronger Singapore dollar will help moderate impact of external cost pressures.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Third, the Government works with a wide range of stakeholders to carefully manage the various cost drivers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In January this year, Minister of State Low Yen Ling shared with Members in detail, our measures to address inflationary pressures.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These include carefully managing the supply of industrial and commercial space to help manage rental costs, working closely with industry partners to ensure that the prices of daily necessities are competitive and affordable, including diversifying food import sources to reduce our vulnerability to global price fluctuations and working with the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE) to promote price transparency and help consumers make informed decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As Second Minister Tan See Leng explained to the House last year and recently in February this year, MTI and the Energy Market Authority (EMA) have put in place several measures to enhance our energy security and resilience and moderate the volatility in electricity prices.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These include ensuring that the electricity gencos have sufficient fuel reserves, establishing a standby fuel facility which gencos can tap on to produce electricity and introducing the Temporary Retail Electricity Contracting Support, or TRECS Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have already extended TRECS from March to May and will extend it further if necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are also working with gencos and electricity retailers to offer more supplies under such contracts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Notwithstanding these measures, with the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine, electricity prices are likely to remain elevated, or even increase further.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Members also spoke about the challenges that businesses faced in labour shortage and rising manpower costs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am heartened that Members appreciate the difficult balance we need to achieve between ensuring sufficient manpower for our enterprises and uplifting the capabilities and employment outcomes of our domestic workforce, especially our lower-income workers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore will continue to build a conducive environment for enterprises to grow, our economy to remain open and competitive, and for our workers to benefit from the growth.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Minister for Manpower Tan See Leng will share more on what the Government is doing to help firms, especially the SMEs, manage the impact of our manpower policy changes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Minister for Finance had also announced a suite of measures in his Budget speech to support businesses, especially SMEs to cope with higher costs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The extension of enhanced Enterprise Loan Schemes will facilitate SMEs continued access to financing and ease their cashflow.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The enhanced SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit, or SFEC, will now be available to more small and microenterprises and the enhancement of the Productivity Solutions Grant will provide support for a broader range of solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Together, more firms will be able to tap on Government support to improve their efficiency and reduce their reliance on manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To encourage take-up, the Government will intensify our outreach to SMEs by proactively reaching out to them through the trade associations and chambers, as well as through Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Households have also been affected by the rise in inflation, especially from higher utilities and grocery bills.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government will continue to lean forward and help them manage the higher cost of living.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Household Support Package introduced as part of this Budget will help HDB households, which will receive double the quantum of their quarterly U-Save Vouchers in 2022 to help them defray the cost of higher electricity bills.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The support measures are not limited to just HDB households.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: All children under the age of 21 will receive a top-up of $200 to their Child Development Account (CDAs), Education Savings Account (ESAs) or Post-Secondary Education Account (PSEA) to help them with their education needs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is in addition to the wide range of support measures for seniors and low-income families that the Government has enhanced such as the Silver Support (SS) Scheme and the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Regular support measures such as the Public Transport Vouchers and the Permanent GST Voucher (GSTV) scheme also help ease the higher cost of living for many Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is a reflection of our commitment to give more support to those who need it most.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Households that still need extra help can also continue to apply to ComCare for financial assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government will monitor the inflation situation carefully and will not hesitate to provide more help should there be a need to.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There is an urgent need for our enterprises to digitalise and improve their productivity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This way, we can face the future with confidence.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Taken as a whole, the Budget is not only fairer, greener and more inclusive for individuals and businesses.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Importantly, it tackles existing challenges and yet, prepares Singapore for opportunities that are before us.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Budget 2022 is a clear step forward as it demonstrates the Government's commitment towards a fairer society, where the better off amongst us contribute more with a progressive and resilient tax system.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The GST hike, higher carbon taxes and wealth tax increases as sources of funds are not immediate and this Budget has provided more clarity and certainty for individuals and firms to plan ahead.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For the above reasons, this Budget, aptly titled "Charting A New Way Forward Together" resonates with me.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Our plan is to ensure that no one – individual or business – will be left behind as we ride the wave into a more complex, more digital and greener world.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To achieve that, I would like to highlight two areas which we will need to focus on: one, supporting and accelerating our SMEs in their recovery and growth in the new economy; and two, redoubling our efforts to tackle escalating crime trends, specifically to safeguard our citizens against digital crimes such as scams as well as to protect our youths from the perils of drug abuse.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I will first speak on supporting our SMEs which are the backbone of our economy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Although Singapore's economy is projected to grow 3% to 5% in 2022, businesses are cautiously optimistic as the world opens up.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: SMEs expect higher business costs for macro-economic risks, such as rising energy and commodity prices, worsening geopolitical conflicts and supply chains disruptions.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This provides payouts to SMEs most affected by COVID-19 restrictions on top of the extension of other financing schemes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: All in, support for SMEs to transform and thrive in the new economy is sizeable.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, what may weigh on the minds of SME owners are the certainty of cost increases against the uncertain benefits of transformation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, beyond funding, what is key to realise our plans for a new economy is good execution.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Government can consider more active role to engage and transform our SMEs quicker.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Jimmy Goh, owner of an SME500 awardee, Sim Chwee Mini-mart, recently told me how grateful he was for the support provided by the Productivity Solutions Grant and advice from an SME Centre.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This helped him to take the bold step to successfully digitised his father's traditional seafood trading business of over 30 years.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While the digitalisation journey was rewarding, he shared the uncertainties that could deter SMEs, such as the heavy reliance on outsourced solution providers and, therefore, the worry of the loss of control of key business data and IT systems.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Another feedback provided to me by the Association of Trade and Commerce noted that SMEs amidst the journey are unclear of the road map to digitalise, such as the need for online marketing after developing a sales website.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: SMEs found themselves underestimating the cost and time required to build new digital channels.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As we speak about a greener future, what has hogged the media and public conversations has been above the line carbon tax increases.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Looking forward, the focus for SMEs should really be about how to remain competitive and in fact capture more opportunities that are ahead.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Increasingly, MNCs and governments will require SMEs to be ESG-compliant to continue to be on their panel of tenders.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These standards are not easy to implement and sometimes confusing so it is no wonder that many SMEs do not quite know where to start and how to measure and report compliance.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While there are different resources available to help businesses in our pursuit of a digital and green economy, SMEs still see transformation as a cost rather than a strategic investment or advantage.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is where the challenge is not about funding alone, but it is about how our Government can play a bigger role in actively engaging our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: More can be done to spark a mindset shift in SMEs, to marshal them towards the right resources, shape role models in different industries and to sustain partnerships in their transformation journey.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: One angle is for the Government to rope in trade associations and chambers of commerce, or TACs, to contribute more as an effective bridge between our agencies and SMEs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, I am glad Minister Gan just raised this point earlier and I hope to hear more details on this at the coming Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If we do this right, SMEs can really benefit and be ahead of the curve against regional competitors in the new economy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that it has catered for the expending resources and capabilities to deal with evolving crime trends.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: At last year's Budget debate, I called for more action and resources to curb the rise of scams.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As we battle scams, it is not difficult to worry that more sophisticated cybercrimes that have emerged in other countries, such as ransomware where perpetuators steal monies and our data can also impact us.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given the above, we need to dedicate more resources, both skilled staff and capabilities, to Singapore Police Force (SPF) to build on the initial success of the Anti-Scam Centre and leverage its partnerships with other stakeholders in the digital ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We need more public engagement with both individuals, as well as businesses.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Everyone has a role to play in this multi-layered strategy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: An equally worrying trend is that of drug abuse by youths.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We owe much thanks to CNB's effectiveness in seizing illicit drugs and apprehending offenders, particularly traffickers, to keep our community safe.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This could be due to the more liberal attitudes they have towards drugs and the advent of new psychoactive substances could make this trend worse.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We know that along with drug addiction come many social ills.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: There is no silver bullet to solve these challenges.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We have to act swiftly and resolutely to protect our citizens.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While challenges remain, we can take heart in the resilience and the unity they have propelled us forward and we can look ahead with renewed confidence.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I support Budget 2022 and the plans in charting Singapore's new way forward together.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, people are most worried about inflation and the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From time to time, we hear complaints from the public that before the implementation of the new GST rate, the prices of utilities, food, coffee and daily necessities have already gradually increased, which makes many families anxious and worried.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Although the Government has announced various assistance packages to offset the impact of the GST hike next year and the year after, people are still worried that the new GST hike will increase their financial burden.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, we also understand that not all price increases are for profiteering.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We understand that, in fact, businesses especially SMEs, coffeeshops and hawkers, are not only affected in terms of labour shortages, but are also under pressure from increased costs of raw materials, ingredients, utility bills, logistics and transportation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Businesses often try to absorb cost increases in the short term in order to retain customers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Prices of goods and food tend not to change every year, but every few years.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a result, price increase tends to be in a step manner.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Businesses must adapt to the needs of the market and, if necessary, change their business models and processes to ensure that the products, food and the services they provide are value-for-money, or even great value-for-money, in the eyes of customers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Then, even with higher prices, consumers continue to patronise their businesses.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given that almost everything in Singapore needs to be imported, we are price takers in the international market.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To ensure that citizens can still afford the products and food, we must ensure that workers' wages grow faster than inflation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, I call on the Government to continue to create opportunities for our workers to upgrade their skills, knowledge and their abilities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, I also call on the Government to pay close attention to and ensure that the wage growth rate and inflation rate can be balanced and that appropriate assistance can be effectively provided when needs arise.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): For workers' wages to outpace inflation and the rising costs of living, they need to have the skills and expertise that are in demand by the market.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to equip and train our workers, give them the opportunity to upgrade themselves as they progress along their careers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will allow them continued access to jobs with higher wages and better work conditions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government, unions and businesses must work together to explore the most suitable training models for their sectors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this regard, I would like to give recognition to NTUC and its affiliated unions for their various initiatives, such as the Company Training Committees (CTCs).

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition to the tasks of identifying what kind of training is needed, the question is whether we can also get enough well-qualified trainers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How would the Government assist our unions in this endeavour?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are plans to establish tripartite academies for sectors where transformation is needed.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will the training be conducted and courses be accredited?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will there be collaboration with our ITEs, Polytechnics and tertiary institutions?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister share more details on this?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do we have long-term studies to track how successful these job matches are and identify the main problems where the matches are not compatible so that we can improve on the process?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For persistent unemployment, mismatched skillsets need to be addressed and retraining for the affected workers is needed to equip them with new skills for growing sectors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, I would like to appeal on behalf of some elderly private property owners regarding the increase in property taxes for owner-occupied residential properties.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are properties that they may have bought long ago.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Upon retirement, they have no income and are burdened with ever-increasing cost of living and now have to pay higher property tax as well.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are their homes, not investment properties that have rental income to offset the property taxes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Government consider assisting this group of residents?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would appear to be fairer and more equitable.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Most measures address concerns such as a green economy, assistance for badly affected businesses and supporting skills upgrading.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The personal income tax rate varies in different countries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is around 37% in the US, 40% in Switzerland, 56% in Japan and 45% in China.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Comparatively, even though our top marginal personal income taxes are 24%, it is still relatively low compared to these developed countries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singapore's top-tier owners should find the revised tax rate favourable.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over the past week, I have spoken to several high-income earning Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is heartening to know that most high earners agree that the business-friendly social and commercial conditions in Singapore have helped them succeed and prosper.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Some are supportive of the higher taxes to provide for heavier social spending.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They understand that the changes to the tax system are necessary for the sustainability and stability of Singapore's infrastructure, conducive policies, secure environment and well-developed digital infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has moved into a different phase of development.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Going forward, Singaporeans should expect more tax changes to meet the demands of the changing demographics and economic conditions, with the top-tier owners expecting to contribute even more towards tax revenues.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Some high-income earners may feel that they have worked very hard for their success and that is not fair to have to share with others who did not work as hard as they did.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I do agree that nothing is absolutely fair and it is never possible to completely justify who should be paying more or less taxes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, it is important to cultivate the growth mindset that those who can afford to pay a little more taxes should do so.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Even with the higher tax revenue, the cost of living and doing business will still continue to rise.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We will have to manage the rising inflation while maintaining our economy's competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: One major area of concern is the push for productivity gains, especially in view of the curbs in foreign labour inflows, as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over the past decades, the availability of low-cost foreign workers has benefited business owners and kept businesses running competitively.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To add, these foreign workers are willing to perform labour-intensive jobs, which Singaporeans tend to eschew.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We have to find a way to win ourselves of the heavy reliance on foreign labour as the easy availability of foreign workers has depressed are blue-collar workers' wages and it will continue to do so.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Through the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) and the Workfare Incentives Supplement (WIS), we have been increasing wages to attract more Singaporeans to take on various jobs, especially those that are currently taken on by foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Though is a difficult period for many businesses that are facing severe manpower crunch, we should persist in this workforce transformation and build a strong Singaporean Core.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must try to continue to hire more locals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In tandem, we need to redesign the operations and job processes and improve the working conditions for lower-wage jobs or Singaporeans need to change their attitude towards low-wage jobs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Business owners should also shift their mindset and relook at how to improve the work conditions that have been deterring Singaporeans to take on such roles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Having said that, workers will always take on jobs with remuneration that justifies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I would also like to appeal to the Government to provide more support to social enterprises.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many social enterprises employ untapped resources that include post-retirement seniors and high-functioning special needs individuals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These senior workers can remain active and sharp.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With some tweaks in the job roles, this particular group of workers can assist in certain jobs, previously done by foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Though easier said than done, we should automate whenever possible.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Understandably, many businesses are reluctant to invest in the capital expenditure required for automation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, new technology and improved business processes is a must.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope the Ministry will consider providing better assistance to our SMEs to offset the upfront costs for automation and innovation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Assistance schemes could be interest-free loans or grants to partially offset initial capex investment, particularly for initial large investments required for scaling-up automation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In Mandarin):   We are heading in the correct direction in revamping our tax system, but the Government can do more.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Assurance Package cash payout and GST Voucher – Cash (Senior's Bonus) will offset the expense increases.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, many retirees have limited savings, they are worried about what would happen after the period of support ends.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Families with special needs members also do not have any additional help.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Will the Government give more support to social enterprises that help to match interested retirees and able persons with special needs with micro jobs?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For those who are able, matched with suitable tasks, they will be able to supplement their household incomes and be meaningfully engaged as they contribute to our community.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In English): We will be starting a Wellness Kampung for seniors in the Sembawang West constituency.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This will be a common space at the void deck where residents come together to socialise and exercise.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There will also be an urban farm on the rooftop of a multi-storey carpark next to it, that will provide micro-jobs for the seniors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It can be a modern-day kampung where residents exchange information about job opportunities like babysitting, tuition, part-time jobs, handy-man jobs and so on.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Green Capital, including carbon taxes and green bonds, is the catalyst to jumpstart our transition to a green economic ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The issuance of green bonds will allow the Government and businesses to invest in new technology and build a strong foundation for a green ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These bonds will greatly reduce the financial risks to our Government, especially for mega infrastructure investment projects for green energy production and for transition to greener business models.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As an example, the transformation to a more sustainable Jurong Island.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Though the newly introduced phased carbon tax increase will help businesses cope and transit more gradually to greener practices, there has been little mention of grants for developing talents needed to support the green economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: R&D for renewable energy production and energy optimisation technologies is important.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Presently, many countries are fighting for talents to support their sustainability related industries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is advisable to start positioning Singapore as a serious regional green hub.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We will need the talent to build our green industries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is also time for us to invest more in the training and nurturing of a new generation of innovators and engineers for the sustainability sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In recent years, many young talents have pursued careers with big IT firms that have set up headquarters in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We also need to proactively plan for some of our very own Singaporeans to pursue engineering, in particular, environment engineering.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Advanced technology is the key to unlocking many constraints in harnessing renewable energy and achieving circularity in waste management.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Government must do more to signal to the nation about the importance of having talents in engineering and R&D.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: On top of channelling resources on geriatric care and building more community hospitals, I urge MOH to focus more on upstream prevention healthcare services, such as free annual health screening services for Singaporeans above 35 years old, as early intervention and treatments are often more effective and less expensive.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The preventive efforts should also focus on encouraging the younger population to live a healthier and more active lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As we recover from the pandemic, more aggressive efforts should be put into community programmes focusing on nutrition and fitness.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Although these programmes will take time and concerted efforts, this may well be the best approach to reverse the rising trend of healthcare spending resulting from diabetes and obesity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In Malay):   With a rapidly ageing population, it is imperative that we get all Singaporeans on early preventive healthcare in order to survive the silver tsunami.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The right direction would be to plan ahead for the long term, by shifting spending towards preventive and community-based healthcare.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There may be genetic, diet and lifestyle differences which need to be addressed, specifically in order to target this problem more effectively.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In English): The frequent consumption of sugary drinks may cause diabetes and obesity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am concerned about the mushrooming of bubble tea outlets all over Singapore over the past few years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Another concern is the prevalence of binge drinking amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Young adults in the 18 to 39 years age group were most likely to binge drink in pubs and bars.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Binge drinking may cause a whole host of health problems, as well as unsafe acts, such as driving under the influence of alcohol.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As part of a suite of preventive healthcare measures, I hope the Government is looking to regulate and reduce the number of bubble tea outlets, pubs and bars.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Another major area of concern is mental health, particularly worsened due to the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Mental health issues are unseen, and it is hard to understand the real extent of this social and health malaise.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is particularly debilitating because many young people are afflicted and the damage can be very long term or dire.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We have no choice but to ensure that we have qualified professionals and allocate sufficient resources in our healthcare systems to provide treatment and support for those affected.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We are a small nation and there are only so few of us.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Budget builds on the strong social compact between our Government with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, our Government has made decisive steps in the ongoing transformation of our labour market, with a clear focus on uplifting lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers understand their critical role in strengthening our social compact and the need for them to build business resilience through fair and progressive employment practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The transitional wage support, along with support grants and schemes to upskill workers and raise firm level productivity will enable employers to sustain these wage increases.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Speaking with other employers, these support measures give us confidence that the Government is with us as we uplift our workforce wages.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many businesses, especially those in consumer-facing sectors, are still reeling from the impact of COVID-19, hence this staggered increase provides the additional time needed for businesses to respond.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A one-off GST hike during a period of inflation concerns would have exacerbated concerns over a potential drop in consumer spending.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond immediate business challenges, we need to adopt a larger resilience agenda grounded in adaptability and decisiveness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This resilience agenda will move beyond defensive measures and short-term goals to encompass strategies aimed at achieving inclusive and sustainable growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my speech, I will expand on two key aspects of resilience: labour resilience and climate resilience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Labour market resilience can be characterised by a low unemployment rate, sufficient supply of skilled labour and productivity and wage growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As observed from Budget 2022, the Government aims to instil labour market resilience through two broad strategies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While most businesses would agree with the rationale behind these strategies to strengthen labour market resilience, they face operational and structural challenges that impede their adoption of these strategies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After many conversations with business owners over the past few months, the difficulty in hiring Singaporeans is a real one.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Job recruitment advertisements for Singaporeans yield low responses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In a recent meeting with a fintech startup, the entrepreneur shared of his difficulty in hiring software engineers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same meeting, a business owner in the manufacturing sector lamented that he was unable to hire sufficient staff to fulfil customers' orders.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Anecdotes like these are repeated by employers from other industries even when all of them show eagerness to hire Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The hiring challenges is also keenly felt in our social services sectors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my constituency in Zhenghua, I have received numerous appeals from young parents for childcare and infant care placements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our anchor operator has just taken possession of a large space at the new Senja BTO development, much to the delight of parents.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, parents will have to wait longer for placements as the operator is still facing challenges in hiring sufficient teaching staff.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The centre is unlikely to run at its optimal capacity when it opens.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a consequence of our ageing population and low birth rates.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our local workforce is anticipated to shrink in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While I agree that we must provide gainful employment for Singaporeans and strengthen the complimentary factor with the foreign workforce, we may soon or already have reached a point where there is simply not enough of us.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond complementing our local workforce, we need to look at supplementing our workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially so for essential services and what I would term also as "enabling" services.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, services such as childcare and infant care enables young parents to dedicate themselves to their jobs, thereby enabling them to be economically active.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we recognise and emphasise the importance of our mental health, there will be a growing need for counsellors in our schools, workplaces and in our communities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With greater mental health capabilities, we can help and enable as many Singaporeans to be at the their best mental and emotional state.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One thing that I believe that all Singaporeans enjoy is our hawker food.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our hawkerpreneurs and culture is recognised by UNESCO.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But will we have enough Singaporeans, especially with other sectors competing for the same local talent, take up the woks as our hawker legends hang up their ladles?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Essential and enabling sectors remain highly dependent on human labour.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For sectors such as healthcare, social work and early childhood, human labour is literally the commodity being traded and digital adoption is commonly seen as complementary to human labour but not a perfect substitute.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also regulatory requirements on service provider-to-client ratios that cannot be changed despite higher levels of productivity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is also growing concerns within the business and international community that Singapore is perceived to be closing up and foreigners are not welcomed.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to address these concerns as such perceptions have grave consequences for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As shared, our workforce is ageing, our labour force growth is declining, and we would not have enough workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For Singapore to stay relevant in this fast-changing world, we need access to the best talent and have them be part of our team.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Domestically, we need essential and enabling workers to support Singaporeans' aspirations and care for our seniors and children.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This need for Singapore to remain open has to be felt both economically and socially to build labour resilience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has always been a talent capital and being welcoming to different nationalities and races to call Singapore their new home is essential for our continuous development.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Marriage data shows that we have also more Singaporeans marrying foreigners and this trend is likely to continue.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: All of this makes social integration and acceptance absolutely important.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This acceptance of differences is occurring at all levels of our society – from preschools where I have seen children who are not yet attuned to our local languages to workplaces where respect for religious beliefs in food and practices require more sophisticated HR practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Retaining and growing our multicultural DNA is absolutely critical and now with even more diversity in it, we need to constantly work at it from our grassroots to our policy officers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our social compact needs to be strengthened through social integration and I believe this is where much more effort can be put in our community with active involvement by companies too.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the productivity front, the time lag between the implementation of productivity enhancement solutions and reaping their results is a very real challenge for businesses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even when businesses successfully leverage on the productivity enhancement schemes and implement more digitisation and skills transformation programmes, there will be a lag time before digital capabilities are running at full steam and employees are up to speed with their skills transformation programmes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During this transitional period, businesses face a shortage of "plug and play" labour to meet their business needs, compounded by labour shortages and the scarcity of tech talent in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a result, even if companies are open to adopting new technologies, there is still apprehension and resistance to operationalising such solutions because of the inability to seize revenue opportunities in the short run.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Inevitably, businesses will eventually reach a tipping point for technology adoption.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The COVID-19 crisis was such one crucial tipping point of historical magnitude.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, the purpose of cultivating labour market resilience is to ensure that businesses can ride on the waves of digitisation instead of being submerged under them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At present, operational and structural challenges are impeding businesses from actualising a resilient labour force.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And what other measures can be put in place to guide businesses as they re-envision their business transformation roadmaps?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With a clear labour shortage on our shores, what is the bigger strategy for our workforce composition that will enable us to remain competitive?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another aspect of the resilience agenda is that of climate resilience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I affirm the Government's commitment towards strengthening Singapore's net zero goals and significantly raising carbon taxes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These steps are necessary and crucial in ensuring Singapore's transition to a green economy and affirm Singapore's commitment towards climate change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Despite our efforts, the sobering reality is that it is unlikely for us to fully escape the effects of climate change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The floods that resulted from torrential rain in many states of Malaysia last December exposed the reality of extreme weather patterns caused by climate change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, there is a need to strengthen our climate resilience through infrastructural interventions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government announced new plans in 2020 for coastal protection measures against rising sea levels to mitigate effects of climate change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The range of options to combat rising sea levels, include engineering feats such as reclamation and building sea walls, as well as nature-based solutions are being considered.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Overall, this Budget will continue to strengthen our common resilience agenda and reinforce Singapore's strong social compact.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In my interaction with various people in business, I can sense an admiration for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Our consistent past achievements and how we are seemingly the only Asian society that managed to move towards endemic COVID-19 are two aspects that they admire.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The interest to invest or expand in Singapore is strong.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: However, one of the most common concerns is whether we have the manpower and talents to support the growth.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This is because of late, the voice of xenophobia has become louder.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We need the business leaders and investors to be clear where we stand.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: As a relatively wealthy nation, some of us might get complacent and believe that economic development is no longer the main priority.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The various vulnerabilities we face as an island city nation must be familiar to Members already.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, unless we can develop and keep our economy vibrant, we will struggle to keep our Budget balanced and start to have surplus again.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Every public policy comes with an underlying trade-off.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: As we become more aware of the trade-offs on the environmental and social aspects, we must not under-emphasise the economic ones.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The concept of "complementarity of foreign labour" is an excellent guiding principle that ingeniously addressed all the conflicting concerns.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Even as some experience huge labour shortage, there will still be a significant number of people who are unemployed or under-employed.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: As businesses are being disrupted at a faster pace, so will the rate of displacement of jobs and skills.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I expect the pace at which people will find their skills and knowledge getting outdated to increase going forward.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For traditional sectors that we want to transform to raise productivity, the more successful we are with the transformation, the more people will be displaced by new machines and talents.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Not to those who are weak and needy.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To stay successful, we have to keep seizing new economic opportunities while we are still doing well.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: If we forego one or two opportunities, we are unlikely to sense any difference.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: By the time we have lost our appeal, it is already too late.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The difficulty for the Government is to convince the public of a future-oriented policy when nothing seems to be broken yet.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: My final point is about a Singapore vision or dream.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I want to, once again, thank the MTF and the whole of Singapore for the way we responded to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The last two years were a big shock to Singapore and the world.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In business, sometimes the best time to reform a company is after it has gone through a major disruption.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, we can use this time to put together a refreshed Singapore vision.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has addressed a similar point, in terms of "renewing and strengthening our new social compact".

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In the 1980s, when I was in Secondary school, the Government's "Vision 1999" had a big impact on me.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It was a vision that covered many different aspects.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
