text: But the parts that I related to the most were the target for Singapore to achieve the Swiss standard of living then by 1999 and the plans for Singapore's New Downtown.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The latter played a part in why I have become an architect and joined URA to be an urban planner.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For mid-career folks like myself, who have gone from having handwritten letters to emails and then social media, what would inspire us?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For the young ones who are digital natives, what would inspire them?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: As we "chart our new way forward", to "emerge stronger" and "towards a low-carbon society", it might be useful to also define the qualitative aspects and value system of our society that we want to have in future.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: After two years of pandemic talk, I like the idea of having a holistic, refreshed and inspiring Singapore Vision to strive towards.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Several residents I spoke with shared that Budget 2022 responded to the needs and aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It tackled some very difficult issues that our people are concerned about and is a big step forward towards a more equitable, harmonious and progressive Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is also encouraging to note that a large part of the Budget is devoted to social well-being, particularly our seniors, who can retire better with stronger financial support and adequate healthcare.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our less privileged families and children will also not be left behind.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The other aspect of this year's Budget that struck a chord is the effort to redistribute wealth through progressive taxes on top-tier earners and expenditures, directing these to the uplifting of those most in need.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is a significantly higher contribution to total income tax revenue than the top 10% of income earners of the US and the UK by at least 10 percentage points.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I believe this redistribution of wealth serves well to build up the social foundation by which our people can thrive together.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If I may share some observations and two considerations on advancing our green transition.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As corporates around the world raced to zero in the weeks and months leading up to COP26, one glaring area of needed change to Singapore's efforts was our $5 per tonne carbon tax.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: My resident and community leader who also serves as the Sustainability Director at Lendlease Singapore shared with me that Lendlease uses a shadow price of US$20 per tonne in 2020, rising to US$100 per tonne in 2030 and US$140 by 2040, which are integrated into Lendlease's investment decisions and prices in financial risks associated with climate change.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Singapore should continue to assess our carbon tax on an ongoing basis, aligning with international best practices, to respond to and aid the transition towards a low-carbon economy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This recognises the ecosystem services that our environment provides and in Doughnut Economics Theory, this points to the ecological ceiling by which we should not cross.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A greener living environment should also ensure that our buildings and infrastructure are climate-resilient so that our people can be.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Flood risk is a significant physical climate risk that low-lying nations must contend with.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I understand that at Lendlease, climate change and adaptation plans are integrated in all major developments to ensure the communities served have access to facilities in case of floods.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Forward planning by the Government, as well as other private developers, should consider climate risks and ecological limits for Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This goes far beyond carbon emissions to include rising water levels, biodiversity loss, amongst other ecological impacts.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While we are cognisant of our limited natural resources and the need to balance economic and societal needs, applying such ecological limits may compel all of us – Government, urban planners, corporates and people sectors – to be truly creative in the way we use our resources and overcome limitations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As for the two considerations, here is the first consideration – reducing our direct emissions in tandem with electrification.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Soaring electricity prices in recent months have impacted economic recovery for businesses.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Even as we move towards electrification for vehicles and land transport, Singapore still has to deal with emissions arising from electricity generated.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While Electric Vehicles (EVs) are inherently more sustainable, producing less emissions per kilometre, EVs still have a significant carbon footprint unless the electricity is from a renewable source.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This recommendation follows the encouraging news that our aviation sector will now have access to sustainable aviation fuel.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: On the land transport front, Singapore has made limited progress, despite the fact that we have Neste, one of the world's leading producers of RD, producing 1.3 million tonnes per year at our doorstep.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To date, I understand that none of this diesel is meant for local consumption, since there are no local distributors, and the supplies are currently shipped to Europe and the US where there are government subsidies for RD.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With oil prices rising, impacting both pump and electric prices, as well as internal combustion engines and EVs, Singapore should consider a third fuel alternative, especially when Neste is producing locally.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The second consideration – accelerating the renewables market.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This can be applied to companies which are large energy consumers, for example, those under GHG Protocol Scope 2, but not the large emitters in Scope 1.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The Singapore renewable market is illiquid at the moment, with much demand and insufficient supply.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With this, I am grateful and I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Those of my generation would fondly remember the 1989 Sound Blaster by Creative Technologies' Sim Wong Hoo.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Just two decades ago, Trek 2000 International Limited, a Singapore company, invented the thumb drive.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Using a USB interface, the thumb drive, the thumb-sized storage device, had a plug-and-play convenience.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It was a wave that swept the floppy discs and mobile storage segments.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Looking at the trend of mobile payments today, a cashless society and the rise of mobile wallets, Network for Electronic Transfers (NETS) started work on their ambition in 1986 with electronic transfers at point-of-sales; the digital or mobile wallet in the form of cash cards was then rolled out in 1996.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore was ahead of our time and spearheading technologies and pushing the frontier of fintech.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today, on the list of the world's 10 most valued and largest companies by market capitalisation, except for two – that is – Berkshire Hathaway and Saudi Aramco, all the rest are IT and tech companies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The future economy will be driven by the fourth IR, moving from traditional digitalisation to an intelligent era – smart home, smart factories, lights out manufacturing – a great way to mitigate manpower and environmental issues, in smart cities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The future powerhouses will be driven by innovation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At the same time in 2017, Israel spent US$16 billion on R&D.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In 2021, Israel was 4.94%, Korea was 4.53% and Switzerland 3.37%.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Slovenia, Czech Republic and Iceland ranked higher for percentage GDP spent on R&D.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To further put into context, Alphabet Inc, the parent company of Google, spent US$31.5 billion on R&D; Amazon, US$42.7 billion; and Microsoft US$19 billion, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Although highly innovative companies with substantive R&D expenditures provide much opportunities and some form of inoculation, it does not guarantee survival.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We know of Kodak, Nokia, Blackberry and Yahoo!.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Interestingly, any keen observer will realise that Kodak and Fujifilm were in the same position.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Kodak filed for bankruptcy but, in 2010, just when Kodak was close to bankruptcy, Fujifilm posted a 57% revenue growth between the years 2000 and 2010.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This was because Fujifilm had the courage to face possible realities, act swiftly and change its business.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There was no time to be incremental, no time for quick wins, no time for low-lying fruits.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These methods would not have been sufficient to steer a behemoth.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The management quickly downscaled production lines, closed redundant facilities and they unified their research efforts, enhanced communications and improved the culture of innovation amongst the engineers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The President of the company ordered a quick stock-take of all of Fuji Film's technologies and quickly mapped out how existing in-house technologies could be used to power future markets.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It was an existential moment for them and Fuji Film survived, moving into pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and functional materials.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: With rapid tech cycles and disruptions to industries, we must be courageous in investing and building our future capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: One example amongst the numerous is oil and gas.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: With peak oil expected to occur between 2025 and 2030, we will expect the subsequent decline of oil and gas within the next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore has substantial investments and revenue from Jurong Island and this is truly one Kodak moment we want to avoid.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Avoiding Kodak moments is only one small aspect.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There is the imperative to recognise long-term trends and the ability to foresee and, most importantly, is Singapore technologically agile and capable to pivot rapidly?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Does it have the ability to build strong networks of ecosystems to solve disruptive and multidiscipline challenges of today and the future?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Is our workforce able to build expertise in different ecosystems and networks to spur collaboration and innovative capabilities?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) ranked Singapore eighth in the Global Innovation Index in 2021.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It has been top 10 in the last 14 years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: More recently, Singapore is second on the Bloomberg Innovation Index.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In a sub-segment of knowledge and technology outputs, Singapore was ranked 13th.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To note, China, Korea and Japan ranked high in knowledge and technology output within Asia.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore's education system, infrastructure, R&D environment as well as business ecosystems are our core strengths.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And we rank very, very high on those categories.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, the ability to produce knowledge products and creative assets have been less than ideal.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To achieve the high level of productivity we aspire, we must maximise our innovation potential and project tangible and quantifiable results.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must not forget that the science, technology and innovation landscape is constantly shifting.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Taking China, for example, China's feat is dramatic.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is global – 37,343 papers, AI patents filed, surpassing any country in the world including the US, a position it continues to hold.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: China also consistently files more AI patents in any other country.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Many countries are systematically gaining ground with China: Malaysia, Thailand, Turkey, Vietnam, India and Philippines, improving their rankings substantially in the last decade.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They are constantly on the move, moving at a rapid pace and gaining ground.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But in reality, science and technology activities are centred around clusters, tech ecosystems that are usually defined by geographical areas.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Some of them are well-known, like Tokyo-Yokohama, which is ranked first.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Second, which Shenzhen, Hongkong, Guangzhou followed by Seoul, Beijing and then San Jose, the famous Silicon Valley at the fifth.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore is ranked at 29th, behind Dejan, Nagoya, Osaka, Nanjing, Hangzhou, Shanghai, Taipei.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore is ranked 47th in in science and technology intensity amongst the top 100 science and technology clusters.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In terms of total IP following activity, Singapore ranks 28th behind Ukraine, Mexico and Thailand.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The term "Start-up Nation" was title of a book in 2009 by Dan Senor and Saul Singer about the economy of Israel.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The presence of thousands of start-ups and more engineers per capita than anywhere else in the world makes Israel a natural hub for innovation, best known for defence and military-inspired technologies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Entrepreneurs across the nation are now focused on building mixed generation applications, helped by government support, societal acceptance and presence of large numbers of multinationals eager to buy innovative technology from start-ups.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Israeli companies are building a wide range of products and services for the world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: So, from Creative Sound Blaster Cards to pioneering cashless payments and disrupting the data storage industry, Singapore has journeyed a long way since Independence.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We progressed from being and having the ambition for innovation in the 1960s, built up a strong core of citizens in engineering and science, attract technology advanced foreign investments, a national plan for research and development the formation of A*STAR, our research investments into biomedical science or Independent Review Entity (IRE) plans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And more recently, our highly successful Smart Nation initiative and a formation of Smart Nation and Digital Government Office (SNDGO) to better serve Singaporeans in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Here are a few suggestions I would like to make.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: First, the breadth and depth for Singapore's research, science and technology capabilities together with our creativity, innovation ambitions are critical in ensuring we remain agile in a disruptive world, navigate global challenges and achieve our strategic and national goals.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today's problems are complex and far-reaching into different domains.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There are significant long-term and substantial science and technology endeavours that require a high level of aggregating efforts at the highest level – MTI with a A*STAR and Economic Development Board (EDB); PMO with National Research Foundation (NRF) and GovTech; MCI with Cyber Security Agency (CSA) and IMDA.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And depending on the sector or domain, it would require further participation of other stakeholders, such as MAS for finance; BCA for building construction or LTA for transport.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Scientific America published an article on the need for the US to establish a Federal Department of science and technology as the STEM-related policies is administered by a bewildering array of entities which dilutes is effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It stated that the failures of producing COVID test kits, slow and ineffective rollout of COVID-19 vaccines and cybersecurity attacks on government agencies, despite multiple warnings.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This reflects the central failure of agencies with science and technology ambitions to meet the challenges of the 21st century.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Similar to events leading up to 9/11 in the US where organisational weaknesses were revealed in scattering of multiple intelligence capabilities across agencies and the federal government.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, there is a need to better organise scientific efforts.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: More recently, the US has elevated the Office of Science and Technology to a Cabinet-level appointment with plans to establish a new Department of Science and Technology.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Many other successful and innovative countries have done so – South Korea, Japan, Israel, India, Denmark.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Next, to succeed, we must keep our pace.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In fact, we must double or triple our pace to maintain our competitiveness and relevance.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These are important decisions and the choices that the Government takes on research, innovation science and technology will set the future trajectory for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To achieve and maintain global leadership requires sustained increase investments, both from a percentage GDP and also from absolute numbers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Third, for Singapore to maintain its competitiveness as a business destination for investments in R&D, the Government should review the speed and agility of business execution in Singapore and balance with the risk reward outcomes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore must keep pace with decision cycle and execution agility of businesses today, especially so when added stability will reduce R&D investment risk, enabling businesses to invest in the long term and build innovative partnerships.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These investments must be coherent with our ambitions to build up local enterprises, manpower and Singapore's overall capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Fourth, building local R&D capabilities by supporting local research and development clusters, collaborate, partner and sharpen product and service quality locally, build portfolio and credentials locally for international markets and accelerate growth through regional and global networks.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For decades, MINDEF has partnered ST Engineering to develop capabilities in-house.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To release R&D and capability development, ST Engineering was able to scale and export capabilities overseas.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We can build more of these such champions and there are numerous opportunities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For example, given that we are the largest customers of elevators in the world, there are opportunities to build a regional, if not, global elevator technology champion.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Our Singapore water stories, one of the most compelling in the world, building capabilities and overcoming challenges, we have co-developed water technologies and there are opportunities to build a multibillion-dollar, Singapore water technology champion.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We had a Singapore company that was a potential unicorn in the renewable energy for Singapore and the region.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Healthcare, such as COVID-19 test kits, high-tech hand sanitisers, and the list goes on.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I have spoken to some entrepreneurs who have mentioned the difficulty that their products having to face immense scrutiny by local registry or authorities, the skepticism of being a locally made product and the fear of endorsing a product.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I think we can do much more to build a collaborative environment that encourages partnerships to help these entrepreneurs navigate through difficult requirements and enable them to build on their capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must seize every opportunity to build long-term R&D partnerships and co-create capabilities with our local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Fifth, Singapore must be open to attract talent from across the world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the United States, evidence shows that immigrants are often the most productive innovators and entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They are vital to competitiveness and fuel growth.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These companies are not only valuable, but they employ a lot of people.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The collective value of some of these 50 immigrant-founded companies far exceed the entire stock market of several countries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: America's ability to attract international students foster entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: About 23% of billion-dollar startup companies had a founder who first came to America as an international student – Slack, Peloton, SpaceX and WeWork are all immigrant founders.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The American education system has embraced international students as part of the learning experience and cultural exchange, which results in more robust, vibrant and competitive landscape.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Sixth, we must strengthen Singapore's skills and competencies by maintaining a strong supply of skilled workers, provide continued training and skills acquisition throughout their careers, build up alternate entry pathways for those who are doing mid-career switches and recognise the transferability of skills.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This will provide the required opportunities for Singaporeans to remain agile and productive longer.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It must also be recognised that present and future challenges are complex and multidisciplinary, which would require a team with diverse skills and expertise.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must stretch the potential Singaporeans to enable them over their lifetime on their own time to achieve the highest education and skills potential.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It can be a diploma, it can be a degree, Masters or PhD or any other professional certifications, working experience that builds upon skillsets.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This OECD average is set to increase to 2.3% by advancing knowledge and research across academia and industry.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Doctoral students and holders can make economies more innovative.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, I want to caution that this is not a narrative about certifications but macro trend of increasing demand for skills and increasing competitive supply of skills worldwide.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must also be mindful not to be overly concerned with degrees and diplomas as we are all reminded by the likes of Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, Mark Zuckerberg, Sean Parker and Mark Darcy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: None of them had University degrees, but a good combination of connective, interpersonal, self leadership and digital skills that set them apart from the rest.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This opens possibilities across education, experience, skill archetypes, everyone that has a role to play.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Most importantly, as we embark on this journey, we leave no one behind.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I believe that everyone deserves an opportunity, an opportunity for a good job for every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The Ensign Infosecurity team also trained to make sure there was a conducive working environment for all it.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It was a team effort and that was what made the difference, all of us doing a bit more for one another.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: When I heard that the programme was a success, it truly touched my heart.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Geraldine, on your birthday, papa would like to wish that you have a Singapore that is tech and rich, inclusive and above all, kind, loving and in all we do, fighting for a better Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am glad that there are actions since by the Government, implementing Progressive Wage Model (PWM) across more sectors, more social programmes to support these families, and in this current Budget, there are more schemes to uplift the lower-income group.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This pandemic has seen our strong dependence on the essential workers in Singapore and globally.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As we speak, the need for frontline workers to get us through this pandemic has not subsided.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Let us remember, we need every segment in our society in good and bad times.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, I am supportive of the measures in this Budget that will drive us forward as a nation and help those that are more in need.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Our ability to accept this and contribute meaningfully in our own way is what defines us as a growing country that keeps up with time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I see Budget 2022 as a crucial turning point as we adapt to a post-pandemic life, pivoting our industries to the new economy and learning what it takes to address nation building with our citizens at different life stages.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: A few things stood out for me in Budget 2022 – our strengthened focus on the green transition, building new capabilities for the future, involving Singaporeans to enable healthy ageing in place and addressing concerns on cost of living.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, strengthening resiliency in critical supply chains locally and globally.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Supply chain bottlenecks have been a pertinent issue in 2021, exacerbating in the last quarter with a spill-over that may persist through a large part of 2022.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The supply chain effects result in rising pressure on all fronts that touches the lives of every individual: from food, transport, utilities and more.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With more severe weather patterns occurring globally and unstable political situations, the likelihood of an end to escalating inflation and costs are nowhere in sight.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am certain the agencies have thought about this, the need for diversification and the vulnerabilities of not doing so, as illustrated in the creation of NEWater and the "30 by 30" plan.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But what I am suggesting is for a more concerted and focused approach by looking across the entire value chain and deepening our access of capabilities into the critical elements of each part of the value chain.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In building these capabilities, a more intentional effort to scale up the number of local enterprises, bringing their expertise international and to better export Singapore's brand beyond education and governance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Due credit is to be given to Enterprise Singapore for its efforts in helping local enterprises internationalise and assisting the startups.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The next steps would be increasing the number and breadth of the different types of enterprises to enable them to create a value chain with scale that can truly create an impact to Singapore's ability in being more self-reliant, especially in the strategic industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While these companies' international growth is important to us, the larger benefit of their growth is the ability to tap on the resources of raw materials, labour and produce overseas to secure the supply for needs back in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There have been some successful enterprises like PSA, CapitaLand and many others, who have scaled its international operations over the years and are able to compete internationally.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We need more of them and the group of enterprises to create different value chains that are significant to our own supply needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To illustrate this, I would use an example of the food industry.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In expanding the food supplies, we need to look beyond just basic procurement of supplies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Instead, help local enterprises to scale with partnership models in Southeast Asia or countries where there are swathes of land for agriculture, but they require technology to increase the yield.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This would help to enable faster experimenting the growth of different crops and allow us for expansion in future, when our local shores are constrained by land availability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The second area I would like to touch on is to increase workers' ability to have more active incomes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Most people are familiar with the concept of active income during their working years until retirement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But with longer life expectancy and later retirement age, the challenge we face is multi-faceted.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Often, we hear feedback about ageism at the workplace, a lack of work scope redesign that caters for part-time work, returnees from expatriate postings overseas that are unable to find suitable roles due to seniority and so on.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As the world becomes more volatile and uncertain, the possibility of a young worker's career being truncated or relocated, due to the competitive external climate and remote nature of work is looming.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, I am glad that we continue to invest in the skills and ensuring our workers' relevance in the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In picking up freelance roles, it will also allow flexibility in learning new skills, augment their savings and buffer the slack in the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For this, I do not mean those in the gig economy that are doing some of the freelance work about deliveries and those where we think more in the blue collar, but really more those in the professional sense, because age will not become a barrier for these individuals and professionals who choose to continue working in the gig economy after the official retirement age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In my previous speeches, I have also raised the need to provide micro jobs for the seniors and the special needs community to better allow more flexibility to provide them a sense of dignity in the road to independence.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Beyond the need for financial retirement adequacy, our ability to increase the worker's ability to have more active income till later years will enable them to be active, mentally and physically, for a much longer time and such interactions will only help lower their need for healthcare services and thus expenses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While it is not uncommon for senior executives to take on advisory roles during retirement, could this practice be expanded to a greater portion of the workforce?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: From the expat returnees guiding local enterprises that are looking for internationalisation opportunities or for them to mentor companies by domain expertise or their area of interest, their wealth of experience and network will benefit the ecosystem.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This would involve a whole-of-society approach and a change in mindset as to how they perceive their golden years to be.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: From a time to enjoy one's retirement – of course, I am not saying that they cannot; they could if they choose to – to another tranche of lifestyle where there is a transfer of knowledge from one generation to another.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Lastly, balancing the taxation structure and intensifying the use of existing resources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Rising cost of living also impacts us as a nation as the Government expenditures increase due to sociological changes in demographics and inflation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While Singapore's comparative advantage is in skilled labour and expertise and the ability to attract investments due to our stable socio-economic political climate, it also similarly exposes the risks we as a nation face.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While this approach may help to enable a more inclusive and equitable society over time, we still run the risk of not being able to address the return of funds into our reserve that we have dipped into or cover the Budget deficits.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Also, many of the highly skilled labour and multinational corporations are global citizens in nature.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: They have the ability to relocate or offshore services as long as the conditions and the new host countries are palatable.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This undeniably would have an impact on our Government revenues in the long run and there will be new constraints or challenges to raise corporate taxes unreservedly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As we rethink our nation's taxation structure, it is equally sensible to be prudent in our use of funds and resources as well.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This involves creative solutioning to problems, existing problems and new ones, working with existing resources and infrastructures instead of investing in new ones each and every time we think of solving a problem.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In the longer term, it involves looking at the social compact and the partnerships between the Government and citizens, including the ones with private sectors as we move towards the green transition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The way to more holistically manage this issue sustainably, in my opinion, is for us to adopt a whole-of-Government and perhaps even a whole-of-society approach.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We need to become more increasingly sustainable for our own basic necessities and having some degree of independence for strategic resources by being prudent and intentional in our use of existing resources in solving our country's problems.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I will end off with a quote from Charles Darwin: "It is not the strongest of the species that survive, nor the most intelligent, but the one that is more responsive to change".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I believe Singapore and Singaporeans have the ability to do so.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With that, Sir, I rise in support of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And finally, what more can we do, to build up the Singapore we love.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We consume public resources; therefore we need to pay for it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, the idea of increasing taxes to fund programmes evokes resistance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In reality, revenue and expenditure are two sides of the same coin.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To spend without regard for revenue, is not sustainable for the future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The question is how to raise revenue from taxes, in a fair and equitable way.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One method is through a progressive tax system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This means that the wealthy and higher income earners will pay more taxes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a slight shift from previous Budgets in the direction of fairness and inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It brings to life our claims of a new social compact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There will always be populist calls for wealth taxes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But if we push the narrative that the wealthy are responsible for driving inequality, we risk provoking resentment and jealousy, against those who may have accumulated wealth through hard work and sacrifices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our current revenue structure is a balanced one, where ultimately, everyone contributes taxes, but those who are richer contribute more.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For the less privileged, I have raised concerns about the GST hike on previous occasions in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I shared my residents' sentiments that the GST hike should only be implemented after the job market stabilises.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This gives more time for the job market and economy to adapt and prepare.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Overall, it is a fair and comprehensive Budget with an eye for the future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, doing more for our people does not necessarily mean we should spend more.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Instead, we should challenge ourselves and think hard about what we should spend less on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is quite a contrarian view, as the Budget is a time when we discuss how Government will increase spending in various areas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The hard truth is that while it is good to have everything, our resources are finite.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should reduce non-essential, duplicative and non-strategic initiatives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Roads are often dug up and closed for various types of works, ranging from the installation of broadband cables, water pipes to electrical cables and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, can we coordinate better amongst the agencies for a fixed period, where the road is dug up and all are repaired at that time?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, frequent road closures slow down traffic, adding to inefficiencies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Another example is the numerous Government apps and websites sometimes offering similar services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The more there are, the more maintenance is needed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It also inconveniences residents who have to navigate numerous websites and install many apps on their phones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we take some inspiration from the UK government, which consolidated their 300 over websites into one in 15 months?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Being prudent with finances is a virtue that is not incentivised enough.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When a department receives a budget, the goal purportedly is to spend it all.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The common mentality is that having surpluses would imply that the department did not work hard enough and need to find new areas to work on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to stop linking expenditure with KPIs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ministries should not feel guilty about having excess money to return to the coffers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In fact, the Government should throw a grand challenge – create an award and recognise Ministries that best reduce their expenditure, streamline their operations and cut out non-essential projects.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The savings can go to the people or be used for more important areas and social programmes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The provision of minimum protections around risks like illnesses, unemployment and old age are better shared by society and the community, rather than individuals, families or employers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we want our seniors to live well.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we need to go beyond monetary incentives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I wish to reiterate my hopes for the Government to play a bigger role in promoting micro jobs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, to offer integrated search and listing platforms, with accreditation and training available for persons who may want to take up micro jobs in the community, such as healthcare assistants and babysitting.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, focus on job redesign by allowing employers to hire and retain senior staff in the long-term.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to look into stronger support for workplace redesign for senior workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How many companies have made use of the Job Redesign Grants for older workers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Government take on a more proactive approach to coax and compel companies to move in the right direction?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, for those seniors who are frail and cannot work, we must ensure that we can better care for them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: From my conversations with my residents, care navigation in Singapore has room for improvement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, Government agencies like MOH and MSF often focus on policy and administrative matters and devolve the actual provision of care to various social service agencies, or SSAs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, some of these organisations have limited resources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may also not be equipped to deal with clients saddled with multiple co-morbidities and complex social issues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, we need an integrated care system that works on the ground.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This means better sharing of information, care plans, resources, networks and financial support schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Caregivers need only to browse this one-stop centre to have all their concerns addressed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A Yio Chu Kang resident, Mr K, confided that he gave up his career and went into full-time caregiving to both his aged parents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The burden fell upon him as he was the only son.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He did not feel safe leaving his parents in the care of a foreign domestic worker, who may neither have the professional experience nor temperament to care for the elderly with special needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He does not regret the decision, but it is no doubt a setback for his career.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Most of us would agree that caregivers like Mr K should be applauded for prioritising family over career.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we should not take the sacrifices of caregivers for granted.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a society, we must do more to uplift caregivers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we need to help seniors at the end of life to leave well.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In my past experience working in the healthcare sector, I see how people die badly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They die in pain, with tubes connected to all parts of their bodies in a sterile hospital environment, just to have life extended by days and at max, by weeks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a torture, both for the individual as well as for the families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to facilitate their departure to be as comfortable as possible, and for them to live out their remaining lives with dignity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must push for higher standards of palliative care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Consequently, most healthcare professionals did not feel prepared to give palliative care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Singapore Hospice Council is doing good work and they are developing a training framework on palliative care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our Budget is well-balanced and provides a path forward as we emerge from COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To be prudent, we should reflect on what we can spend less on – cut waste, reduce redundancies and for the Government to coordinate better.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Resources should be channelled to areas where more help is needed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One clear area is in caring for an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We may be an ageing society, but what we face need not be a "silver tsunami".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It can be a "silver fountain" – one of vitality and productive longevity, where we all keep well, age well and die well.
